Boeing Product Development · war game on the game-theory dashboard · ExCo and Board agents · BOEING PROPRIETARY

Airbus wins on value as NGSA leads fps by three years; Boeing settles at 47% of narrowbodies, and no veto stops a decision

Airbus won on value (ΔPV +$23.37B, against Boeing's +$0.66B). Rolls-Royce had the best yield (118.68%, ΔPV +$20.55B). CFM/GE lost most (−$38.29B); Pratt & Whitney (P&W) ended at −$2.93B. Why: Boeing launched fps in 2030 on the 10-year ramp-up, where its Board had recommended the 7-year, so NGSA (in service 2037) leads fps (2040) by three years, and Boeing settles at 47% of narrowbody deliveries from 2049. In 2035 P&W and Rolls-Royce formed a Joint Venture, on conditions both their Boards had set in 2030; it cost CFM/GE $7.09B. Twenty AI agents played four sealed rounds (2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050) on your dashboard, each company as an executive committee (ExCo) of CEO, CFO and operating head under a Board agent. No veto stopped a decision, and the Boards approved all nine orders put to them. The record shows the limits came earlier: each Board named in advance the orders it would veto, and no CEO ordered one. Whether those limits changed any choice is not observed: every final order was the CEO's opening lean.

Boeing took the 10-year ramp-up against its Board's advice, and NGSA leads by three years. On the dashboard the two ramps were $0.46B apart in Boeing's expected case, inside the $1B margin its rules treat as a tie, so the CEO chose on his stated preferences.
  • The Boeing Board recommended the 7-year ramp for its better worst case (−$1.50B against −$1.96B if Airbus re-engined the A350 beside NGSA), but said it would approve either.
  • The CEO agent, profiled on Kelly Ortberg, chose the 10-year: a bill $4.68B smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B) and about $6.0B a year of spend against $9.3B. He logged the $0.46B he gave up as a premium paid for that preference. His CFO (Jay Malave) and operating head (Stephanie Pope) recommended the same, and the Board approved his reasons.
  • Malave's own worst-column test preferred the 7-year, as the Board did. He set it aside on "balance sheet first", recommended the 10-year, and "would not veto the 7-year".
  • fps enters service in 2040, three years after NGSA. Boeing falls from 40% of narrowbody deliveries to 37% in 2039 while NGSA is alone. It then gains 1 point a year, from 38% in 2040 to 47% in 2049. On the dashboard the first in service keeps its lead for good.
  • Airbus launched NGSA with no A350 Re-engine and no Delay Tactics, the case that came true. There the 7-year ramp was worth +$1.12B to Boeing against +$0.66B, so the $0.46B premium was the real cost. The CEO and the Board had also recorded the share cost when choosing: Boeing below 40% for some years, and its incumbency objective missed.
Airbus finishes far ahead: its gain comes earlier and is discounted less, and its debt penalty is far smaller.
  • In PV the narrowbody gain is +$39.13B for Airbus and +$20.30B for Boeing. Airbus's starts in 2037, at an 8% discount rate; Boeing's starts in 2040, at 10.5%.
  • The fps bill ($14.91B in PV) and the debt penalty ($4.73B) leave Boeing +$0.66B. NGSA's bill ($15.23B in PV) and debt penalty ($0.53B) leave Airbus +$23.37B.
  • In nominal terms Boeing's operating profit ends the higher. From 2048 it earns more than Airbus each year ($16.57B against $16.23B in 2048, $16.86B against $15.94B from 2049), and over 2026-60 its gain over the status quo is the larger ($200.71B against $191.74B).
The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on conditions both Boards had set in 2030. No message passed between the companies. Each Board had set, in its private guidance, a matching condition for the public record to meet: the partner's commitment, or a live airframe carrying the partner's engine. Rolls-Royce's published line named only P&W's commitment, and P&W published none. NGSA's selection of all three engine makers met the airframe clause for both.
  • In 2030 the RTX Board (the Board of P&W's parent) ruled out a commitment until one of those held, and the Rolls-Royce Board set the mirror condition. Both CFOs opposed a 2030 commitment in their memos.
  • In 2035 both CEOs committed on sealed orders, and both Boards approved: on their grids the commitment was never worth less than holding. The RTX Board had recommended it.
  • P&W went from −$8.44B to −$2.93B, Rolls-Royce from +$18.26B to +$20.55B, and CFM/GE from −$31.20B to −$38.29B.
  • The Joint Venture moved 4.8 points of narrowbody engines from CFM/GE to P&W in every year from 2037. On the dashboard's engine rules a Joint Venture puts the two partners level, and the extra share comes from CFM/GE. Rolls-Royce's UltraFan already had the larger share, so only P&W rose.
  • Rolls-Royce's share and engine value did not change. Its gain is its R&D halving from $8B to its $4B share, less a $1.71B write-off on UltraFan spend beyond that share.
Engine selections set the narrowbody engine split, and CFM/GE's share tracks Boeing's. Boeing put fps on CFM alone. Airbus opened NGSA to all three makers, on its Board's, CFO's and operating head's advice: CFM plus a second maker for supply security, and a selection that could never clash with Boeing's.
  • CFM/GE falls from 76% of narrowbody engines to 51.7% in 2037 and a low of 50.5% in 2039. It recovers to 56.8% from 2049 as Boeing's CFM-only fps gains share. It keeps a majority in every year, narrowly.
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce share the rest equally: 24.1% each in 2037, 21.6% from 2049. Rolls-Royce enters from 0%. P&W is above its status-quo 24% only in 2037-41.
  • CFM/GE ends −$38.29B: $32.29B of engine value lost against the status quo (the narrowbody loss net of the GEnx widebody gain), plus $4B of ducted-engine R&D and a $2B strain charge for three live programmes.
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce launched only once NGSA selected them, so no engine was built without an airframe.
Nobody re-engined a widebody, and nobody used Delay Tactics. Both airframers held, each on its own rules. In 2045 and 2050 neither Re-engine cleared its own company's $1B launch bar even if the rival held, and both CEOs said the hold did not rest on the rival.
  • Boeing: its rule allows one development at a time, and fps was in development until 2040. In 2045 and 2050 its Board would have vetoed the 787 Re-engine on its business case.
  • Airbus: the A350 Re-engine fell short of the $1B bar, and its CFO and operating head each opposed it with a binding veto in their memos: Toepfer on his added-move test, Wagner because no widebody engine would be ready.
  • Rolls-Royce would spend nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine on the record. With Wagner's readiness test, that is the one mutual wait in the record (observed).
  • Delay Tactics: the Airbus Board ruled out the bottleneck on integrity. In 2030 it ruled out poaching too: with no fps yet on the record, one move risked the $48.32B fine. In 2035 poaching was worth +$1.65B, but it took peak spend $0.07B over the Board's $5.2B cash line, and Faury kept the team's stricter condition, which on its own keeps poaching off.
  • Measured ex post, the 2030 holds cost Boeing $2.20B and Airbus $3.30B (regret table).
No veto stopped a decision: the Boards set their limits in advance, and no CEO crossed them. The CFOs' and operating heads' binding vetoes ruled options out before the CEO chose, never his opening lean. Details under How the companies decided.
  • Nine orders went to a Board (seven in 2030, two in 2035), and the Boards approved all nine. The veto checks on the CEOs' decisions raised no binding veto or red-line flag, so nothing was revised or reverted.
  • Each Board's guidance named, with numbers, the orders it would veto. None of them was ordered: among them a 737 rate increase beside fps, Delay Tactics, an A350 Re-engine beside NGSA, and a 787 Re-engine in 2045.
Objectives: Rolls-Royce met both of its own, Boeing neither; five of ten were met.
  • Boeing missed both: 50% of narrowbodies in 2040-50 (38%, 43%, 47%) and holding 40% (38% in 2040). Its true low, 37% in 2039, falls between the tested years.
  • Airbus lost its 60% share target (53% in 2050) but protected the A320 family (60% until NGSA).
  • CFM/GE kept narrowbody dominance, narrowly (51.1% in its worst tested year), and missed its Open Fan objective (never launched).
  • P&W met one: credibility, its engine on NGSA through the Joint Venture. It missed the other, a ΔPV of at least zero (−$2.93B).
  • Rolls-Royce met both: narrowbody entry (21.6% in 2050) and widebody dominance (55.2% at worst).

Market shares

  • Narrowbody. NGSA enters service in 2037 and gains 1 point a year while alone, taking Airbus to 63% in 2039. fps enters service in 2040 and Boeing recovers 1 point a year to 47% in 2049. NGSA's three-year lead is kept for good, so Boeing settles at 47% of narrowbody deliveries (Airbus 53%), not 50%. Boeing's projected path never changed after 2030.
  • Widebody. Untouched: nobody re-engined.
  • Engines. fps's CFM-only selection and NGSA's three-way split set the narrowbody engine shares, and the Joint Venture puts P&W and Rolls-Royce level. Nothing counts before 2037, NGSA's entry into service. The GEnx upgrade, ready in 2033, moves 2.8 points of widebody engines to CFM/GE only from 2042: the dashboard counts widebody engine upgrades from its default Re-engine date.

Financials

  • The airframers' ΔPV is narrowbody profit above the status quo, less the new airplane's bill, charged at entry into service as the dashboard does, and the debt penalty. Neither airframer's widebody profit moved.
  • Boeing's fps bill ($14.91B in PV for $60.32B charged in 2040) and debt penalty ($4.73B) absorb all but $0.66B of its +$20.30B narrowbody gain.
  • Airbus's NGSA bill ($15.23B in PV for $35.52B charged in 2037) and debt penalty ($0.53B) leave it +$23.37B of a +$39.13B gain.
  • Engine value is the lifetime value of the engines each maker delivers. Rolls-Royce's narrowbody entry takes its yearly engine value from $4.39B in 2036 to $11.82B in 2037. CFM/GE's is $18.97B in 2037, against $26.34B in the status quo.
  • Engine R&D and write-offs are undiscounted, as on the dashboard: CFM/GE $4B for the ducted engine plus $2B of strain; P&W $2B and Rolls-Royce $4B, their Joint Venture shares; and Rolls-Royce's $1.71B write-off.

Programme dates

Every programme but one was launched in 2030; the Joint Venture was launched in 2035, and nothing was cancelled outright. NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040. P&W's GTF2 and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB, each launched once NGSA selected its maker, folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. It inherits GTF2's schedule and is ready in 2036; a fresh Joint Venture would have been ready only in 2041. CFM/GE's ducted engine (ready 2036) and Embraer partnership (2037) count from 2037, NGSA's entry into service. Its GEnx upgrade, ready in 2033, counts only from 2042, the dashboard's default Re-engine date.

How the companies decided

The chain never needed its later steps: no binding veto at the veto check, red-line flag, revision, Board veto or reversion in 20 company-rounds. Each company ran the same chain every round. The Board gave guidance. The CEO framed the choice, and the CFO and operating head tested the options independently. The CEO decided; the CFO and operating head then ran a veto check on that decision, and the CEO could revise once. Any order other than hold then went to the Board, with one more revision and a reversion to the default if a Board veto stood. Two kinds of veto appear below. In their test memos the CFO and operating head could mark any option a veto, some binding; the CEOs treated the binding ones as ruling those options out before choosing. Only the veto check on the CEO's actual decision, or a Board review, could send a decision back, and neither did. The record shows what came earlier: each Board's guidance, and the tests the CEO wrote into his opening framing. Whether they changed any choice is not observed. Names below are the agents profiled on those executives, not the people.

A Board item is any order that differs from the default (hold). A binding ExCo veto or a red-line flag sends the decision back to the CEO for one revision; a Board veto sends it back once more, and a still-vetoed item reverts to the default.

The Boards set the limits in advance, with numbers.
  • Each Board's guidance listed the orders it would veto and why, with the item's value in each case. No CEO submitted one of them.
  • The CEOs answered each Board recommendation in writing: 167 answers, of which one says "Not taken".
  • They wrote the Boards' tests into their own reasons. Ortberg, on the 787 Re-engine in 2030: "The Board's Downside test also bars the Re-engine".
The ExCos agreed at the decision; their binding vetoes fell on the options left out.
  • In all 40 test memos, the CFO's and the operating head's recommended orders were the CEO's final orders. In all 20 company-rounds, the final orders were the CEO's opening lean.
  • The memos marked 58 vetoes binding (50 CFO, 8 operating head, all Wagner's), all on options the CEO did not choose. The other 80 entries in their veto lists were advice, standing conditions or explicit non-vetoes.
  • Two failed CFO tests fell on chosen orders. Malave's worst-column test preferred the 7-year ramp, and he set it aside. The volumes-first test of Rahul Ghai, CFM/GE's CFO, failed the Embraer partnership; Larry Culp, the CEO, answered it with a $0 premium declaration, as the team rule allows.
  • 61 of the CFOs' 297 tests returned a fail, and 20 of the operating heads' 213.
  • Some seats had little record of their own, and said so. Pope (Boeing): "My record is thin". Lars Wagner (Airbus): "My tests are role-derived; confidence Very low".
Boeing's ramp: the one open divergence from a Board.
  • The Board: "We therefore recommend the ramp with the higher worst column", the 7-year, and "If you choose the 10-year, state why in the rationale."
  • Ortberg chose the 10-year, as he had leaned from the start. Entering service alongside a 2037 NGSA "would time our airplane to theirs, which I will not do."
  • Malave's own worst-column test preferred the 7-year, as the Board did. He set it aside: "Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet comes first", and "I would not veto the 7-year." Pope: "The 7-year also passes every test of mine."
  • The Board approved: "We recommended the 7-year ramp; the CEO answered with reasons, which is not a veto ground." It recorded the incumbency objective as not met, with Boeing below 40% for some years.
  • At the same review the Board corrected its own guidance. It had parked the 787 Re-engine to 2035, but on the 10-year ramp a 2035 Re-engine overlaps fps by 5 years, so that window was "closed by arithmetic".
The Joint Venture: matching private conditions, one public trigger.
  • 2030, the RTX Board (the Board of P&W's parent): "No Joint Venture commit until Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record or a live airframe carries a Rolls-Royce code". The Rolls-Royce Board: a commitment "fails partner alignment" until the same holds for P&W. Both were private guidance.
  • 2035: NGSA's selection of all three makers met the airframe clause for both. Neil Mitchill, P&W's CFO, had opposed a commitment in his 2030 memo for booking unproven upside: "That condition is met, so the objection is cleared." Helen McCabe, Rolls-Royce's CFO, co-signed the commitment in her memo.
  • The RTX Board recommended the commitment in 2035. The Rolls-Royce Board "would approve a commit, but we do not press it". Its CEO's red line allowed one once a live airframe's engine selection included P&W, the Board's own partner test.
  • Both Boards approved: on their grids the commitment was never below holding.
Airbus: the cash line and the team's stricter condition kept Delay Tactics out in 2035.
  • 2030: the Board's guidance ruled out the bottleneck on integrity, and poaching as "naked": with no fps on the record, one move could cost $15.74B through the $48.32B fine.
  • 2035: poaching passed the value test (+$1.65B) and the fps-on-the-record condition. The Board still ruled it out: "Its cash, not its value, decides it this round." NGSA was spending $5.07B a year against a $5.2B line, and one move took the peak to $5.27B. If the CEO had not recorded setting aside the team's stricter condition, it added, poaching "fails on integrity as well".
  • Thomas Toepfer, the CFO: "an override is arithmetically open, but the Board's own line still vetoes it". The team's stricter condition, that the move must change who enters service first, cannot be met on this dashboard: "On that condition alone, poaching stays off." Toepfer and Wagner also barred the bottleneck on integrity.
  • Guillaume Faury, the CEO, did not set that condition aside, and "the cash line decides it". He logged the 2030 gap to the best plan on his grid, $3.30B, as "the cost of the red lines, not a premium".
The widebody: both airframers held on their own rules; the one mutual wait was between Airbus and Rolls-Royce.
  • Boeing held the 787 Re-engine on different grounds each round: its one-development-at-a-time rule and the Board's downside test in 2030, its 2-year overlap limit in 2035, and in 2045 and 2050 the Board's $1B business case plus Ortberg's tie-break toward doing less and paying debt first. Ortberg in 2045: "I'm not holding because of Airbus either."
  • The Airbus Board on the A350 Re-engine in 2045: "The Board does not press for the launch and will not stand in its way." Toepfer failed it on his added-move test. Wagner failed it on readiness: "The engine leads the airframe." Faury held in both rounds: "The decision rests on our own tests, not on our read of Boeing."
  • No override was available, since the margin was under $1B. Airbus's rules let the CEO overrule one ExCo veto per game; that override, open only for poaching in 2035, closed unused. Toepfer in 2050: "Waiting bought the same case, smaller."
  • Wagner's readiness test waited on a widebody engine, and Rolls-Royce would launch UltraFan WB only with a Re-engine on the record (observed).
  • Rolls-Royce also held the Trent 1000 upgrade, which still carried a $5B strain charge while the Joint Venture ran. Tufan Erginbilgic, the CEO, in 2050: "the 2035 widebody plan assumed the strain would lift ... It did not." The misread cost nothing: on the Board's 2045 estimate, without the strain the upgrade was still worth about −$1.48B (and −$1.73B on its 2050 estimate).
CFM/GE: a package within its Board's conditions, and a declined objective.
  • The GE Aerospace Board's guidance had set the conditions under which it would approve all three 2030 items (the ducted engine, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade), and Culp's package met them. The package was the best plan on CFM/GE's grid in four of six cases, so no premium was paid.
  • The Board ruled out the Open Fan in every round, as a downside with no airframer to fly on: −$8.00B to −$57.60B against holding in 2030, −$19.17B in 2050. In 2050: "we make no end-of-game exception for the Open Fan objective."
  • On the advice of Ghai, the CFO ("Book about −$50B"), Culp, the CEO, expected −$50.41B in 2030. The value after the round was −$31.20B, and −$38.29B once the Joint Venture formed.

Round 1 · decision year 2030

2030: both new narrowbodies launch, and Boeing takes the 10-year ramp-up

  • Airbus launched NGSA, open to all three engine makers, for entry into service in 2037. Its Board, CFO and operating head advised CFM plus a second maker, for supply security. Its Board's guidance ruled out an A350 Re-engine beside it, and every Delay Tactics move.
  • Boeing lifted its rule against a first-round launch: by its CEO's reading the 777X and MAX 7/10 were done and debt repair was on track. It launched fps on the 10-year ramp-up, on CFM alone, where its Board had recommended the 7-year. No rate increase and no 787 Re-engine.
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce ordered launches conditional on selection for NGSA, and Airbus selected both. Both Boards ruled out a Joint Venture commitment until the partner's was on the record or a live airframe carried the partner's engine.
  • CFM/GE launched the ducted engine, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade. Its Board's guidance had set the conditions under which it would approve all three, and Culp's package met them.
  • The Boards approved all seven orders put to them.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingLaunch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: CFM)

Public statement: “When I started, I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We've spent these years earning that. The 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are delivering. Our production lines are stable on the KPIs. Our balance sheet is healthier. I think we've turned this ship. I don't think the work is done. Today we are launching a new single-aisle airplane. It is a Boeing airplane, and we will own the design. We are taking the ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. That is a planning date with headroom built in, not a stretch target. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We have tested the plan against a harder case, including disruption in the supply chain or our engineering workforce around entry into service, and it still stands. If the schedule moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once. A few things will not change. We will certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll share risk with our suppliers on terms that work for both of us, and we'll keep the supply chain funded and healthy. We'll fund this from our operations and our debt capacity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade. We are not changing production rates today. The 737 stays where its KPIs have it, and we are not starting a second development alongside this one. Doing less, and doing it better, is what got us here. This decision rests on our own readiness, not on anyone else's timeline. The financials will follow our production performance. We have a lot of work in front of us, and we're going to do it one step at a time.”

AirbusLaunch NGSA (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We are launching it on its technology clock. Entry into service is planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies have matured, and not before. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it are protected. We have invited all three engine makers to propose engines for the new aircraft. Our aim is CFM and at least one other maker on the aircraft, to give customers choice and to secure supply. We will also strengthen the European supply chain behind this programme. Securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths remains a priority. On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We will fund this investment within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility. On trade, we will keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.”

CFM/GELaunch ducted engine
Partner with Embraer
GEnx upgrade

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: nobody has launched a new narrowbody yet. When one comes, we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM, together with our partners at Safran, is launching a new ducted engine now. That way a new CFM engine is there for whichever new airframe comes first. We don't expect it ready before 2036. We'll report against that gate every year, on test, not on slides. It is not our next-generation engine. That's still RISE. We're all in on that technology, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that. CFM is also teaming with Embraer. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, GE is upgrading the GEnx for our 787 customers. What we don't know: when the airframers move, and what they pick. So we plan on the low case, and we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyLaunch GTF2 if selected

Public statement: “Pratt & Whitney has no new engine programme to announce today, and our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% for four years. That is not where we want to be. We know we have to earn the dependable-engine reputation every day, so the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. Control what you can control. Our commitment is this. In any round in which an airframer names Pratt & Whitney on a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside another engine, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2. It will be ready six years from launch, so no earlier than 2036, with time on wing and full-life parts proven before entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not buy a selection: standard terms, no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we ever enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.”

Rolls-RoyceLaunch UltraFan NB if selected

Public statement: “So, let me be clear. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and only then. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed, and with support in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership is our preference: we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today. Widebody is our franchise. No new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.”

How each company decided: Board guidance, ExCo, Board review (private during the game)

Boeing: the decision chain (Kelly Ortberg, Jay Malave, Stephanie Pope; Boeing Board)
StepWhat happened
Board guidanceBoeing Board: risk appetite: 4.5 of 5, easing slowly: at most one Solo fps launch, and only with the H1 ruling and Pope's readiness results. Our limits: no Board item below -$1B in any of the five plausible columns, and no plan more than $2B below Do Nothing in S5. Nothing that leans on …
FrameKelly Ortberg: initial lean: Orders I lean to: - fps: launch (10-year ramp-up); - fps engine code: 3 (CFM); - 737 rate: hold; - 787 Re-engine: hold. That is one Solo launch, standing alone. Why: - It beats Do Nothing by $2.86-4.30B in every column. That passes debt-first and doing less, better. - It sits …
Test (CFO)Jay Malave recommends: Launch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: CFM). Options failing a test: Buffer test (slip leg), plan H: every fps launch via Embraer row; Meet and beat: ramp, launch (10-year ramp-up) (B) against launch (7-year ramp-up) (C) (ask 4); Rate step: 737 Rate Increase (ask 6); 787 Re-engine beside fps: strain and downside (ask 5); via Embraer outside the grid (ask 7). Vetoes: Any plan with fps: launch via Embraer (all four rows: with holds, + 787 Re-engine, + 737 rate up, + both) (binding); 787 Re-engine: launch in Round 1 (beside either fps ramp, or alone) (not binding); 737 rate: increase beside any fps launch (not binding)
Test (operating head)Stephanie Pope recommends: Launch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: CFM). Options failing a test: Capacity follows demand: 737 Rate Increase (inference from one remark [BX-1329]). Vetoes: 737 rate: increase (any combination) (not binding); fps launch (7-year ramp-up) + 787 Re-engine launch (option G) (not binding); fps launch (10-year ramp-up) + 787 Re-engine launch (option F) (not binding); fps launch via Embraer (option H) (not binding)
DecideKelly Ortberg: Launch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: CFM)
Veto check (CFO)Jay Malave concurs
Veto check (operating head)Stephanie Pope concurs
Board reviewBoeing Board: approve; approved fps

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and production readiness first. No launch and no Rate Increase without Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, so the readiness test turns on her memo [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236].
  • The rating comes first. Whatever the ExCo submits must be no more than $2B below Do Nothing in the risk-case column S5. Do Nothing scores -3.64 there, so the floor is -5.64. Every Solo plan clears it. fps via Embraer does not: at -18.83 it is $15.19B below Do Nothing [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327].
  • One well-founded launch, not a bet. If the ExCo lifts H1 with evidence, we would approve one Solo fps (7-year or 10-year) on its own, with no 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase alongside it [BG-0068, B-2303, BG-0066].
  • Each Board item stands on its own item value. A launch needs an item value above $1B in the expected column, and a Rate Increase needs one above zero. No item may fall below -$1B in any column. All five columns count as plausible this round, because the bulletin rules none out [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581].
  • The long cycle and disclosure. No fps date before launch, a conservative EIS at launch, and every premium logged against the $2B cap [B-2315, BG-0006, BG-0022].

Expects to see. Ortberg's frame and expected_scenario. The submitted row from the grid and, for each Board item, the same row with that item at its default, in all five columns (S1 to S5). Malave's buffer test with the numbers: the plan's S5 value against Do Nothing's -3.64 (floor -5.64). His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result: fps fundable from 2029 [BX-0547], against a 2030 launch. Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results, and her veto check on any Rate Increase. A written Round-1 ruling on H1 and H3 citing evidence: the 777X reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 anti-ice certification [BX-1873], the 777X cash path [BX-0547] and debt repair on track [B-2327]. A launch without the H1 ruling fails our Boeing-ready test. The engine code with its maker's readiness by fps EIS. premium with its reason. A public statement with no fps EIS date unless fps is launched, and a conservative EIS if it is.

Would approve.

  • fps: launch (7-year ramp-up), with 737 rate: hold and 787 Re-engine: hold. Plan row: S1 +2.20, S2 +1.12, S3 -0.42, S4 -1.50, S5 -0.83. Item value against fps: hold: +2.20, +4.76, +2.20, +4.76, +2.81, so it is above $1B in every column and never below -$1B. S5 at -0.83 is above the -5.64 floor. EIS 2037 (2035 or later). Approval is subject to the H1 ruling with evidence, Malave's fundable test (2030 is not before 2029) and Pope's readiness results. It has the higher worst column of the two ramps (-1.50 against -1.96).
  • fps: launch (10-year ramp-up), with 737 rate: hold and 787 Re-engine: hold. Plan row: S1 +3.50, S2 +0.66, S3 +0.88, S4 -1.96, S5 -0.78. Item value: +3.50, +4.30, +3.50, +4.30, +2.86. EIS 2040. The same conditions as the 7-year ramp apply. It passes all our tests and has the better average.
  • fps engine code: any code (1-7) that rides with an approved Solo launch. The code does not change Boeing's payoff, so it is never a veto ground.
  • 737 rate: increase, only with fps: hold, and only if the expected column is S1 or S3. Its item value is +2.30 there, and -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5, which is within the -$1B limit. It also needs stable KPIs, no live problem, no standing KPI veto from Pope, and a rationale that does not cite Airbus (H6).
  • hold on any field. A hold is never a Board item and never vetoed.

Would veto.

  • fps: launch via Embraer, in any combination. Item value: -14.55, -13.75, -14.56, -13.75, -15.19. It fails Business case, Downside ($14.55B or more below the -$1B limit) and Rating first (-18.83 in S5 against the -5.64 floor; it never beats the best Solo ramp). Acceptable alternatives: launch (7-year ramp-up), launch (10-year ramp-up), hold.
  • 787 Re-engine: launch, in any combination this round. Its item value in S3 and S4 (Airbus A350 Re-engine, not ruled out) is -2.48 with fps: hold, -3.58 with the 10-year ramp and -4.51 with the 7-year ramp. That fails Downside. With launch (7-year ramp-up) the overlap is also 5 years against our 2-year limit (H4), and H3 bars a Round-1 Re-engine unless the CEO lifts it with evidence. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • 737 rate: increase paired with any fps launch. Its item value is -0.74 in every column (for example 2.76 against 3.50 with the 10-year ramp, 1.46 against 2.20 with the 7-year), so the business case fails. It also pulls the fps item value below $1B in S1 and S3: -0.84 for 7-year, +0.46 for 10-year. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • 737 rate: increase with fps: hold when the expected column is S2, S4 or S5 (item value -0.74, which fails the business case), while Pope's memo or the brief reports a live KPI, quality, FAA or supplier problem, or when the rationale cites Airbus (H6). Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any fps launch without a Round-1 ruling on H1 backed by evidence that the 777X and MAX 7/10 are done and debt repair is on track (Boeing-ready test). The same applies to any launch Pope's memo fails on KPIs, suppliers or strain without her veto check showing it resolved. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any plan whose logged premium exceeds $2B, or carries a binding ExCo veto (Malave's buffer test, Pope's KPI veto) still standing after revision. In that case we would veto the item whose reversion cures the breach.

Recommendations.

  • Rule explicitly on H1 and H3 in the decision, citing evidence. The H1 conditions were written for 2026. By 2030 our record has the 777X reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix expected to certify in 2026 [BX-1873], 777X cash near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and debt first [B-2327]. Ortberg's own test is that market, technology and finances must all be ready [BG-0068, B-2303]. If you lift H1, say so and say why. A launch without that ruling fails our Boeing-ready test.
  • Show the risk-case column against Do Nothing. Do Nothing scores -3.64 in S5, so no plan may fall below -5.64. Both Solo ramps clear it (-0.83 and -0.78). Fund any launch within the investment-grade rating and from operations and debt capacity. A plan that needs new equity or puts the rating at risk will not pass this board.
  • On the ramp, as a risk-averse board: the two ramps are not within $1B of each other in every column. The 10-year is better by 1.30 in S1 and S3; the 7-year is better by 0.46 in S2 and S4 and by 0.05 in S5. We therefore recommend the ramp with the higher worst column: launch (7-year ramp-up) (worst -1.50 in S4, against -1.96 for the 10-year). Either ramp passes our tests. If you choose the 10-year, state why in the rationale. Do not choose either ramp because of Airbus's timing.
  • One development at a time: no 787 Re-engine this round. Its item value is -2.48 to -4.51 in the A350 Re-engine columns (S3 and S4), which this board cannot rule out, and with a 7-year fps the overlap is 5 years. Bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3) and the overlap with fps is no more than 2 years.
  • Keep the Rate Increase apart from any fps launch. With fps launched, the Rate Increase is worth -0.74 in every column, and it pulls the fps item value below $1B in S1 and S3, which puts the launch itself at risk at review. If fps holds, bring the Rate Increase only on stable KPIs agreed with the FAA, with Pope's results, and with a rationale that does not cite Airbus (H6).
  • Log premium with its reason, within the $2B cap (H8). Measure it against the best plan that respects the hard rules and passes this board's tests, which this round means the Solo fps rows without a Re-engine or Rate Increase. Record any value forgone to H3 or to our Downside test separately, as a hard-rule cost, not a soft premium. Under the public share rules no plan reaches 50% of the narrowbody market by 2040, so no objective premium buys the 2040 test (inference).
  • Engine code: request a maker whose engine will be ready by fps EIS (2037 on the 7-year ramp, 2040 on the 10-year). CFM is always available as the fallback. A request for RR, P&W or the Joint Venture is acceptable, but say how you will judge that maker's readiness. This is not a veto ground.
  • Disclosure: no fps date unless fps is launched. At launch, a conservative EIS with headroom, and publish the nominal and risk-case range. Never blame the FAA or suppliers. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions, and we judge this choice on the long cycle.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. Is 2030 the year the three work streams finally converge? Are the market, the technology and Boeing (finances and capacity) all ready, with the 777X and MAX 7/10 behind us? If so, we lift H1 and launch one Solo fps, and I need to know on which ramp. Then: does anything else earn a place beside it (737 Rate Increase, 787 Re-engine, the Embraer route), or is this a round for doing less and doing it better? I am putting my four questions to this ExCo. (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and I want Pope's seat to confirm it [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]? (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave's risk-case column, S5, read before we decide [BX-1319]. (4) Is each plan doing less, better when set against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239]?

Situation. Decision year 2030, Round 1. Nobody has launched anything. Observed shares were flat over 2026-29: narrowbody 40/60, widebody 58.8/41.2, engines unchanged. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The game board has no FAA, so my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. Do Nothing scores 0.00 only if the rivals hold (S1). It scores -3.64 if Airbus launches NGSA (S2), -2.62 against an A350 Re-engine (S3), -6.26 against both (S4) and -3.64 in the risk case, NGSA plus Delay Tactics (S5). Waiting is not free. Grid against Do Nothing, by column (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5): - fps launch (10-year ramp-up) alone: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. - fps launch (7-year ramp-up) alone: +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.81. - Both Solo ramps beat Do Nothing by more than epsilon in every column, and both clear the S5 floor of -5.64 (10-year -0.78, 7-year -0.83). - fps via Embraer: -14.55 / -13.75 / -14.56 / -13.75 / -15.19, and -18.83 in S5. It fails the buffer test outright. - 737 Rate Increase: -0.74 in every column when fps is launched. With fps on hold it is +2.30 in S1 and S3 and -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5. - 787 Re-engine on top of the 10-year fps: +2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, but -3.58 in S3 and S4. The strain overlap is 2 years on the board's measure. On top of the 7-year fps it is +1.27 / -4.51 with a 5-year overlap. - Debt penalty and two-front strain are already netted in the grid. I will not subtract them again. For scale only, the undiscounted penalties in dashboard_game.md §2 are: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B. Debt is $45B on an EV of $130B. Objective (the company's mission, not my ranking). Holding 50/50 is not met at 40%; incumbency is met. No plan can reach 50% by 2040: the earliest fps entry into service is 2037, and capture is 1 pp a year. The record I bring into 2030: - 777X first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550]; - MAX 7/10 anti-ice certification in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299]; - 777X cash near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; - my own July 2026 view: about two more years to financial readiness, with launch around 2029-30 [BG-0068]; - Spirit closed December 2025 [BG-0064]; - 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069]. Board risks (from its guidance; they are not my red lines). It would veto: - launch via Embraer in any combination; - 787 Re-engine: launch in any combination this round (Downside test fails in S3 and S4); - 737 rate: increase paired with any fps launch, or with fps on hold when the expected column is S2, S4 or S5; - any launch without my written H1 ruling or without Pope's readiness results; - any premium above $2B; - any plan with a binding ExCo veto still standing. It would approve one Solo fps on either ramp, standing alone.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing (fps hold, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold): 0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. The baseline for every comparison. It sets the S5 floor of -5.64 for Malave's buffer test.
  • B. fps launch (10-year ramp-up), 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. Against Do Nothing: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. S5 is 4.86 above the floor. EIS 2040. Lowest Solo bill and debt penalty. My lean.
  • C. fps launch (7-year ramp-up), 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold: +2.20 / +1.12 / -0.42 / -1.50 / -0.83. Against B: -1.30 / +0.46 / -1.30 / +0.46 / -0.05. Inside epsilon in S2, S4 and S5; 1.30 behind in S1 and S3. It has the higher worst column (S4 -1.50 against -1.96), which is the Board's preference. I am testing it to price the H3 ruling.

Red lines.

  • H1 (no fps in Round 1). My provisional ruling: lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds no longer hold. The 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550]. MAX 7/10 certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299]. The 777X cash is positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so fps is fundable from 2029 and a 2030 launch is not early. Debt repair is on the path I set in July 2026 (about two years, launch around 2029-30) [BG-0068, BX-1305, B-2327]. The developments that had to finish first are done [B-2326, B-2276]. The lift is final only if Malave's buffer and fundable tests and Pope's readiness results come back clean.
  • H2: cannot bind. The earliest fps EIS is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year.
  • H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1). My provisional ruling: held for Round 1, on a re-founded ground. Its literal 2026 ground, the 777X first, has lapsed. Its principle has not: one major development at a time, with the next one feathering in only as the last rolls off [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393]; finish what is in hand before what's next [B-2326]; doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336]. Any value forgone is logged as a hard-rule cost, not a premium. H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine, ever, once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine.
  • H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine. launch (7-year ramp-up) with 787 Re-engine (5 years) is struck.
  • H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Re-baseline once instead [BX-1251, BX-1321].
  • H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus, and none under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem [BX-1259, BX-1322].
  • H7: no trigger on this board. If a brief ever reports certification trouble, I treat it as a failed FAA-process gate and launch no fps that round [BX-1309].
  • H8: plans within epsilon ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides. Doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B. Every premium is logged.
  • My own lines: - no rate request without stable KPIs [BX-1259, BX-1271]; - no production-certification concurrency in the fps plan [BX-1263]; - no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments (folded into the H1 ruling) [BX-1247]; - no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]; - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); - no order justified by Airbus's timing [B-2313, B-2315].

Initial lean. Orders I lean to: - fps: launch (10-year ramp-up); - fps engine code: 3 (CFM); - 737 rate: hold; - 787 Re-engine: hold. That is one Solo launch, standing alone. Why: - It beats Do Nothing by $2.86-4.30B in every column. That passes debt-first and doing less, better. - It sits 4.86 above Malave's S5 floor, and the risk case (-0.78) is slightly better than the 7-year's (-0.83). - The fps is fundable now that the 777X has turned [BX-0547]. Expected column (provisional): S4, NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine, with S2 a close second. This is doctrine's reading of Airbus (profile §7), not my record; my confidence on Airbus is low. The lean is the same in S2 and S4, and that is the point: it does not hang on guessing Airbus [B-2313]. On the ramp: - In S2 and S4 the 7-year is 0.46 ahead, inside epsilon. - The tie goes to the plan with less to execute and more headroom. That is the 10-year: about $4.7B smaller bill, lower debt penalty, "right than fast" [BX-1241, BX-1275, BX-0548]. It is also 1.30 ahead if Airbus holds or only re-engines the A350. - I log a soft premium of 0.46 in S2 and S4, and none in S1, S3 or S5. - I am not choosing either ramp because of NGSA's date. - I note honestly that the 7-year, by entering service with a 2030 NGSA, would hold incumbency in the NGSA columns where the 10-year dips below 40% for a few years. It also has the Board's higher worst column. If Malave and Pope show the 7-year carries the same buffer and strain headroom, I will weigh it in the decide step. Rate Increase: hold. It is worth -0.74 beside any fps launch, and fps beats it alone in every column. No premium, and no Airbus in the reasoning. 787 Re-engine: hold under my H3 ruling. One development at a time; bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap is within H4. The cost is a hard-rule cost: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, and nil in S3 and S4, where the Re-engine would lose 3.58. Via Embraer: rejected. H1: lifted, subject to both memos. Public line: no fps date before launch. At launch, a conservative EIS with the nominal and risk-case range; no blame on the FAA, suppliers or Airbus. We're turning it; I don't think it's turned.

With the 7-yr (2030-37) the overlap is 5 years and $3.0B, which breaches H4. Item value against B: +2.20 / +2.20 / -3.58 / -3.58 / +2.20; against C: +1.27 / +1.27 / -4.51 / -4.51 / +1.28. Row F passes my buffer test (S5 +1.42), so I have no veto. But a second programme while we deleverage adds about $1.0B a year in 2030-34 on top of about $6.0B a year of fps spend, and -3.58 in two plausible columns is a downside I would not take. Hold; revisit in 2035 only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap is within H4.
via Embraer outside the grid (ask 7)Anything off the grid (risk transfer, partner capital) would have to close a gap of $13.75B or more to Do Nothing, and $15.19B in S5.failThe board books $100B to Boeing in 2040 with a $52.5B undiscounted penalty, against $60.32B and $19.1B for the Solo 10-yr with the same 2040 EIS. No objective premium: no plan reaches 50% by 2040. Kelly, I ran your grid the way we ran the 777X baseline: the risk case is the baseline, not a sensitivity. Buffer test. Do Nothing scores -3.64 in S5, so the floor is -5.64. The 10-year ramp scores -0.78 and the 7-year -0.83: both pass with about $2.8B to spare. Every Embraer row fails, at -17.47 to -19.58, at least $13.8B below Do Nothing. Under the team rule that is my binding veto. Nothing else fails it. Fundable. The 777X is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so a 2030 launch passes. Cash path. The board books $60.32B in 2040 for the 10-year ramp and $65.00B in 2037 for the 7-year, with penalties of $19.1B and $22.0B undiscounted, already netted. Phased over development, that is about $6.0B a year against $6.7B of airplane operating profit, or about $9.3B a year, which we would borrow to cover. Ramp. The 7-year has the higher worst column and leads by 0.46 in S2 and S4, inside $1B; the 10-year leads by 1.30 in S1 and S3. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet comes first [BX-0556]. I recommend launch (10-year ramp-up) with code 3, and log 0.46 as premium. I would not veto the 7-year. Hold the Rate Increase (-0.74 in every column) and the Re-engine (-3.58 in S3 and S4). At launch, publish entry into service in 2040, barring a supply-chain or talent disruption around EIS, and hold any earlier date as upside. That baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

Kelly Ortberg decides

Orders. Launch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: CFM)

Rationale. ExCo deliberation, Round 1 (2030), team rule of teams.md §9: I propose and decide; Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can block. 1. Vetoes in force. Malave holds one binding veto: every fps launch via Embraer row fails his slip leg. In S5 they score -18.83, -17.47, -19.58 and -18.21, against a floor of -5.64 (Do Nothing -3.64). Embraer is out and I do not contest it. Pope ran the KPI check on a Rate Increase and did not invoke her veto: the brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's H4 flag on fps 7-yr + Re-engine (5 years of overlap) is correct; that row is struck. Neither colleague vetoes the 10-year Solo, so overrides is empty. 2. My four questions. - KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live problem, with 800 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries a year, flat over 2026-29. 47 a month cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069] is company record, not in the brief. - Market, technology and Boeing ready? - Market: waiting is not free. Do Nothing scores -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 if Airbus moves. - Technology: H2 cannot bind; EIS 2040 is well after 2035. - Boeing: see the H1 ruling below. - If certification takes longer? Read S5 first. The 10-year scores -0.78 there, +2.86 against Do Nothing and 4.86 above the floor. - Doing less, better? The 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 in S1-S5, so it is above ε in every column. It carries the smallest bill of the launches. 3. H1 ruling (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were unfinished developments and unrepaired debt [B-2326, BX-1305], and they no longer hold: - the 777X is delivering from 2027 [BX-0550]; - the MAX 7/10 anti-ice fix certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299]; - 777X cash was near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547], so Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes for a 2030 launch; - debt repair ran on the path I set at Farnborough, about two more years with a launch around 2029-30 [BG-0068, B-2327]; - Spirit is inside [BG-0064]. The post-2025 outcomes rest on the teams.md §9 script and Board-file record, not on my own words, and the brief reports no certification trouble. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] therefore passes. 4. H3 ruling, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): held on a re-founded ground. The literal 2026 ground (the 777X first) has lapsed. The principle has not: one major development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], finish what is in hand first [B-2326], do less and do it better [BX-1239]. From 2030 the program in hand is the fps. The Board's Downside test also bars the Re-engine: -3.58 in S3 and S4 beside the 10-year. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. 5. The ramp, my main call. In my expected column S4 (doctrine's reading of Airbus, profile §7; my own confidence on Airbus is Low), C (7-year) scores -1.50 and B (10-year) -1.96. That is 0.46 apart, inside ε, so doctrine breaks the tie. I take the 10-year: - Doing less [BX-1239]: the bill is $4.68B smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B). The undiscounted debt penalty is $2.9B lower ($19.1B against $22.0B; Malave confirms the 16.3/21.7 set on my card is stale), about $2.6B lower discounted. - Headroom [BX-1275, B-2295, BX-1241]: about $6.0B a year of spend against about $9.3B. The 7-year would need about $2.6B a year borrowed above airplane operating profit. Malave supports the rating only on the 10-year phasing. - Honest date: Pope's clean-sheet slip prior (central +3 years, doctrine) puts a 7-year launch at 2040 anyway. So 2040 is a date we can meet and maybe beat [BX-0553]. - Robustness: B leads C by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5, and trails by only 0.46 in S2 and S4. Its five-column mean is +0.46 against +0.11. - Airbus does not set the date [B-2313]. The 7-year's one structural edge is entering service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched in 2030. Choosing it for that edge would time our airplane to theirs, which I will not do. I log 0.46 as a doctrine premium, within the $2B cap. The Board recommended the 7-year for its higher worst column. I take that seriously, but the 10-year's worst column (-1.96) is still $4.30B above Do Nothing's in the same column. Doctrine (profile §11.4) tilts the same way as my record here. 6. Rate Increase: hold. Beside any fps launch its item value is -0.74 in every column (B 3.50 / 0.66 / 0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78 becomes 2.76 / -0.08 / 0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52). It fails the value condition and the Board's business case. Declining in 2030 is final, but it costs nothing in any column beside the fps. Airbus played no part in this reasoning (H6). 7. Embraer: out on Malave's binding veto and Pope's IP test. It costs $39.68B more bill for the same 2040 EIS. 8. Board items and rows. - fps launch (10-year ramp-up) (with code 3 riding with it). Submitted row: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. With the item at its default (Do Nothing): 0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. Item value: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. It is above $1B in the expected column, never below -$1B, and S5 clears the floor by 4.86. - No other Board item: the rate and the Re-engine are held. - Premium 0.46 (S4, doctrine). Hard-rule cost from H3: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4. Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the expected column (profile §7); the re-founded H3 ground (company record on one development at a time); engine code 3 (Low on my record; doctrine and inference); the supplier-readiness and strain tests (Pope's seat is doctrine-played).

Weighing the CFO. Malave is my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. His seat is thin (one call, Low), so beyond the buffer test I weighed his views as advice. - Buffer test: binding, and applied. The Embraer rows (-17.47 to -19.58 in S5) are out. B passes with -0.78, C with -0.83. - Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. 777X cash is positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and the launch year is 2030. - Taken on his word: - the corrected debt-penalty set (19.1 / 22.0 / 52.5 undiscounted, already netted, never subtracted again; 16.3 / 21.7 is stale); - the funding arithmetic: about $6.0B a year on the 10-year against $6.7B of operating profit, with no new equity, and the rating supportable on the 10-year phasing standing alone; - the disclosure: 2040, risk case stated as a condition, earlier date held as upside. - His 'higher worst column' rule pointed to the 7-year by 0.46. He set it aside himself on balance sheet first and logged the premium. I agree. - His advice on the Re-engine (-3.58 in S3 and S4, side-by-side spend in 2030-34) and the Rate Increase (-0.74) matched my own holds. I note one limit: his per-year spend is an even spread, which is inference; real programs peak mid-development.

Weighing the operating head. Pope's seat is played by the [NOW] operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence. Her delivery, IP and cash tests are her record applied by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine. I weighed her memo as readiness results, which the Board requires, not as independent airplane judgment. - KPI veto: checked and not invoked. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. She was right to flag that the 2-3 stable months [BX-1271] and 47 a month [BG-0069] are company record I passed in, not brief data. - Strain: the fps alone has 0 years of overlap and $0 of strain. The 10-year + Re-engine counts 2 years ($1.2B) on the board but runs side by side in 2030-35. Her H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine (5 years) is correct, and I struck that row. - Ramp: the 10-year holds its date under doctrine's +3-year slip prior. It has less value riding on the nominal date ($1.44B lost from S2 to S5, against $1.95B), and the 7-year carries a 54% heavier annual load. That headroom finding is what kept me on the 10-year after I had said in the frame I would weigh the 7-year. - IP: Solo; Embraer adds neither capital nor capacity. - Engines: CFM is always available by EIS. Other makers count only with a ready date on or before EIS. - Supplier caveat taken into other_moves: beyond 47 the supply base binds [B-2340], and the fps ramp loads the same base.

The Board approves fps: launch (10-year ramp-up), with engine code 3 riding with it. Its item value against Do Nothing is +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86 (S1-S5): above $1B in the expected S4 and never below -$1B. S5 at -0.78 sits 4.86 above the -5.64 floor. The CEO's written H1 ruling cites the 777X, the MAX 7/10, 777X cash from 2029 and debt repair. Malave's buffer and fundable tests and Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results pass, with no ExCo veto standing. The premium of 0.46 is logged within the $2B cap. We recommended the 7-year ramp; the CEO answered with reasons, which is not a veto ground. One correction to our own guidance: on this ramp a 2035 Re-engine would overlap the fps by 5 years, so its earliest window is 2045. We ask for yearly funding and rating reports to Finance, and KPI results direct to Aerospace Safety. The fps is to be re-baselined, never cancelled.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S4 (Airbus launches NGSA and an A350 Re-engine), with S2 a close second. This is doctrine's reading of Airbus (profile §7); my own record on Airbus is Low. The decision does not hang on it: the 10-year Solo beats Do Nothing by more than ε in all five columns, and B and C are within ε in both S2 and S4.

Best grid plan in that scenario. In S4, the best grid row is fps 7-yr + 787: hold at -1.50. It is also the best plan that respects the hard rules and the Board's tests. My plan, fps 10-yr + 787: hold (rate hold), scores -1.96 there: 0.46 behind, inside ε, and logged as a doctrine premium. In S2 the best grid row is fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine at +2.86, which H3 (my Round-1 ruling) and the Board's Downside test exclude; among H3-legal rows the 7-year leads at +1.12, against +0.66 for the 10-year.. Premium paid: +0.46 $B. This is a doctrine premium of $0.46B in the expected column S4, and the same in S2: launch (10-year ramp-up) (-1.96) against launch (7-year ramp-up) (-1.50), measured against the best plan that respects the hard rules and the Board's tests. Grounds: - doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]: a bill $4.68B smaller and a debt penalty $2.9B lower undiscounted; - right than fast, with headroom [BX-1241, BX-1275]: about $6.0B a year of spend against $9.3B; - balance sheet first [BX-1305, BX-0556]; - a 2040 date that holds under doctrine's clean-sheet slip prior [BX-0553]. The premium is nil in S1, S3 and S5, where the 10-year is ahead. There is no objective premium, since no plan reaches 50% by 2040. Logged separately as a hard-rule cost, not a premium: the 787 Re-engine forgone under my H3 ruling, 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5 and nil in S3 and S4. The total doctrine plus objective premium is 0.46, within the $2B cap (H8). The figure holds only if the fps schedule does not slip, which the board does not price.

Answers to the Board.

  • Rule explicitly on H1 and H3, citing evidence. Taken up in full. H1 is lifted for 2030: - 777X first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550]; - MAX 7/10 anti-ice certified in 2026 [BX-1873, BX-1299]; - 777X cash near neutral in 2028 and positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; - debt repair on the path I set (about two years, launch around 2029-30) [BG-0068, B-2327, BX-1305]; - market, technology and finances all ready [B-2303, BX-1296]. H3's first half is held for Round 1 on a re-founded ground: one development at a time, and from 2030 the program in hand is the fps [B-0341, B-1526, B-2326, BX-1239]. H3's second half applies as written.
  • Show the risk-case column against Do Nothing; fund within investment grade from operations and debt capacity, no new equity. Taken up. - The submitted plan scores -0.78 in S5, against Do Nothing's -3.64: +2.86, and 4.86 above the -5.64 floor. Malave's buffer test passes. - Funding comes from operations and debt capacity, about $6.0B a year over 2030-39 against $6.7B of operating profit. - No new equity. Malave supports the rating on the 10-year phasing standing alone, which is one reason I declined any second program.
  • On the ramp, prefer launch (7-year ramp-up) (higher worst column); if choosing the 10-year, state why; not for Airbus's timing. Not taken. I chose launch (10-year ramp-up) and logged a 0.46 premium. Why: - In the expected column S4 the two ramps are 0.46 apart, inside ε. - The 10-year leads by 1.30 in S1 and S3 and by 0.05 in S5. Its mean is +0.46 against +0.11. - Its bill is $4.68B smaller and its debt penalty $2.9B lower undiscounted. - It spends about $6.0B a year, against $9.3B (about $2.6B a year borrowed above operating profit on the 7-year). - Its 2040 date holds under doctrine's +3-year clean-sheet slip prior. - Malave and Pope both recommend it. Its worst column (-1.96) is still $4.30B above Do Nothing's. Airbus's timing played no part. I declined the 7-year's one structural edge, entering service alongside a 2037 NGSA, precisely because it would time our airplane to theirs.
  • One development at a time: no 787 Re-engine this round; bring it back in 2035 only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap is within 2 years. Taken up: 787 Re-engine hold under my H3 ruling. The Re-engine is parked to Round 2 on exactly your conditions: the A350 not re-engined (H3, second half) and an overlap with the fps of no more than 2 years (H4). Widebody growth meanwhile comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336].
  • Keep the Rate Increase apart from any fps launch; if fps holds, only on stable KPIs, Pope's results, no Airbus in the rationale. Taken up: 737 rate hold. Beside the fps launch it is worth -0.74 in every column and would have pulled the fps item value down. Pope's KPI check passed and her veto was not invoked, but the value condition fails. I accept that 2030 was the only round for it. Airbus is not in this reasoning (H6).
  • Log premium with its reason within the $2B cap; record H3 or Downside forgone value separately as a hard-rule cost. Taken up. premium is 0.46, a doctrine premium in S4 (and S2) against the 7-year Solo, the best plan passing the hard rules and your tests. It is nil in S1, S3 and S5, and there is no objective premium. The hard-rule cost of H3 (the Re-engine forgone) is logged separately: 2.20 in S1, S2 and S5, nil in S3 and S4. The total is within the $2B cap.
  • Engine code: request a maker ready by fps EIS; CFM is the fallback; say how readiness is judged. Taken up: code 3 (CFM), ready by 2040, as a LEAP derivative at worst. Readiness is judged on a matured engine with durability shown before EIS [BX-1298, BX-1325] and on CFM's capacity across both airframers' rates [BX-1264]. If NGSA also takes code 3, the board moves the later airframe to code 7 at no payoff change.
  • Disclosure: no fps date unless launched; at launch a conservative EIS with headroom, nominal and risk-case range; never blame the FAA or suppliers. Taken up. The public statement gives entry into service in 2040 as a planning date with headroom. It states the risk case as a condition (supply-chain or engineering-workforce disruption around EIS) and holds any earlier date back as upside. It blames neither the FAA nor suppliers nor Airbus, rules out fixed-price development, and commits to resetting once, early, if the date moves.

Objective. The company's mission (objectives.md §1) is not on my ranked list and does not change the payoff. - Hold 50/50 (Boeing NB share of 50% or more in 2040, 2045 and 2050): not met under any plan. The earliest fps EIS is 2037, and the board moves share 1 pp a year, so 2040 tops out near 43%. - Defend incumbency (40% or more in 2030-50): - With the 10-year ramp it is met in S1 and S3, where Boeing climbs from 2040. - In S2 and S4 an NGSA entering service in 2037 would be alone for three years. On my reading of the public share rules, Boeing then falls to about 37% by 2040, before climbing toward a 47/53 long-run split, so incumbency is missed for roughly 2038-43 (inference from rules.md). - In S5 both ramps miss it (Delay Tactics take 5 pp from EIS). - The 7-year would hold incumbency in S2 and S4 by entering service with NGSA. I did not take it for that, because it would time our airplane to Airbus [B-2313] and give up the headroom above. - The objective is logged as not fully met. No PV was given up for the objective, so the objective premium is 0.

Predictions. My record gives me little on Airbus (Low), so these lean on doctrine. Airbus: - Most likely in 2030: an NGSA launch (S2 or S4), with roughly even odds of an A350 Re-engine alongside it. - Any covert Delay Tactics would only show around our 2040 EIS. I attribute nothing before exposure. Engines: - CFM stays our available engine by 2040 under code 3. Any rival maker's new narrowbody engine counts only with a public ready date on or before 2040. Boeing on the board, under my orders: - Narrowbody share holds at 40% through the 2030s unless NGSA enters service in 2037. In that case it dips to about 37% by 2040, then recovers toward 47% over the 2040s once the fps is in service. - Widebody share holds at 58.8% unless the A350 re-engines (from 2035), in which case it erodes. - ΔPV by column: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. Round 2 (2035): - I expect to revisit the 787 Re-engine only if the A350 has not re-engined and the overlap stays within H4. - I expect no cancel of the fps under any column (H5).

Expected ΔPV. −1.96 $B (board after the round: +0.66 $B)

Other moves.

  • Conservative EIS disclosure at launch (public): Publish entry into service in 2040, no earlier, as a planning baseline with buffer in it. State the risk case as a condition: a supply-chain or engineering-talent disruption around EIS. On the board that is S5: 5 pp of share lost for 5 years from EIS, -0.78 against Do Nothing's -3.64. Keep any earlier internal date as upside and never publish it. If the date moves, reset once and say so early [BX-0553, BX-1318, BX-1306].
  • No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms (public): Contract fps development on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. This is not priced on the board.
  • Certify before building at rate (public): The fps program plan carries no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. The 10-year ramp leaves room to certify before the line goes to rate.
  • Fund from operations and debt capacity; keep deleveraging (public): No new equity. Stay solidly investment grade on the 10-year phasing, about $6.0B a year over 2030-39 against $6.7B a year of airplane operating profit (Malave's arithmetic). Debt stays the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327].
  • Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot (private): Fund fragile suppliers so they stay above our rate as the fps ramp loads the same base as the 737 at 47 a month. Embed staff, buffer, requalify; acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2264]. Attribute no bottleneck to anyone before exposure.
  • Engine request: code 3 (CFM), durability first (private): Request CFM. It is always available by 2040, as a LEAP derivative at worst. Require a matured engine before EIS, with durability proven on the ground [BX-1298, BX-1325], and watch CFM's load across both airframers' rates [BX-1264]. If NGSA also takes code 3, the board moves the later airframe to code 7 at no change in payoff.
  • Independent estimate check and early-warning rule (private): Malave reviews the fps estimate and schedule independently every quarter [BX-1316]. Any slip is reported early with the mitigation attached, and costed once in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost [B-2349, BX-1299].
  • 787 Re-engine parked to 2035 on conditions; widebody growth from Charleston (private): Bring the Re-engine back in Round 2 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half) and its overlap with the fps is no more than 2 years (H4). Until then, widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336].
