Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety and maturity first: any narrowbody engine must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves, with nothing compressed. A 2030 UltraFan NB launch is ready in 2037, which is zero margin against a 2030 NGSA (EIS 2037) or a 7-year fps (2037) and three years against a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (2040). No EIS earlier than launch plus development years should be disclosed, and a support plan must be in place before EIS [RG-0027, RG-0025, R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296, RX-0283].
  • The balance sheet and the reasonable worst case: no unconditional commitment before an airframe names us. Each Board item's downside must stay within its own bill in every plausible column (NB Solo -$8B, Joint Venture -$4B, UltraFan WB -$4B, upgrade -$2B). The grid models no balance sheet, so McCabe's co-signature, worst column and capex a year are our evidence [RX-0242, RG-0033, RG-0041, RG-0060].
  • An airframe first, through launch if selected. It is the only form that can catch an airframe launched this round. A 2035 launch would be ready in 2042, too late for a 2030 NGSA or fps, so this round's conditional is the narrowbody entry the briefing goal asks for. It costs nothing unless we are selected [R-0994, R-1005, RX-0058, R-1011].
  • A partner only on aligned terms, once P&W's commitment is on the public record. Formed in 2035, the Joint Venture would be ready in 2041, so it stays open as a next-round option [R-1010, R-0318, R-0916].
  • One big programme at a time, and the widebody core held. Trent keeps 58% of widebody engines through 2060 on the grid and no Re-engine is on the record, so there should be no widebody spend this round and nothing that stacks the $5B strain on a narrowbody trigger [RG-0019, RX-0214, R-0929, R-1127, R-1574, RG-0068].

Expects to see. For each Board item we expect the following. (1) The grid row of the submitted orders and the row with that item at hold, column by column: for example "UltraFan NB if selected" against "UltraFan NB: hold". (2) The CEO's expected scenario and predictions by column (S1-S8). (3) McCabe's co-signature on every launch, launch if selected or commit, with her column weights, worst column and capex a year. If triggered, UltraFan NB is about $1.14B a year for 7 years ($8B ÷ 7). We also want her confirmation that this fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the 2026-2028 buyback plan with no leverage above about 1.5x. (4) Watson's ready year against each live or launching airframe's EIS: UltraFan NB 2037 against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, and fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040. We also want his support plan before EIS, given no narrowbody MRO scale. (5) Both veto checks (CFO and Civil), with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in rationale, and overrides empty. (6) Any premium in premium, item by item, with its reason. (7) A public statement with no EIS earlier than launch plus 7 (2037 for a 2030 launch) and nothing on an airframer's dates. If a figure is missing we will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected, with Joint Venture with P&W, UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade at hold. Against the hold row ('UltraFan NB if selected' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') the item is S1 0, S2 +32.60, S3 0, S4 +28.24, S5 +44.54, S6 0, S7 0, S8 0. It is at or above 0 under any weights: +3.26 at the ExCo's 0.1 'nothing on the record' weight on S2, and +2.82 on S4. Its worst case is 0, against a limit of -$8B. It passes safety by construction, since it triggers only if ready by EIS. It is the form the doctrine prefers, conditional on McCabe's co-signature and no standing Civil veto [R-0994, R-1005, RX-0058, RG-0033].
  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch only with UltraFan NB Solo and UltraFan WB both at hold, and only as a declared premium. Against the hold row ('UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') it is -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8. The premium of at most $0.98B is inside the $3B cap and its worst case is above -$2B. It needs premium declared with a durability reason and McCabe's co-signature. We would approve it, but we do not recommend it this round [RG-0068, RX-0246, R-1574].
  • Every hold: never a Board item and never vetoed.

Would veto.

  • UltraFan NB Solo: launch (unconditional) fails the airframe-on-the-record test. No airframe is launched and none carries code 1, 5, 7 or 4 [R-1005, R-0994]. Against hold it is S1 -8.00, S2 +32.60, S3 +3.57, S4 +28.24, S5 +44.54, S6 +3.57, S7 -8.00, S8 -8.00. At the ExCo's 0.1 rule weight the weighted value is about -3.94 (NGSA case) or -4.38 (fps case), which fails our 0 floor and the ExCo's +$2B bar. Break-even needs a selection probability of about 0.20-0.22, or 0.25-0.28 for +$2B. Its only edge over the conditional form is +3.57 in S3/S6, which does not justify an unconditional $8B. Acceptable alternatives: launch if selected or hold.
  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit fails partner alignment. P&W's commitment is not on the public record and no live airframe carries code 2, 4, 6 or 7 [R-1010, R-0318]. Against the hold row ('hold + commit to JV' minus 'hold', or with launch if selected in both) it is -4.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, so it is below 0 under any weight on S7 and fails profit over share (narrowbody carries no premium) [R-1011, R-1582]. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • UltraFan WB: launch fails the airframe test because no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record [R-1574]. Against hold it is -4.00 in S1-S7 and -0.90 in S8, a premium far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Beside launch if selected it is -9.00 in S2/S4/S5, below its -$4B bill, and it overlaps a narrowbody programme [RG-0033, R-0929]. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch beside launch if selected, launch or UltraFan WB fails one big programme at a time, because an UltraFan could be triggered or in development this round. Against 'UltraFan NB if selected' it is -5.98 in S2/S4 and -5.97 in S5, below its own -$2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks [R-1127, RX-0214, RG-0033]. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any launch, launch if selected or commit without McCabe's co-signature, with a binding ExCo veto left unrespected, with an unresolved red-line flag or with a non-empty overrides. Also any item on which Watson's binding Civil veto still stands against the final orders: compressed maturity, an early disclosed EIS or ready date, or no support plan [RX-0213, R-1579, RG-0044, R-1476, R-0970].

Recommendations.

  • Submit UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected with everything else at hold. This keeps the narrowbody entry open at no cost unless an airframer names us this round, and it is the last timing-feasible route for any airframe launched in 2030. Answer it in board_response.
  • McCabe should give explicit column weights for S1-S8 and the worst column for each item. If she gives none, we will use the CEO's predictions, then the ExCo's rule (0.1 with nothing on the record). She should state capex a year if triggered (about $1.14B for 7 years) and confirm it fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the £7-9bn buyback plan for 2026-2028, with no leverage above about 1.5x.
  • Watson should record the zero margin of a 2030 UltraFan NB (ready 2037) against a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps (EIS 2037) and his test pacing to hold it. He should also give a support and MRO plan before EIS, since we have no narrowbody MRO scale. We treat a zero-margin pass as advice, not a veto ground.
  • Public statement: say UltraFan is available to a new narrowbody that selects it in time, ready seven years from launch, and give no date earlier than 2037 and nothing on any airframer's dates. Say we remain open to a partnership with P&W on aligned terms, without committing. 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.'
  • Hold the Joint Venture this round and revisit it in 2035 if P&W's commitment appears on the public record. Formed in 2035, it would be ready in 2041, in time for a 2035 airframe launch.
  • Defer the Trent 1000 upgrade. With no Re-engine it counts only from 2042 whenever it is launched, it is -0.98 on every non-Re-engine column, and the franchise test does not trigger (58% widebody share throughout, no rival-engined Re-engine). Revisit it once a Re-engine is on the record or the narrowbody question is settled. Hold UltraFan WB until a Re-engine is on the record. Even S8 shows -0.90, so it would need a better case within the $1B sub-cap.
  • Next round: if launch if selected triggers and the selecting airframe later drops our code, bring a cancel of the orphaned programme. If no airframe launches in 2030, expect the same conditional discipline in 2035.
  • Other moves, reported qualitatively: we support recording the UltraFan 30 demonstrator path (ground test, public R&D money, partner sought) and continued Trent 1000 durability work as public context. Neither changes a payoff.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, the 2030 question, put in cash and quality of earnings: nothing is on the public record. Do we put any cash at risk for narrowbody, widebody or the Trent 1000 this round? Or do we take only the conditional order, which costs nothing unless an airframer names Rolls-Royce on an airframe UltraFan can serve in time? We are not after market share. I will not spend $8B blind on narrowbody, I will not fund widebody without a Re-engine, and the Trent 1000 upgrade goes ahead only if it pays on this board. The one thing this round alone can do is catch an airframe launched in 2030. A 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, which is too late for any 2030 airframe.

Situation. Public record, 2030: no programme has been launched. There is no fps, no NGSA, no 787 Re-engine and no A350 Re-engine, so there are no engine selections or codes. P&W has made no Joint Venture commitment. Markets 2026-29 sit at the status quo: narrowbody Boeing 40 / Airbus 60; narrowbody engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; widebody engines GE 42 / RR 58. Our position on hold: ΔPV +0.00, yield 100.0% (EV $110B, debt $40B, WACC 10%). Objective: narrowbody entry is NOT met (RR narrowbody share 0% in 2045 and 2050). Widebody dominance is MET (58% every year to 2060; worst year 58%). Timing that decides this round: - An UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037. - An NGSA or a 7-year fps launched in 2030 enters service in 2037. That is zero margin. - A 10-year fps or fps via Embraer enters service in 2040. That is three years of margin. - A 2035 UltraFan is ready in 2042, too late for any 2030 airframe. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041: too late for a 2030 airframe, in time for a 2035 one. - 2035 is the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045. Grid facts against the hold row (columns S1-S8): - 'UltraFan NB if selected': 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is never below hold. - Unconditional 'UltraFan NB Solo': -8.00 in S1, S7 and S8; +3.57 in S3 and S6, because the board credits RR +15 pp once any new narrowbody flies, even if we are not selected; the selected columns match the conditional. - Trent 1000 upgrade alone: -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8. With no Re-engine it counts only from 2042. - UltraFan WB alone: -4.00, or -0.90 in S8. - Joint Venture commit alone: -4.00 in S7 only. - Beside a triggered UltraFan NB, the $5B strain takes the upgrade to -5.98 against the conditional, and UltraFan WB to -9.00. Board (risk aversion 4 of 5, time horizon 2.5): - Would approve launch if selected with everything else at hold. - Would approve the upgrade alone only as a declared premium, and does not recommend it. - Would veto an unconditional Solo, a first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, and the upgrade beside any UltraFan order.

Options to test.

  • Weights for every row (mine; Helen to confirm or replace): S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.15. Selection in total is 0.10, our weight for 'nothing on the record'. The expected scenario is S1 (rivals hold), the single most likely column.
  • A. 'UltraFan NB if selected', everything else at hold (my proposal). Expected gain over hold +3.37; worst column 0 (S1, S3, S6-S8). It triggers only in S2, S4 and S5. At the Board's weights (0.1 on S2, 0.9 on S1) it is +3.26. Four-part gate [RX-0030]: differentiated, since UltraFan is about 10% better [RX-0069]; a large market of 4,000 narrowbody engines a year; a viable business model, since it is spent only when selected; synergy with the UltraFan demonstrator. It passes, conditionally. It is not options management: it is no standing programme, and it lapses if not triggered. The Board would approve it.
  • B. 'UltraFan NB: hold' (Do Nothing on all four). 0 in every column. Safe, but it closes the only route onto a 2030 airframe, and the narrowbody objective stays unmet. This is the benchmark row.
  • C. 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade'. Expected -0.88; worst -0.98; a premium of up to $0.98B. My record backs it ('regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]; 787 share 'Why not?' [RX-0117]). On this board, though, it counts only from 2042 without a Re-engine, and it rules out the conditional (red line). It fails the gate on business model this round. I test it; it is not my lean.
  • D. 'UltraFan NB if selected + T1000 upgrade'. Expected +1.99, which is 1.38 below A. Against A it is -0.98 in the untriggered columns and -5.98 (S2, S4) or -5.97 (S5) where the conditional triggers, because the $5B strain stacks: below the upgrade's own -$2B bill. It breaks the rule of no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development; the Board would veto it. Tested only to price the cost.
  • E. 'UltraFan NB Solo', unconditional. Expected -0.94; worst -8.00 (S1, S7, S8). Its only edge over A is +3.57 in S3 and S6, where we are not selected. At the Board's weights it is -3.94. It fails airframers first [RX-0058], the +$2B bar and the Board veto. Rejected; the test shows that the premium for keeping A over it is zero.
  • F. 'UltraFan NB if selected + commit to JV'. Expected +2.97, 0.40 below A; worst -4.00 in S7. P&W has not committed: a first commit is options management and a Board veto. Hold, and revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the record.
  • G. UltraFan WB, alone or beside A ('hold + UltraFan WB' or 'if selected + UltraFan WB'). Expected -3.54 or -0.67; worst -4.00, and -9.00 against A where the conditional triggers. No Re-engine is on the record, and even S8 shows -0.90, above the $1B sub-cap. Rejected.

Red lines.

  • Safety first: no compressed maturity, and never disclose an EIS earlier than launch plus development years. For UltraFan NB that is launch + 7, so 2037 for a 2030 launch; for UltraFan WB and the Joint Venture it is + 6. Nothing on any airframer's dates [R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296].
  • No unconditional UltraFan NB launch without an RR selection on the public record (codes 1, 5, 7, or 4 with a formed Joint Venture). There is none in 2030, so the only forms are launch if selected or hold [RX-0058, R-1005, R-0994]. The Board would veto it.
  • No Joint Venture with P&W: commit until P&W's commitment is on the public record, or a live airframe's code includes P&W. A commitment is public at once [R-1010, R-0318]. The Board would veto it.
  • No UltraFan WB without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan. Never beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected. Any UltraFan WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574, R-0929]. The Board would veto it.
  • No Trent 1000 upgrade in any round where an UltraFan is in development, launched or ordered launch if selected. A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs $5B of strain [R-0929, R-1127]. The Board would veto it.
  • cancel only a programme no live airframe flies. There is nothing to cancel in 2030 [R-1573].
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column (NB Solo -$8B, Joint Venture -$4B, UltraFan WB -$4B, upgrade -$2B).
  • Every launch, launch if selected or commit needs McCabe's co-signature against mid-to-high-teens hurdles [RX-0213, R-1579]. Watson's Civil veto binds: compressed maturity, an early disclosed EIS, or no support plan before EIS. overrides stays empty; we revise once within any veto.
  • No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x net debt to EBITDA, and no levering up for buybacks.
  • Doctrine premium: at most $3B per round against the best expected grid plan, declared item by item. Narrowbody items carry no premium with the Board: weighted value at least 0 against hold.
  • No price concessions to buy share: 'win-win', and value remunerated [R-1582, RX-0097].

Initial lean. Proposal: UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected; Joint Venture with P&W: hold; UltraFan WB: hold; Trent 1000 upgrade: hold. On my weights the expected gain is +3.37 over hold and the worst column is 0. The premium is $0B: the order doctrine favours is also the best grid plan in expectation. An unconditional Solo is -0.94 and is rejected on red lines. The expected scenario is S1 (rivals hold). If an airframer launches and names us, the conditional catches it, and only this round can. - Upgrade deferred. On this board it loses 0.98 and cannot sit beside a conditional UltraFan. Revisit it once a Re-engine is on the record or the narrowbody question is settled. - Joint Venture held until P&W commits on the public record. Revisit in 2035. - UltraFan WB held until a Re-engine is on the record. - Other moves (public, qualitative): the UltraFan demonstrator path continues, and so does Trent 1000 durability work. Draft public statement: 'So, let me be clear. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and only then. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that: we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today. No widebody spend without a Re-engine. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.' This is subject to Helen's co-signature and Rob's readiness check. Until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing.

We've always said safety, then we said the balance sheet. Nothing is on the public record, so no cash goes at risk unless an airframer asks for it. The conditional order is zero wherever we are not selected, and +28.24 to +44.54 where we are. On the CEO's weights, confirmed, it is +3.37 over hold; on the Board's case, +3.26. It clears the bar and I co-sign it. If it triggers, it is $8B over seven years: about £0.84bn a year, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance, funded from cash, no equity, no leverage. It fits a broadly flat R&D envelope only as redeployment, so nothing widebody runs beside it. Plan for failure: if a selecting airframe later drops us, a 2035 cancel writes off $5.71B, inside the bill. I withhold my signature on everything else. An unconditional Solo is -0.94 expected and loses the full $8B in S1, S7 and S8. A first Joint Venture commit only costs: -4.00 in S7. UltraFan WB is -3.54 alone, -9.00 beside a trigger. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -0.98 and earns nothing before 2042; beside the conditional it is -5.98, worse than its own bill. Time on wing continues as an other move. My record is thin on engine-launch economics: these are the board's numbers, not mine. So hold it this way: no cash out unless we are selected, about +3 on paper, nothing booked until a customer is announced. That's our best view at the minute.

The test pacing is the full seven years: if a phase slips, the engine slips. - Statement: the public statement gives no EIS earlier than launch + 7, no 2037 next to any airframe, and no airframer date. No veto stands. overrides is empty. 3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5/S6/S7/S8). Weights, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.15 (selection 0.10 in total, our rule for 'nothing on the record'). - UltraFan NB Solo launch if selected ('UltraFan NB if selected' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold'): 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0. RED LINES, AGAINST THE FINAL ORDERS. None breached. Both colleagues flagged option D (the upgrade beside launch if selected) as a red-line breach. It is struck: not ordered. The one Board item, UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected, spends nothing unless an airframer names us and UltraFan can be ready by that aircraft's entry into service. Provided in her memo and carried into the rationale. Weights: S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.15. Worst column: 0 for the conditional; -8.00 for the Solo, -4.00 for a Joint Venture commit, -9.00 for UltraFan WB and -5.98 for the upgrade beside the conditional, all rejected. Capex if triggered: $1.14B a year for 7 years, about £0.84bn a year and about £5.9bn in total, 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance. It is funded from FCF as redeployment inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, after the 2026-28 returns programme, with no equity and no leverage above about 1.5x. She co-signs.
  • Watson should record the zero margin of a 2030 UltraFan NB against a 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps and his test pacing, and give a support and MRO plan before EIS. Recorded. Ready in 2037 against EIS 2037 is zero margin, a pass with a note; against a 10-year fps or fps via Embraer (2040) there are three years. Pacing over the full 7 years: design and gearbox sizing, then ground and flight test, then certification and maturity. If a phase slips, the engine slips. The support plan is in the rationale and other moves: partner MRO shops on the Singapore model, repair technology, a spares pool and field service, supplier and partner-shop contracts by the 2035 round, and an EIS-readiness review. No Civil veto stands.
  • Public statement: UltraFan available to a new narrowbody that selects it in time, ready seven years from launch, no date earlier than 2037 and nothing on airframers' dates; open to P&W on aligned terms without committing; 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.' Taken up. The statement says we launch UltraFan in the round an airframer selects it, with entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch and support through partner shops before EIS. It includes 'We do not want to underestimate the risks', is open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms with no commitment today, and names no airframer or date.
  • Hold the Joint Venture this round and revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment appears on the public record. Taken up. Joint Venture with P&W: hold. A first commit is -4.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere (expected -0.40), and McCabe withholds her signature on it. Revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the record: formed then, it is ready in 2041, in time for a 2035 airframe. The test then is an expected gain above 0 against the same row without it.
  • Defer the Trent 1000 upgrade; revisit once a Re-engine is on the record or the narrowbody question is settled. Hold UltraFan WB until a Re-engine is on the record. Taken up. Trent 1000 upgrade: hold and UltraFan WB: hold. The upgrade is -0.98 alone and earns nothing before 2042 without a Re-engine. Beside the conditional it is -5.98, beyond its own bill, and it breaks a red line. UltraFan WB is -4.00 alone and -9.00 beside a trigger, with no Re-engine on the record. Widebody stays at 58%. I revisit the upgrade in 2035 if no UltraFan is in play, as a declared premium within $3B or against a Re-engine on the record.
  • Next round: if launch if selected triggers and the selecting airframe later drops our code, bring a cancel; if no airframe launches in 2030, expect the same conditional discipline in 2035. Agreed and recorded as a private other move. If it is orphaned, I bring a 2035 cancel (write-off $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, inside the bill); no orphan is kept. If nothing triggers, 2035 gets the same conditional discipline: it is the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045.
  • Other moves, reported qualitatively: the UltraFan 30 demonstrator path and continued Trent 1000 durability work as public context. Taken up. Both are public other moves with no payoff: the UltraFan demonstrator continues (ground test, public R&D money, partner sought, technology pull-through to the Trent fleet), and Trent 1000 and fleet durability continues as funded. The Trent 1000 upgrade order itself stays at hold.

Objective. Briefing goal: enter narrowbody, keep widebody dominance. Widebody: met. RR stays at 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, with no widebody order. About 53% under a GEnx upgrade is still above 50%. Narrowbody: met only if the conditional triggers (S2, S4, S5; weight 0.10). RR then has a narrowbody engine in service from 2037, so its share is above 0 in 2045 and 2050. The unconditional Solo would also meet it in S3 and S6, through the +15 pp the board credits once any new narrowbody flies, lifting the probability to about 0.35. But that costs -4.31 expected against the conditional, is -8.00 in S1, S7 and S8, breaks the airframers-first red line and draws a Board veto. I pay no premium for the objective: 'We won't do anything not profitable.' Route left for 2035: if no airframe selects us now, 2035 is the last round whose narrowbody launch can deliver by 2045. That could be a conditional against a 2035 airframe, or the Joint Venture if P&W's commitment is on the record (formed 2035, ready 2041).

Predictions. Column weights, with McCabe's confirmation: - S1 0.40: rivals hold. - S2 0.05: Airbus launches NGSA and selects RR (code 7). - S3 0.15: NGSA launched without RR (code 6). - S4 0.03: Boeing fps 10-year selects RR (code 5). - S5 0.02: both launch and select RR. - S6 0.10: both launch, RR on neither. - S7 0.10: P&W commits to the Joint Venture. - S8 0.15: 787 Re-engine and A350 Re-engine. Selection in total is 0.10, our rule for 'nothing on the record'. My payoff on the orders submitted: +0.00 in S1, S3, S6, S7 and S8; +32.60 in S2; +28.24 in S4; +44.54 in S5. Expected +3.37. Reading of rivals, from the public record only: the airframers move first and the engine makers follow. CFM and P&W hold the narrowbody duopoly and have no reason to invite us in unless an airframer pulls us in. I say nothing on any airframer's dates or rates. Next round: - If triggered: the programme is in development until 2037. Hold all widebody items and check that the selecting airframe keeps our code. - If not triggered: the same conditional discipline in 2035, and test a Joint Venture commit if P&W's commitment is on the record.

Expected ΔPV. +3.37 $B (board after the round: +18.26 $B)

Other moves.

  • UltraFan demonstrator path continues (public): UltraFan continues as a technology demonstrator: ground test, public R&D money where available, partner sought. Some of its technology goes into today's Trent fleet for time on wing. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0057, RX-0094, RG-0065].
  • Trent 1000 and Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded (public): The durability programme (about £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money) continues [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.
  • Narrowbody support plan, ready to activate on trigger (Watson's plan, adopted) (private): If launch if selected triggers: (1) name partner MRO shops on our Singapore joint-venture model near the selecting airframe's launch operators, without building our own narrowbody MRO scale [RX-0287]; (2) develop repair technology for those shops alongside the test programme; (3) set up a spares pool and field-service team for EIS and the early years; (4) by the 2035 round, contract the partner-shop agreements and castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers [RX-0286], with Watson reporting status in his 2035 memo; (5) hold an EIS-readiness review before EIS. Test pacing over the full 7 years: years 1-2 detailed design and gearbox sizing, years 3-5 ground and flight test, years 6-7 certification and maturity. If a phase slips, the engine slips; no tests are cut.
  • Plan for failure on a triggered programme (private): If the conditional triggers and the selecting airframe later drops our code before EIS, bring a cancel in 2035 (write-off $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, inside the bill). No orphan programme kept: 'that activity is gone' [R-1573].
  • Pricing discipline (private): No price concessions to buy share on any campaign. 'Win-win' terms, value remunerated, every new contract through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.
  • Open door to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms (public): Stated as openness only, in the public statement. No Joint Venture with P&W commitment this round. Revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the public record. Formed then, the Joint Venture is ready in 2041.

Round 2 · decision year 2035

2035: the Joint Venture forms; Airbus's cash line and its stricter condition keep Delay Tactics out

  • P&W and Rolls-Royce both committed to the Joint Venture on sealed orders. Both solo programmes folded into it. It inherits GTF2's schedule and is ready in 2036. Rolls-Royce writes off $1.71B.
  • Airbus left poaching out. It was worth +$1.65B, but it took peak spend $0.07B over its Board's $5.2B cash line, and Faury kept the team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first), which on its own keeps poaching off.
  • Boeing held the 787 Re-engine: on the 10-year ramp it would overlap fps by 5 years, against its 2-year limit. It logged the $0.65B forgone as the cost of that fixed rule.
  • CFM/GE held everything and declined the Open Fan objective.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingDo Nothing

Public statement: “Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once. We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line. A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade. There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it. Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline. We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected. We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s. On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility. On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines. The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that. Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers. What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyCommit to Joint Venture with RR

Public statement: “Let me start with what is not done. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% since 2026, and that is not where we want to be. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. We launched it in 2030, when we were named on a new single-aisle, and it is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. We will not compress the programme to make a date. If that date comes under risk, we will say so early, with the plan. Control what you can control. The GTF fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers, ahead of GTF2. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection, and there are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. That commitment is ours alone. A Joint Venture forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits. That is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture would share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. The Joint Venture would carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.”

Rolls-RoyceCommit to Joint Venture with P&W

Public statement: “So, let me be clear. UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and on its seven-year clock: ready in 2037, seven years from launch, and not before. The full test programme runs and nothing is compressed. If a phase slips, the engine slips. Support goes in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms. That means shared risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. We are actually bringing a technology. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise. There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.”

FrameKelly Ortberg: initial lean: Orders I lean to: Do Nothing. - fps: hold (we keep building the fps toward 2040); - fps engine code: 3 (CFM), unless Pope shows a second source adds supply security with durability shown before 2040; - 737 rate: hold; - 787 Re-engine: hold. Row: +0.66 / -0.80 / …

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Keep the fps whole on its 2040 date. It is now a core development: re-baseline it, never cancel it (H5). Keeping it beats cancelling by +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 (S1 / S2 / S3). Our Cancellation test protects it unless keeping it loses at least $1B in every plausible column, and the grid shows the opposite by about $17.5-19B [BG-0022, B-1729, BX-0553].
  • One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine in 2035. The fps 10-year counts 2033-40 (EIS - 7 to EIS), and a Re-engine launched now counts 2035-40: 5 years of overlap against our 2-year limit (H4). Its item value is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. It is never above $1B, and in S2 it is $1.99B past our -$1B limit. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine this round [B-2167, BX-0248, BG-0068].
  • The rating comes first. The risk case is S3 (Airbus Delay Tactics). Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, so no plan may fall below -2.78. Every fps: hold plan clears it, and every cancel row fails it (-18.33 and -16.66). Fund the programme from operations and debt capacity, with no new equity; debt stays the first call on free cash [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BX-0556].
  • Safety and production readiness. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, and it offers the 737 rate only at hold. We still want Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results, and the Chief Engineer's certification results heard directly by Aerospace Safety. Supplier and engineering-talent readiness is our hedge against S3 [BG-0043, BG-0025, BG-0014, BX-1263].
  • Candour and the long cycle. Hold the 2040 date publicly and reset once and early if it moves. Report the incumbency path honestly. Log every premium, and log hard-rule costs separately [B-2315, BG-0006, BG-0022].

Expects to see. 1. Ortberg's frame and his expected_scenario (S1, S2 or S3). 2. The submitted row from the round-2 grid. For each Board item, the same row with that item at hold, in all three columns. Do Nothing (fps: hold + 787: hold) is +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78. 3. Malave's buffer test with its numbers: the plan's S3 value against Do Nothing's -0.78 (floor -2.78). 4. Malave's yearly funding report, which we asked for at the round-1 review: the actual fps phasing against airplane operating profit, the debt path and the rating outlook, with no new equity. The brief's own table shows operating profit falling from 6.7 to 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39. His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passed at the 2030 launch; it needs restating only if a new launch is proposed. 5. Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results and her veto check. The brief reports no live problem, and 737 rate is offered only at hold. 6. The CEO's ruling on H4 and on the second half of H3 for the 787 Re-engine (5 years of overlap), and on H5 for the fps. H1 is not at issue, since the fps is launched. 7. The engine code, with each named maker's public ready date against the 2040 EIS. 8. premium with its reason, and hard-rule costs logged separately. 9. A board_response answering each of our seven round-1 review recommendations. 10. A public statement that holds 2040 as a planning date with headroom.

Would approve.

  • fps: hold, 787 Re-engine: hold and 737 rate: hold, which is Do Nothing: continue the launched 10-year fps toward its 2040 EIS. Row: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 / S2 / S3). S3 sits $2.00B above the -2.78 floor. Holds are not Board items and are never vetoed. If every order is a hold, the GM does not call us for review, and our recommendations carry into the 2045 guidance.
  • fps engine code: keep 3 (CFM), or move to any code whose makers have a public new-engine ready date on or before 2040. Those dates are CFM ducted 2036, P&W GTF2 2036 and RR UltraFan NB 2037, so codes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 qualify. NGSA's code 7 creates no forbidden pair. With the fps on hold, a code change is not a Board item, and a code is never a veto ground: it does not change Boeing's payoff.

Would veto.

  • fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine: hold. Item value: -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. It fails four tests. Cancellation (H5): keeping the programme beats cancelling by $17.55B or more in every column. Downside: every column is far below -$1B. Rating first: S3 at -18.33 against the -2.78 floor. Business case. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine: launch. Item value: -17.97 / -17.97 / -16.53, and S3 is -16.66 against the -2.78 floor. It fails on the same grounds. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • 787 Re-engine: launch, with fps: hold. Item value: +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65 (row +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13 against Do Nothing's +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78). It fails three tests. Business case: no column is above $1B, so it fails whichever column the CEO expects. Downside: -2.99 in S2, and the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine. One development at a time (H4): 5 years of overlap (fps 2033-40, Re-engine 2035-40) against our 2-year limit. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • 787 Re-engine: launch, with fps: cancel. Item value: +1.67 / -1.97 / +1.67. It fails Downside in S2, and it rides with a cancel we would veto. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any plan that has a binding ExCo veto still standing after revision (Malave's buffer test), a red-line flag the CEO neither struck nor rebutted, or a premium above $2B or unlogged. We would veto the item whose reversion to hold cures it.

Recommendations.

  • Re-baseline the fps, never cancel it. Keeping it beats cancelling by +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55, and H5 bars a cancel for a slip, a charge, a supplier problem or Airbus entering service first. Keep Malave's quarterly independent check of the estimate and schedule. If the 2040 date moves, report it early with the plan to fix it, cost it once and in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to this board.
  • Hold the 787 Re-engine this round. A 2035 launch overlaps the fps by 5 years and fails H4 and our One development test. Its item value is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65, so it never reaches our $1B business case. Log the 0.65 forgone in S1 and S3 as a hard-rule cost (H4), not a premium; in S2, holding saves 2.99. The earliest window is the 2045 round (EIS 2050, no overlap with the fps), and only if Airbus has not re-engined the A350 by then (H3, second half). Until then, grow the widebody from Charleston capacity.
  • Bring the Finance Committee its yearly report: actual fps phasing, the debt path and the rating outlook. The brief shows airplane operating profit falling to 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39 as share dips. Against about $6.03B a year of even-spread fps spend, cover rises from 90% to 94%, and the cushion shrinks from about $0.67B to about $0.37B a year. The grid already carries -4.73 of debt penalty. If peak-year spend runs above operating profit, show how debt capacity covers it within investment grade. No new equity. Any threat to the rating comes back to this board before it is committed.
  • The Aerospace Safety Committee asks to hear the 737, 787 and fps KPI, supplier and certification results directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. It also asks that certify-before-rate, with no production-certification concurrency, be written into the fps plan. Against our risk case S3, which costs 1.44 against S1, keep fragile suppliers funded and engineering staff in place through the fps ramp. Attribute no bottleneck to anyone before it is exposed.
  • Engine code (recommendation only). Code 3 remains acceptable. All three makers now have public ready dates before our 2040 EIS: CFM ducted 2036, GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037. A second source (code 5, 6 or 7) is acceptable if management judges each maker on a matured engine with durability shown before EIS and on its capacity across both airframers. Code 4 is not advisable: no Joint Venture has formed, and one formed in 2035 would be ready only in 2041. This is not a veto ground.
  • Disclosure and the long cycle. Hold 2040 publicly as a planning date with headroom, keep any earlier date back, and reset once if it moves. Report the incumbency path honestly. The brief shows narrowbody share at 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 and 38% in 2040, recovering to 47% by 2049. Both objectives are recorded as not met, and no order offered this round can change that, so no objective premium applies. Attribute nothing to the FAA, suppliers or Airbus, and tie no order to Airbus's timing. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions.
  • Premium log. This round, the best plan that respects the hard rules and our tests is Do Nothing (every field at hold), so the premium should be 0. Carry forward the round-1 premium of 0.46, and log hard-rule costs (H4: 0.65 in S1 and S3) separately. Answer each of our seven round-1 review recommendations in board_response; an unanswered one will be raised again in 2045.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. 2035 is a round for carrying what we started, not for starting something new. The fps is five years into a ten-year plan. The brief shows it on its 2040 date, with no slip and no certification trouble, and no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. So the question is narrow. Does anything earn a place beside the fps this round: a 787 Re-engine, a cancel or an engine-code change? And does our 2040 date still carry the headroom we said it had? I'm putting my four questions to this ExCo. (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live problem, and I want Pope's seat to confirm it on the record for the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet ready for a second development while the fps is in its heaviest years [BX-1296, BX-1305]? (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave to read the risk-case column S3 before anything else, and to tell me whether anything shows our fps estimate is wrong [BX-1319]. (4) Is each plan doing less, better? I want every row set against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

Situation. Where we are (bulletin and brief). - Round 1 was adjudicated. Our fps launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp, with EIS 2040 and CFM selected. Airbus launched NGSA in 2030, with EIS 2037 and code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). No A350 Re-engine has been launched. - Engine ready dates on the public record: CFM ducted 2036, P&W GTF2 2036, RR UltraFan NB 2037, CFM-Embraer partnership 2037. The GEnx upgrade has been in service on the 787 since 2033. - Observed shares were flat over 2026-34: narrowbody 40/60, widebody 58.8/41.2, 800 NB and 100 WB deliveries a year. - The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and lists the fps as "in development; EIS 2040". My FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. Do Nothing (fps continues, 787 hold, rate hold) scores +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 rivals hold / S2 A350 Re-engine / S3 risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics). Its components: - narrowbody operating profit +20.30; - programme investment -14.91, booked at EIS; - debt penalty -4.73, already netted, never subtracted again. For scale only, the undiscounted penalty on the 10-year fps is $19.1B. Incumbency path. Narrowbody share runs 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while NGSA is alone, then 38% in 2040, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049. That is a 47/53 long-run split for a 3-year NGSA lead. Both objectives (50/50 and incumbency) are recorded as not met, and no order offered this round changes that. So no objective premium applies. Funding. Airplane operating profit is 6.7 through 2036, then 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39. Against about $6.03B a year of even-spread fps spend (inference), cover rises from 90% to 91 / 93 / 94%, and the cushion shrinks from $0.67B to $0.57B / $0.47B / $0.37B a year. Grid against Do Nothing (S1 / S2 / S3; S3 floor -2.78): - 787 Re-engine with the fps: row +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13; item +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. - Launched now, it enters service in 2040. The board's strain counts it 2035-40 against the fps's 2033-40: 5 years of overlap and $3.0B of strain undiscounted, already netted. - Its $5B bill lands in 2040, the same year as the fps's $60.32B. My own arithmetic, for Malave to confirm: the convex penalty then adds about $3.1B undiscounted (about 0.77 PV), against $0.6B for the Re-engine alone. - Real spend of about $1.0B a year over 2035-39 takes total spend to about $7.03B a year. That is 105-110% of operating profit, about $2.25B borrowed above it over five years. - Cancel the fps: row -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33; item -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. The write-off is $30.16B in 2035 (60.32 × 5/10), and the penalty stays. - Cancel with a Re-engine: row -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66; item -17.32 / -20.96 / -15.88. The Re-engine item beside a cancel is +1.67 / -1.97 / +1.67. Board risks (from its guidance; these are not my red lines). It would veto: - any fps cancel, with or without a Re-engine; - 787 Re-engine: launch with the fps on hold, for three reasons: it never clears $1B in any column; it is -2.99 in S2, which the bulletin does not rule out; and it carries 5 years of overlap against its 2-year limit; - 787 Re-engine: launch with a cancel; - any plan with a binding ExCo veto still standing, a red-line flag neither struck nor rebutted, or a premium above $2B or unlogged. It would approve Do Nothing, and code 3 or any code whose makers are ready by 2040. If every order is a hold, it is not called to review, and its recommendations carry into 2045.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing: fps hold (continue to 2040), 787 Re-engine hold, rate hold, code 3. - Row: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78. - It is the baseline, and it sets the S3 floor at -2.78. It sits exactly $2.00B above that floor. - It is the best H4- and H5-legal row in every column. - My lean.
  • B. fps hold + 787 Re-engine. - Row: +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13; item against A: +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. - S3 passes the buffer test (-0.13, 2.65 above the floor). - It never clears ε. In S1 and S3 it is a tie that 'doing less, better' gives to A anyway. In S2 it loses $2.99B. - 5 years of overlap against H4's 2-year limit. Both bills land in 2040. About $2.25B is borrowed above operating profit over 2035-39. - Struck on H4. Tested only to price the hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2.
  • C. Cancel the fps + 787 hold. - Row: -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33; item: -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. - S3 misses the floor by 15.55. - Struck by H5, and it fails the buffer test and the Board's Cancellation test. - For the record only.
  • D. Cancel the fps + 787 Re-engine. - Row: -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66; item: -17.32 / -20.96 / -15.88. - S3 misses the floor by 13.88. - Struck by H5. - For the record only.
  • E. Engine code on row A, with no payoff change: - keep 3 (CFM), my lean; - or add a second source: 6 (P&W and CFM), 5 (RR and CFM) or 7 (all three). Judge each on a matured engine with durability shown before EIS [BX-1298]: GTF2 and UltraFan NB would have about three years in service on NGSA by 2040 if fitted there. Also judge on each maker's capacity to support both airframers' rates and the aftermarket [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Code 4 is out (ready 2041 at the earliest).

Red lines.

  • H1: not at issue. The fps is launched.
  • H2: cannot bind. EIS 2040 is after the 2035 technology-ready year.
  • H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): it lapsed by its own terms after 2030. The ground I re-founded it on in Round 1, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393, BX-1239], now works through H4. H3, second half (no 787 Re-engine, ever, once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine): not triggered, since the bulletin shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round (S2), it bars our Re-engine from 2045 on, and I accept that.
  • H4 binds. A 2035 Re-engine overlaps the fps for 5 years (2035-40) against the 2-year limit, so 787 Re-engine: launch is struck this round. The earliest H4-legal window is the 2045 round (EIS 2050, no overlap), and only if the A350 has not re-engined. The forgone value is a hard-rule cost (0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2), logged apart from any premium.
  • H5 binds. Never cancel the launched fps. If the date moves, re-baseline once and early, costed in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost [BX-1251, BX-1321, B-2349]. Every cancel row is struck.
  • H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus or under a live problem. Not in play: the rate is offered only at hold.
  • H7: no trigger. The brief reports no certification trouble, so the FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
  • H8: plans within ε ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides. Doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B. Every premium is logged, the Round-1 premium of 0.46 is carried forward, and hard-rule costs are logged separately.
  • My own lines: - no production-certification concurrency in the fps plan [BX-1263, B-2228]; - no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]; - no second development before the one in hand is done [B-2326]; - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; - no attribution of a supplier or talent problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); - no order timed to Airbus [B-2313, B-2315]; - no rate request without stable KPIs [BX-1259].

Initial lean. Orders I lean to: Do Nothing. - fps: hold (we keep building the fps toward 2040); - fps engine code: 3 (CFM), unless Pope shows a second source adds supply security with durability shown before 2040; - 737 rate: hold; - 787 Re-engine: hold. Row: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78. None of these is a Board item, so the Board is not called to review. I will still answer its seven Round-1 recommendations in board_response. Why: - It is the best row that respects H4 and H5 in every column. - The Re-engine adds only +0.65 in S1 and S3. That is inside ε, so doing less, better [BX-1239] takes A even before H4 strikes B, and the Re-engine loses $2.99B in S2. - A Re-engine now would put two developments and two 2040 bills on a balance sheet that still has debt as the first call on cash [BX-1305]. It would have us borrowing above operating profit. - A cancel throws away $17.55-18.99B and breaks H5. We do not walk away from a core programme [BX-1251]. The rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem. - Her flags are both correct, so I confirm them and strike the rows: - H4 on B: 5 years of overlap against a 2-year limit. - H5 on C and D. - No flag is mistaken and nothing needs a rebuttal, so overrides is empty. 2. My four questions. - Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and deliveries were flat at 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies over 2026-34. Pope rightly says the board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI record comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259]. - Are market, technology and balance sheet ready for a second development? No. - Market: the Re-engine's item is +0.65 in S1, inside ε, and -2.99 in S2. - Balance sheet: Malave finds the Re-engine not fundable from operations. On his curve it adds $7.69B of borrowing above operating profit over 2035-39 ($2.26B on an even spread), and he would not support investment grade with a second bill in the fps peak years [BX-1305]. - The fps is the development in hand. We finish it first [B-2326]. - What if certification takes longer? I read S3 first. Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, 2.00 above the floor. Malave's quarterly check finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong [BX-1319], so there is no reset to make, and I will not make one for the sake of it. One reset, if it comes, made early [BX-1318]. - Is this doing less, better? A and B are within ε in S1 (+0.66 against +1.31) and in S3 (-0.78 against -0.13). A leads by 2.99 in S2. Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both give it to A. Malave's worst-column rule picks A by 2.99. 3. Rulings on the hard rules. - H1 is not at issue; the fps is launched. - H2 cannot bind. - H3: - First half: it lapsed after 2030. Its re-founded ground, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], now works through H4. - Second half: not triggered, since the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars ours from 2045, and I accept that. - H4 binds. The fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years against 2. 787 Re-engine stays at hold. - Hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. Logged apart from any premium. - Earliest window: the 2045 round (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap). - H5 binds. The fps stays whole. - Keeping it beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55, so H5 forgoes nothing. - A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying. - H6 is not in play. - H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. - H8: premium 0 this round. Cumulative 0.46 (Round 1), within the $2B cap. 4. Debt and funding, Malave's figures, adopted as the Finance Committee baseline. - Do Nothing carries -4.73 of debt penalty already netted ($19.1B undiscounted for scale). It is never subtracted again. - On his planning curve: - spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit; - 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34; - 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. - That is fundable within investment grade with no new equity, on the fps alone. - His curve is an inference, because the brief gives no phasing. I have asked him to replace it with programme actuals each quarter. His triggers go to the Board before anything is committed. 5. Engine code: 3 (CFM). This is the last code decision before EIS. - CFM ducted is ready in 2036, with the LEAP derivative as a floor. - Code 3 against NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair. - I considered a second source (5, 6 or 7): GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so all qualify by date. I rejected it: - none of these engines is in service today, and about three years on NGSA by 2040 is short of durability shown [BX-1298]; - it would add a second propulsion integration and certification inside the fps's heaviest years, the same capacity ground as H4; - Pope cannot show it adds supply security on matured, durable engines. - CFM's load across both airframers is real [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We manage it with allocation tracking and contracted delivery commitments. - My confidence on engine choice is Low, so doctrine plus Pope's test drove this. 6. Expected scenario: S1, provisional; my confidence on Airbus is Low. My Round-1 read of an A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA did not happen. A move is real only when it is launched. The orders are the same in every column, so the read does not drive the decision. 7. Doctrine and record. Several of these calls rest on company doctrine, not my own record: H4, H5, the code-3 default and the 2044 hedge window. Others are my record: one development at a time, debt first, never walk away from a core programme, reset once, no fixed-price development and certify before rate. 8. The Board. All four orders are holds, which matches its would-approve list, so no item goes to review. Its seven recommendations are answered in board_response. 9. What would change this: - a finding that the estimate or date is wrong: we reset once, now, costed in full and brought to the Board; - a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem; - an A350 Re-engine, which closes our 2045 Re-engine window under H3.

Weighing the CFO. Weighed as my independent check on the estimate [BX-1316]. His veto binds only on the slip leg. It is a thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and his phasing curve is his own inference because the brief gives no phasing. Taken in full: - Buffer results: A is 2.00 above the floor, B 2.65 above, C 15.55 below and D 13.88 below. I accept his binding veto on C and D. - Debt penalty: Do Nothing's -4.73 is confirmed. B would add $3.10B undiscounted (0.765 PV) against $0.60B for the Re-engine alone. B's strain is $3.0B. Both are netted already and never subtracted again. - Cancel arithmetic: $30.16B written off, and keeping beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55. - His finding that the estimate is not wrong, so there is no reset. - The premium log. Taken as advice: - Hold on B. It agrees with my H4 strike, so it is not decisive. - The worst-column rule. It agrees with A by 2.99. His funding report becomes the Finance Committee baseline: - peak in 2036 at about $8.44B; - $3.66B drawn over 2035-38 against $8.77B built over 2030-34; - the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt; - investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity. I treat his curve as a plan, not a fact, until programme actuals replace it.

Weighing the operating head. Weighed as the operations doctrine. It is a thin seat with Very low airplane evidence, which she states herself. Her KPI veto was checked and not invoked. That is correct: the rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem. Taken in full: - H4 flag on B: 5 years of overlap and $3.0B of strain. Confirmed and struck. She confirms we lack the engineering capacity for a second development in these years. - H5 flag on C and D: confirmed and struck. - The board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI and certification results come directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. - The S3 window runs 2040-44. I extend the supplier and talent hedge through 2044. - Exposure framed as ordinary market moves, with nothing attributed to anyone. - Engine code 3, with CFM allocation tracked, since this is the last code round before EIS. Useful sensitivities: - each fps share point is worth about $0.28B a year nominal, against $0.08B on the 737; - the $2.74B even-spread cushion absorbs a 9.1% overrun on the remaining spend. Noted: Charleston can carry the 787 to the 2045 window, and widebody growth beyond 100 a year is commercial and unpriced. Nothing material was rejected.

Final

Best grid plan in that scenario. The grid's top row in S1 is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine at +1.31. It is only 0.65 above Do Nothing, inside ε. It breaches H4 (5 years of overlap against 2), loses 2.99 in S2 and is not fundable from operations. Struck. The best plan that respects H4, H5 and every ExCo and Board test, and the one chosen, is fps: hold + 787: hold (Do Nothing), with code 3 and the rate at hold: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 / S2 / S3).. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. No doctrine or objective premium this round. It is logged separately and is not a premium. It is also inside ε, so doing less, better would choose Do Nothing anyway. - H5 forgoes nothing: cancelling is worse by 17.55 or more in every column. - No objective premium: no order on offer changes the narrowbody share path. - Running log: Round-1 premium 0.46 (10-year over 7-year, S2 and S4), carried forward. Cumulative 0.46, within the $2B cap. - Hard-rule cost log: Round 1, the Re-engine forgone under H3 and H4. Round 2, H4 at 0.65 in S1 and S3.

  • 1. Re-baseline the fps, never cancel it; keep Malave's quarterly check; if 2040 moves, report early, cost it once in full and bring it to the Board. (Carries Round-1 recommendation 4.) Keeping beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55. - Malave's quarterly independent check continues. It finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong, so there is no reset this round. - If the date moves, I report it early with the plan, reset once, and cost it in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost. My H4 ruling: the fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40, so 5 years of overlap against 2.   • 3. Bring the Finance Committee its yearly report: actual fps phasing, debt path, rating outlook; no new equity; any threat to the rating comes back before commitment. (Carries Round-1 recommendation 2.) Taken up. Malave's report is in his memo and is now the Finance Committee baseline. - Phasing (his planning curve): fps spend of 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43 in 2035-39, against operating profit of 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4. - Peak: 2036, at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit. - Debt path: 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34. 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. - The -4.73 penalty is already netted. - Rating: investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity. Aerospace Safety hears 737, 787 and fps KPI, supplier and certification results directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer; certify-before-rate is written into the fps plan; suppliers funded and staff held against S3; no attribution. H5 forgoes nothing. - All seven Round-1 review recommendations are answered here, each mapped to the Round-2 recommendation that carries it.

Objective. The PD-briefing objective (hold the 50/50 split, defend incumbency) is the company's mission, not on my ranked list. Both parts are recorded as not met: - The worst year is 38.0%: 2040 38%, 2045 43%, 2050 47%. - Share is below the 40% incumbency line over 2037-41: 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while NGSA flies alone, 38% in 2040, 39% in 2041, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049. - The long-run split is 47/53 for a 3-year NGSA lead. No order on offer this round changes that path: - The 787 Re-engine is a widebody lever. - A cancel would throw away the fps recovery. So no objective premium applies. The objective is best served by protecting the 2040 date, since each year of slip costs 1 pp of long-run share for good. That calls for funded suppliers, engineers in place and certify-before-rate, not for any order. I report this path honestly and tie no order to Airbus's timing.

Airbus likely keeps code 7, or narrows it to CFM plus one second source. - Delay Tactics are covert and unobservable until the fps enters service; S3 is priced as the risk case. Engine makers: - CFM ducted is ready in 2036, and GTF2 and UltraFan NB on their 2036 and 2037 dates. - An RR and P&W Joint Venture is unlikely this round, since both already run Solo programmes. If one forms in 2035, it is ready in 2041, after our EIS. Boeing: - The Board is not called to review, since all four orders are holds. - Next round (2045): the fps in service from 2040, narrowbody share 38% in 2040 rising to 43% in 2045. - The 787 Re-engine is reconsidered in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined. - No fps reset expected, but the 2035-37 peak spend and the 2040-44 supply ramp are the watch items. - Expected ΔPV is +0.66 in S1; -0.80 and -0.78 in S2 and S3.

Other moves.

The board carries deliveries only, so those results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record [BX-1271, BG-0043]. Public as a commitment; the reports themselves are internal.
  • No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms continue (public): fps development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Not priced on the board.
  • Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee: fund from operations and debt capacity, no new equity (private): Malave's planning curve is the baseline until programme actuals replace it each quarter: fps spend 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43 in 2035-39 against operating profit 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4. Peak 2036 at about $8.4B, $1.74B above operating profit; 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B room built in 2030-34; 2039 turns positive; the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. Investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity and debt the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Triggers back to the Board before commitment: operating profit below 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39, peak spend above about $8.4B, 2035-38 borrowing above the 2030-34 room, or any threat to the rating.
  • Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, and engineering teams in place, through 2044 (private): Our hedge against the risk case S3 (5 pp for 5 years from EIS, $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV). The window runs 2040-44, so the hedge runs through 2044, not 2040. Keep the fps long-lead airframe structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth-dependent parts and the CFM engine line funded above our rate; embed staff where a supplier falls behind; requalify or acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. Long-term supply agreements sized to our own 2040 plan, on our own schedule. Hold the fps engineering and certification teams through 2044; retention and hiring as needed; none assigned to a second development. Others' supply agreements and hiring are ordinary market moves; we attribute nothing to anyone before exposure.
  • Engine request stays code 3 (CFM); allocation tracked (private): This is the last code decision before EIS 2040. CFM ducted is ready 2036, four years before EIS, with the LEAP derivative as the floor. Code 3 beside NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair. Require a matured engine with durability proven on the ground before EIS [BX-1298]. Track CFM engine allocation by airframer and contract delivery commitments, because CFM supports NGSA, the A320neo, the 737 aftermarket and the fps [BX-1264, BX-1325].
  • Independent estimate check continues; early-warning rule (private): Malave reviews the fps estimate and schedule every quarter [BX-1316]. Watch items, none a reset trigger today: peak spend 2035-37 above operating profit; operating profit falling to 6.4 by 2039; CFM ducted on its 2036 gate; supply-base tightness for the 2040-44 ramp. Any finding is reported a year ahead, not at the gate [BX-1306].
  • 787 Re-engine parked to the 2045 window; widebody growth from Charleston (private): No second development while the fps is in its heaviest years (H4: 5 years of overlap against 2). Bring the Re-engine back in 2045 (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap) only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), it passes Malave's buffer test and its bill does not land in a peak year. Until then the 787 grows from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board holds Boeing at 100 widebodies a year, so that growth is commercial and unpriced.
  • Hold the 737 MAX base through the gap, campaign by campaign (private): Narrowbody share dips to 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while a newer airplane flies before ours. Deliver the 737 MAX on the dates promised; quote fps slots only against the 2040 planning date, never an earlier internal date; make every transaction trust-building [BX-1273, B-2315]. Pricing is decided campaign by campaign. Not priced on the board.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety first, and NGSA kept whole on its technology clock through entry into service in 2037. The Board wants it continued, not cancelled and not accelerated. Cancelling would lose $39.65B against continuing in both columns (S1 and S2). Boeing's fps launch (10-year path, EIS 2040) changes nothing in the NGSA plan [AG-0038, AG-0063, A-0225, A-0409, AG-0055, A-0364].
  • Liquidity and the A+/A1 rating through NGSA's last two cash years. Spend in 2035-36 is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line, which is one year's FCF. That leaves $0.13B of headroom ($0.15B against the unrounded $5.23B). Nothing added this round may break the line. An A350 Re-engine would take spend to $6.67B a year. One Delay Tactics move would take it to $5.27B [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104, A-0343].
  • Integrity in the last round in which Delay Tactics can be ordered (fps enters service in 2040; the next round is 2045). Bottleneck and both remain integrity vetoes. Poaching now meets the fps-on-the-record and downside conditions (+1.65 in S1, +1.66 in S2), but it fails the Board's cash line in 2035-36. The default stays none [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, A-0331].
  • One programme at a time. The A350 Re-engine stays in reserve until NGSA cash rolls off: 2037 at the earliest, which means the 2045 round. It should come back as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round, company rule 3 closes it [A-0343, A-0401, A-0302, AX-0019].
  • Returns kept fundable. The 30-50% payout stays inside policy. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State money is upside only and is not assumed in the case [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0034, AG-0054, A-0348].
