Would approve.

  • NGSA: hold, meaning NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037. This is the default, not a Board item, and it is never vetoed. The default row is +23.37 in S1 and +22.88 in S2, and continuing beats cancelling by $39.65B in each column.
  • NGSA engine code 7 kept. CFM plus two second sources are all public and ready by the 2037 entry into service: CFM ducted and GTF2 in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037. Code 7 is in no barred pair with fps's CFM code. The code is a recommendation and never a veto ground.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold. This is the default and is never vetoed.
  • Delay Tactics: none. This is the default and is never vetoed. The Board records that a single poaching move would otherwise meet the downside test (+1.65 / +1.66) and the fps-on-the-record and NGSA-in-development conditions. Its cash, not its value, decides it this round.

Would veto.

  • NGSA: cancel. Ground: reactive cancellation. Continuing beats cancelling by $39.65B in S1 and S2 (by $39.09B and $39.08B on the A350 Re-engine rows), far above the $1B the Board's test requires against continuing in every column. A Boeing move is never a ground. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch in 2035. Ground: balance sheet. Development runs 2035-39 and overlaps NGSA in 2035-36. Spend in those two years is $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B a year, $1.47B over the $5.2B line. The item value is +1.54 in S1 and -1.21 in S2, so it also fails the downside test if the CEO expects S2. As an override on a Qualified Majority item, it would trail the best passing option by $1.21B to $1.22B in S2 and fail the Board's override review. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Delay Tactics: bottleneck or both. Ground: integrity and abnormal risk. 'Both' also loses $0.47B against one move in each column, for no added effect. Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Delay Tactics: poaching. Ground: balance sheet. The $1B is spread over 2035-39 to fps entry into service at $0.20B a year, so spend peaks at $5.27B in 2035-36. That is $0.07B over the $5.2B line, or $0.05B over the unrounded $5.23B. The Board signalled this in its round-1 review. If the CEO has not recorded setting aside the team's stricter condition, it fails on integrity as well. Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Any plan that combines the A350 Re-engine with Delay Tactics (2035 peak about $6.87B). Under the plan-level rule the Board vetoes the A350 Re-engine first, then Delay Tactics, and never NGSA. Any override of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp or supply tests is also vetoed.

Recommendations.

  • Hold course on NGSA. It is launched, funded and on its technology clock, entering service in 2037, three years ahead of fps in 2040. Do not accelerate it, re-time it or cancel it because of Boeing's launch. Cancelling loses $39.65B in both columns. The ExCo's job this round is execution: maturity, the production system and certification ahead of rate.
  • Let NGSA's cash roll off before adding anything. The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) should take the CFO's 2035-37 schedule and confirm that 2035 and 2036 stay within the $5.2B line at $5.07B a year. It should also report whether any round-1 break point was triggered. Re-phasing inside NGSA remains the only remedy. It must never be used to make room for another item.
  • Keep the A350 Re-engine in reserve this round. On the Board's line, a 2035 launch peaks at $6.67B a year, and its value turns to -1.21 if Boeing re-engines the 787. The first year that passes is 2037, which means the 2045 round. Bring it back then as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column, after Wagner confirms the A350F and Spirit absorption. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round, company rule 3 closes it.
  • Delay Tactics: none, and the Board expects this to close the question for the game. Bottleneck and both are integrity vetoes. Poaching would add +1.65 / +1.66, but the money cannot be spent within the cash line while NGSA spends. The supply agreements must stay sized to Airbus's own NGSA and A320 needs, and the hiring programme must never target Boeing's fps teams. The ECSC should review both again this year.
  • Returns and rating. In round 1 the Board asked for a base case to sit beside the CFO's stress case, and for the A+/A1 headroom metrics. It now asks for both. The CFO should confirm that net cash still carries the 30-50% payout through 2036, and should flag any year in which the EUR 3.20 dividend depends on FCF above about $5.9B. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State support stays upside only.
  • Engine supply. Keep code 7. All three makers now have public engines that are ready by NGSA's 2037 entry into service, and CFM backstops UltraFan NB, which is ready only in 2037 itself. Avoid code 3, which would form a barred pair with fps's CFM selection. The code is not a veto ground.
  • Safety and ramp. The Board's twice-yearly safety review should take Wagner's NGSA readiness report together with the A320 ring-fence and ramp report. Entry into service comes only once the technologies and the production system are mature. A quality or supply issue on the A320 line comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line.
  • Read Boeing only from the bulletin. Its fps entering service in 2040 gives NGSA a three-year lead and a long-run split of 47/53 (Boeing/Airbus). Its statement against a second development makes S1 the likely column, but S2 remains plausible and the case must show it. The briefing objective (60% in 2045 and 2050) is not a Board test, and the Board will not trade value or integrity for it.
  • Public statement. Lead with the five pillars. Say NGSA is on track for the second half of the 2030s, with windows and not dates and no internal targets. Do not link NGSA's timing to Boeing's. Never mention Delay Tactics. The Board vets the final text.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. Do we hold course in 2035, keeping NGSA unchanged on its own technology clock to entry into service in 2037, engine code 7, the A350 held and Delay Tactics at none, which closes that question for the game? Or does any addition (an A350 Re-engine or one poaching move) pass the five pillars, Toepfer's $5.2B cash line while NGSA spends its last two years at $5.07B, Wagner's tests and the Board?

Situation. Round 2, decision year 2035. Public record (bulletin): - Boeing launched fps in 2030 on the 10-year path, entering service in 2040, with CFM (code 3). It calls 2040 "a planning date with headroom built in", will "certify before we build at rate", is not changing 737 rates, and is "not starting a second development alongside this one". - NGSA launched in 2030 and is in development for entry into service in 2037. That is a three-year lead: 1 pp a year while we are alone, then a long-run split of 47/53 (Boeing/Airbus) under the rules. - Engines: all three makers launched in 2030 on our code 7. CFM ducted and P&W GTF2 are ready in 2036; RR UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, our entry-into-service year itself. NGSA is set to fly CFM + PW + RR, and CFM backstops any late maker. CFM also launched the Embraer partnership (ready 2037) and the GEnx upgrade for 787 customers (in service since 2033). RR says it will make no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. P&W says the GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts and shops. - No 787 Re-engine and no Boeing Rate Increase is on the record. - Observed shares for 2026-34 are the status quo: 60% narrowbody, 41.2% widebody. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem, no engine slip and no inject. Our position (brief section 1): - If nobody moves, ΔPV is +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). That is narrowbody profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 (booked at the 2037 entry into service) and debt penalty -0.53. - In the Board's cash view NGSA still spends $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 (about $10.15B left), and nil in 2037, against the $5.2B one-year-FCF line. Headroom is $0.13B ($0.15B to the unrounded $5.23B) [AX-0104]. Columns: - S1: rivals hold. This is my provisional expected scenario, on Boeing's own words about no second development. - S2: Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round. Boeing statements have reversed before (profile section 7), so S2 is the worst plausible column and the case must show it. Objective (scored by the GM, never in the payoff): - "Protect the A320 family" is met: 60% through 2036. - "Defend the 60/40 edge" is not met: 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045, 53% in 2050. - My reading of the rules is that no order on this round's menu restores it. Delay Tactics act only in 2040-44 (5 pp for 5 years from fps entry into service), when we are already above 60%, and the A350 Re-engine has no narrowbody effect. I trade no PV for the objective. Board guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 4 of 5): a quiet round. - NGSA continues; it is not accelerated and not cancelled. - Nothing new while NGSA spends. - Delay Tactics stay at none, which closes the question for the game. - The A350 Re-engine stays in reserve until the 2045 round, as a staged widebody case that shows the 787 Re-engine column. - It expects no Board item and would approve the defaults as they stand. This is the last round in which Delay Tactics can be ordered: fps enters service in 2040 and the next round is 2045.

Options to test.

  • A. NGSA hold + code 7 + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none. This is my lean and the company default for this round. - Grid: +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). Positive in both columns. - No Board item. - Continuing beats cancelling by $39.65B in both columns.
  • B. A + one poaching move. I test it for the record and expect to strike it. - Grid: +25.02 / +24.54. Item value against A: +1.65 / +1.66. - It meets the grid's $1B test. - It meets rule 4: fps is public and not in service, and this would be the first move of the game. - It meets rule 5: NGSA is in development. - Cash: peak $5.07B + $0.20B = $5.27B in 2035-36. That is $0.07B over the $5.2B line ($0.05B over the unrounded $5.23B). It fails Toepfer's cash test and the Board's line. - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board. Read literally, it keeps the move off unless I record setting it aside. I do not intend to. - The Board vetoes it on the balance sheet. - Bottleneck in place of poaching is an integrity veto and is struck outright.
  • C. A + both moves. Deleted; listed for the record only. - Grid: +24.55 / +24.07, which is -0.47 against one move in each column. - It breaks rule 4 (both counts as two moves) and the integrity pillar. - The Board vetoes it on integrity.
  • D. A + A350 Re-engine launched in 2035. I expect to strike it. - Grid: +24.91 / +21.67. Item value against A: +1.54 in S1, -1.21 in S2. - It is one launch, with a 2-year overlap (2035-36) and $1.2B of strain, so it sits at the edge of rule 6. - Rule 3 is not yet binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. In S2 both would launch this round and enter service in 2040, so share would not move. - Cash: $6.67B a year in 2035-36, $1.47B over the line. - It fails the added-move $1B test in S2. - The Board vetoes it on the balance sheet. An override would trail the best passing option by $1.21B in S2 and fail the Board's override review. - Wagner's absorption and capacity results are pending.
  • E. A + A350 Re-engine + one poaching move. Record only. - Grid: +26.56 / +23.32. It is the best grid row in S1. - Peak is about $6.87B. The Board vetoes the A350 Re-engine first, then Delay Tactics.
  • F. Cancel NGSA, on any row. Deleted. - On the hold row: -16.28 / -16.77, which is -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows). - It breaks rule 7 (never in reaction to Boeing). There is no failed case behind it, and the Board vetoes it.
  • G. Engine-code sub-test, on supply certainty only. Wagner to recommend. - 7 (all three): CFM backstops UltraFan NB, which is ready only in 2037 itself. - 5 (RR + CFM) or 6 (P&W + CFM). - 3 is barred with fps's CFM code. - For the record: the best grid row is $3.19B above A in S1 (row E) and $1.66B above A in S2 (row B). Both rows fail the cash line and the Board's tests, so the gap is a cost of discipline, not a doctrine premium.

Red lines.

  • The five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). Every order and every public word must stand on them. They are never overridden and never traded for PV [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 1. NGSA enters service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. No acceleration and no re-timing [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
  • Rules 2 and 7: our own clock. Boeing's fps launch (10-year path, entry into service 2040) changes nothing in the NGSA plan. NGSA is never cancelled in reaction to Boeing, so the cancel rows are deleted (-39.65 in both columns) [A-0364, AG-0063].
  • Rule 3. It is not binding today, because no 787 Re-engine is on the record. If Boeing launches one this round (S2), the A350 Re-engine is closed for 2045 and 2050.
  • Rule 4: at most one Delay Tactics move in the game. - Both counts as two moves, so it is deleted. - A move is allowed only after fps is public and before it enters service, which makes this the last round. - Delay Tactics are never named in public.
  • Rule 5. Poaching only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development. NGSA is in development through 2036, so the rule is met.
  • The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it cannot, so read literally it keeps Delay Tactics off. That is the default, and I do not plan to set it aside.
  • Rule 6. At most one new launch per round, and an NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more. A 2035 A350 Re-engine sits at the 2-year limit.
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried into this round: - NGSA: cancel; - A350 Re-engine: launch ($6.67B a year in 2035-36; -1.21 in S2); - Delay Tactics: bottleneck or both (integrity and abnormal risk); - Delay Tactics: poaching (balance sheet: $5.27B against the $5.2B line); - any plan that combines the A350 Re-engine with Delay Tactics ($6.87B); - any override of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp or supply tests.
  • The Board's tests: - peak programme cash at or under the $5.2B line in 2035-36; - re-phasing inside NGSA is the only remedy, and is never used to make room for another item; - no item worse than its default in the worst plausible column beyond the Board's limits; - the 30-50% payout stays fundable; - no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis; - state money is upside only [AX-0022, AG-0062].
  • Override budget: one per game, none used so far, none planned. An override needs at least $1B over the best passing option, must stay ahead in the worst plausible column, and is recorded as a Board item. It is never used against the five pillars, a company red line or Wagner's safety, quality, ramp or supply results. I have no override against the Board.
  • Disclosure: - no internal long-term-plan targets [AX-0005]; - windows, not dates ("the second half of the 2030s"); - NGSA is never tied to Boeing's timeline; - the Board vets the text [AX-0004]; - Delay Tactics are never mentioned.

Initial lean. Plan A, the company default for this round, as the Board guides: - NGSA: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037; in public, "the second half of the 2030s". - NGSA engine code: 7, unchanged, pending Wagner's supply view. - A350 Re-engine: hold. - Delay Tactics: none. That carries no Board item. It gives +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible), positive in both columns. Why, in the order I am paid to protect: - Five pillars: nothing in plan A puts safety, quality or integrity in question [AX-0073, AX-0081]. - The ramp: no new concurrency while the A320 ramp and NGSA industrialisation run, "disciplined and controlled" [AX-0010, AX-0054]. - The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA stays whole on its technology clock, three years ahead of fps. Boeing's launch moves nothing (rules 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225]. - The Board: it would approve the defaults and expects no item. The rows above plan A do not survive on present numbers, and I do not plan to buy them back with an override: - Delay Tactics: one poaching move adds +1.65 / +1.66. - It breaks the $5.2B line by $0.07B while NGSA spends, and the Board vetoes it on the balance sheet. I have no override against the Board. - I do not set aside the team's stricter condition. Bottleneck and both are integrity vetoes, and both also breaks rule 4. - With fps entering service in 2040, this closes Delay Tactics for the game, as the Board expects. Nothing is said in public. - A350 Re-engine: +1.54 in S1 but -1.21 in S2, and $6.67B a year in 2035-36. It stays in reserve for the 2045 round as a staged widebody case with the 787 Re-engine column. Rule 3 closes it if Boeing re-engines the 787. - Cancel NGSA: deleted on rule 7, at -39.65. For the record, the best grid row is $3.19B above plan A in S1 and $1.66B above it in S2. Those gaps are the price of the cash line, integrity and the Board's veto, not a doctrine premium. No PV is traded for the briefing objective. Public line: - the five pillars first; - NGSA on track for the second half of the 2030s; - a disciplined and controlled A320 ramp; - three engine makers on the aircraft for customer choice and supply; - a more sovereign European supply chain; - the A350 family, including the A350F, as our widebody focus; - our financial framework; - zero-for-zero trade. Nothing on Boeing's timeline, and nothing on Delay Tactics. What would change my lean: - Toepfer shows a round-1 break point already triggered. Then the answer is re-phasing inside NGSA only, never acceleration. - Wagner reports a safety, quality, ramp or supply problem. Then we act at once, with no new concurrency. - An engine is late. An unready maker is dropped and CFM backstops it, so NGSA does not change. A Boeing statement on its own would not change it.

Guillaume Faury decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision: plan A, the company default. - NGSA: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037. - NGSA engine code: 7, unchanged. - A350 Re-engine: hold. - Delay Tactics: none. Grid: +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible). The plan is positive in both columns, carries no Board item and uses no override. The team rule, step by step. 1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches. - Cancel NGSA (every cancel row) is deleted under rule 7. It would be a reaction to Boeing with no failed case behind it: -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), with a $25.37B write-off. - Both moves (on every row) are deleted. They break rule 4, since both counts as two moves, and they fail the integrity pillar because both contains a bottleneck. They also lose $0.47B against one move. - Bottleneck in place of poaching is deleted on integrity. Toepfer and Wagner both fail it as more than a first claim on our own capacity. 2. Survivors of both colleagues' tests. - Only plan A passes Toepfer's tests and Wagner's tests together. - Plan B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails Toepfer's peak-cash test: $5.27B in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, a binding soft veto. It also trips round-1 break point (d). - Plan D (A350 Re-engine, +24.91 / +21.67) fails peak cash at $6.67B and fails robustness at -1.21 in S2. - Plan E (+26.56 / +23.32) fails peak cash at $6.87B, and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2. - Wagner passes poaching and passes the A350 Re-engine on capacity at the limit, but recommends hold. 3. Choice. The highest-grid survivor in my expected column, S1, is plan A. No tie-break is needed. 4. Overrides considered and declined. - Poaching clears $1B over plan A in both columns (+1.65 / +1.66), so an override of Toepfer's cash test is arithmetically open. I decline it for five reasons: - The Board applies its own $5.2B line and has said it would veto, and I have no override against the Board. - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and I do not set it aside. - Toepfer flags that three of its five spend years (2037-39) would run with no Airbus programme in development, which is the spirit of rule 5. - Nothing in my record shows me using or favouring such a lever. - The money cannot be spent inside the line while NGSA spends. - The A350 Re-engine trails plan A by $1.21B in S2, so it fails both the override rule and the Board's override review. - No override is used; the budget of one per game stays intact. 5. What discipline costs on the grid. - S1: $3.19B below row E and $1.65B below row B. - S2: $1.66B below row B. - These are costs of the binding cash test, the integrity pillar and the Board's vetoes. They are not a doctrine premium. 6. Delay Tactics are now closed for the game. fps enters service in 2040, and the next round is 2045. No move was ordered in either round, and nothing is said in public. 7. Against what I am paid to protect. - Five pillars: plan A adds nothing that tests safety, quality or integrity [AX-0073, AX-0081]. - Ramp: there is no new concurrency on the shared NGSA/A350 teams while NGSA industrialises. The A320 ring-fence holds [AX-0010, AX-0054]. - The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA is kept whole on its technology clock, entering service two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Boeing's fps on the 10-year path moves nothing (rules 1, 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225]. - Board: the defaults are what it would approve. 8. Engine code. I keep 7 on Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's. All three makers are ready by 2037, CFM backstops UltraFan NB (which has no margin), code 3 is avoided, and the code is not a veto ground. 9. Board-gate lines. There is no Board item. For the package: - five pillars: pass; - Toepfer: pass on every test, with peak $5.07B, headroom $0.13B, no break point triggered (phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief), +22.88 in the worst column, and returns fundable at the lower end of the policy with no equity raise; - Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and NGSA readiness; supply crunch not applicable; - grid: +23.37 / +22.88. 10. What I take to the Board outside the orders. - Toepfer's flag that the per-share dividend in 2035-36 depends on FCF of about $5.9B or more. The payout is set each year inside the 30-50% policy on actual FCF. - Wagner's watch item on P&W new-build engines for the A320neo. - The 2045 staged case for the A350 Re-engine, which now needs a widebody engine ready by its entry into service as well as the A350F and Spirit confirmation.

Weighing the CFO. Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence), and his numbers match the brief's grid and the Board's figures. Passed: - plan A on peak cash: $5.07B against $5.2B, 97% of the line, $0.13B of headroom; - the round-1 cash gate: no break point triggered, with phasing and the euro rate honestly marked as not observable from the brief; - net cash and returns: the 30-50% payout is fundable at its lower end in both cases, and no equity raise is needed; - robustness: +22.88 in S2; - Board items: none; - rule 6 for plans D and E: two years of overlap, at the limit. Failed, all binding: - plan B on peak cash ($5.27B; a soft veto); - plan D on peak cash ($6.67B) and robustness (-1.21 in S2); - plan E on peak cash ($6.87B) and robustness (-1.22 in S2); - plan C on a red line and a pillar; - bottleneck on a pillar; - plan F on a red line. I accepted every veto. The B override was arithmetically open (+1.65 / +1.66), but I declined it: the Board's own line vetoes it, I have no override against the Board, and I do not set aside the stricter team condition. The D and E overrides fail the $1B rule in S2. I took up his flag that the 2035-36 per-share dividend needs FCF of about $5.9B. It goes to the Board as a choice inside the payout policy. I also adopted his 2045 A350 preview gates.

Weighing the operating head. Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence). His report rests on the brief, which reports no safety, quality, ramp or supply issue. Passed: - safety and quality, on every plan; - the A320 ramp shield; - NGSA readiness for 2037 and rule 1; - engineering capacity for a 2035 A350 Re-engine, at the limit (two years of overlap and $1.2B of strain). A one-year NGSA slip would make it three years and $1.8B; - A350F and Spirit absorption, on the game proxy only; - poaching, on his own tests (cash and the stricter condition he leaves to Toepfer and to me); - the integrity limits on our other moves. Supply crunch: not applicable. Failed, all binding: - both moves (rule 4 and integrity); - bottleneck (integrity); - cancel (rule 7). These are pillar and red-line results. I accept them; neither I nor the Board overrides them. He vetoes nothing else but recommends hold on the A350 Re-engine, because capacity sits at the limit and no widebody engine is on the record (an UltraFan WB launched in 2035 is ready only in 2041). I accepted that. I also took his engine-code recommendation (keep 7), his post-EIS supply priorities (engines, wing, titanium, rare earths, sized to our own needs), his P&W GTF watch item in the quarterly ramp report, and his request that the NGSA readiness and A320 ramp reports go to the Board's safety review together.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1: rivals hold. Boeing says it is "not starting a second development alongside this one" and is not changing 737 rates, so I put a 787 Re-engine this round at about 20%. S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) is the worst plausible column, and the case shows it: plan A stays at +22.88 there.

Best grid plan in that scenario. NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine + one Delay Tactics move (row E): +26.56 in S1 and +23.32 in S2. It fails Toepfer's peak-cash test ($6.87B in 2035-36), and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2. The Board vetoes both added items. The best row that every test and the Board pass is plan A: NGSA hold + A350 hold, +23.37 in S1 and +22.88 in S2. That is $3.19B below row E in S1. Row B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails the cash line and the Board's veto.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. No doctrine premium is paid. Plan A is the only option that passes Toepfer's and Wagner's tests together, and the Board would approve it. The $3.19B gap to row E in S1 and the $1.65-1.66B gap to row B are the price of binding tests: the $5.2B cash line, robustness in S2, integrity, and the Board's would-veto list. They are not a premium I chose to pay under the $3B allowance. No PV is traded for the briefing objective.

  • Read Boeing only from the bulletin; S1 is likely, but the case must show S2; the briefing objective is not a Board test and no value or integrity is traded for it. Taken up.   • Public statement: lead with the five pillars, windows not dates, no internal targets, NGSA not linked to Boeing's timing, never mention Delay Tactics; the Board vets the final text. Taken up. The statement leads with the five pillars and says "the second half of the 2030s". It gives no internal targets, no reference to Boeing and no mention of Delay Tactics. It is submitted for the Board's vetting [AX-0004, AX-0005].

Objective. Briefing goal "Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family", scored by the GM and never part of the payoff. - Protect the A320 family: met. Narrowbody share is 60% in every year before NGSA enters service. - Defend the 60/40 edge: not met. Share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050, on the long-run 47/53 split after fps enters service. No order on this round's menu restores it: - a Delay Tactics move acts only in 2040-44, when we are already above 60%, and leaves 2045 and 2050 unchanged; - the A350 Re-engine has no narrowbody effect. I trade no PV for it and size no premium. We defend the edge with our own NGSA ramp and the A320 family, not with programme moves against Boeing.

Predictions. Boeing: - About 80% that it holds this round: no 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase, with fps kept at entry into service in 2040 on CFM. About 20% that it launches a 787 Re-engine (S2), which would close our A350 Re-engine under rule 3. - I expect no public Boeing move aimed at NGSA, and no fps re-timing announced this round. Engines: - CFM ducted and P&W GTF2 ready in 2036 as stated. - UltraFan NB ready in 2037 with no margin. I put a slip at about 25%; if it slips, RR is dropped and NGSA enters service in 2037 on CFM + PW. - No RR-P&W Joint Venture formed this round. - The CFM-Embraer partnership continues toward 2037, with no new effect on our grid. Our board path if nobody moves: - narrowbody share 61% in 2037, 63% in 2039, 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% from 2049; - ΔPV +23.37 in S1 and +22.88 in S2. The 2045 round: the A350 Re-engine comes back as a staged case only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record and a widebody engine can be ready by its entry into service.

Expected ΔPV. +23.27 $B (board after the round: +23.37 $B)

Other moves.

  • NGSA engine selection confirmed: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7 unchanged) (public): We confirm three engine makers on the next single-aisle for customer choice and supply certainty. Internal basis (Wagner): CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, and UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. A late maker is dropped without moving entry into service, and CFM backstops. Code 7 forms no barred pair. The code does not change our payoff [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].
  • Secure supply for the NGSA ramp after entry into service (public): Long-term agreements in Wagner's order of priority: (1) engine rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop; (2) the rate-capable wing work packages; (3) titanium forgings; (4) rare earths. All are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and never over-contracted to deny anyone capacity. The ECSC reviews them this year. Presented in public as a more sovereign European supply chain [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0441, A-0457].
  • A320 ring-fence and quarterly ramp report, with a P&W new-build watch item (private): A320 line staff and supplier slots stay protected from NGSA industrialisation. The quarterly ramp report now tracks P&W new-build engine deliveries, because P&W gives its GTF fleet first call on parts and shops; CFM is the second source on the A320neo. A shortfall goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line [AX-0010, AX-0054, A-0366].
  • NGSA readiness report to the Board's twice-yearly safety review (private): Wagner's readiness report goes to the safety review together with the A320 ramp report. It covers technologies, the production system, the rate-capable wing, certification ahead of rate and the engine gates, with UltraFan NB carrying no margin. Entry into service comes only on maturity. If an engine slips, we drop the maker and re-test readiness; we never cancel [AX-0015, A-0225, A-0441].
  • Audit Committee cash gate, 2035-37 (private): The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) takes Toepfer's schedule: NGSA at $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 against the $5.2B line, and nil from 2037. The round-1 break points stand: an overrun above $0.88B, a peak year more than 2.5% above the average, a euro below about $1.07, or any Delay Tactics spend. Annual phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief, so they are to be reported from actuals. The only remedy is re-phasing inside NGSA, never acceleration and never to make room for another item [AX-0104, AX-0022, AX-0107].
  • Capital allocation inside the policy (private): The payout is set each year within the 30-50% policy on actual FCF, with no equity raise and state support kept outside the case as upside. Toepfer's flag goes to the Board: holding the per-share dividend in 2035-36 needs FCF of about $5.9B or more. On a 30% payout, net cash stays positive in both his cases. The per-share level is the Board's choice each year. Net cash turns back up once NGSA cash stops in 2037 [AX-0102, AX-0001, AG-0058, AG-0059].
  • Open European engineering recruitment continues (public): Ordinary public hiring for the Airbus of the 2030s, sized for NGSA industrialisation and entry into service. It never draws on A320 ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year. It is not a Delay Tactics move [A-0366, A-0485].
  • A350 Re-engine kept in reserve: staged widebody case for the 2045 round (private): No launch while NGSA spends. Gates for 2045: (1) rule 3, meaning no 787 Re-engine on the record (if S2 happens this round, the case is closed); (2) Wagner confirms the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate; (3) a widebody engine on the record that is ready by the entry-into-service year (an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051); (4) the grid row in the rivals-hold and 787 Re-engine columns, with the added move worth at least $1B in the expected column and not negative in the 787 column; (5) peak cash, with no overlap and $1.0B a year; (6) a Board item on a Qualified Majority [AX-0082, AX-0019, A-0343, AG-0049].
  • Zero-for-zero trade advocacy (public): We continue to press for a tariff-free regime for civil aerospace through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic [AX-0088].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and readiness first. The Ducted's 2036 ready year and Embraer's 2037 date must be confirmed on test evidence (turned on and turned off), not on analysis. The margin to the NGSA's 2037 entry is one year. Any safety or durability flag goes to a cross-functional review with Safran's engineers and comes to us before orders. If a date has to move, it moves. A slip is never answered by trading away durability margin or by a cancel [CG-0009, CG-0018, CX-0009, CX-0012, CX-0208, CX-0658].
  • Keep what we launched in 2030. Hold everything is the best grid plan in all three columns (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31). Cancelling the Ducted loses -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 against hold and writes off $3.33B ($4B x 5/6). Cancelling Embraer loses -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44. Neither passes our cancellation test in any column [CG-0017, CX-0564, CX-0609, CG-0065].
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, and launch no product into a wait. The NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040, both before a 2035 Open Fan could be ready in 2045, so the 35 pp wait penalty applies in every column. Against hold the Open Fan is -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09, and with Lobby -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99, against an $8B ($9B) bill. 2035 is the last launch round that could be ready by 2050. The 'Introduce the Open Fan' objective is therefore given up on the dashboard, and the record should say so plainly. RISE is never cancelled for cost [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0147, CX-0174, CX-0398, CG-0065].
  • Keep the balance sheet and the payout whole. No new R&D or strain is needed this round. The round-1 package commits about $1.0B a year to 2036, against about $2.5B of room after returning at least 70% of roughly $8.5B of free cash flow. Premium $0 this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game, and the RISE allowance unused [CX-0645, CG-0063, CG-0022, CG-0002, CG-0064, CG-0012].
  • Serve the customer, and Safran with it. Airbus revisits its NGSA code in 2035 against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance. Our lever is off the grid: on-time LEAP deliveries and spares, a test-gated 2036 Ducted, and a CFM engine offered to every airframer on standard terms. Any price or terms are agreed jointly with Safran [CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0613, CX-0529, CX-0184, CG-0013].

Expects to see. (1) Your expected_scenario (S1, S2 or S3) and column weights in predictions, reasoned from the bulletin. Nothing in the bulletin rules out any column, so we treat all three as plausible. Hold everything is best in each (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31; -56.00 on equal weights), so the weights should change the expected PV booked, not the decision. Book it low, as in round 1. (2) The grid rows for every alternative against hold, column by column. For any Board item: the submitted row, the row with that item at its default, and the expected and worst columns named. Our reading: Ducted cancel -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65; Embraer cancel -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (0.00 beside a Ducted cancel, since it needs a CFM engine); Open Fan -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09; Open Fan + Lobby -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99; Lobby beside an Open Fan +20.26 / +20.25 / +4.10. (3) Ali's report on readiness and safety. The Ducted's 2036 and Embraer's 2037 confirmed on test evidence against the NGSA's 2037 and fps's 2040 entry, with any safety or durability flag and its cross-functional resolution. No Open Fan date before 2045. (4) Ghai's numbers. New R&D and strain this round, which should be $0. The round-1 run-rate of about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room after a payout of at least 70%. Any rating effect, only if his memo shows one. (5) The Safran gate for any ducted, Open Fan, Embraer partnership or emissions lobbying order, and for any cancel a stated reason why Safran would agree. RISE continuation is presented as a 50-50 decision. (6) objective_note. 'Dominate NB engines' is met in S1 (worst year 55.9%). On our reading of the public rules (inference; the brief gives no share path by column), CFM's NB share in 2040 is about 36% in S2 and about 20% in S3, and no order on this menu restores it. 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard, because 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050. Meeting it would cost $35.99B to $57.60B, far above the $2.0B round cap and the $15B RISE allowance. (7) premium in dollars. We expect $0, with any RISE allowance stated separately in premium_reason; we expect none, and the allowance stays unused. (8) Risks outside the columns, named in predictions: a P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment (CFM -10 pp; RR said it would revisit in 2035), and the GTF2 and UltraFan NB ready dates (2036, 2037) that Airbus will weigh. (9) board_response to our round-1 review recommendations: the 2036 test gate, supplier readiness, Embraer presented as a CFM decision with Safran, and 2036 kept as a floor. (10) A public statement that names no rival, blames no one, gives no Open Fan date, has no CFM price talk without Safran, and does not call the Ducted the next generation.

Would approve.

  • hold on every field (ducted, Open Fan, Embraer partnership, emissions lobbying, genx). This is the best grid plan in all three columns (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31), with a premium of $0. A hold is not a Board item and is never vetoed.
  • No Board item on this round's menu passes our tests. Every cancel loses value in every column, and every Open Fan or Lobby order waits on an airframe and loses more than its bill. We say so now so the package is not built around one.
  • Unpriced other_moves that serve the customer: on-time LEAP and spares delivery on the A320neo and 737, supplier readiness on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, and a CFM engine offered privately to every airframer on standard terms. RISE continues 50-50 as technology with no product date. Any price or terms are agreed jointly with Safran. These are recommendations, not Board items.

Would veto.

  • ducted engine: cancel. Item value against hold is -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 (S1-S3), and -13.50 / -8.72 / -2.67 beside an Open Fan. It fails the cancellation test, which needs at least zero in every plausible column, and it writes off $3.33B. CFM parity rule (Safran consent): this cancels the new CFM engine offered to an fps that has selected CFM, a move Safran has never been seen to make. No reason why Safran would agree is on the record. Acceptable: hold.
  • Embraer partnership: cancel. Item value against hold is -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44, and -5.56 / -5.94 / -1.35 beside an Open Fan. It fails the cancellation test. CFM parity rule: withdrawing from a third airframer runs against serving every airframer. It is 0.00 beside a Ducted cancel only because Embraer counts nothing without a CFM engine, so we would veto the two together. Acceptable: hold.
  • Open Fan: launch. Item value against hold is -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09 against an $8B bill, so the downside is unbounded in every column. The airframer-path test fails: the NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) enter service before a 2045 Open Fan, and our horizon allows no exception. The cost against the best non-RISE plan (hold) is $40.09B to $57.60B, or $35.99B to $37.35B with Lobby, above the $15B RISE allowance and the $2.0B premium cap. This is not a RISE cancel: holding keeps RISE whole as technology. Acceptable: hold.
  • emissions lobbying: launch. It passes only with a live Open Fan, and on its own it does nothing (-$1B). Beside a vetoed Open Fan it falls with it, even though it would add +20.26 / +20.25 / +4.10 to that Open Fan, because the pair is still -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99 against hold. Acceptable: hold.
  • Any premium above $2.0B this round less a declared RISE allowance, and any use of the RISE allowance outside the airframer-path test. On this grid every RISE route waits in every column, so the allowance cannot be used this round.

Recommendations.

  • Safety and readiness. Have Ali report the Ducted's 2036 gate and Embraer's 2037 date on test evidence, with gate calls made cross-functionally alongside Safran's engineers. The margin to the NGSA's 2037 entry is one year. If durability needs more time, bring us the flag and move the date. On the grid a late Ducted still earns from its ready year, whereas a cancel loses $15-18B and a traded durability margin is never acceptable.
  • Keep what we launched. Hold the Ducted and Embraer, and show each cancel against hold in all three columns: Ducted -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 with a $3.33B write-off, Embraer -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44. The Ducted is the defence we bought in 2030, and fps has selected CFM. A cancel would also need a stated reason why Safran would agree.
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, and hold the Open Fan and Lobby. Say plainly in objective_note that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard. Every new narrowbody on the record enters service before 2045, and a launch after 2035 cannot be ready by 2050. Meeting the objective would cost $35.99B to $57.60B. We will not stretch the airframer-path test, the RISE allowance stays unused, and RISE is never cancelled for cost.
  • The customer comes first in the code revisit. Airbus will judge its NGSA code in 2035 on published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance. Put the effort where we control it: on-time LEAP and spares, finishing the supplier work, and a test-gated 2036 Ducted. Offer every airframer a CFM engine on standard terms in private talks. Any price or terms are agreed jointly with Safran. This is not priced on the board, and nothing is ordered only because a rival moved.
  • Weights and risks. Treat S1-S3 as plausible and give weights in predictions. Hold is best in each column, so book expected PV low (-56.00 on equal weights). Name the risks no column carries: a P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment (CFM -10 pp), and the 50% share line. On our reading of the rules (inference) that line falls to about 36% in S2 and about 20% in S3 in 2040, whatever we order this round.
  • Keep the payout whole. State that this round commits no new R&D or strain, that the round-1 package runs about $1.0B a year to 2036 against about $2.5B of room after returning at least 70% of free cash flow, and that premium is $0 ($0 of $4.0B for the game).
  • Public statement: name no rival, blame no one, give no Open Fan or RISE date, and no CFM price talk without Safran. Keep 2036 as a test-gated floor, never call the Ducted the next generation, and present Embraer as a CFM decision taken with Safran. RISE goes into product when airframers and airlines want it.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] In 2030 the game was getting a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That part is done. Both airframes launched. fps selected us and enters service in 2040. NGSA selected all three engine makers and enters service in 2037. Our Ducted is due in 2036 and Embraer in 2037. The game now is the installed base on airframes that are already launched [CX-0422]. We play it on delivery, not on new launches. Each airframer can still change its code until its airframe enters service. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. Nothing on our menu wins a slot: hold is the best grid plan in every column (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31). We win by keeping what we launched and being on time with LEAP engines and spares. The 2036 Ducted has to be proven on test, not on slides, and every airframer gets a CFM engine on standard terms, priced together with Safran. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." [CX-0564] That still holds until 2040. We earn the order by delivering, not by spending. The one hard call is to say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard. We do that without touching RISE as technology. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2035. - fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on a 10-year ramp, entry 2040, code 3 (CFM alone). - NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, entry 2037, code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR). - P&W GTF2: launched solo, ready 2036. RR UltraFan NB: launched solo, ready 2037. Both are fitted on NGSA. - Ours: Ducted ready 2036; Embraer partnership ready (counts) 2037; GEnx upgrade in service since 2033, counting from 2042 (no re-engine on the record). - No Joint Venture commitment is on the record. P&W says it has made none. RR is 'open' and said it would revisit in 2035 only if P&W's commitment were on the record. It is not. - Airbus revisits its NGSA code in 2035, judged on published ready dates, CFM's choice between Ducted and Open Fan, fps's code, and A320 engine delivery performance. Its stated aim is 'CFM and at least one other maker'. - Observed shares from 2026 to 2034 were flat: NB engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; WB engines GEnx 42 / Trent 58. WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T [CX-0436]. Last round I called S2: NGSA alone, on CFM plus P&W. The market gave us both airframes and three engines on NGSA. Our ΔPV moved from 0.00 to -31.20 (yield 80.5%). Of that, -25.20 is engine value, mostly NGSA's slot split three ways, and the rest is the round-1 R&D ($4B) and strain ($2B). That is the market, not our orders. THE H3 TRIGGER IS NOW ON THE PUBLIC RECORD. Two rival new NB engines are launched and selected on NGSA. The Ducted is a defence by the book, and it earns in the record column: cancelling it costs $15.30B in S1. OBJECTIVE. 'Dominate NB engines' (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is met in S1, worst year 2040 at 55.9%. My reading of the public rules (inference; my arithmetic reproduces the brief's S1 path of 56.5 / 55.2 / 55.9) puts CFM at about 36% in 2040 in S2 and about 20% in S3. No order on this menu restores it. 'Introduce the Open Fan' (launched and ready by 2050) is not met. 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050, and every route waits on an airframe. COLUMNS. - S1: rivals hold. This is the record. - S2: NGSA moves to code 2 (P&W alone), and Airbus's slot leaves CFM. It costs $27.30B against S1. - S3: fps moves to code 1 (RR alone), and Boeing's slot leaves CFM from 2040. It costs $47.11B against S1. In both S2 and S3 a rival selection takes our slot, and no lever we hold answers it. Read them hard: no birthright [CX-0564]. THE GRID. Hold everything is the best plan in all three columns. Every alternative loses in every column. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision). It WOULD VETO: - ducted engine: cancel (-15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 against hold; writes off $3.33B; no reason on the record why Safran would agree). - Embraer partnership: cancel (-3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44; vetoed together with a Ducted cancel). - Open Fan: launch (-57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09; waits on the NGSA's 2037 and fps's 2040 entry; the cost to meet the objective, $35.99B to $57.60B, is above the $15B RISE allowance and the $2.0B cap). - emissions lobbying: launch (falls with a vetoed Open Fan; does nothing alone). - Any premium above $2.0B, and any RISE allowance used outside the airframer-path test. It WOULD APPROVE hold on every field, which is not a Board item, plus unpriced customer moves: LEAP and spares on time, supplier readiness at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, a private CFM offer on standard terms, and RISE continuing 50-50 as technology. It EXPECTS: - the expected column and weights; - every alternative against hold, column by column; - Ali's report on the 2036 and 2037 dates on test evidence, with any flag; - Ghai showing $0 of new R&D and strain, and the run-rate against the room; - the Safran gate; - an objective_note that says 'Introduce' is given up; - premium $0; - the Joint Venture and rival-ready-date risks named; - answers to its round-1 recommendations (the 2036 test gate, supplier readiness, Embraer as a CFM decision with Safran, 2036 as a floor); - a clean statement.

Options to test.

  • 1. Hold everything (my lean; the default): -31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31 (S1-S3). Best grid plan in every column. Weighted -46.08 on my initial weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20) and -56.00 on equal weights. Worst column S3. Premium $0. No Board item, no new R&D, no new strain.
  • 2. Ducted cancel (the row is the same with or without an Embraer cancel): -46.50 / -75.17 / -95.96. Against hold -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65; weighted -16.04 (mine) / -16.54 (equal). It writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B, kills Embraer's +5 pp, and drops our only new NB engine one year before NGSA enters service. It fails additive-or-nothing and the Board's cancel test in every column. Tested to record why we keep it.
  • 3. Partner Embraer cancel: -34.29 / -62.95 / -83.75. Against hold -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44; weighted -3.83 / -4.33. Nothing is saved on the board, since there is no R&D to stop. It runs against H1 (serve every airframer). Tested to record.
  • 4. Open Fan alone: -88.80 / -116.10 / -118.40. Against hold -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09; weighted -54.10 / -51.76. The S1 row is the launch's own effect now that new NBs are on the record: $8B of bill plus the 35 pp wait. H2 bars it. It is the only route to 'Introduce the Open Fan', at a cost of $40.09B to $57.60B.
  • 5. Open Fan + Lobby (the cheapest route to the objective): -68.54 / -95.85 / -114.30. Against hold -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99; weighted -37.07 / -36.89. Lobby beside an Open Fan adds +20.26 / +20.25 / +4.10, but the pair is still $35.99B to $37.35B behind hold. That is above the $15B RISE allowance, the $2.0B round cap and the $4.0B game cap. Tested to put the objective premium in dollars.
  • 6. Open Fan combined with cancels: all dominated. OF + Embraer cancel -63.16 / -63.54 / -41.44 against hold; with Lobby -41.85 / -43.21 / -37.19. Ducted cancel + OF -71.10 / -66.32 / -42.76; with Lobby -50.85 / -50.85 / -38.75; with Embraer cancel -77.38 / -67.14 / -44.28; with both -56.06 / -57.42 / -40.03. Beside an Open Fan, a Ducted cancel still loses -13.50 / -8.72 / -2.67 and an Embraer cancel -5.56 / -5.94 / -1.35. Listed only so nobody builds a package around them.
  • 7. Lobby alone: not a grid row. $1B with no board effect, so about -1.00 in every column (rules; Board figure). Fails pays-for-itself.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No date is held by trading away durability margin, and safety and durability calls are made by a cross-functional team, with Safran's engineers on a CFM engine [CX-0012]. If a date has to move, it moves.
  • H1: never refuse an airframer, never lock one out. Every airframer, Embraer included, is offered a CFM engine on standard terms [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Cancelling Embraer would run against this.
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan, so there is no launch this round. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B, against a $15B cap [CX-0205, CX-0469].
  • H3: the Ducted is a defence only, never our next generation. The trigger is now on the public record: GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and selected on NGSA [CX-0564; CX-0183].
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it. RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398, CX-0166].
  • H6 (through Ali): no date without test evidence. The Ducted's 2036 is a test-gated floor, not a promise. No Open Fan date before 2045, and no RISE demo, ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0009, CX-0008].
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM NB order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby). Hold orders none. Any cancel needs a stated reason why Safran would agree. Any CFM price or terms are set jointly with Safran [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals or on any airframer's code decision [CX-0625, CX-0580].
  • H9: doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B in the game (game to date $0). One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan. Unused.
  • My 20% line: a next-generation engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn reduction [CX-0217]. It binds RISE. It does not bar the defensive Ducted, which is never offered or described as the next generation [CX-0183, CX-0180].
  • Durability is not traded for fuel burn or for schedule [CX-0208]. This applies to the Ducted's run into 2036 too.

It is not our next generation. - Embraer is a CFM decision with Safran. - RISE: all in on the technology; the entry date is 'really not for us to say'. - No rival named, no blame, no price talk. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

Real testing, not analysis. I report against last year's promise: Ducted not ready before 2036, launch plus six. That floor stands. Nothing earlier. It clears NGSA's 2037 by one year and fps's 2040 by four. If durability needs time, the date moves. It is never traded. What I can't show you: my record holds no ducted turn-on, turn-off result. What is in real testing is the base: LEAP-1A HPT hardware, turned on, turned off, certified; RISE, over 350 tests with an early durability focus; compact-core HPT blades in dust testing. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise. Say 'not before 2036', not 'on track'. Embraer counts from 2037, launch plus seven, and rides on the Ducted. Slip the Ducted past 2037 and Embraer moves with it. No safety or durability flag in the evidence. No single person can make a safety decision: gate calls stay cross-functional, with Safran's engineers. Supply: no new project, no new strain. LEAP OE and spares first. On supplier work since 2025, no evidence: following doctrine.

Larry Culp decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. DECISION: hold on every field. No Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain, premium $0. THE FRAME [CX-0467]. In 2030 the game was to get a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That is done. fps selected CFM (code 3, entry 2040). NGSA selected all three makers (code 7, entry 2037). The game now is the installed base on airframes already launched [CX-0422], and it is won on delivery, not on new launches. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564] holds until 2040. THE GRID (brief §3). I checked it myself and Ghai confirmed every figure. Hold everything is -31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31 (S1 / S2 / S3): -46.08 on my weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20) and -56.00 on equal weights. It is the best plan in every column. Each alternative against hold (S1 / S2 / S3; my weights / equal): - Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 (-16.04 / -16.54). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board ($0.67B of R&D plus the $2B strain handed back) against about $18-20B of engine value given up. - Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33). - Open Fan: -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09 (-54.10 / -51.76). In S1 that is the $8B bill plus about $49.6B of wait penalty. - Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99 (-37.07 / -36.89). - Lobby alone: about -1.00. - Every combination with cancels is dominated. Nothing on the menu is positive in any column, S1 included. Weights move the booking, not the decision. MY TESTS. - Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: no order beats hold anywhere, so nothing is ordered. - H3: the trigger is now on the record. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and fitted on NGSA, so the Ducted stands as a defence by the book, and keeping it is worth +15.30 in the record column. - H2: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan. Every route waits in every column, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B against $15B, and even the allowance plus the full $4.0B game cap is $17-19B short. - H5: RISE continues whole as technology. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel. - Strain: no new project, so no new strain. Supply load is the live risk, but it is unpriced (see Ali). - 20% and durability lines: unaffected. The Ducted is never called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded for the 2036 floor. - Tie-break: not needed, since no alternative comes within ε. LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, the selections on the record. I book low at the equal-weight -56.00 and treat S1's -31.20 as upside. Ghai agrees and would not go lower. We raise only when the next bulletin confirms the codes. SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. Keeping the Ducted and Embraer continues decisions taken jointly in 2030. No reason exists why Safran would agree to a cancel: it would cut Safran's half of the same installed base. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. Any price, terms or narrowbody capacity commitment is joint [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove three parts. My record is silent on Embraer, so I followed doctrine (profile.md §6) and kept it, since a cancel runs against H1. My record has no lobbying evidence, so Lobby follows doctrine: only beside a live Open Fan. My record is silent on a Joint Venture and on Delay Tactics, so I followed profile.md §5 and §7: no public reaction and no price cut. BIAS NAMED. My installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. Admission buys a seat, and here there is no seat to buy: both airframes are in service before 2045. My ramp optimism [CX-0590, CX-0592] is checked by publishing no Ducted rate and using the one year of board slack before 2038. WHAT CHANGES MY MIND: - A durability flag on the Ducted: the date moves; it is not cancelled. - Supply that can't carry the Ducted's entry with LEAP on time: LEAP comes first, and the Ducted's ramp moves. - A Joint Venture on the record: re-priced next round. Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444]. No veto stands. Ghai's and Ali's vetoes all fall on orders I don't make, so there are no overrides.

Weighing the CFO. Weighed in full. His record is High confidence on money and his profit calls land [CX-0910]. He reproduced every grid row and confirmed that hold is best in all three columns. I adopted his three corrections: - a Ducted cancel saves $2.67B on the board, not $0.67B (the $2B strain comes back too), with the item value unchanged at -15.30; - the worst objective year in S3 is 2050 (about 17%), not 2040 (19.7%); - the Joint Venture is a two-sided risk, about +$7B if it folds in both solos and about -$14B if it stacks on top. On the stacked reading 'Dominate' fails even in S1 (about 46% in 2040). I name it in predictions and don't book it. His volumes-first test passes on the record, so no carve-out is needed. I note his caveat that a selection is not an agreed volume: rates stay the airframers'. Capex passes: $0 new, and the standing $1.00B a year sits against $2.55B of room, leaving $1.55B of headroom with no rating effect. The premium is $0, $0 of $4.0B for the game, with the RISE allowance unused. On his advice I book -56.00 and no higher until the codes are confirmed. His binding vetoes (any cancel, any Open Fan, Lobby without an Open Fan, any price talk without Safran) all fall on orders I don't make. The statement carries no price or terms language. He concurs with hold.

Weighing the operating head. Weighed as a thin record. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, so he is Medium confidence on durability, test standard and RISE physics. On supply and capacity his record is only my own description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts against doctrine (dashboard_game.md §2 strain; LEAP OE and spares first). On dates I deferred to him fully: - The Ducted's 2036 passes as launch + 6 and nothing earlier, and Embraer's 2037 as launch + 7, riding on the Ducted. - An Open Fan could be ready no earlier than 2045, so it cannot make 2037 or 2040. - The public record carries no RISE demo or test date. I took his wording advice: 'not before 2036, reported against that gate on test', not 'on track', because he holds no ducted turn-on, turn-off result. The statement uses it. He raises no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, the LEAP fleet or RISE hardware, and gate calls stay cross-functional with Safran's engineers [CX-0012]. I adopted his slip arithmetic as his inference: a slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board, and a slip to 2038 costs about $1.2B PV, against $15-18B for a cancel. His raw-materials flag (titanium forgings, rare earths) is unpriced and unquantified, and I carry it into the supplier-readiness move. His track record on demonstration dates, which ran about a year late [CX-0151, CX-0211], is why we publish no Ducted ramp rate. He concurs with hold, and no date in the statement fails his test.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold): the selections on the public record, fps on CFM (code 3) and NGSA on all three (code 7). It is the backlog we hold, not a hoped-for selection [CX-0248]. Airbus's stated aim of 'CFM and at least one other maker' argues against S2 (P&W alone). Boeing's selection of CFM and the 737's CFM-only history [CX-0632] argue against S3 (RR alone). Codes can still move until entry and we have no birthright [CX-0564], so 40% of my weight sits on the two switch columns. I book on equal weights to stay low.

Best grid plan in that scenario. Hold everything: -31.20 in S1 (yield 80.5%). It is also the best plan in S2 (-58.50) and S3 (-78.31), so it is the best plan on any weights: -46.08 on mine and -56.00 on equal weights. My submitted plan is this plan.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. $0.00 this round and $0.00 of the $4.0B game cap. RISE allowance: $0 of $15B, unused. The submitted plan (hold everything) is the best grid plan in every column, so no doctrine or objective premium arises. The objective premium I decline to pay, in dollars, for 'Introduce the Open Fan' against the best non-RISE plan (hold): - Cheapest route, Open Fan + Lobby: $37.34B / $37.35B / $35.99B (S1 / S2 / S3), or $37.07B on my weights and $36.89B on equal weights. - Open Fan alone: $57.60B / $57.60B / $40.09B. Either is far above the $2.0B round cap and the $15B RISE allowance, and still $17-19B short even with the allowance and the whole game cap combined. The RISE allowance also fails the airframer-path test, because every route waits on an airframe in every column. 'Dominate NB' raises no premium question. It is met in S1, and no order on the menu restores it in S2 or S3.

Objective. PD-briefing objective: Dominate narrowbody engines; introduce the Open Fan. It never changes the payoff. (1) Dominate NB engines (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is MET in S1. My shares there are 55.9% (2040), 59.0% (2045) and 61.6% (2050), worst year 2040. Ghai's reading of the public rules (inference) gives: - S2: about 36.2% (2040), 41.0% (2045) and 44.8% (2050), so not met, worst year 2040; - S3: about 19.7% (2040), 18.1% (2045) and 16.8% (2050), so not met, worst year 2050. No order on this menu restores 50% in S2 or S3. A Joint Venture that stacked on top of the solos could take S1 to about 46% in 2040 (Ghai, inference). It is named as a risk, with no lever on this board. (2) Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050) is GIVEN UP ON THE DASHBOARD. 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050 (launch + 10, not before 2045). NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service first, so every route waits in every column (H2). Meeting it would cost $35.99B to $57.60B, above every cap. RISE is not given up: it continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214]. It goes into product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].

Predictions. COLUMN WEIGHTS: S1 0.60, S2 0.20, S3 0.20. Hold is -46.08 on these weights and -56.00 on equal weights. I book -56.00. S1 (rivals hold), 0.60. The record carries the selections. Airbus's stated aim is CFM plus at least one other maker, and Boeing picked CFM. I expect P&W and RR to keep their solos on their published dates (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037). S2 (NGSA to P&W alone), 0.20. It contradicts Airbus's stated aim of CFM plus at least one other, but Airbus weighs A320 engine delivery performance in its revisit, and we don't control its read. It costs $27.30B against S1. S3 (fps to RR alone), 0.20. Boeing gave no signal of a switch, but a code is a request until entry, and RR would be ready by 2040. It costs $47.11B against S1. It is the worst column. RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMNS (named, not booked): (a) A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment. P&W says it has made none. RR said it would revisit in 2035 only if P&W's commitment were on the record. Both would need to commit in the same sealed round, so I put it at about 15-20% this round. On Ghai's reading it is worth +$7B to CFM if it folds in both solos on their dates, and -$14B if it stacks on top. On the stacked reading 'Dominate' fails even in S1 (about 46% in 2040). (b) Rival ready dates slipping past NGSA's 2037 entry. That maker would be dropped and CFM would carry more of the slot. Upside I don't book. (c) Our own Ducted slipping. A slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board; a slip to 2038 costs about $1.2B PV (Ali, inference). Embraer moves with it. (d) Delay Tactics on the fps: Boeing -5 pp for 5 years from 2040, which cuts our fps slot in S1. It is covert, so we would see it only at game end. No reaction (doctrine). (e) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths for the Ducted's ramp. Unpriced and unquantified (Ali's flag). (f) Codes lock after this round. The next bulletin tells us our column, and I raise the booking only then.

Other moves.

  • LEAP delivery first: OE engines and spares on time on the A320neo and 737 (public): Today, tomorrow, the future, in that order [CX-0552]. LEAP OE and spares are the operating lever nearest Airbus's code revisit, which weighs A320 engine delivery performance. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529, CX-0542]. No rate, unit or growth number is published: my own LEAP ramp calls ran hot in 2023-24 [CX-0590, CX-0592], so we guide low and raise. Unpriced; not on the board.
  • Ducted gate reported on test: not before 2036 (public): The Ducted is held at 'not before 2036' (launch + 6), and we report against that gate each round on core and hot-section results that have been turned on and turned off in test, not on analysis [CX-0009, CX-0008]. Gate calls on ready year, durability and safety-critical parts are made by one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on this CFM engine [CX-0012, CX-0633]. Any safety or durability flag reaches the Board before the next round's orders. If durability needs more time, the date moves; it is never traded and never answered with a cancel [CX-0208]. Embraer rides on the Ducted, so a Ducted slip past 2037 moves Embraer with it. No ramp rate is published. Never described as the next generation [CX-0183].
  • Supplier readiness at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites before the Ducted's 2036-37 production load (private): Run by Ali's supply, engineering and quality team [CX-0633] at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites where 80% of our 2024 shortages sat [CX-0613]. The priority order is fixed: LEAP OE and spares first. If the base can't carry the Ducted's entry alongside LEAP and the durability-kit shop-visit flow, the Ducted's ramp moves, not LEAP. We use the one year of board slack before 2038 rather than publish a rate. The work includes a review of our exposure on titanium forgings and rare earths, which Ali flags as an unpriced, unquantified risk while an airframer locks up the same materials for its own programme. Any capacity commitment on CFM narrowbody work is taken jointly with Safran. Unpriced.
  • Private CFM offer to every airframer on standard terms, with Safran (private): Every airframer, Embraer included, is offered a CFM engine. Nobody is locked out and nobody is refused [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Any price or terms are set jointly with Safran [CX-0184]: no launch-era pricing, no concession, and nothing ordered or offered only because a rival moved [CX-0609]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Unpriced.
  • RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran (public): Ground and component testing continues, funded as technology with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades while it matures [CX-0162]. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given (Ali's date ground). RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5).
  • No reaction to rival or Joint Venture news (private): If a P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment, a rival ready-date change or a Delay Tactics effect on the fps comes onto the record, we make no public comment and no price cut, and we re-price it inside the columns at the next round (company doctrine, profile.md §5 and §7; my record is silent on both) [CX-0580, CX-0600, CX-0609]. Unpriced.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • 1. Protect the live GTF2 that NGSA has selected. GTF2 (launched 2030) is ready in 2036. NGSA (code 7: RR, PW and CFM; EIS 2037) is live and has not yet entered service. That selection is what meets the credibility objective today. This is also the last round in which a cancel is possible, because GTF2 is ready before 2045. On the grid, GTF2 Solo: cancel reads -29.42 in every column. Against hold that is -20.98 (S1), +0.34 (S2), -32.79 (S3) and -20.98 (S4). Break-even needs P(S2) of about 0.98. The Board expects GTF2 Solo: hold [P-1347, P-1342, P-1191, P-0746].
  • 2. Durability and readiness before NGSA's entry into service. The margin is one year: ready 2036 against EIS 2037. Time on wing and full-life parts must be proven before entry into service, with no compression and no late engine presented as on time. The GTF fleet keeps first call on parts and shops. Any Joint Venture must carry GTF2's schedule, not reset or squeeze it [P-1360, P-1214, P-1215, PG-0050].
  • 3. The Joint Venture trigger is now met on the public record. NGSA is live, not yet in service, and its code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. Joint Venture with RR: commit reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 against hold, so it is never below Do Nothing. It adds no new R&D while GTF2 is live, because GTF2's spend folds in. Its engine (the folded GTF2, 2036) is ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS. The Board would approve it on aligned terms that share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233, P-1875, PG-0047, P-1563].
  • 4. The dividend first, then debt on its pre-ASR path. GTF2's remaining spend (about $0.33B a year to 2036) sits inside the roughly $6B self-funded envelope, and a commit adds nothing. No stretch is needed; the Board's once-in-the-game stretch stays in reserve. premium should be 0 [P-0566, P-0686, PX-0353, P-0499, PX-0268].
  • 5. Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV >= 0) is not met, at -8.44. Only S3 (Boeing moves fps to code 7: +3.37) meets it, and that is Boeing's choice. Win selections with product and time on wing, on standard terms. A rival's discount never moves the answer, and the public statement must support Airbus's 2035 code review without overclaiming [P-0731, P-1165, PG-0017, PG-0039].
