Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: hold. This is not a Board item, and it is the Board's preferred order. It keeps P&W on NGSA (code 7, ready 2036 against EIS 2037), which keeps the credibility objective met. It also keeps P&W eligible for fps (EIS 2040) if Boeing moves to code 7 (S3, +3.37), the only column where Capitalise is met.
  • Joint Venture with RR: commit beside GTF2 Solo: hold, on any weights. The Joint Venture test passes: NGSA is live and not yet in service, and its code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. Its item value against hold is 0 (S1) / 0 (S2) / 0 (S3) / +5.51 (S4), so its weighted value is 5.51 x P(S4) >= 0 and Return hurdle passes with premium 0. Bounded downside passes: the worst column against hold is 0.00. Proof before commitment passes: its S4 value is its own condition, since the Joint Venture forms only when both partners are committed, and is not booked upside. Durability first passes: the folded GTF2 is ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS, rather than formation + 6 = 2041. Dividend and envelope passes: GTF2's spend folds in, with no new R&D. The approval holds on these conditions: - no unresolved veto from Mitchill (grounds 3 and 4) or Eddy; - the gear and core red-line flag is struck or rebutted; - the terms share risk and investment, with P&W keeping the gear and core as its own module; - the statement books no Rolls-Royce commitment.
  • If a cancel were somehow paired with a commit, the commit would read +24.82 in S4 against cancel alone. The Board would still veto the cancel (see would_veto), and the commit would stand beside hold.
  • Expected PV of hold + commit = the hold row + 5.51 x P(S4). On any weights this is at least the hold row's expected PV, so no premium is needed.

Would veto.

  • GTF2 Solo: cancel, on two grounds. - Premature exit: NGSA (EIS 2037) is live, not yet in service, and has code 7, which includes P&W, and GTF2 can be ready by 2036. The cancel must therefore beat hold in every plausible column. It is behind hold by -20.98 in S1, -32.79 in S3, and -20.98 in S4 (-1.67 beside a commit), and ahead only in S2 (+0.34). - Return hurdle: it is negative unless P(S2) >= 0.98 (0.83 with all other weight in S4 beside a commit). It would also turn the credibility objective from met to not met, and it books a $1.67B write-off to save $0.33B. Acceptable alternative: GTF2 Solo: hold.
  • Joint Venture with RR: commit if any of the following holds: - it carries an unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, any entry in overrides, or a Joint Venture red-line flag (gear and core) that the CEO neither struck nor rebutted; - its terms hand P&W's gear or core technology to the Joint Venture or to Rolls-Royce, or are aggressive (subsidising UltraFan, launch-style discounts); - it adds new R&D beyond GTF2's folded spend without Mitchill showing the envelope and dividend whole; - its case or the statement books Rolls-Royce's commitment, partner money or a Joint Venture selection that is not on the public record; - Eddy fails durability because the fold would compress or reset GTF2, or the Joint Venture engine would not be ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS. Acceptable alternative: Joint Venture with RR: hold.
  • Any Board item that carries a declared premium above $0.5B, an undeclared premium, or a premium outside the objective, or that strains the dividend.

Recommendations.

  • Keep GTF2 Solo: hold through to the 2036 ready year, and write the cancel test into the rationale. - Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 / +0.34 / -32.79 / -20.98. - Write-off: $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, to save $0.33B. - Break-even P(S2): about 0.98. This is the last round a cancel can be taken; after 2036 GTF2 is ready and the S2 risk can no longer be hedged, at a cost of only $0.34B in that column. This is the annual programme NPV review the Board kept in 2017, applied to GTF2. The Board does not cut a programme a customer has asked for.
  • Take the Joint Venture to the ExCo gate this round. Its public trigger is now met (NGSA code 7 includes Rolls-Royce), and Joint Venture with RR: commit is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51). It adds no R&D while GTF2 is live. It also puts P&W's commitment on the public record, which is Rolls-Royce's own stated condition for revisiting. Both partners now have a new narrowbody engine on the same airframe (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037), the alignment whose absence ended IAE. This is a recommendation; the decision is Eddy's proposal, Mitchill's gate and Calio's call.
  • Joint Venture terms. Share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms; partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge, and that is the model. P&W keeps the gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. Calio's rationale should address the red line, given that GTF2 folds in. Mitchill should test the terms on ground 3. If a Joint Venture design ever needs the gear or core handed over, Eddy's proposal to withdraw stands, and the Board would veto the commit.
  • Write a 2045 withdraw test into the plan. The commitment stands until withdrawn. By 2045, NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) will be in service, and the Board books no Rolls-Royce commitment it has not seen. If Rolls-Royce has not committed by then, test Joint Venture with RR: withdraw against hold on the 2045 grid. 'P&W and RR then hold equal NB shares' can cut either way once both engines are fitted.
  • Durability and readiness. Eddy should report GTF2's progress toward 2036 on test, not on slides: severe-environment testing, full life for life-limited parts, and time on wing. He should state plainly and at once if the one-year margin to NGSA's 2037 EIS is at risk. The fleet keeps first call on parts and shops. A Joint Venture must carry GTF2's schedule and must not compress or restart it.
  • Disclosure. Airbus revisits its NGSA code this round against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance, so the statement matters, and it must not overclaim. - Report GTF2 as in development and ready in 2036, six years from launch, with time on wing and full-life parts as standards to be proven before entry into service, not as proven claims. - Offer GTF2 to any airframer on standard terms, with no discounts. - Say nothing on Boeing's or Airbus's dates, rates or codes. - If P&W commits, state it as P&W's own standing commitment, sharing risk and never the gear or core. - Book no Rolls-Royce commitment, and give no Joint Venture engine date beyond GTF2's own 2036, so that Eddy's dating rule is respected. This also takes up the round-1 recommendation to promise no more than the orders do.
  • Return, dividend and envelope. - Show expected PV against Do Nothing and against a buyback. - Keep premium at 0; none is needed, because the commit weakly dominates hold. - Mitchill should confirm that GTF2's remaining spend to 2036 sits inside the roughly $6B envelope, that the commit adds nothing, that the dividend is covered and that debt is on its pre-ASR path. - The Board's one envelope stretch stays in reserve.

Chris Calio frames the round

Question. Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Airbus has named us on NGSA (code 7, alongside Rolls-Royce and CFM). So GTF2 launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, one year before NGSA's planned 2037 entry into service. Two things make this round final. It is the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service. It is also the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled. What we do not control: Airbus's code review (S2), Boeing's fps code (S3), and whether Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture (S4). What we do control gives three questions for 2035: 1. GTF2 Solo: do we hold the selected GTF2 through to its 2036 ready year, or cancel it, writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B? 2. Joint Venture with RR: the public trigger is now met, because a live code includes Rolls-Royce. Do we put a standing Joint Venture commitment on the record? The terms would share risk and investment, never the gear or core [P-1233], and GTF2 would fold in and keep its own schedule. 3. Disclosure: Airbus is reviewing its code against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance. What do we say, without claiming durability we have not yet proven on test? Each order must pass the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035], then Neil's gate, then the Board.

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2035 (bulletin) - Airframes: - NGSA (Airbus) launched in 2030. EIS 2037, code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). - fps (Boeing) launched in 2030 on the 10-year path. EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM). - Both are live and not yet in service. Both enter service before 2045, so neither can change its code after this round. - Engines: - P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036. - RR UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030, ready 2037. - CFM ducted engine: launched 2030, ready 2036. - CFM-Embraer partnership: ready 2037. - GEnx upgrade: in service since 2033. - Fitted if nothing changes: NGSA gets CFM + PW + RR; fps gets CFM. - Rolls-Royce: - No Joint Venture with P&W commitment on the record. - Its stance: 'open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms', 'not committing today', revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the public record. - Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so Rolls-Royce decides this round without seeing ours. A commitment from us would be public from the next bulletin. - Airbus is revisiting its NGSA code this round. Its criteria: - published ready dates (GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine) against the NGSA entry year; - CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan; - Boeing's fps code; - A320 engine delivery performance. - Observed NB engine share 2026-34: CFM 76% / P&W 24% / RR 0%, unchanged. OUR POSITION (brief) - ΔPV is -8.44 $B if nobody moves (-6.44 engine value, -2.00 GTF2 R&D). Yield 92.3%. - On the hold row our NB share falls from 24.0% to 19.4% in 2037, when NGSA enters service with three engines. It then drifts to 16.8% by 2049. OBJECTIVE STATUS - Restore credibility: MET (GTF2 on NGSA). - Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV >= 0): NOT MET at -8.44. No order of ours meets it. Only S3 (+3.37) does, and that is Boeing's choice. - The Board's open round-1 recommendations: a narrower disclosure, a readiness report on test, and cash against the envelope. GRID (ΔPV $B, columns S1 / S2 / S3 / S4) - S1: rivals hold. S2: Airbus moves NGSA to code 5 (RR and CFM). S3: Boeing moves fps to code 7. S4: Rolls-Royce commits to the Joint Venture. - hold: -8.44 / -29.76 / +3.37 / -8.44 - hold + commit: -8.44 / -29.76 / +3.37 / -2.93 - cancel: -29.42 in every column - cancel + commit: -29.42 / -29.42 / -29.42 / -4.60 THE BAD NEWS FIRST The miss-a-cycle loss is in front of us. If Airbus drops us (S2), the hold row loses another $21.32B against S1, and no order of ours recovers it; a cancel saves only $0.34B in that column. Every grid column this round is decided by someone else. Our only lever on S2 is product, time on wing and what we say, and the board does not price any of that.

Options to test.

  • A. Default and the Board's comparator: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR hold. - Row: -8.44 / -29.76 / +3.37 / -8.44. - It keeps GTF2 on NGSA (credibility stays met) and keeps us eligible for fps if Boeing moves (S3). - It leaves +5.51 on the table if Rolls-Royce commits (S4).
  • B. My lean: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR commit. - Row: -8.44 / -29.76 / +3.37 / -2.93. - Against A: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. It is never below Do Nothing, and its weighted value, 5.51 x P(S4), is >= 0 on any weights. - No new R&D: GTF2 folds in. - Conditional on terms: risk and investment shared; the gear and core stay ours as our own module, with no licence; GTF2's 2036 schedule is carried, not reset or compressed.
  • C. GTF2 Solo cancel, Joint Venture with RR hold. - Row: -29.42 in every column. Against A: -20.98 / +0.34 / -32.79 / -20.98. - Break-even P(S2) = 20.98 / 21.32, about 0.98. - It writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B, turns credibility from met to not met, and walks away from an airframer that has named us. - Tested so the cancel is written into the record, not because I expect it to pass.
  • D. GTF2 Solo cancel + Joint Venture with RR commit. - Row: -29.42 / -29.42 / -29.42 / -4.60. - Against B: -20.98 / +0.34 / -32.79 / -1.67. Break-even P(S2) is about 0.83, even with all the remaining weight in S4. - For the record only.

Red lines.

  • Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. - GTF2 must be ready, with durability proven on test, by NGSA's 2037 EIS, and by fps's 2040 EIS if Boeing moves. - No compression, and no late engine presented as on time. - A Joint Venture carries GTF2's schedule; it does not reset or compress it. - Eddy's ground-1 veto binds on me.
  • Fleet first [PX-0080]. GTF2's production ramp and any Joint Venture work may not take pacing parts, shops or engineers from the GTF fleet or from A320neo deliveries. Eddy's ground-2 veto binds.
  • No cancel of a selected engine while the airframer that named us can still be served. My lever rule rejects harvesting; reading my $575M reset [PX-0064] across to engines is inference. The Board vetoes a cancel unless it beats hold in every plausible column.
  • Joint Venture [P-1233]: share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology. - P&W keeps the gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. - Aligned, standard terms, with no subsidy of either partner's solo engine. - If a design ever needs the gear or core handed over, we withdraw. - Flag on the record: 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours' assumed we would join UltraFan. Here GTF2 folds in, so our technology is the one at stake. I must strike or rebut the flag in the decision.
  • Book no unproven upside (Mitchill's ground 4; a Board veto). - No Rolls-Royce commitment, partner money, code-4 selection or durability gain is booked. - No Joint Venture engine date beyond GTF2's own 2036. - 'Proven before entry into service' is a standard we set, not a claim.
  • Never speak for an airframer's dates, rates or codes [PX-0062]. Nothing on NGSA's or fps's entry dates or codes, and nothing on Airbus's review.
  • Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. Standard terms; no launch-style discounts or free upgrades in other moves or the statement, including to sway Airbus's code review. A rival's discount never moves the answer.
  • Capital order [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. No envelope stretch; the Board's once-in-the-game stretch stays in reserve.
  • Premium. - Expected: 0. - Doctrine plus objective premium never exceeds $1B. - The Board passes at most $0.5B, declared and serving the objective.
  • Sole source [P-0746]. The shared-source relief declared in round 1 still covers NGSA code 7: it is franchise defence, and the company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292][PX-0058]. No order this round changes it.
  • No widebody [PX-0027]. overrides stays empty; on a binding veto I revise once, within it.
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in. - A cancel: premature exit, and it fails the return hurdle. - A commit that carries any of these: - an unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, or any entry in overrides; - a gear-and-core flag I have not struck or rebutted; - terms that hand over the gear or core, or that are aggressive; - new R&D beyond GTF2's folded spend; - a booked Rolls-Royce commitment or Joint Venture selection; - a fold that compresses or resets GTF2. - Any premium above $0.5B, any undeclared premium, or any that strains the dividend.

Initial lean. My lean is Option B: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR commit, premium 0. GTF2 Solo: HOLD - An airframer has named us. The Board does not cut a programme a customer has asked for, and neither do I. - My lever rule is to cancel only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can. - Cancel trails hold by $20.98B to $32.79B in three columns and gains $0.34B in one; it needs P(S2) of about 0.98. - Writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B is not a responsible bet [PX-0010]. - Hold also keeps us eligible for fps if Boeing moves (S3, +3.37), the only column where Capitalise is met. Joint Venture with RR: COMMIT, ON CONDITIONS - My trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. - The commit is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51) and adds no R&D. If the Joint Venture forms, its engine is the folded GTF2, ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS. - I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture (Low). This is doctrine plus the grid, and I will decide on Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test. - I name my bias: architecture loyalty ('the GTF is the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]) would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it. - For it: 'The strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038]; partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge [P-1563]; and IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]. Here both would be. THE RED-LINE FLAG AND MY PROPOSED REBUTTAL - The red line: 'You spread risk, you spread investment through JVs, but you don't share technologies' [P-1233]. - The commit is an order to share risk and investment. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are ours to set: the gear and core stay P&W's own module, with no technology licence. - GTF2's fold-in counts our spend toward our $2B share. It does not transfer intellectual property. - Rolls-Royce says it does not need partnership for capability and rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours. - If Shane finds a design that needs our gear or core, his withdraw proposal stands and the commit goes. I keep the flag open until both memos confirm. PREMIUM: 0 - The commit weakly dominates hold, so no doctrine premium is needed. Once the trigger is met, commit is the doctrine-favoured order on my lever rule. - Objective: credibility stays met under hold. Capitalise is not met in any column we control; the commit narrows the gap in S4 (-2.93 against -8.44). MY PROVISIONAL COLUMN READ (I will take Neil's weights) - S1 0.62, S2 0.15, S3 0.08, S4 0.15. - Expected PV: A -10.69; B -9.87; C -29.42; D -25.70. - My incrementalism bias leans to S1. It does not move the answer: B is never below A, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98. WHAT COULD CHANGE MY LEAN - The commit comes off if: - Shane fails durability, or finds the fold compresses GTF2; - the terms need our gear or core; - Neil sustains a ground-3 or ground-4 veto. In that case I revise to A. - Nothing on this grid moves me to a cancel. PROPOSED OTHER MOVES 1. GTF durability kit for the installed fleet (public): sold on standard terms, with no dated AOG recovery [PX-0100][PX-0098][PX-0104]. 2. Joint Venture terms (public, with the commit): share risk, investment and revenue; P&W's gear and core stay its own module; no technology licence; no subsidy of either partner's solo engine. 3. GTF2 readiness report to the Board each round (private): severe-environment testing, LLP life and time on wing, with a flag at once if 2036 is at risk. 4. Standing 2045 review (private): a withdraw test if Rolls-Royce has not committed. PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement) 'Let me start with what is not done. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. It launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. If that date comes under risk, you will hear it from us first, early, with the plan. Control what you can control. The GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection; we're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. It forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits; that is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence, and the Joint Venture carries GTF2's schedule; it does not reset it. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.' If the commit is struck, the Joint Venture sentences become: 'We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core.'

Chris Calio decides

Orders. Commit to Joint Venture with RR

Rationale. THE DECISION: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR commit, premium 0, overrides empty. 1. Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073] - GTF2 (launched 2030) is ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service (code 7, which includes P&W). It would also be ready for fps's 2040 entry into service if Boeing moves to code 7 (S3). - If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2. It is ready in 2036, not at formation + 6 = 2041, and UltraFan NB's 2037 does not pull it later. - Eddy passes both of his veto grounds on rows A and B. The fold neither compresses nor resets GTF2, and its configuration stays frozen through certification. - I name my own bias here. My operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024][PX-0098]. So I take Eddy's number, not mine: the one-year margin is not shown at risk on the board, and nothing proves it safe. His ground-1 veto binds the moment test data say otherwise. 2. Starting point: Eddy's proposal Eddy proposes hold and commit. Mitchill recommends the same orders. No binding veto stands from either of them. 3. GTF2: HOLD. The cancel test, written out - A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035 to save the last ~$0.33B. This is the last round a cancel exists, because GTF2 is ready in 2036 and the next round is 2045. - Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 (S1) / +0.34 (S2) / -32.79 (S3) / -20.98 (S4). Weighted: -18.73. - Break-even P(S2) is 0.98, or 0.83 beside a commit with all the remaining weight in S4. - My lever rule cancels only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can, and an airframer that has named us is not harvested [PX-0064 read across, inference]. - The $0.34B gain in S2 is not worth hedging. A cancel would also turn credibility from met to not met. - Not a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010]. 4. Joint Venture: COMMIT - The trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. - Against hold the commit reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. That is never below Do Nothing, weighted +0.55, for $0 of new R&D, because GTF2's $2B folds into P&W's share. - My record on a Joint Venture is Low and holds no evidence of my own. This is doctrine plus the grid, decided on Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback directs. - I name my architecture loyalty bias ('the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]). It would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it. - For: 'the strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038], and partners carried 49% of the 2023 charge [P-1563]. IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]; here both are on NGSA. - Rolls-Royce decides this round without seeing our order. The commitment therefore mainly puts P&W on the public record for Rolls-Royce's stated revisit. That is why S4 is weighted only 0.10. 5. Red-line flag (gear and core [P-1233]): REBUTTED, and its condition written into the terms - The flag said 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours'. That assumed we would join UltraFan. Here GTF2 folds in, so our technology is the one at stake. - The order commits risk, investment and revenue sharing, not technology. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are on the record before Rolls-Royce can commit: - the gear and core stay one P&W module and one P&W team, with design authority through certification; - there is no technology licence. - Counting the fold-in toward our $2B share transfers no intellectual property. - Rolls-Royce rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours. - Eddy confirms that module ownership works for a GTF2-based engine [P-1240]. If any design ever needs the gear or core handed over, his withdraw proposal stands, and we withdraw before formation. - The flag is therefore rebutted on these terms. The terms are a public other move and part of the statement. 6. Mitchill's four grounds - Ground 1 (dividend and debt): not engaged. The envelope passes, and the dividend and debt path are intact. - Ground 2 (unselected engine): passes. GTF2 is selected. - Ground 3 (terms): passes on the final text. Standard terms, no discounts, no subsidy of UltraFan, and the durability kit is sold. - Ground 4 (unproven upside): passes. His round-1 objection named its own condition (a live Rolls-Royce code and a commit row never below hold), and both now hold. The booked number is -8.44. Nothing for S4 is booked, and no Joint Venture date beyond 2036 is given. - His cancel objection rests on return, not on one of his grounds. I adopt it anyway, on my lever rule and the Board's would-veto list. 7. Tie-breaks - The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, ahead of GTF2. - 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] applies here on visible demand, a live selection. It is RTX-wide in my record; applying it to GTF2 is inference. It argues for holding, not cancelling. - No rival's price entered the answer [PX-0055]. 8. Shared source [P-0746] NGSA's code 7 stays covered by the shared-source relief declared in round 1, as franchise defence, at 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292][PX-0058]. No order of ours changes a code this round. 9. Capital order The dividend first, then debt to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. GTF2's last $0.33B is 5.5% of the ~$6B envelope [PX-0268], and the commit adds nothing. No stretch is used. 10. Premium: 0 - Hold/commit (B) is the best expected PV at -10.14, against -10.69 for hold/hold, -29.42 for cancel and -26.94 for cancel/commit. - No doctrine-favoured order trails the best, and no objective premium is needed. The total is $0 against the $1B cap. 11. Disclosure - The statement leaves out the round-1 promise to launch in any round we are named. It keeps 2036 and 'proven before entry into service' as standards we set, not claims. - It offers GTF2 only where we can be ready by an airframer's entry into service. It says nothing on Airbus's code review or on any airframer's dates [PX-0062]. It puts the fleet and A320neo deliveries ahead of GTF2. - Its only lever on S2 is product, time on wing and delivery performance. The board prices none of that. 12. Incrementalism My incrementalism leans me to S1. It does not move the answer: B weakly dominates A on any weights, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

Weighing the CFO. Mitchill's memo is the cash basis for this decision. Per the team rule, I trust his numbers over my operating dates. Where his work changed or anchored the decision: - I adopted his column weights (S1 0.67 / S2 0.15 / S3 0.08 / S4 0.10) over my provisional 0.62 / 0.15 / 0.08 / 0.15. His reasoning on S4 is right: Rolls-Royce's stated condition is P&W's commitment on the record, and it decides this round sealed, without seeing ours. On either set of weights the ranking is the same (B -10.14 on his, -9.87 on mine). - His cancel arithmetic is my cancel test: a $1.67B write-off against $0.33B saved, -18.73 weighted, break-even P(S2) of 0.98. - His cancel objection is advice, not binding: it rests on return, not on one of his four grounds. I took it on my own lever rule and the Board's would-veto list. - He cleared his round-1 ground-4 objection on its own stated condition. - I kept his standing ground-3 and ground-4 conditions. The final text offers no discount, no subsidy of UltraFan and no booked Rolls-Royce commitment, and gives no Joint Venture date beyond 2036. Taken into the plan: - his off-grid exposures (a 2045 acceptance under equal NB shares, and a possible fresh $2B share); - his question on whether a withdraw in the same round that Rolls-Royce commits stops formation. Both go into the 2045 review, with an ask to the GM. I also note his named V2500 bias and his own counter-evidence to it [P-1875].

Weighing the operating head. I started from Eddy's proposal (hold, commit), and his readiness check binds me. His seat rests on one event (June 2023), so his record is Low. I weight his engineering judgement as the seat's doctrine, and his honesty on data as his own. What I accepted: - His plain report that the brief holds no severe-environment, LLP or time-on-wing data, and that he will not fill it in. That is the readiness report I give the Board. - His caution that the one-year margin to 2037 is exposed on the company's 1.5-2-year slip prior. No Joint Venture or UltraFan design content enters GTF2's certification baseline before 2036. Any merged content comes later as a derivative, fully tested before its own entry into service. Before 2036, Joint Venture work is limited to commercial, support and interface work. Eddy runs the daily choice between the two on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0123][PX-0131]. Powder-metal capacity is added with records discipline, because the 2015 ramp is where the contaminant came in [P-1040]. Castings are built up in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125]. The ramp from 960 GTF engines (2036) to about 775 mostly GTF2 engines (2037) runs on commonality with the Advantage. Eddy flags that no factory makes that step in one year, so it is planned in steps and not promised publicly.

We withdraw if the withdraw row is not worse in any column weighted at 0.2 or more, or if its expected gain clears its break-even odds. Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety and maturity first. UltraFan NB was launched in 2030 on NGSA's selection and is ready in 2037, against NGSA's EIS of 2037: zero margin. We expect the full test programme with nothing compressed; if a phase slips, the engine slips. We also expect Watson's report on gearbox sizing and on the castings, forgings, gearbox and partner-shop contracts he undertook to place by this round, and support in place before EIS. Nothing earlier than 2037 in public, and nothing on any airframer's dates [RG-0027, RG-0025, R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284, RX-0286, RX-0287].
  • Keep the programme an airframe flies. NGSA carries code 7 (RR, PW and CFM), and it is live and not yet in service. UltraFan NB is therefore no orphan, and cancelling it would break the company's hard rule. The grid agrees: against 'UltraFan NB: hold', cancelling is -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54 (S1-S5). It is worse even in S2, where Airbus drops us. The round-1 plan for failure has not triggered [R-1573, R-0986, R-1005, RG-0033].
  • One big programme at a time, and the widebody core held. UltraFan NB is in development until 2037, so neither the Trent 1000 upgrade nor UltraFan WB may run beside it. The $5B strain puts each beyond its own bill: -6.02 and -9.00 against hold in S1. Our widebody share is 58% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, both above 50%, and no Re-engine is on the record. The widebody question comes back in 2045, once UltraFan NB is ready [RG-0019, RX-0214, R-0929, R-1127, R-1574, RG-0068].
  • A partner only on aligned terms. A Joint Venture with P&W: commit now meets our partner test, because NGSA's code includes P&W. On the grid it is never below hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. It is the CEO's call, not our ask. We would approve it with McCabe's co-signature and Watson's ready check, on terms that share risk and investment, and with a withdrawal review in 2045 if the Joint Venture has not formed [R-1010, R-0318, R-0916, R-0920].
  • The balance sheet and returns. The remaining Solo spend is about $2.29B ($8B x 2/7), roughly $1.14B a year to 2037. It should stay inside a broadly flat R&D envelope and after the 2026-2028 returns programme, with no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x and no borrowing for distributions. The test does not apply unless McCabe invokes a balance-sheet veto [RX-0242, RG-0041, RG-0059, RX-0214, RG-0033].

Expects to see. For each Board item we expect the following. (1) The grid row of the submitted orders and the row with that item at hold, column by column (S1-S5). Examples: 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV' against 'UltraFan NB: hold'; for a widebody item, its row against the same row without it ('hold + commit to JV + T1000 upgrade' against 'hold + commit to JV'). She should also confirm the plan fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the returns programme, with leverage at or below about 1.5x. The brief shows 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 against 197 widebody a year. (5) Both veto checks (CFO and Civil), with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in rationale and overrides empty. (6) Any premium in premium, item by item, with its reason. We expect $0B: 'hold + commit to JV' is never below 'UltraFan NB: hold' and is the best or tied-best row in every column. Would approve.

  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit, with UltraFan NB Solo, UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade at hold. Recommendations.

  • Keep UltraFan NB to readiness. Describe it publicly as ready in 2037, seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed. Make no price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps: narrowbody is an option, not a need, and we are not after share.
  • Watson's 2035 memo should report on the support plan he undertook in 2030. That covers the partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model; castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers; gearbox sizing, the one item that would turn the zero margin into a maturity concern; confirmation that no test phase has been cut to hold 2037; and the date of the EIS-readiness review. Capacity is advice, not a ground: the brief shows 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 against our 197 widebody a year.
  • McCabe should give weights for S1-S5 and the worst column for each item. She should give the remaining Solo spend (about $2.29B, roughly $1.14B a year to 2037). If a Joint Venture is ordered, she should give the cash and write-off effect of a 2035 formation, in which the live Solo folds in and spend beyond our $4B share is written off. She should confirm the fit with a broadly flat R&D envelope, the 2026-2028 returns programme and leverage at or below about 1.5x.
  • On the Joint Venture: we would approve a commit, but we do not press it; the CEO has said he dislikes options management. If he brings it, the terms should be aligned: shared risk and investment, our UltraFan technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. The rationale should also address a case the grid does not show: Boeing naming RR (S3) and P&W committing (S4) in the same round. Under a formed Joint Venture, RR and P&W hold equal narrowbody shares, so part of the S3 upside would be given up. Finally, set a withdrawal review for 2045. If the Joint Venture has not formed by then, NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) will be in service and no live airframe can use its engine in time. A later formation would also bring the $5B strain back onto any widebody item.
  • Hold both widebody items this round. Revisit the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2045, when UltraFan NB is ready and no longer in development: either against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium inside $3B. UltraFan WB waits for a Re-engine on the record and must come within the $1B sub-cap. Without strain it is still -1.95 against a Re-engine and -4.00 without one. Watch the GEnx upgrade (55.2% from 2042) and any rival-engined Re-engine, which would trigger the franchise test.
  • Public statement: UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development, ready in 2037, with nothing compressed and support through partner shops before entry into service. Put no date beside any airframe. If committing to the Joint Venture, describe it as aligned terms with no ready date. 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.'
  • Other moves: keep the UltraFan demonstrator path and Trent fleet durability as public, qualitative moves. Retire the round-1 plan for failure: NGSA still carries our code, holding beats cancelling in every column (S2 included), and 2035 is the last round in which a cancel is possible before UltraFan NB is ready.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, the 2035 question, put in cash and quality of earnings. We have $5.71B in an UltraFan NB that NGSA's code 7 flies. It is ready in 2037 against NGSA's 2037 EIS, which is zero margin. On hold the board gives us +18.26 and both legs of the objective. The question is narrow. Do we protect what is working and add nothing? Or do we add one item: a Joint Venture commitment that costs nothing in any column and avoids the last $2.29B of Solo spend if Pratt & Whitney comes in? Everything else on the grid destroys value or breaks a red line. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.02 and UltraFan WB is -9.00, because the $5B strain beside a narrowbody programme takes each beyond its own bill. A cancel is -24.54 in S1 and -42.25 in S3 on a programme an airframe flies. We are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582]. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].

Situation. Public record, 2035. - NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, EIS 2037, code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). Fitted if nothing changes: CFM + PW + RR. Airbus said it revisits the code in 2035. Its tests are published ready dates for GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine against the NGSA entry year, CFM's ducted-or-Open-Fan choice, Boeing's fps code and A320 engine delivery. - fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on the 10-year path, EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM). Boeing said it is not starting a second development alongside this one. - Our UltraFan NB (Solo): triggered in 2030 by NGSA's selection, ready 2037. - Rivals: P&W GTF2 (Solo) ready 2036; CFM ducted ready 2036; CFM-Embraer partnership ready 2037. GEnx upgrade in service since 2033. - P&W has made no Joint Venture commitment. Its stated terms: any partnership would 'share risk and investment, never our gear or core technology'. It 'will not buy a selection'. - No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says the A350 family remains its focus. - Observed markets 2026-34 at the status quo: narrowbody engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; widebody engines GE 42 / RR 58. Our position on hold: ΔPV +18.26 $B, yield 116.6%. Engine value +26.26, R&D -8.00. RR narrowbody engines: 965 in 2037, a peak of 990 in 2039, 863 a year from 2049. Widebody: 197 a year to 2041, 188 from 2042. Objective: both legs met on hold. - Narrowbody entry: RR share 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050. - Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050; worst year 55.2%, after the GEnx upgrade counts from 2042. - In S2 (Airbus drops us to code 6) the hold row is still -3.06, not -8.00. So the board still credits some RR narrowbody value; I read entry as surviving at far lower value (inference, Rob to confirm). The round-1 plan for failure (cancel if the selecting airframe drops our code) has not triggered: NGSA still carries code 7. 2035 is the last round in which a cancel is possible before UltraFan NB is ready. Grid, each item against the same row without it (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5): - Commit to JV: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. - T1000 upgrade: -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 / -5.87. - UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -6.95. - Cancel UltraFan NB: -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54 (beside the JV, -4.00 in S4). Best grid plan by column: hold in S1, S2, S3 and S5 (tied with hold + JV); hold + JV in S4 (+20.55). Board guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 2.5): - It would approve the JV commit with McCabe's co-signature and Watson's ready check, on aligned terms with a 2045 withdrawal review. It does not press it. - It would veto a cancel, the upgrade, UltraFan WB, a JV commit without co-signature or under a standing Civil veto (or beside a widebody item), and any package with an unrespected veto, an unresolved red-line flag or a non-empty overrides.

Red lines.

  • Safety first. No compressed maturity: if a phase slips, the engine slips. No date earlier than launch plus development years: UltraFan NB 2037 (2030 + 7), UltraFan WB launch + 6, Joint Venture formation + 6. No Joint Venture ready date in public at all. Nothing on any airframer's dates [R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296].
  • No cancel of a programme a live airframe flies. NGSA (code 7, EIS 2037) flies UltraFan NB, so UltraFan NB Solo stays at hold. The round-1 plan for failure has not triggered and is retired [R-1573]. Board veto.
  • One big programme at a time. No Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (UltraFan NB to 2037). No UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected. Any narrowbody project (Solo or Joint Venture) beside a widebody project costs $5B of strain [R-0929, R-1127]. Board veto on both widebody items.
  • No UltraFan WB without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan. None is on the record. Any UltraFan WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574].
  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit only with P&W's commitment on the record or a live airframe whose code includes P&W. NGSA's code 7 meets the second test. It also needs McCabe's co-signature, no standing Civil veto from Watson and no widebody item beside it. A commitment is public at once and standing: if the Joint Venture has not formed by 2045, I withdraw it then, because no live airframe could use it in time [R-1010, R-0318, RX-0051].
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column (Joint Venture -$4B, UltraFan WB -$4B, upgrade -$2B). A narrowbody item needs a weighted value of at least 0 against hold, with no premium.
  • McCabe's joint sign-off on every commit or launch against mid-to-high-teens hurdles [RX-0213, R-1579]. Her balance-sheet vetoes: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Watson's Civil veto binds: compressed maturity, an early disclosed date, or no support in place before EIS. overrides stays empty; we revise once within any veto.
  • Doctrine premium at most $3B per round against the best expected grid plan, declared item by item.
  • No price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps: win-win terms, value remunerated, every contract through the Investment Committee [R-1582, RX-0097].

Initial lean. Proposal: UltraFan NB Solo: hold (kept to readiness, no cancel); Joint Venture with P&W: commit, on aligned terms; UltraFan WB: hold; Trent 1000 upgrade: hold. So, frankly, this round is about delivery, not new bets. UltraFan NB stays on its seven-year clock with the full test programme; NGSA flies it, and cancelling it would be value destruction in every column. The Joint Venture is the one addition. - It is never below hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights, worst column 0, premium $0B. - It avoids the last $2.29B of Solo spend if Pratt comes in, which is cash as an input [RX-0042]. - NGSA's code 7 flies both makers, so a live airframe can use it: a choice, not options management [RX-0051]. - Partnership has always been our preference [RX-0118], 'to derisk things a little bit' [RX-0072]. - The terms must credit what we bring: shared risk and investment, our UltraFan technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. - A withdrawal review is set for 2045: if it has not formed by then, no live airframe can use it, and it goes. The lean flips to B (all hold, premium $0.23B declared, 'we are actually bringing a technology') if: - Helen withholds her co-signature, or her off-grid reading puts the S3+S4 giveaway above the S2+S4 hedge; or - Rob finds the fold compresses anything, or the support plan is not on track. Widebody: nothing this round. The upgrade comes back in 2045, once UltraFan NB is ready. Other moves: - Public: the UltraFan demonstrator path and Trent fleet durability continue. - Private: Rob's support build and contracting status; pricing discipline (no concessions to keep NGSA or win fps); the round-1 plan for failure retired. Draft public statement: 'So, UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and ready in 2037, seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed, and support in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, sharing risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise: no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.' If we hold the JV instead: 'Partnership remains our preference; we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today.' Subject to Helen's co-signature and Rob's ready check.

Tufan Erginbilgic decides

Orders. Commit to Joint Venture with P&W

Rationale. So, the decision, by the team rule. 1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL. UltraFan NB Solo: hold, which keeps the programme to readiness with no cancel. Joint Venture with P&W: commit. UltraFan WB: hold. Trent 1000 upgrade: hold. Both memos recommend exactly these orders, and the Board says it would approve them. 2. BINDING VETO CHECKS. - CFO. McCabe co-signs the commit against the hurdle. It is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 against 'UltraFan NB: hold', +0.23 expected, worst column 0, with no new cash in any column. She withholds her signature on the upgrade, on UltraFan WB and on a commit beside either widebody item. None of these is ordered. She invokes no balance-sheet veto. The remaining $2.29B of Solo spend ($8B x 2/7, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year in 2036-37, £1.68bn in total) comes from free cash flow, after the 2026-28 returns programme and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. No equity, no borrowing, leverage at or below about 1.5x. - Civil. Watson invokes no Civil veto. UltraFan NB, ready 2037 (2030 + 7), against NGSA's 2037 EIS is zero margin: a pass with a note. His concurrence rests on three conditions, and all three are met in these orders. (a) The public statement gives no UltraFan NB date before 2037, no Joint Venture ready date and no airframer date. 2037 is not placed next to NGSA, and the date is framed as a clock, 'not before'. (b) I count the Joint Venture engine only at a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, or GTF2 2036) and otherwise at formation + 6 (2041). I promise no new combined design for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan, no core change. The folded programme keeps its own test clock (private other move). (c) The support plan is carried as a private other move with its dates. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox contracts are placed in 2035. The spares pool and field service stand up in 2036, and the EIS-readiness review is in 2036. - No binding veto stands, and overrides is empty. 3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5). My weights, which McCabe confirmed: S1 0.55, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05. - S2 is a signal: Airbus's 2035 code review is on the record. - S3 and S4 have nothing on the record. - S5 sits below 'nothing': Boeing has said no second development, and Airbus says the A350 family is its focus. Item by item: - JV commit ('hold + commit to JV' minus 'hold'): 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights and on the Board's case (0.55 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.10); +0.11 to +0.46 with S4 at 0.05-0.20. Worst column 0, against a $4B limit. In S4 the whole +2.29 is spend not made: the $1.71B beyond our $4B share is already spent, sunk, with no new cash. - Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 (-6.03 beside the JV) / -5.87. Expected -6.01, worst -6.03. That is beyond its own $2B bill and above the $3B cap, and it is a red line. Not ordered. - UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -6.95. Expected -8.90, worst -9.00. There is no Re-engine on the record, it overlaps UltraFan NB, and it is far above the $1B sub-cap. Not ordered. - Cancel UltraFan NB: -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54. Expected -22.05 (-19.99 beside the JV, -4.00 in S4). Worst -42.25. NGSA's code 7 flies it. Not ordered. Row EVs: 'hold + commit to JV' +15.99; hold +15.76; 'hold + JV + T1000' +9.98; 'hold + T1000' +9.75; 'hold + JV + UltraFan WB' +7.09; 'hold + UltraFan WB' +6.87; 'cancel + JV' -4.00; cancel -6.28. 4. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND BEST PLAN. I expect S1, rivals hold. Its best plan is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +18.26, tied with 'hold + commit to JV' at +18.26. The commit is best or tied-best in every column and best outright in S4 (+20.55). Premium $0B. 5. OFF-GRID (inference, nothing booked). If S3 and S4 come in the same round, equal shares could hand P&W up to about $8.9B of the fps upside, at a joint weight of about 0.01. If S2 and S4 come together, the Joint Venture keeps us on NGSA and recovers about $10.7B, at a joint weight of about 0.02. Net about +0.12. The two roughly offset, the S2 hedge is the larger, and the sign of +0.23 does not change. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so P&W cannot time its commit to Boeing's or Airbus's code. 6. WHY COMMIT, ON MY RECORD. 'We don't commit that easily' [RX-0124], so I do not take this lightly. The commitment costs nothing in any column, and an airframe can use it: NGSA's live code 7 includes both makers, and a 2035 formation is ready by 2037 from the folded UltraFan. So it is a choice, not options management [RX-0051]. Partnership is the preference, not a need [RX-0118]. The terms credit what we bring [RX-0072]: shared risk and investment, our technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. It saves the last $2.29B if P&W comes in, which is cash as an input [RX-0042]. The test is binary [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table, or we deliver alone. It is not open-ended. A sealed withdrawal is planned for 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and no widebody item goes beside it. The thresholds and the Joint Venture terms are doctrine and inference, not my record: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms. 7. Strain $0. - Joint Venture with P&W commit: met on the partner test (NGSA's live code 7 includes P&W), co-signed, with no Civil veto and no widebody item beside it. - No early date and no airframer date: met. - No item loses more than its own bill: the commit's worst column is 0. - Premium within cap: $0B. - No price concessions. No colleague flagged a red-line breach against these orders. The flags both raised (upgrade, UltraFan WB, cancel) apply to options that are not ordered. 8. CAPACITY AND THE FRANCHISE (advice). Narrowbody volume is 965 engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes through partner shops and our best suppliers. Widebody is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, so the franchise holds above 50%. The franchise test comes back in 2045.

Weighing the CFO. Taken in full. Her weights confirm mine (0.55 / 0.20 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05), and no item changes sign on the Board's set. Remaining Solo spend is about £0.84bn a year, £1.68bn in total, funded from free cash flow with no balance-sheet veto. Her withheld signatures on the upgrade, UltraFan WB and any commit beside a widebody item are binding, and I respect them: none is ordered. I adopt both of her conditions as private other moves: a sealed withdraw in 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and nothing widebody beside a standing commitment. I also adopt her off-grid bound (S3+S4 -0.09 against S2+S4 +0.21) and book nothing from it. On cash, the hurdle and the downside, her test is my evidence.

Weighing the operating head. Taken in full; I defer to him on readiness, strain and support. UltraFan NB at 2037 against NGSA's 2037 entry is zero margin, a pass with a note. Gearbox sizing closed at design; gearbox durability is what the private 2036 EIS-readiness review must clear. If a phase slips, the engine slips. His three conditions for concurrence on the commit are all carried: (a) no Joint Venture date, nothing before 2037 and no airframer date in public, with 2037 framed as a clock, 'not before'; (b) the Joint Venture engine counted only at a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036), otherwise 2041, with no new combined design for 2037; (c) the support plan carried privately with its dates: contracts in 2035, spares and field service in 2036, review in 2036. I take his advice to place forgings contracts now, given Airbus's lock on titanium, and not to count on P&W's shops. I also take his 2045 sequencing: withdraw in the same round as any upgrade, so the strain does not return. His capacity view is advice and is carried in the support move.

The spares pool and field service stand up in 2036. Gearbox sizing closed at design in 2030-32, and gearbox durability is what the review must clear. Widebody is not touched: no spend while UltraFan NB is in development, and the franchise test returns in 2045.

Predictions. Weights: S1 0.55, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05. - Airbus keeps NGSA on code 7 (likely, 0.80). On its own published test, UltraFan's 2037 ready date meets the NGSA entry, GTF2 is ready in 2036 and CFM's ducted engine in 2036, and its stated aim is CFM plus at least one other maker. - Boeing keeps fps on CFM (0.90). It is on the 10-year path to 2040 and has said it starts no second development. - Pratt & Whitney does not commit to the Joint Venture this round (0.90). Its record says it has made no commitment, it protects its gear and core, and GTF2 is already on NGSA. - No 787 or A350 Re-engine this round (0.95). Airbus says the A350 family is its focus. - CFM continues the ducted engine and the Embraer partnership, with RISE as technology. GEnx stays in service. - RR: UltraFan NB ready 2037 on its clock, with nothing compressed. The 2036 readiness review clears gearbox durability, or the engine slips. Expected ΔPV of the chosen orders: +15.99 $B on my weights (+17.05 on the Board's case). S1 outcome +18.26.

Expected ΔPV. +15.99 $B (board after the round: +20.55 $B)

Other moves.

  • Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms (public): Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney (the Joint Venture with P&W: commit order). The terms: shared risk and investment, and each side's technology protected. Our UltraFan technology is protected the way P&W protects its gear and core. If P&W comes to the table, we form it; if not, UltraFan goes on alone. No ready date and no airframer date are given for any Joint Venture engine [RX-0118, RX-0072, R-1010].
  • Joint Venture internal conditions (structure and maturity) (private): (1) RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. (2) If the Joint Venture forms, a folded programme keeps its own test clock and certification path. Internally the Joint Venture engine counts only at that programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036), and otherwise at formation + 6. (3) No new combined design is offered for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan and no core change. A gearbox change at year 5 of 7 would restart maturity testing. (4) Our support plan carries over unchanged, and we do not count on P&W's shops, because the GTF fleet keeps first call on them [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0287].
  • 2045 withdrawal review of the standing commitment (private): If the Joint Venture has not formed by the 2045 round, we place a sealed Joint Venture with P&W: withdraw in the 2045 orders, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above hold. By then NGSA and fps are in service, so no live airframe could use a Joint Venture engine in time, and keeping it would be options management [RX-0051, R-1573]. No widebody item goes beside a standing commitment. The withdrawal goes in the same round as any Trent 1000 upgrade, so the $5B strain cannot come back.
  • UltraFan NB test programme held to its seven-year clock (private): Launched 2030, ready 2037, which is year 5 of 7 now. Certification and maturity testing run 2035-37. Gearbox sizing was closed at design in 2030-32. Gearbox durability is the item the EIS-readiness review must clear. That review is in 2036 and stays private, with a final certification gate before the first engine is delivered. If a phase slips, the engine slips. At zero margin we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test [RX-0296, RX-0284].
  • Narrowbody support build: 2035 contracting (Watson's plan, step 4 due) (private): Placed in 2035: (a) partner-shop agreements on our Singapore joint-venture model near the launch operators, with no narrowbody MRO scale of our own [RX-0287]; (b) castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts with high-performing suppliers. Airbus is locking titanium forgings for its own ramp, so ours go now [RX-0286]. Repair technology continues alongside the test programme. The spares pool and field-service team stand up in 2036. The EIS-readiness review is in 2036. Support is in place before entry into service. The plan is resized if Airbus changes its code, and carries over unchanged if the Joint Venture forms. Capacity, as advice: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes to our best suppliers, not spread thin.
  • Round-1 plan for failure retired (private): NGSA still carries code 7, so the cancel trigger has not fired. Holding beats cancelling in every column, S2 included (-3.22). 2035 was the last round for a cancel before readiness. UltraFan NB is held to readiness [R-1573, R-1005].
  • UltraFan demonstrator path and technology pull-through continue (public): UltraFan technology continues to feed the Trent fleet for time on wing. Public R&D money is used where available. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0094, RG-0065].
  • Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded (public): About £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.
  • Pricing discipline (private): No price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.
  • Widebody franchise watch for 2045 (private): RR widebody share is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, a headroom of 5.2 pp. The franchise test triggers in 2045 on any of three events: a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, a further CFM widebody gain, or a projection below 55%. The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, once UltraFan NB is out of development: against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium within $3B. UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap [R-1574, RX-0101].

Round 3 · decision year 2045

2045: everyone holds; neither airframer re-engines its widebody

  • Both new narrowbodies are in service. The live levers were the Re-engines, the Open Fan and Rolls-Royce's widebody engines, and every company held.
  • Airbus: the A350 Re-engine was worth +$0.89B if Boeing held, under its $1B bar, and no widebody engine would be ready for it.
  • Boeing: its Board would have vetoed the 787 Re-engine on its business case: +$0.29B if Airbus held, −$1.26B if Airbus re-engined too.
  • Rolls-Royce found the Trent 1000 upgrade still carrying a $5B strain charge while the Joint Venture ran.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave you. That's five years of airplanes in customers' hands, and we're climbing the ramp the way we said we would. We take one step at a time, on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line has shown it's stable at the rate it's on. We've come a long way. There's still a lot of work in front of us, and we're not going to hurry the last part of the climb. We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready. Today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched. Paying down debt is far and away our priority. We're funding the business from our operations, with no new equity. I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers. We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 43% this year, up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and still climbing. That's short of half, and I won't dress it up. We earn the rest one delivery at a time. A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us. We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates. Others make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. The financials will follow our production performance.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We continue its production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family, and we put fleet safety and operational integrity above all. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected. On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We keep studying the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock. We will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before. We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes. We also continue to recruit the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft. We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility. On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: both new single-aisle airplanes are in service, and there's a CFM engine on both. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 has been in service since 2036. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We didn't take those positions for granted then, and we don't now. We don't have a birthright on the next order, so we earn it the way we earned the last one: by delivering. That means LEAP and the new engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines. What we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up over years of service, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. So we'll measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we'll report it on field data, not on analysis. Where we find something, we fix it with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery. The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that. We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. Any commitment on CFM capacity, we make together with Safran. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyDo Nothing

Public statement: “Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them. What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected. Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready six years from launch, with durability proven before entry into service. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.”

Rolls-RoyceDo Nothing

Public statement: “So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our job now is the fleet. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.”
