Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality of the fps in service and through its ramp. The fps has been in service since 2040, and narrowbody deliveries climb from 760 (2040) to 940 (2049). The Aerospace Safety Committee wants the fps, 737 and 787 KPI, supplier and in-service results, including the durability of the CFM ducted engine, from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer directly. Every production step stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem [BG-0043, BG-0025, BG-0014, BX-1263, B-2236, BG-0069].
  • The rating comes first. The $60.32B fps bill was booked at EIS. Airplane operating profit is now 15.7 in 2045 and rises to 16.9 by 2049, against 6.7 in the status quo, which is about $48.0B of nominal uplift over 2045-49. Debt is the first call on that cash until we are solidly investment grade, with no new equity. Shareholder returns come last, and any dividend or buyback proposal is a matter reserved to this board [BG-0029, BG-0062, BG-0034, B-2259, B-2327, BX-0556, BG-0044].
  • One well-founded launch, not a bet. The only Board item available this round is 787 Re-engine: launch. Its item value is +0.30 / -1.26 (S1 / S2): it clears $1B in neither column and falls below -$1B in S2, which the bulletin does not rule out. We expect 787 Re-engine: hold. Launching it in the same year as an A350 Re-engine would deepen S2 rather than hedge it [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581, BG-0066, BX-1239].
  • The long cycle and candour. Report narrowbody share honestly: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045 and 47% from 2049. Both objectives are recorded as not met, and no order on offer changes that path. Tie no order to Airbus's timing, attribute nothing to anyone, and log every premium [BG-0006, BG-0005, B-2313, BG-0022, BG-0026].

Expects to see. 1. Ortberg's frame and his expected_scenario (S1 rivals hold, or S2 Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine), argued from the bulletin. Airbus calls the A350 family its widebody focus, and Rolls-Royce says it will spend nothing new on a widebody engine without a Re-engine. Neither rules S2 out. 2. The submitted row from the round-3 grid. If 787 Re-engine: launch is submitted, show the same row with 787 Re-engine at hold, column by column. Do Nothing is +0.66 / +0.34. fps: hold + 787 Re-engine is +0.96 / -0.92. The Re-engine's item value is +0.30 / -1.26. 3. Malave's buffer test with its numbers. If S2 is the risk case, the floor is -1.66: Do Nothing passes by 2.00 and the Re-engine row by 0.74. His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test does not apply, since no fps launch is possible. 4. Malave's yearly funding report to the Finance Committee, carried from rounds 1 and 2. It should show the actual fps phasing against his planning curve (the 2030-39 decade ended about $6.1B down on debt), the post-EIS debt path using 14.3-16.9 a year of operating profit (2040-49), the rating outlook, the date he expects solidly investment grade, and confirmation of no new equity. 5. Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results and her veto check. The KPI veto is not in play because 737 rate is offered only at hold, but we want her results on the fps ramp from 760 to 940 deliveries, on CFM ducted supply and durability in service, and on the 737 and 787. She should also give strain for any Re-engine (0 years of overlap with the fps, which was counted 2033-40). 6. The CEO's rulings for any Re-engine. H3, second half: not triggered, because the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. H4: 0 years of overlap. H5: the fps is in service and cannot be cancelled. H1 and H2 do not apply. 7. premium with its reason. If S1 is expected and the Re-engine is held, 0.30 is forgone. That is within epsilon, a tie decided by doctrine, and it brings the cumulative premium to 0.76 against the $2B cap. If S2 is expected, the premium is 0. The objective premium is 0, since no order on offer moves narrowbody share. 8. A board_response answering each recommendation below, including those carried from our round-2 guidance (funding and rating report, safety reporting, disclosure, premium log). 9. A public statement that gives no Re-engine date before any launch, makes no attribution, and ties no order to Airbus.

Would approve.

  • fps: hold, 737 rate: hold and 787 Re-engine: hold, which is Do Nothing. The launched fps stays in service and continues its ramp. Row: +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). In the S2 risk case it sits 2.00 above the -1.66 floor, and it has the higher worst column of the two rows (+0.34 against -0.92, by 1.26). Holds are not Board items and are never vetoed. If every order is a hold, the GM does not call us to review, and our recommendations carry into the 2050 guidance.
  • fps engine code: none. The fps has flown CFM since its 2040 EIS, and the code can no longer change. This is not a Board item and never a veto ground.

Would veto.

  • 787 Re-engine: launch (with fps: hold). The row is +0.96 / -0.92 against Do Nothing's +0.66 / +0.34, so the item value is +0.30 / -1.26. It fails two tests. (1) Business case: a launch needs an item value above $1B in the expected column. It falls short by 0.70 in S1 and by 2.26 in S2, so it fails whichever column the CEO expects. (2) Downside: -1.26 in S2 is $0.26B below our -$1B limit, and the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine this round. It passes Rating first (S2 -0.92 against the -1.66 floor, by 0.74), One development at a time (0 years of overlap, the fps counted 2033-40 and the Re-engine 2045-50), H3 (no A350 Re-engine on the record) and, as far as the brief shows, Safety. Funding is not our ground: the $5B bill is about 6% of 2045-49 operating profit. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any plan with a binding ExCo veto still standing after revision (Malave's buffer test), a red-line flag the CEO neither struck nor rebutted in the rationale, or a premium above $2B or unlogged. We would veto the item whose reversion to hold cures it, here 787 Re-engine: launch, and name hold as the alternative.

Recommendations.

  • Hold the 787 Re-engine this round. Its item value is +0.30 / -1.26. It clears $1B in no column, and in S2 it is $0.26B past our -$1B limit. A 787 Re-engine entering service in the same year as an A350 Re-engine changes no share and costs more than it gains, so it deepens S2 rather than hedging it. In S1 the 0.30 is within epsilon, a tie that doing less, better and the higher-confidence plan decide. Grow the widebody from Charleston capacity. Bring the Re-engine back in the 2050 round only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half) and that brief's grid shows an item value above $1B in the expected column and no column below -$1B. Publish no Re-engine date before any launch.
  • Bring the Finance Committee its yearly report, carried from rounds 1 and 2. It should cover the actual fps phasing against Malave's 2030-39 curve, and the post-EIS debt path as operating profit runs at 14.3-15.4 in 2040-44 (74.4 in total) and 15.7-16.9 in 2045-49 (81.5 in total), about $48.0B above the status quo over 2045-49. It should also give the rating outlook and the year he expects to be solidly investment grade. Debt stays the first call on free cash, with no new equity. Shareholder returns stay last: any dividend reinstatement or buyback comes to this board as a reserved matter, and only once the rating is solid.
  • The Aerospace Safety Committee asks to hear directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer each year, covering: fps in-service safety and reliability; the CFM ducted engine's durability in service; supplier and quality KPIs through the fps ramp from 760 to 940 deliveries; and the 737 and 787 results. Every production step on the fps and the 737 stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next step. Certify before building at rate on any derivative, with no production-certification concurrency. Track CFM engine allocation across both airframers. The engine code is no longer a lever.
  • Disclosure and the long cycle. Report the narrowbody path honestly: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 39% in 2041, 40% in 2042, 43% in 2045 and 47% from 2049, the 47/53 long-run split. Both objectives stay recorded as not met. No order on offer this round can change that, so no objective premium applies. Tie no order to Airbus's timing and attribute nothing to the FAA, suppliers or Airbus. We will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions, and we judge this plan on the long cycle.
  • Premium log and board_response. If S1 is expected and the Re-engine is held, log 0.30 as a doctrine premium within epsilon, bringing the cumulative total to 0.76 against the $2B cap. If S2 is expected, log 0. Keep hard-rule costs in their own log: H4 at 0.65 in round 2, and none this round, because H3 and H4 both pass. Answer each recommendation here in board_response; any left unanswered will be raised again in 2050.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. 2045 is the first round with the fps in service. It entered service in 2040, on its date, and the brief shows it ramping: 760 narrowbody deliveries in 2040, 860 this year and 940 by 2049. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. So the question is narrow, and only one order is live: does a 787 Re-engine, launched now to enter service in 2050, earn a place beside the fps ramp? Or do we hold and keep doing less, better? Two questions I owe the Board sit under it: is the fps ramp stable on its KPIs, and when will we be solidly investment grade? My four questions to this ExCo: (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live problem. I want Pope's seat to confirm it on the record, for the fps ramp, the 737 and the 787 [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready for a second development? A Re-engine is that second development, even with the fps out of development [BX-1296, BX-1305]. (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? The brief labels no column "Risk case" this year: the fps is in service, so it has no slip leg. I still want Malave to read S2 first, as the Board does, and to cost a Re-engine slip for scale [BX-1319]. (4) Is each plan doing less, better? I want every row set against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

Situation. Where we are (bulletin and brief). - Rounds 1 and 2 are adjudicated. Our fps launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and has been in service since 2040, flying CFM. - NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, with CFM, the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine and RR fitted. - Engine ready dates on the public record: - CFM ducted 2036; - CFM-Embraer partnership 2037; - the GEnx upgrade, on the 787 since 2033; - the P&W-RR Joint Venture, formed in 2035, with its narrowbody engine in service since 2036 and both Solo programmes folded into it. - No A350 Re-engine is on the public record, and no 787 Re-engine. - Observed narrowbody share: - 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39, while NGSA flew alone; - 38% in 2040, then up a point a year to 42% in 2044. That is the plan path, with no dip in the 2040-44 window. - Widebody share is flat at 58.8%, 100 airplanes a year. - The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. My FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. Do Nothing (every order at hold) scores +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 rivals hold / S2 Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine). - Components: - narrowbody operating profit +20.30; - programme investment -14.91, booked at EIS 2040; - debt penalty -4.73, already netted and never subtracted again ($19.1B undiscounted, for scale only). - An A350 Re-engine alone costs us 0.32. Operating profit and funding. - Airplane operating profit stepped from 6.4 in 2039 to 14.3 in 2040. - 2040-44: 14.3 to 15.4 a year, 74.4 in total, 40.9 above the status quo. - 2045-49: 15.7 to 16.9 a year, 81.5 in total, 48.0 above the status quo. - Malave's 2030-39 planning curve ended the decade about $6.1B down on debt. - On the board, the $60.32B was booked as debt at EIS. - Debt stays the first call on cash, with no new equity. Shareholder returns come last. Grid against Do Nothing (S1 / S2): - A. Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.34. - B. fps hold + 787 Re-engine: row +0.96 / -0.92; item +0.30 / -1.26. - It enters service in 2050, with $5B booked at EIS. - Strain is 0: the fps counted 2033-40 and the Re-engine would count 2045-50. - In S2 both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2050. Share does not move, and our 787 margin falls to 15.77%. So B deepens S2 rather than hedging it. - B beats A in expectation only if the chance of S2 is below about 19% (0.30 ÷ 1.56). Even with S2 ruled out, its gain is inside ε. Incumbency path. Narrowbody share is 43% this year and 47% from 2049, for a long-run split of 47/53. Both objectives are recorded as not met (worst year 38%, in 2040). No order on offer moves that path, so the objective premium is 0. Board risks (from its guidance; these are not my red lines). - It would veto 787 Re-engine: launch on two tests: - business case: +0.30 / -1.26 clears $1B in neither column; - downside: -1.26 in S2 is $0.26B past its -$1B limit. - It would also veto any plan with a standing ExCo veto, a red-line flag neither struck nor rebutted, or a premium above $2B or unlogged. - It would approve Do Nothing and fps engine code none. - If every order is a hold, it is not called to review, and its recommendations carry into 2050.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing: fps hold, fps engine code null, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. - Row: +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). - Best row in S2, by 1.26. - In S1 it trails B by 0.30, inside ε, so doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] give it the tie. - Higher worst column, by 1.26. - It sits 2.00 above the Board's S2 floor of -1.66. - Not a Board item. - My lean.
  • B. fps hold + 787 Re-engine (code null, rate hold). - Row: +0.96 / -0.92; item against A: +0.30 / -1.26. - Passes: - H3, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record; - H4, with 0 years of overlap; - the Board's S2 floor, by 0.74. - Fails: - my debt-first test: a second development must beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and it does in neither column [BX-1305]; - doing less, better: inside ε in S1, -1.26 in S2; - the Board's business-case and downside tests. - It wins in expectation only if S2 is less likely than about 19%. - Tested to price the premium (0.30 if S1 is expected) and to answer the Board. - It is not a hedge. Doctrine reads the widebody as a Chicken game, where whoever moves first holds. Launching first for that reason would tie the order to Airbus's timing [B-2313], and the grid shows that entering service in the same year costs us 1.26. I am not testing it on that ground.

Red lines.

  • H1: not at issue. The fps is launched and in service.
  • H2: cannot bind.
  • H3, first half: lapsed after 2030. Its ground, one development at a time, works through H4. H3, second half (no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine): not triggered, since the record shows no A350 Re-engine. Orders this round are sealed together. If Airbus launches one now, from 2050 on it bars any 787 Re-engine, and I accept that: we stand aside, as with the A330neo [B-0917, B-0858].
  • H4: passes. The fps counted 2033-40 and a Re-engine launched now would count 2045-50: 0 years of overlap against the 2-year limit.
  • H5: the fps is in service and can no longer be cancelled. A Re-engine, once launched, is never cancelled for a slip, a charge or Airbus [BX-1251, BX-1321]; we re-baseline once instead.
  • H6: not in play. The rate is offered only at hold.
  • H7: no trigger. The brief reports no certification trouble.
  • H8: plans within ε ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides, and doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B, every premium logged. - Carried forward: 0.46 from Round 1 and 0 from Round 2. - This round: 0.30 if S1 is expected and we hold; 0 if S2. - Hard-rule costs are logged apart: Round 1, the Re-engine forgone under H3 (2.20 in S1, S2 and S5); Round 2, H4 at 0.65 in S1 and S3; Round 3, none.
  • My own lines: - no production-certification concurrency on any derivative [BX-1263, B-2228]; - no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]; - no rate request without stable KPIs [BX-1259, BX-1322]; - never walk away from core customers' programmes [BX-1251]; - no second development until it beats Do Nothing by more than ε with debt still first [BX-1305, B-2326]; - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; - no attribution to suppliers or Airbus before exposure (company doctrine, not my record); - no order timed to Airbus [B-2313, B-2315].

Initial lean. Orders I lean to: Do Nothing. - fps: hold - fps engine code: null - 737 rate: hold - 787 Re-engine: hold Row: +0.66 / +0.34. Every order is a hold, so no item goes to the Board. I will still answer each of its five recommendations in board_response. Why: - The Re-engine's +0.30 in S1 is inside ε, so doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] take the tie. - In S2 it loses 1.26. It is a bet that Airbus holds, not a hedge, and I don't time orders to Airbus either way [B-2313]. - Debt first: a second development has to beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and it does in neither column [BX-1305]. - Stability first: the fps is in its ramp, and Pope's results will tell me whether the technology work stream is even ready. Expected column, provisional: S1, rivals hold. My confidence on Airbus is Low. - Airbus repeated last round's line, "the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus", and it held in both 2030 and 2035. - Rolls-Royce's line is a condition on its own spending, not an Airbus commitment. - A move is real only when it is launched (doctrine §7). - S2 stays plausible: NGSA has been in service since 2037, which frees Airbus engineers, and doctrine expects an A350 Re-engine attempt. - The orders are the same either way: hold ties in S1 and wins by 1.26 in S2. Premium: 0.30 if S1 (cumulative 0.76 of $2B); 0 if S2. No objective premium and no hard-rule cost this round. What would change my lean: a grid where the Re-engine clears ε in the expected column with no column below -$1B, with Pope's readiness and strain results behind it. A live problem would only make the hold stronger. Public line: - The fps is in service and climbing, and we're ramping on our KPIs, step by step with the FAA. - We're not starting a second development today. The 787 grows from Charleston, and we'll look at its next step when it earns its place. - Debt stays first, with no new equity. - No date for anything we haven't launched, no order tied to anyone else's clock, and no blame on anyone. - "the financials will follow our production performance" [BX-1287].

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision: Do Nothing. The orders are fps hold, fps engine code null, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. The row is +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board. 1. Team rule, applied. - Malave's buffer test is not applicable. The brief labels no column 'Risk case', and the fps has been in service since 2040, so it has no slip leg. He confirms he holds no veto this round, and no plan is out on this ground. - Board proxy on S2 (floor 0.34 - 2.00 = -1.66): A passes by 2.00 and B by 0.74. - KPI doctrine (Pope's seat): not in play. 737 rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. She checked the veto and did not invoke it. - No colleague flagged a red line, and I override nothing. The rest is my call. 2. The grid (from the brief): - A, Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.34. - B, fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.96 / -0.92. - B's item: +0.30 / -1.26. It breaks even at a 19.2% chance of S2. - Malave rebuilt the item from the rules and tied out to rounding (+0.29 / -1.27). 3. My tests. - KPI stability: pass. No live problem in the brief. Pope rightly says delivery counts are not the KPI record, so the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report to Aerospace Safety [BX-1271, BX-1259]. - Three work streams: not converged [BX-1296]. - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2050, share does not move and our 787 margin falls to 15.77%. - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been on the 787 since 2033, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, after a 2050 EIS. My technology risk appetite is low [BX-1298]. This is unpriced, and it is not why I hold, but it means the work stream isn't there. - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 6.1% of the 81.5 of operating profit in 2045-49. Readiness is not the issue; the return is. - Debt before the next airplane: B fails. A second development must beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does so in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326]. - Malave corrects the penalty: +$3.10B undiscounted, which on the grid's pro-rata allocation is about 0.50 PV, not the 0.28 Pope and I used. The grid governs, and nothing is subtracted twice. - B would also move his conservative investment-grade year from 2053 to 2054. - Certification slip: there is no risk-case column, so this is for scale only. - Malave: one year of slip costs about 0.15 all-in in S1. - Pope: doctrine's central +2-year prior takes 40-50% of the S1 item. - So B's +0.30 rests partly on a nominal date with no headroom. I won't plan that way [BX-1318, BX-1319]. - Doing less, better: +0.30 in S1 is inside ε, so the plan with less to execute wins [BX-1239]. It is also the higher-confidence plan, with a worst column higher by 1.26 [BX-0548]. In S2, A leads by 1.26, outside ε. A wins whichever column I expect. - Airbus does not set the date: both directions apply. - I'm not launching to pre-empt an A350 Re-engine. That is doctrine's Chicken-game reading, which I did not use [B-2313]. - I'm not holding because of Airbus either. The hold rests on ε, debt-first and readiness. 4. Hard rules. - H1, H2, H6 and H7: not at issue. - H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars a 787 Re-engine from then on, and I accept that. - H4: 0 years of overlap (the fps counted 2033-40). - H5: the fps is in service and cannot be cancelled. - H8: the premium below. 5. The 2050 window. Malave estimates that a 2050 launch scores about +0.04 in S1, about $0.96B short of the Board's bar. So holding now very likely forgoes the 787 Re-engine on this board. That is a loss we accept, not a wait. On an item inside ε, with a technology work stream that hasn't converged, I'd rather be a year late than a year early [BX-1322]. 6. The Board. It would veto 787 Re-engine: launch on business case (+0.30 / -1.26 clears $1B in neither column) and on downside (-1.26 against its -$1B limit). It approves Do Nothing. Weighed: no conflict. 7. Record versus doctrine. - My record drove: the tie-break [BX-1239, BX-0548], debt-first [BX-1305], the three work streams [BX-1296] and under-disclosure of the rating year [BX-1268]. - Doctrine drove: Pope's supplier binding order, the slip prior and the reading that the engine code is locked. - Malave's investment-grade year is his inference (debt back to $45B). I keep it internal.

Weighing the CFO. Weighed heavily, as my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. It is still a thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and beyond the buffer test his views are advice. What I took: - His buffer test is not applicable, since there is no risk-case column. He holds no veto, which confirms my reading. - The S2 proxy: A +2.00, B +0.74 against -1.66. - His independent rebuild of B: +0.29 / -1.27 against the grid's +0.30 / -1.26. - His penalty correction: about 0.50 PV, not my 0.28. I accept it. The grid governs, and nothing is netted twice. - The cash path: one $5B bill at 2050, no two bills landing together, fundable from operations. - The slip cost, for scale: about 0.15 all-in in S1. - The 2050 window: about +0.04, so the Re-engine is likely forgone on this board. - The premium log: 0.30, cumulative 0.76. His funding report is the Finance Committee baseline: - fps phasing ran on his curve, and no trigger tripped. - Debt was $105.32B at EIS (81% of EV). - Conservative case: $60.9B at end-2049, back to $45B in 2053. - Upper bound: back to $45B during 2047. His 'Meet and beat' rule and mine agree: A in either column. Caveats: the pro-rata penalty allocation and the 2053 year are his inferences, not grid outputs. I keep the year internal and give no public date.

Weighing the operating head. Weighed as advice from a doctrine seat. Pope's evidence on the airplane business is Very low; her own record covers delivery, cash and IP, applied by inference. What I took: - KPI veto: checked and not invoked. There is no live problem, and 737 rate is offered only at hold. - Her point that delivery counts are not KPIs. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer give that record directly. - Ramp tempo: 860 to 940 is about one step of 5 every three years, well inside doctrine. - Supply binding order: the CFM line, structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth parts. All funded and hot through 2049. - CFM allocation: 78% of CFM's 2044 narrowbody output. We need 1,720 engines in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. No durability flag is on the record, though durability is not yet shown by the board. - Strain: 0 years, $0. The engineers feather in after the fps handover. - IP: a Solo airframe with an engine partner is the right split. - Charleston can grow the 787 without a Re-engine. Her technology-readiness fail mattered to my three-work-streams test as an unpriced input, not as a veto. No matured widebody engine can meet 2050, and UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051. Her +2-year slip prior is doctrine, and the record runs both ways (MAX 8 early; 777X and MAX 10 late). I read it as a sensitivity, not a forecast. Her 0.28 PV penalty is superseded by Malave's 0.50 on the grid's allocation. Her reading that the board carries no new-build 737 deliveries is noted. The 737 fleet and aftermarket are off the board.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Other moves.

The board carries deliveries only, so their results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record. The commitment is public; the reports are internal [BG-0043, BX-1298].

Development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Neither is priced on the board.
  • Supply base funded and hot through 2049 (private): Pope's binding order: (1) the CFM engine line, (2) long-lead airframe structures, (3) titanium forgings, (4) rare-earth parts. All four categories stay funded and hot above our rate through 2049, not just 2044. Staff are embedded at any supplier that falls behind [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. We name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing to anyone.
  • CFM allocation tracked by airframer; delivery commitments contracted for the ramp (private): In 2044 we took 1,680 of CFM's 2,148 narrowbody engines (78%). Our need rises to 1,720 in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. CFM is sole source and the code is locked, so we track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and contract delivery commitments for each ramp step [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923]. A durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step.
  • Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee; debt first, no new equity (private): Malave's report is the baseline. Debt was $105.32B at EIS 2040 (81% of EV) and is the first call on the $48.0B of operating-profit uplift over 2045-49. Planning case: solidly investment grade (debt back to $45B) by 2053, with 2047 held as upside. It is restated once, before any commitment, if deliveries or operating profit fall below the brief's path, a live problem appears, or a second development is proposed. No new equity. No dividend or buyback proposal: that is reserved to the Board, and only once the rating is solid [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Publicly we say debt first and give no rating year.
  • 787 grows from Charleston; no Re-engine launch this round (public): The 787 holds 100 a year on the board. Charleston has headroom above that [BX-1317, B-2336]. We give no Re-engine date. Internally, readiness work on the 787's next step continues without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. Pope finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 EIS [BX-1296].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety first, and NGSA's ramp after entry into service. NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce engines. The Board's twice-yearly safety review should take Wagner's NGSA ramp report together with the A320neo transition report. Nothing added this round may draw on the people or supplier slots that carry either line [AG-0038, AX-0081, AX-0015, A-0303, A-0331].
  • Liquidity and the A+/A1 rating, now with room. NGSA's cash rolled off in 2037. The Board's line stays at $5.2B, one year's FCF. An A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 would spend $1.0B a year over 2045-49, $4.2B under the line, with no overlap with NGSA development and no two-front strain. Cash is not the constraint this round. Value and widebody robustness are [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104, A-0343].
  • The widebody position, decided on proof. The A350 Re-engine is the only possible Board item. It is a staged, funded derivative of the kind the Board approves, but its case is thin: +0.89 in S1 (rivals hold) and -0.50 in S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine). It breaks even when the chance of a 787 Re-engine is 64%. In 2035 Boeing said it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service, and fps has been in service since 2040, so S2 is a live column. The Board does not press for the launch and will not stand in its way. The ExCo should decide it on its own tests and on its own read of Boeing [A-0302, AX-0019, A-0364, AX-0007, AG-0029].
  • Governance of any Board item. An A350 Re-engine is a launch above EUR 800m, so it needs a Qualified Majority. No override can carry it. At +0.89 in S1 it falls short of the $1B the Board's override review requires over hold. As a Qualified Majority item it would also trail hold by $0.50B in S2, the worst plausible column. The game's one override stays unused [AG-0049, AG-0011, AX-0008, AX-0027, AG-0026].
  • Integrity and returns. Delay Tactics are closed for the game: fps entered service in 2040, and the menu offers only none. No unpriced move may do by other means what the Board refused. Shareholder returns stay within the 30-50% payout and the AGM buyback authority, sized after the year's programme cash. There is to be no equity raise, and state money is upside only [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0034].

Expects to see. (1) The grid rows. On the Board's reading of round3.md: - NGSA hold + A350 hold: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2; - NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine: +24.26 in S1 and +22.76 in S2; - item value of the A350 Re-engine: +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2; - holding loses only $0.11B in S2, the cost of a lone 787 Re-engine. (2) The CEO's expected column, with a probability, read from the bulletin. In 2035 Boeing said it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service. fps has been in service since 2040. S2 is therefore the worst plausible column and cannot be ruled out. The A350 Re-engine has positive expected value only if the chance of S2 is below 64%. (3) Toepfer's cash case: - if launched: $1.0B a year in 2045-49, entry into service in 2050, no overlap, no strain, $4.2B of headroom; - if held: no programme cash; - the net-cash path with NGSA's bill behind it (operating profit on the brief is about $17.1B in 2045, against $8.8B in the status quo); - the payout and any buyback room under the AGM authority; - the A+/A1 headroom metrics, with the base case beside the stress case; - his added-move robustness result against his own 2035 gate (at least $1B in the expected column and not negative in the 787 Re-engine column). The Board reads +0.89 / -0.50 as failing that gate. (4) Wagner's results: - safety and quality; - the NGSA ramp after entry into service, and the A320neo transition; - his own 2035 gates: the A350F in service and the Spirit A350 packages at rate; - engineering capacity on the shared NGSA/A350 teams; - the widebody engine path for any A350 Re-engine. None is on the record, and an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 would be ready only in 2051, a year after a 2050 entry into service. (5) Overrides. None is expected. Any override should be reported with its margin over hold in both columns. (6) Confirmation of the remaining fields: - ngsa hold, with no cancel on the menu since NGSA is in service; - NGSA engine code none; - Delay Tactics none. (7) The staged widebody case the Board asked for in 2035, presented whatever the decision, including the 787 Re-engine column and the gates the ExCo recorded then. Among them: rule 3 (no A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine), which no 787 Re-engine on the record breaches. (8) A public statement that: - leads with the five pillars; - gives windows, not dates; - does not tie any widebody step to Boeing; - never mentions Delay Tactics. Where a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so. A missing piece alone is not a veto ground.

Would approve.

  • NGSA: hold. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so this is not a Board item and cancelling is no longer on the menu. NGSA engine code none: the fitted engines (CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce) stand.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold. This is the default and is never vetoed. The row is +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2, and it gives up only $0.11B in S2.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch (entry into service 2050), if every one of these conditions holds: - the CEO's expected column is S1, where the item adds +0.89; - its worst plausible column is S2 at -0.50, inside the Board's $2B loss line; - spend is $1.0B a year over 2045-49 against the $5.2B line, with no overlap with NGSA, no strain and one launch in the round; - rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record; - Toepfer and Wagner pass it on their own tests, with no override; - Wagner confirms the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate, and names the engine path; - it carries a Qualified Majority as a launch above EUR 800m.
  • Delay Tactics: none. This is the only value on the menu. The question has been closed since fps entered service in 2040.

Would veto.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch where the CEO's expected column is S2. Ground: downside. The item does not gain in his expected scenario: it is -0.50 against hold. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch carried by an override of a CFO or Wagner soft veto. An example is Toepfer's added-move gate, which +0.89 / -0.50 fails. Ground: governance, because the override fails the Board's review. +0.89 is under $1B over hold in S1, and it trails hold by $0.50B in S2, the worst plausible column of a Qualified Majority item. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch that carries a binding ExCo veto the CEO neither respected nor overrode as the rule allows, or a red-line flag he neither struck nor rebutted. Ground: governance. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch that Wagner fails on safety, quality, the NGSA or A320 ramp shield, or a supply crunch. Ground: safety and ramp. The Board accepts no override of these tests. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Delay Tactics value other than none, or any NGSA cancel, should either appear. Neither is on the brief's menu. Integrity and reactive cancellation would be the grounds. Acceptable alternatives: none and hold.

Recommendations.

  • Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and on an explicit read of Boeing. Put a probability on S2 and reason it from the bulletin. In 2035 Boeing said it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service, and fps has been in service since 2040. The item breaks even at a 64% chance of S2: it is worth about +0.40 in expectation at 35% and about +0.20 at 50%. If Toepfer's added-move gate fails it, the right answer is hold. The Board will not read that as a lost opportunity: the item is worth at most $0.89B, and the Board would not accept an override to carry it.
  • If the ExCo launches the A350 Re-engine, treat it as a commitment to entry into service in 2050. - The Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) should run an annual cash gate at $1.0B a year over 2045-49. - Cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. A 787 Re-engine launched in 2045 or 2050 cannot enter service before 2050, so no Boeing move left in this game is a ground to cancel. - The write-off would be $5B x years elapsed / 5.
  • Engine path for any A350 Re-engine. Rolls-Royce is the incumbent on the A350, but no widebody engine for a re-engine is on the record. Rolls-Royce says it spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched in 2045 would be ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 entry into service. The board does not price this. Wagner should still name the engine, its readiness and the fallback. The engine path is not a veto ground on its own unless Wagner fails the launch on production readiness.
  • Safety and ramp. The twice-yearly safety review should take Wagner's NGSA ramp report together with the A320neo transition report. Any widebody engineering assigned to an A350 Re-engine must come from neither NGSA in-service support nor the NGSA ramp. A quality or supply issue on either line comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line.
  • Returns and rating. NGSA's bill is behind the company. The CFO should show: - the payout within the 30-50% policy; - any room for a further buyback under the 18-month AGM authority, sized after the year's programme cash, with the A350 Re-engine first if it is launched; - the base case beside the stress case; - the A+/A1 headroom metrics. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State support stays upside only.
  • The briefing objective. The 60/40 edge is not met: narrowbody share is 57% in 2045 and 53% from 2049, on the long-run split. No order on this menu moves narrowbody share, and the A350 Re-engine is widebody only. The Board will not trade value or integrity for the objective. Defend the edge with NGSA ramp execution, deliveries and customer support. No unpriced move should recreate Delay Tactics by other means: - supply agreements stay sized to Airbus's own needs; - hiring never targets rival teams; - pricing stays within ordinary competition. The ECSC should review all three this year.
  • Unpriced other moves. In the real company, any commitment above EUR 300m is a reserved matter, for example an NGSA derivative or a new A220 variant. Present such a move as a study or a staged case with its own cash line, not as a launch in public. Keep technology work for the generation after NGSA as funded research and technology, not a programme. The board prices none of this.
  • Public statement. - Lead with the five pillars and the NGSA ramp. - If the A350 Re-engine is launched, give a window, not a date, and make no reference to Boeing. - If it is held, say the A350 family remains the focus and commit to nothing either way. - Never mention Delay Tactics. The Board vets the final text.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. It is 2045. NGSA has been in service since 2037 and its cash is behind us. Do we keep the A350 at Do Nothing, the default (+23.37 in S1, +23.26 in S2)? Or do we launch the A350 Re-engine for entry into service around 2050 (+24.26 / +22.76, so the launch alone is worth +0.89 / -0.50)? To launch, it must pass all of these: - the five pillars; - the company's $1B launch test; - Toepfer's added-move gate from 2035; - Wagner's 2035 gates: the A350F, the Spirit A350 work packages, a widebody engine ready by entry into service, and no draw on the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition; - a Qualified Majority of the Board.

Situation. Round 3, decision year 2045. Public record (bulletin) - Boeing. fps launched in 2030 on the 10-year path and has been in service since 2040 on CFM. No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase is on the record. - In 2035 Boeing said "We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service" and "We're not starting a second development alongside this one". It also said debt reduction and a solid investment-grade rating stay its priorities. - fps has now been in service for five years, so that look is due. S2 is a live column. - Airbus. NGSA has been in service since 2037, three years ahead of fps. It flies CFM, P&W and RR (code 7). - Engines. - CFM ducted engine: in service since 2036. - P&W-RR Joint Venture: formed in 2035, with GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded in. Its engine has been in service since 2036. - CFM-Embraer: in service since 2037. - GEnx upgrade for 787 customers: in service since 2033. - Rolls-Royce: "There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine." No widebody engine for an A350 Re-engine is on the record. Red lines.

  • The five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). Every order and every public word must stand on them. They are never overridden and never traded for PV [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 1: met. NGSA entered service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. Nothing in 2045 re-times it.
  • Rules 2 and 7: our own clock. There is no NGSA cancel, and none is on the menu. Boeing's 2035 statement on the 787 neither launches nor stops our widebody step. No public word ties any widebody step to Boeing.
  • Rule 3: not binding today, because no 787 Re-engine is on the record. If Boeing launches one this round (S2), the A350 Re-engine is closed for 2050.
  • Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed for the game, and none is the only value. No unpriced move may do the same by other means: - supply agreements stay sized to our own needs; - hiring never targets rival teams; - pricing stays within ordinary competition. Delay Tactics are never named in public.
  • Rule 6: at most one launch per round. A 2045 A350 Re-engine has no overlap with NGSA, so this is met.
  • The company A350 Re-engine launch test: at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile section 6). Doctrine default: take hold when it is within $1B of the best row in my expected column.
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried into this round. It vetoes an A350 Re-engine launch: - where my expected column is S2; - carried by an override of a Toepfer or Wagner soft veto; - carrying a binding ExCo veto I neither respected nor overrode as the rule allows, or a red-line flag I neither struck nor rebutted; - that Wagner fails on safety, quality, the NGSA or A320 ramp shield, or a supply crunch. It also vetoes any Delay Tactics value other than none, and any NGSA cancel.
  • The Board's ring-fence: nothing added may draw on the people or supplier slots that carry the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition [AX-0015, A-0303, A-0331].
  • Override budget: one per game, unused, and none planned. It cannot carry the A350 Re-engine: +0.89 is under $1B in S1, and it trails hold by $0.50B in S2. It is never used against the pillars, a red line or Wagner's safety, quality, ramp or supply results. I have no override against the Board.
  • Capital: - the $5.2B line; - the 30-50% payout; - buybacks within the AGM authority, sized after the year's programme cash; - no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis; - state money upside only [AX-0022, AX-0001].
  • If launched, the A350 Re-engine is cancelled only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B.
  • Disclosure: - no internal long-term-plan targets [AX-0005]; - windows, not dates; - no widebody step tied to Boeing; - never Delay Tactics; - the Board vets the text [AX-0004].

Initial lean. My lean is plan A, the company default: - NGSA: hold; - NGSA engine code: none; - A350 Re-engine: hold; - Delay Tactics: none. That gives +23.37 in S1, my expected column at about 60%, and +23.26 in S2 at about 40%. There is no Board item. Expected PV is about $23.33B. Why, in the order I am paid to protect - Five pillars. Neither option tests them. Hold adds nothing to review [AX-0073, AX-0081]. - The ramp. The job this round is the NGSA ramp after entry into service and the A320neo transition, "disciplined and controlled" [AX-0010]. Hold puts no new demand on shared teams or supplier slots, which keeps the Board's ring-fence intact. - The Airbus of the 2030s. That aircraft is delivered: NGSA has been in service since 2037. The widebody derivative is where my instinct pulls, as with the A330neo, re-engined late and cheaply [A-0090, A-0091]. On this grid it does not clear the company's own tests: - At +0.89 it falls short of the $1B launch test even if Boeing never moves. My decision therefore rests on our tests, not on a read of Boeing, which keeps us on our own clock. - It fails Toepfer's 2035 added-move gate on both counts. - No widebody engine ready by 2050 is on the record. An UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051. - The company doctrine had already named 2035-37 as the last A350 Re-engine window. - The Board. It approves hold as readily as a launch, and no override could carry the launch. Robustness. Hold's worst column (+23.26) is better than the launch's (+22.76). The expected cost of holding, about $0.33B at 40% for S2, is inside the $1B doctrine default. It is not a premium, and no PV is traded for the 60/40 objective. My read of Boeing (it is not decisive). In 2035 Boeing said it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service, and fps has now been in service for five years. Against that, Boeing has kept to one development at a time and puts debt reduction first. I put S2 at about 40%, within a range of 30-50%. S2 stays the worst plausible column. What would change my lean. Toepfer and Wagner would both have to pass the launch on their own tests, and the launch would have to clear $1B in my expected column without going negative in S2. This grid cannot show that. A safety, quality or supply issue on either line would only strengthen hold. Public line - The five pillars first. - NGSA in service and ramping in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family. - The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We commit to nothing either way. - A more sovereign European supply chain. - Our financial framework, in Toepfer's register. - Zero-for-zero trade. - Windows, not dates. Nothing on Boeing, and nothing on Delay Tactics.

Production readiness: a widebody engine ready by the A350 Re-engine's entry into service, plan B (a soft-veto ground; not priced on the board)Launch an A350 Re-engine only with a named engine on the record that is ready at or before the airframe's entry into service. This is the discipline of rule 1 for NGSA (no entry into service before the technology is ready) applied to the widebodyfailLaunched in 2045, the A350 Re-engine enters service in 2050 (launch + 5). The engine: - Rolls-Royce is the A350's incumbent with the Trent XWB [A-0253]. It says: 'There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine.' - An UltraFan WB launched alongside us in 2045 would be ready in 2051 (launch + 6), one year after our entry into service. - The other new engines on the record do not fit. The GEnx upgrade serves 787 customers (in service since 2033), and the CFM ducted, CFM-Embraer and Joint Venture engines are narrowbody engines. - No second widebody engine is on the record, and no Trent XWB derivative with a ready date. There is no fallback. So a 2050 entry into service has no engine. The real window opens in 2051 at the earliest, which the board's launch + 5 Re-engine cannot represent. The gap is built into the clocks; 2045 is not special. If Rolls-Royce launches only alongside a Re-engine, a 2050 launch (entry into service 2055) meets an engine ready in 2056. The gap closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe. Grid margin against the best option that passes (A, hold): +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2, under $1B in both columns.
Engine maturity slipIf the brief reports one, re-time so that entry into service stays at or after the new technology-ready year; never cancelnot applicableNo slip is reported, and all of NGSA's engines are in service. The A350 Re-engine's problem is not a slip: no engine has been committed in time (see the readiness test).
NGSA engines and supply; engine code (a recommendation, not a veto ground)CFM in the set plus at least one second maker; flag any supply watch itempassThe only code on the menu is None. The fitted set, CFM + P&W + RR, stands and meets my rule with three sources. The CFM ducted and P&W-RR Joint Venture engines have been in service since 2036, and NGSA since 2037. Narrowbody engine shares in 2044 were CFM 53.7%, P&W 23.2% and RR 23.2%. No shortfall is reported, so I can confirm delivery on the board but not from line data. Watch items: 1. P&W said in 2035 that its GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts, shops and engineers. That priority now sits inside the Joint Venture. 2. Our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both ride on the one Joint Venture engine, since GTF2 and UltraFan NB were folded into it. A single Joint Venture problem would therefore hit two of our three engine sources. CFM is the backstop.
Integrity limits and Delay Tactics, rules 4 and 5, for the ECSC review (a pillars result)Supply agreements sized to our own NGSA and A320neo needs and never over-contracted; hiring that never targets rival teams; pricing within ordinary competition; Delay Tactics nonepassDelay Tactics: none, the only value on the menu. The window closed when fps entered service in 2040, and no move was ordered in round 1 or round 2. Supply: the agreements were sized for the ramp to the 2039 peak of 1,260 aircraft. Our needs fall to 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. The ECSC should resize the engine, wing-package, titanium and rare-earth agreements to those needs. Holding slots at the peak while our needs fall would be over-contracting, which is what a bottleneck looks like. Hiring: open European hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support and any approved widebody work, never aimed at rival teams. Pricing is Faury's call. From my side, no supply or hiring lever is used to do what Delay Tactics would do.
Rule 1 and NGSA readiness (red line)No NGSA entry into service before the 2035 technology-ready yearpassNGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Nothing in 2045 re-times it: ngsa is hold only, and no cancel is on the menu.
Boeing Rate IncreaseNo programme reaction to Boeing's rate; we keep our own disciplined rampnot applicableNo Rate Increase is on the record, and the order existed only in 2030.

My tests come from my role, not from anything I have said on record. Confidence: Very low. I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, engine code none, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Safety and quality: pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality, supply or ramp problem. NGSA flies CFM, P&W and RR. The CFM ducted and Joint Venture engines have been in service since 2036, and no shortfall is reported. Watch items: P&W's first call for its GTF fleet, and our P&W and RR slots both riding on one Joint Venture engine. CFM backstops. Ramp: pass. Our narrowbody deliveries fall from 1,260 in 2039 to 1,060 from 2049 as share settles. That is the market, not a ramp problem, but supply agreements must be resized to those needs, never held at the peak. A350 Re-engine: capacity passes, with no overlap, $0 strain and one launch. The A350F and Spirit pass on the game proxy only. The brief is silent, so I cannot confirm either. Readiness fails. The A350 flies Rolls-Royce, which spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched this year is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 entry into service. No other widebody engine is on the record. The engine leads the airframe. That is a soft veto, binding: the launch is +0.89 / -0.50 against hold, under $1B in both columns, so no override carries it. It moves the window, not the idea. Re-test once an engine is committed that is ready by entry into service.

Guillaume Faury decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision: the company default. NGSA hold, engine code none (the only code on the menu), A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. - Grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2. - No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item. 1. Red-line and pillars screen (the team rule's first step) Neither option breaks a company red line or the five pillars. - Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. - Rules 2 and 7: there is no NGSA cancel on the menu. - Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, and none is the only value. - Rule 6 is met: a 2045 A350 Re-engine would be one launch with zero overlap with NGSA. - Wagner confirms safety and quality pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem and no inject. Both options therefore go on to the colleagues' tests. 2. Survivors - Plan A (hold) passes all of Toepfer's tests: peak cash $0, robustness +23.26 in the worst column, net cash and rating proxy. It passes all of Wagner's: safety and quality, ramp shield, engine code, integrity, rule 1. - Plan B (A350 Re-engine, entry into service 2050) fails two binding soft vetoes: 1. Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B launch test. The item is +0.89 in S1, $0.11B short of $1B, and -0.50 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column. 2. Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine on the record is ready by 2050: Rolls-Royce spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine, an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback. Neither failure is a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result. Both are soft vetoes. - Override. None is available. B's margin over A, the best passing option, is +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2: under $1B in both columns. The Board's override review would also fail it, as a Qualified Majority item that trails hold in its worst column. The game's single override stays unused. I concur on the merits in any case. A is the only survivor. It is also the doctrine default: within $1B of the best grid row in my expected column, a $0.89B gap in S1. 3. Tie-breaks all point to A: less strain, a later capex start, and fewer Board items (0 against 1). 4. My read of Boeing, and the expected column Expected column: S1, at about 60%. S2 at about 40%, within a 30-50% range. - For S2: in 2035 Boeing said "We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service". fps has been in service since 2040. Boeing also said the 787 "has room to grow from our Charleston capacity". - Against S2: "We're not starting a second development alongside this one", "Doing less and doing it better", and debt reduction with a solid investment-grade rating as its priority. S2 stays the worst plausible column. At 40%, the launch is worth about +0.33 in expectation (+0.40 at 35%, +0.20 at 50%). It breaks even at 64%. Even at 0% for S2 it is only +0.89, under the $1B test. The decision rests on our own tests, not on our read of Boeing. That keeps us on our own clock and ties no widebody step to Boeing. 5. The staged widebody case the Board asked for in 2035, gate by gate | Gate | Result | |---|---| | Rule 3 | Met. No 787 Re-engine is on the record. | | A350F in service and Spirit A350 packages at rate | Passes on the game proxy only. The record is silent after 2025 and Wagner has no line data, so the Board's condition that he confirm both is not met. | | Widebody engine ready by entry into service | Fails. The gap is built into the clocks: an engine launched alongside the airframe is ready at launch + 6, the airframe enters service at launch + 5. | | Grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 column) | Fails at +0.89 / -0.50. | | Peak cash | Passes: $1.0B a year over 2045-49, $4.2B under the $5.2B line. | | Qualified Majority | Required. | The option to wait: on Toepfer's reconstruction (an inference), a like-for-like 2050 launch is worth about +0.6 in a rivals-hold column. It is still under $1B. A 787 Re-engine in 2045 would close it under rule 3, and the company already named 2035-37 as the last window. The case stays staged and is not launched. 6. Board-gate line There is no Board item this round. For the record, the hold package: - five pillars: pass; - Toepfer: pass, with a peak programme cash of $0 against the $5.2B line; - Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the ramp shield and integrity; - grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2. The Board says hold is never vetoed. 7. Cost and objective - Holding gives up $0.89B in S1, about $0.33B in expectation at 40% for S2. It gains $0.50B against B in S2. - Plan A's worst column (+23.26) is better than plan B's (+22.76), so it meets the robustness preference. - No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective, which no order on this menu can move. 8. Operating actions - Supply agreements are resized down to our own falling needs (Wagner). - The Joint Venture engine is carried as a watch item, with CFM as backstop. - Buybacks are sized after programme cash (Toepfer). - Studies stay studies, below EUR 300m each until a Board gate.

Weighing the CFO. Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence), and I weighed them as such. His arithmetic matches the brief. Plan A: passes everything. - Peak programme cash $0 against the $5.2B line. - Robustness +23.37 / +23.26. - Net-cash proxy positive through 2049 in both the base case (+$43.6B) and the stress case (+$3.7B), with the full buyback. - No Board items. Plan B: - Passes peak cash ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom), rule 6 (zero overlap, one launch) and the plan-level robustness test (positive in both columns). - Fails his added-move gate, the company's $1B launch test: +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2. Soft veto, binding. - His expected-value schedule confirms my figures: +0.33 at 40% for S2, break-even at 64%. Even at 0% the item is +0.89, under $1B. - His override arithmetic confirms that no override can carry B, under the team rule or the Board's review. Accepted: the veto is binding, no override is allowed, and I agree on the merits. I also adopted: - his rule that buybacks are sized after programme cash, the trim he would make first under stress; - his staged sizing of the studies, below EUR 300m each and about EUR 0.9bn in aggregate; - his option-to-wait estimate (about +0.6 for a 2050 launch, still under $1B); - his finance line for the public statement. He uses proxies he labels as inference: operating profit for EBIT Adjusted, an FCF/EBIT ratio of 0.667, and net cash at or above zero standing in for the agency thresholds, which are not in his record. I take them as indicative.

Weighing the operating head. Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence), and I weighed them as such. Where his record is silent, he says so. Results: - Safety and quality: pass on both options. It is a pillars result, but there is no line data after 2025, so it rests on the brief reporting no issue. - NGSA ramp shield and A320neo transition: pass. A ramp result. - Supply crunch: not applicable, as none is reported. - Engineering capacity and rule 6: pass for B, on two conditions: a named widebody team ring-fenced from NGSA and the A320neo, and the studies staying studies. - A350F and Spirit absorption: pass on the game proxy only. The record is silent, so he cannot confirm the Board's condition from data. - Production readiness: fail for B. No widebody engine is ready by a 2050 entry into service. UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback. Soft veto, binding. It is not a safety, quality, ramp or supply result, and it moves the window rather than closing the idea. - Engine code: None only; the fitted CFM + P&W + RR set stands. - Integrity and Delay Tactics: pass. - Rule 1: pass. Accepted: B's margin over hold (+0.89 / -0.50) is under $1B, so no override is allowed. On the merits, an entry into service without a ready engine is the very discipline we hold NGSA to under rule 1. I adopted: - his finding that the supply agreements must be resized down from the 2039 peak (1,260) to our own falling needs (1,140 in 2045, 1,060 from 2049). Holding slots at the peak would be over-contracting; - his Joint Venture watch item, with CFM as backstop; - his condition that the studies stay studies and draw on no NGSA or A320neo engineers; - his request that both ramp reports go together to the safety review.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), at about 60%. S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) is at about 40%, within a 30-50% range, and is the worst plausible column. - For S2: Boeing said in 2035 it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service. fps has been in service since 2040, and Boeing has said the 787 has room to grow. - Against S2: Boeing's one-development-at-a-time discipline and its priority on debt reduction and investment grade. The decision does not depend on this read: the launch fails the $1B test even at 0% for S2.

Best grid plan in that scenario. In S1, NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine scores +24.26, against +23.37 for NGSA hold + A350 hold. The Re-engine row fails two binding soft vetoes: Toepfer's added-move gate (the company's $1B launch test) and Wagner's production readiness (no widebody engine ready by 2050). Its margin of +0.89 / -0.50 over hold allows no override. The best surviving plan, and the doctrine default within $1B, is NGSA hold + A350 hold: +23.37 / +23.26. It is also the best plan against S2.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. No premium is paid. Hold is the only plan that survives both colleagues' tests, so it is the highest-grid survivor. It is also within the $1B doctrine default of the best S1 row: the gap is $0.89B, or about $0.33B in expectation at 40% for S2. Hold is the better plan in S2 (+0.50) and in the worst column. No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective, which no order on this menu can move.

Answers to the Board.

  • Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and on an explicit read of Boeing, with a probability on S2. Taken up. My read of Boeing puts S2 at about 40%, within 30-50%. - For S2: the 2035 "look at its next step once this airplane is in service" (fps in service since 2040), and the 787's Charleston room to grow. - Against S2: "not starting a second development alongside this one", and Boeing's priority on debt reduction. At 40% the item is worth about +0.33 (+0.40 at 35%, +0.20 at 50%), and it breaks even at 64%. Two binding soft vetoes fail it: Toepfer's added-move gate and Wagner's production readiness. The right answer is hold, as the Board says. The decision does not depend on the probability: even at 0% the item is +0.89, under $1B.
  • If launched, treat the A350 Re-engine as a commitment to entry into service in 2050, with an Audit Committee cash gate at $1.0B a year, the cancel rule and the write-off schedule. Not applicable: we hold. The governance is recorded for any future staged case: - an annual Audit Committee cash gate at the programme's yearly spend; - cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B; - a write-off of bill x years elapsed / development years, shown in reported EBIT and never adjusted away.
  • Wagner should name the engine path for any A350 Re-engine, its readiness and the fallback. Taken up. Wagner named it: - Rolls-Royce is the A350 incumbent and spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine. - An UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, one year after a 2050 entry into service. - No Trent XWB derivative with a ready date and no second widebody engine is on the record, so there is no fallback. He fails the launch on production readiness, a soft veto. That is not a safety, quality, ramp or supply result. Together with Toepfer's gate, it makes hold the decision. Any re-test requires an engine committed and ready by the airframe's entry into service. Talks with Rolls-Royce stay at technical-readiness level, with no commitment.
  • Safety and ramp: take Wagner's NGSA ramp report together with the A320neo transition report at the twice-yearly safety review. No widebody engineering from NGSA in-service support or the ramp. Quality or supply issues come to the Board first. Taken up in full. - The two reports go to the safety review as one package. - No widebody engineering is assigned this round. - Wagner's Joint Venture watch item goes to the review: our P&W and RR positions both depend on the one Joint Venture engine, with CFM as backstop. - Any quality or supply issue on either line comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. - The supply agreements are resized down to our own falling needs.
  • Returns and rating: the payout within 30-50%, buyback room under the AGM authority sized after programme cash, the base case beside the stress case, the A+/A1 headroom metrics, no equity raise, no dividend cut outside a crisis, state support upside only. Taken up on Toepfer's schedule. - With no programme cash in 2045, buyback room after a 50% payout is about $5.1B in the base case and $2.4B in the stress case. - The EUR 5bn three-year programme (about $1.83B a year) is fundable in every hold case. - The net-cash proxy at end-2049 is about +$43.6B in the base case and +$3.7B in the stress case, with the full buyback. - Buybacks are sized after programme cash and trimmed first under stress. - The agencies' thresholds are not in our record, so we use Toepfer's proxy: net cash at or above zero every year, and programme spend within one year's FCF. - The share price is not in our record, so the 10% AGM cap is not expressed in dollars. - No equity raise, no dividend cut, and state money upside only.
  • The briefing objective: the 60/40 edge is not met, and no value or integrity is to be traded for it. Defend it with NGSA ramp execution, deliveries and support, and have the ECSC review supply sizing, hiring and pricing. Taken up. The objective is not met (57% in 2045, 53% from 2049), and no PV is traded for it. We defend the edge with ramp execution, deliveries and customer support. The ECSC reviews all three integrity limits this year: - supply agreements resized down to our own needs, never held at the peak; - hiring that never targets rival teams; - pricing within ordinary competition.
  • Unpriced other moves: anything above EUR 300m is a reserved matter. Present it as a study or staged case with its own cash line, not as a launch in public, and keep next-generation technology as funded research and technology. Taken up. - The NGSA derivative and A220 variant studies each stay below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate. - Research and technology for the generation after NGSA stays inside the Board-approved R&D budget. - In aggregate, about EUR 0.9bn over the study phase. - Anything crossing EUR 300m comes to the Board, and a launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority. - None is presented as a launch in public, and none draws on the NGSA or A320neo engineers.
  • Public statement: lead with the five pillars and the NGSA ramp. If held, say the A350 family remains the focus and commit to nothing either way. No reference to Boeing, never Delay Tactics, and the Board vets the text. Taken up. The statement: - leads with the five pillars and the disciplined and controlled NGSA ramp alongside the A320neo; - gives windows, not dates; - says the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus, commits to nothing either way, and decides on our own technology and industrial clock; - makes no reference to Boeing and no mention of Delay Tactics; - gives no internal targets. It is submitted for the Board's vetting.

Objective. The briefing goal, "Defend 60/40 edge; Protect A320 family", is scored by the GM and never part of the payoff. - Protect the A320 family: met. Narrowbody share was 60% in every year before NGSA entered service. - Defend the 60/40 edge: not met. Share was 62% in 2040, is 57% in 2045 and will be 53% from 2049, as share settles on the long-run 47/53 split. No order on this menu moves narrowbody share; the A350 Re-engine is widebody only. Delay Tactics are closed, and no unpriced move may do the same work by other means. I trade no PV and no integrity for the objective. We defend the edge with NGSA ramp execution, deliveries and customer support, and the ECSC reviews supply sizing, hiring and pricing this year.

Predictions. Boeing, this round - About 60%: it holds, with no 787 Re-engine. - About 40%: it launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). That would close our A350 Re-engine under rule 3 for 2050. - No public Boeing move aimed at NGSA, and no new narrowbody programme announced. Engines - No new widebody engine launched by Rolls-Royce without a Re-engine. - CFM ducted and the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine keep delivering to the NGSA ramp, with no slip or shortfall reported. - Narrowbody engine shares hold near CFM 54% / P&W 23% / RR 23%. Our board path if nobody moves - Narrowbody share 57% in 2045 and 53% from 2049. Widebody share flat at 41.2%. - ΔPV +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2. 2050 round - If Boeing holds, the A350 Re-engine returns only as a staged case. I expect it to fail the $1B test (about +0.6 on Toepfer's discount) unless an engine is committed ahead of the airframe. - If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine, the case is closed.

Expected ΔPV. +23.33 $B (board after the round: +23.37 $B)

Other moves.

  • Resize the NGSA and A320 supply agreements down to our own needs (public): This is Wagner's finding, and I adopt it. The long-term agreements for engines from all three makers, the wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths were sized for the ramp to the 2039 peak of 1,260 narrowbody deliveries. Our own needs fall to 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. The ECSC resizes each agreement to those needs this year. Holding slots at the peak while our needs fall would be over-contracting, and we will not do it. Any agreement committing more than EUR 300m comes to the Board. In public we present this as a more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0331, A-0457].
  • Twice-yearly safety review: the NGSA ramp report and the A320neo transition report, taken together (private): Wagner reports the two lines to the Board's safety review as one package [AG-0038, AX-0015]. No widebody engineering is assigned from NGSA in-service support, the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. Any quality or supply issue on either line goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. Wagner flagged one watch item, and the review carries it: our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both depend on the one Joint Venture engine, and P&W's GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts, shops and engineers. CFM is the backstop. A Joint Venture shortfall would lead to a supply response through CFM, never to an NGSA re-timing or a cancel.
  • A350 Re-engine kept as a staged widebody case, with gates for any re-test (private): We do not launch in 2045. We re-test only if all of these hold: 1. no 787 Re-engine is on the record (rule 3); 2. a named widebody engine is committed and ready at or before the airframe's entry into service. Today an UltraFan WB launched alongside us would be one year late; 3. Wagner confirms from line data that the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate; 4. the item is worth at least $1B over hold in the expected column and is not negative in the 787 Re-engine column; 5. peak cash stays under the $5.2B line; 6. it carries a Qualified Majority. On Toepfer's discount, a like-for-like 2050 launch is worth about +0.6, so I do not expect it to pass. The company already named 2035-37 as the last window. Talks with Rolls-Royce, the A350 incumbent, stay at technical-readiness level, with no commitment and no money above the study line.
  • Staged studies outside the board: an NGSA derivative, an A220 variant, and research and technology for the generation after NGSA (private): Each runs as a staged study with its own cash line, using Toepfer's sizing: - the NGSA derivative and the A220 variant each stay below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate; - research and technology stays inside the annual R&D budget the Board approves; - in aggregate, about EUR 0.9bn (about $1.0B) over the study phase, roughly $0.3B a year. Anything that crosses EUR 300m comes to the Board as its own item, and a launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority [A-0298, AG-0049]. In line with Wagner's condition, none becomes a second programme on the engineers who carry the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. None is presented as a launch in public.
  • ECSC integrity review of supply sizing, hiring and pricing (private): The ECSC reviews three things this year: - supply agreements sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and resized down as those needs fall; - open European hiring that never targets rival teams; - pricing within ordinary competition. No unpriced move may do by other means what a Delay Tactics move would do. Delay Tactics stay at none, the only value on the menu, and no move was ordered in this game [A-0299, A-0474, AG-0053].
  • Capital allocation inside the policy, with buybacks sized after programme cash (private): These are Toepfer's figures. - The payout stays within 30-50%. - Buybacks stay within the 18-month AGM authority and are sized after the year's programme cash. - With no programme cash in 2045, buyback room after a 50% payout is about $5.1B in the base case and $2.4B in the stress case. - The EUR 5bn three-year programme, about $1.83B a year, is fundable in every hold case. - No equity raise, and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State money is upside only [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035, A-0348]. The agencies' A+/A1 thresholds are not in our record, so we use Toepfer's proxy: net cash at or above zero every year. On that proxy, hold stays positive through 2049 in both the base and the stress case.
  • Open European engineering recruitment continues (public): Ordinary public hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support, the A320neo transition and the staged studies. It never draws on ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year [A-0366, A-0485].
  • Zero-for-zero trade advocacy (public): We continue to press, through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic, for a tariff-free regime in civil aerospace [AX-0088].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality in service come first. The Ducted has been in service since 2036 and Embraer since 2037, alongside the LEAP fleet on the 737, the A320neo, fps and NGSA. The safety question is now in-service durability and fleet safety, not a ready date. Ali should report on test and field evidence (turned on and turned off, not analysis), with gate calls made cross-functionally alongside Safran's engineers. Any safety or durability flag reaches us before orders, and durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn. Nothing on this round's menu answers a flag; it is an operating matter [CG-0009, CG-0018, CX-0009, CX-0012, CX-0208, CX-0658, CX-0633].
  • Hold everything is the only plan that bounds the downside. In the brief's single column, S1 (rivals hold), hold is -38.29. Against hold, the Open Fan is -30.56: its $8B bill plus about $22.56B of wait penalty. Open Fan + Lobby is -21.89: a $9B bill plus about $12.89B of penalty. Both lose more than their own bill. On our reading of the rules (inference), either would also take 'Dominate NB engines' below 50% in 2045 and 2050. That objective is met today: worst year 51.1% (2040), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050 [CG-0017, CG-0022, CG-0032, CX-0205, CX-0493].
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, and say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' cannot be met in this game. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 at the earliest. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056. The board gives the Open Fan no share gain, so on this dashboard it is only bill and wait penalty. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel. The RISE allowance stays unused, and RISE is never cancelled for cost [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0147, CX-0174, CX-0214, CX-0398, CG-0065].
  • Keep the balance sheet and the payout whole. No new R&D or strain is needed. The 2030 package is complete: Ducted R&D of $4B and $2B of strain, already booked. That leaves the full ~$2.5B a year of room after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow. Premium $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game; RISE allowance $0 of $15B [CX-0645, CG-0063, CG-0022, CG-0012, CG-0002, CG-0064].
  • Earn the installed base by delivering. Narrowbody codes are locked: both new airframes are in service and the Joint Venture is formed. What remains in our control is LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares, delivered on time to every airframer. We also continue a CFM engine offered on standard terms, with any price or terms set jointly with Safran. There is no reaction or price cut on rival news. Book low, on the one column [CX-0529, CX-0542, CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0184, CX-0609, CX-0564, CX-0248].

Expects to see. (1) expected_scenario S1, with predictions weighting S1 at 1.0. It is the brief's only column and the only plausible one. (2) Every alternative against hold, from the brief's grid: - hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%); - Open Fan: -68.85, or -30.56 against hold, which is the $8B bill plus about $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty; - Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18, or -21.89 against hold, which is the $9B bill plus about $12.89B of 20 pp penalty, with no added strain implied; - Lobby beside an Open Fan: +8.67; - Lobby alone: about -1.00.
