Would approve.

  • hold on every field (ducted, Open Fan, Embraer partnership, emissions lobbying, genx). It is the best grid plan in S1, the only column, at -38.29, with premium $0. A hold is not a Board item and is never vetoed. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx menus offer hold only this round, so nothing we launched is at risk.
  • No Board item on this round's menu passes our tests. The only non-hold values are Open Fan: launch and emissions lobbying: launch, and both lose more than their bill in the only column. We say so now so the package is not built around one.
  • Unpriced other_moves that serve the customer and safety. These are recommendations, not Board items: - in-service durability reporting on the Ducted and LEAP, cross-functional with Safran's engineers; - LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time to every airframer, with spares never crowding out OE; - RISE continued whole as technology, 50-50, with no date; - a private CFM offer on standard terms, with any price or terms set jointly with Safran; - no public reaction or price cut on rival or Joint Venture news.

Would veto.

  • Open Fan: launch (alone). Item value against hold in S1 (expected and only plausible column) is -30.56, against an $8B bill. That is about $22.56B of wait penalty beyond the bill, so it fails the bounded-downside test. - Airframer path (hard rule 2): it fails (a). NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) entered service long before a 2055 Open Fan, so the penalty applies. - The RISE allowance: it fails (b). The cost against the best non-RISE plan (hold) is $30.56B, above the $15B allowance. - Objective: it buys nothing toward 'Introduce the Open Fan' (ready 2055, not by 2050). On our reading (inference) it would break 'Dominate NB' in 2045 and 2050. - Not grounds: the payout floor would pass ($0.8B a year), and holding is not a RISE cancel. - CFM parity rule (Safran consent): a RISE product with no airframer path is outside joint practice, so it would need a stated reason why Safran would agree. None is on the record. Acceptable: hold.
  • Open Fan: launch with emissions lobbying: launch. The pair is -21.89 against hold in S1: a $9B bill plus about $12.89B of 20 pp wait penalty. It fails the bounded-downside and airframer-path tests. - The RISE allowance: $21.89B exceeds the $15B allowance, and exceeds the allowance plus the $2.0B round cap by $4.89B. - Lobby: it adds +8.67 beside an Open Fan, but it passes only with a live Open Fan, so it falls with the vetoed one; we would veto the two together. - CFM parity rule: Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but this is moot. Acceptable: hold on both.
  • emissions lobbying: launch without an Open Fan. On its own it does nothing on the board, so it is about -1.00 (its $1B bill; not on the grid, computed by us). It fails 'paid for the risk' and the rule that Lobby goes only with a live Open Fan. Acceptable: hold.
  • Any premium above $0 not tied to a grid plan, or above $2.0B less a declared RISE allowance. Any use of the RISE allowance outside the airframer-path test: every Open Fan route waits on this grid, so the allowance cannot be used this round or in 2050.

Recommendations.

  • Safety and quality in service. Ali should report the in-service durability and safety of the Ducted (since 2036), Embraer (2037) and the LEAP fleet: - on test and field evidence, turned on and turned off, not analysis; - with gate calls made by the one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, alongside Safran's engineers. Any flag reaches us before the next round's orders, together with its fleet action (inspection, shop visit, spares). Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn.
  • Hold everything. Show both Open Fan rows against hold in S1, with the wait penalty broken out: - Open Fan: -30.56, which is the $8B bill plus $22.56B of penalty; - Open Fan + Lobby: -21.89, which is the $9B bill plus $12.89B of penalty. Also state the effect on 'Dominate NB', which is met today (51.1% worst year). On our reading (inference) an Open Fan would take it below 50% in 2045 and 2050. Nothing is ordered only because a rival moved.
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP and the fleet, and a product follows only when an airframer and its airlines want one. Say plainly in objective_note that 'Introduce the Open Fan' cannot be met in this game: ready no earlier than 2055 from this round, and 2060 from 2050, after the 2056 window. The RISE allowance stays unused. RISE is never cancelled for cost, and holding the Open Fan is not a cancel.
  • Keep the payout whole. State that this round commits $0 of new R&D and strain, and that the 2030 package is complete. The full ~$2.5B a year of room stands after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow, with no rating effect. Premium is $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.
  • Book low and learn from the last call. Weight S1 at 1.0 and book -38.29 or below, never above. - Ask Ghai to reconcile his round-2 Joint Venture reading (+$7.1B / -$14.2B) with the ~-$7.09B the record now shows (inference). - Name the risks outside the column, without booking them: rival widebody moves against GEnx's 44.8% (about -$0.8B PV for a Trent 1000 upgrade, about -$1.3B for a re-engine with UltraFan WB; our inference from our own economics), Ducted in-service durability, and raw materials. - There is no GEnx lever on this menu.
  • The customer comes first. - LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time on the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer; spares never crowd out OE, and no rate is published. - A CFM engine offered to every airframer on standard terms, with any price, capacity or terms decided jointly with Safran. - No public reaction and no price cut on the Joint Venture.
  • Public statement. Name no rival and blame no one. Give no Open Fan or RISE date, and no CFM price talk without Safran. Never call the Ducted the next generation, and publish no ramp rate. RISE goes into a product when the airframers and their airlines decide.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] For this horizon the narrowbody contest is decided. Both new airframes are in service: NGSA since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR on it, and fps since 2040 with CFM alone. The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine is fitted on NGSA. No code can move, no narrowbody slot is open, and the brief has one column, S1. In that column no rival selection takes our slot. So the game now is the installed base we already hold [CX-0422]: LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, the Ducted on fps, NGSA and Embraer, and the GEnx on the 787. We win it the way we always have: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. That means durable engines in service, OE engines and spares on time to every airframer, and the balance sheet and payout kept whole. The only real question on the menu is the Open Fan. A 2045 launch could not be ready before 2055. That is eight years after NGSA's entry, five after fps's, and outside the objective's 2050 date. On the grid it loses $30.56B against hold on its own and $21.89B with Lobby. It would also trade an objective we meet today (Dominate NB, 54.3% in 2045) for one we can no longer reach (Introduce the Open Fan by 2050). My aim is to say that plainly, keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, and book low. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2045 (bulletin). - fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on a 10-year ramp, in service since 2040, selection CFM (code 3), fitted CFM. Boeing: 'Our engine partner stays CFM.' - NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037, selection RR, PW and CFM (code 7), all three fitted. - P&W GTF2 (Solo, ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (Solo, ready 2037) both folded into the P&W-RR Joint Venture in 2035. The Joint Venture NB engine launched in 2035 and has been ready and in service since 2036, carrying a folded solo's schedule. - Ours: Ducted launched 2030, in service since 2036. Embraer partnership launched 2030, in service since 2037. GEnx upgrade launched 2030, in service since 2033, counting from 2042. - Observed NB engine shares: CFM 76.0% to 2036, then 51.7% (2037), 50.5% (2039, the low), 51.1% (2040) and 53.7% (2044). P&W and RR are equal at about 23%. - Observed WB engine shares: GEnx 42.0% to 2041, then 44.8% from 2042. - NB airframes: Boeing troughed at 37% in 2039 and is climbing 1 pp a year from fps's entry (42% in 2044). That pulls our share up, because fps and the 737 are CFM. - No Delay Tactics effect is visible on the fps path. WIDEBODY SIGNALS (nothing on our menu answers them). - Boeing will 'look at [the 787's] next step once this airplane is in service', and fps now is. - RR: 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine.' - Airbus: the A350 family stays its focus. It is locking up titanium forgings and rare earths for NGSA and A320 needs. OUR POSITION (brief §1). If nobody moves again: ΔPV -38.29 (yield 76.07%). That is engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00, the 2030 package, all booked. The path is NB 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% from 2049 to 2056; WB 44.8%. WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T [CX-0436]. - Last round's S1 row (the record) was -31.20. Today's hold is -38.29, a move of $7.09B. Codes and dates did not change; the Joint Venture is the only new fact on the record. - My arithmetic (inference): about -4.8 pp of NB share every year from 2037 (2037: 56.5% to 51.7%; 2040: 55.9% to 51.1%; 2045: 59.0% to 54.3%; 2050: 61.6% to 56.8%), at about $1.47B PV per point over 2037-56. - That lies between Ghai's round-2 readings: +$7.1B if the Joint Venture folded both solos, -$14.2B if it stacked on top. The sign was on the stacked side, at about half the size. - I booked -56.00 last round. The switch columns did not happen; the backlog held. The hit came from a risk we named but did not book. OBJECTIVE (brief §2; it never changes the payoff). - Dominate NB engines: MET. 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year, now locked), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050. - Introduce the Open Fan: NOT MET, and unreachable in this game. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 at the earliest (launch + 10). A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056. - An Open Fan launch would also break Dominate. My arithmetic, inference, ignoring renormalisation: about 19% in 2045 and 22% in 2050 on its own, and about 34% and 37% with Lobby. That holds if the penalty starts in the decision year; 2050 fails either way. THE GRID (brief §3, one column, S1: rivals hold). Hold everything is -38.29 (76.1%), the best row. - Open Fan: -68.85 (57.0%). - Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18 (62.4%). - No row is positive against hold. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision). It WOULD VETO: - Open Fan: launch, alone. It is -30.56 against hold: the $8B bill plus about $22.56B of wait penalty. It fails the airframer-path test, and the RISE allowance cannot cover it ($30.56B against $15B). With no airframer path it would need a stated reason why Safran would agree. - Open Fan + emissions lobbying: -21.89, the $9B bill plus about $12.89B of penalty. That is $4.89B above the $15B allowance plus the $2.0B round cap. - emissions lobbying without an Open Fan: about -1.00. - Any premium above $0 not tied to a grid plan. Any RISE allowance used outside the airframer-path test; it says that cannot happen in this round or in 2050. It WOULD APPROVE: - hold on every field (not a Board item); - unpriced moves: in-service durability reporting with Safran's engineers; LEAP and Ducted OE and spares on time; RISE whole, 50-50, with no date; a private CFM offer on standard terms set with Safran; no reaction or price cut on Joint Venture news. It EXPECTS: - S1 at weight 1.0; - every alternative against hold, with the penalty broken out; - Ali's in-service safety and durability report on test and field evidence, with any flag and its cross-functional answer; - Ghai's $0 new R&D and strain, the payout kept whole, and a reconciliation of his round-2 Joint Venture reading; - the Safran gate; - an objective_note saying 'Introduce' is unreachable; - premium $0, with the declined objective premium in dollars ($21.89B cheapest, $30.56B for the Open Fan alone); - risks outside the column named and not booked: GEnx widebody (about -$0.8B for a Trent 1000 upgrade and about -$1.3B for a re-engine with UltraFan WB, its inference), Ducted durability and raw materials; - a clean statement.

Options to test.

  • 1. Hold everything (the default and my lean): -38.29 (76.1%) in S1, the only column. Best row. No Board item, $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0. Dominate stays met (54.3% in 2045, 56.8% in 2050).
  • 2. Open Fan alone: -68.85 (57.0%), which is -30.56 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus about $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty, about $0.645B per point (my arithmetic). New NBs are on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect, and it is all cost: ready 2055, after both airframes and after the 2050 objective date. Barred by H2. It would break Dominate in 2050, and in 2045 if the penalty starts in the decision year. The RISE allowance ($15B) does not cover it. Tested to put the declined premium in dollars.
  • 3. Open Fan + Lobby (the cheapest Open Fan route): -60.18 (62.4%), which is -21.89 against hold. That is the $9B bill plus about $12.89B of 20 pp penalty, with no added strain implied. Lobby beside an Open Fan is +8.67 (15 pp x about $0.645B, less $1B). The pair is still $21.89B behind hold: above the $15B RISE allowance, and $4.89B above the allowance plus the $2.0B round cap. It fails H2, and it buys nothing toward 'Introduce' (ready 2055). Tested for the record.
  • 4. Lobby alone: not a grid row. A $1B bill with no board effect, so about -1.00. It fails 'paid for the risk' and the doctrine that Lobby goes only beside a live Open Fan. Tested to close it off.
  • Weighting: one column, S1 at 1.0. Weights change nothing; the ranking is hold, then Open Fan + Lobby, then Open Fan. No alternative comes within the $1B epsilon of hold, so no tie-break is needed.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. In-service safety and durability calls are made by one cross-functional team, with Safran's engineers on CFM engines [CX-0012, CX-0633]. No single person makes a safety call. Any flag is answered on the fleet (inspection, shop visit, spares), not traded against delivery.
  • Durability is not traded for fuel burn or delivery [CX-0208]. This covers the Ducted, Embraer and LEAP fleets in service, and the GEnx.
  • My 20% line: a next-generation engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn reduction [CX-0217]. It binds RISE. The brief makes no fuel-burn claim, so it applies as a wording check: the Ducted is never called the next generation [CX-0183, CX-0180].
  • H1: never refuse an airframer, never lock one out. A CFM engine is offered to every airframer, Embraer included, on standard terms [CX-0587, CX-0185].
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait. Both new NBs are in service, and the Open Fan is ready no earlier than 2055, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $21.89B against $15B [CX-0205, CX-0469].
  • H3: the Ducted is a defence only, never the next-generation product. It is in service, and its trigger (the Joint Venture engine on NGSA) is on the record.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it. RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398, CX-0166]. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel.
  • H6 (through Ali): no date without test evidence. No Open Fan or RISE date of any kind (entry, demo, ground or flight test), and no ramp rate. In-service years are facts on the record [CX-0009, CX-0008].
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM NB order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby). Hold orders none. Any CFM price, terms or NB capacity commitment is joint with Safran [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals, the Joint Venture or any airframer's plans [CX-0625, CX-0580].
  • H9: doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B in the game ($0 used to date). One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan. Unused, and unusable this round: every Open Fan route waits.

Initial lean. LEAN (to be tested, not decided): hold on every field: ducted hold, Open Fan hold, Embraer partnership hold, emissions lobbying hold, genx hold. Hold is the best and only sensible row in the only column (-38.29). Nothing else is additive, so nothing else gets ordered [CX-0301]. That means no Board item, $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0 ($0 of $4.0B for the game) and the RISE allowance unused. EXPECTED COLUMN: S1 at weight 1.0. It is the backlog we hold on the record, not a hoped-for selection [CX-0248]. BOOKING: about -39.60. That is S1 less about $1.3B for the largest named widebody risk (Board inference), held below the record [CX-0536]. Ghai may move it. I raise only on results. OPEN FAN: hold. It is -30.56 alone and -21.89 with Lobby, all bill and wait penalty. It is ready 2055 at the earliest, so 'Introduce the Open Fan' is unreachable in this game whatever we order. Launching it would break 'Dominate', which we meet today. I'll name my own bias. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. But admission buys a seat, and both airframes are already flying. There is no seat to buy until an airframer wants one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214], with no date. Its technology keeps flowing into the LEAP and Ducted fleets [CX-0162]. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel (H5). SAFRAN GATE: hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate. - RISE stays a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. - An Open Fan with no airframer path would need a stated reason why Safran would agree. There is none: a 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same narrowbody base. - Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but it is moot. - Any price, terms or capacity is joint [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone. OTHER MOVES (unpriced; from the Board's approve list): - in-service durability and safety reporting with Safran's engineers, any flag to the Board before orders; - LEAP and Ducted OE and spares on time to every airframer (737, A320neo, fps, NGSA, Embraer), spares never crowding out OE, no rate published [CX-0529, CX-0542, CX-0552]; - RISE whole, 50-50, no date; - a private CFM offer on standard terms, set with Safran [CX-0586, CX-0587]; - supplier and raw-materials work, sized to our own needs; - no public reaction or price cut on Joint Venture or rival news [CX-0580, CX-0600, CX-0609]; - GEnx 787 fleet support: we don't get ahead of the airframer on its 787 plans. WHAT CHANGES MY MIND: - A safety or durability flag in the fleet: that is fleet action first, and it goes to the Board before orders. - Ghai finding an error in my reading of the grid. - A firm airframer launch that wants RISE [CX-0469]. There is none on the record. Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444]. STATEMENT PLAN: tell you what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]. - Safety first. - The engines in service and on time. - The Ducted is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us, not the next generation. - RISE: all in with Safran, and when that architecture enters service is 'really not for us to say'. - No rival named, no blame, no price, no rate, no date. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

Rationale. DECISION: hold on every field. There is no Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain and a premium of $0. THE FRAME [CX-0467]. The narrowbody contest is decided. Ghai reproduced every row. - Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%). That is the $8B bill plus $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty from 2045. - Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18, or -21.89 against hold. That is the $9B bill plus $12.89B of 20 pp penalty. - Lobby beside an Open Fan: +8.67. Lobby alone: about -1.00 (not a grid row; it has no board effect on its own). Nothing is positive against hold. Every alternative loses more than its own bill (3.8x and 2.4x). CORRECTIONS TO MY FRAME, accepted: - Ali: 2055 is 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's, not 'eight and five'. That was my arithmetic slip. It never reached a statement or a move. - Ghai: the penalty starts in 2045. He reproduces it within $0.03B on a 2045 start, and a 2046 start does not match. $0.645B per raw point and $0.678B per point of share are the same rate. - Ghai: no new strain arises because the $2B is a one-time charge already in hold, not because it is 'one project'. Open Fan + Lobby would be two projects. - Ghai: on renormalised shares, Dominate falls to 21.0% (2045) and 23.5% (2050) with the Open Fan alone, and to 35.2% and 37.8% with Lobby. My rough figures ran 1-2 points low; the conclusion stands. MY TESTS. - Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]. The new NBs are on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect, and it is all cost: the board gives the Open Fan no share gain. Nothing is ordered. - H2. RISE continues whole; holding the Open Fan is not a cancel. - My 20% and durability lines are unaffected. OBJECTIVE. Dominate is met (51.1% worst year, 2040; 54.3% in 2045; 56.8% in 2050). Introduce is unreachable. Launching an Open Fan would give up an objective we meet for one we can't reach. Those risks are not put into any grid row or column. On Ghai's advice I go no lower: the narrowbody is locked, and booking below the low case misinforms too. I raise toward -38.29 only if the next bulletin shows no widebody move. THE JOINT VENTURE LESSON. The record moved from -31.20 to -38.29, which is -$7.09B. The board took 20 raw points off us, not 15: the Joint Venture's 10 stacked on one solo-sized 10. That sits between Ghai's two readings (+$7.1B fold, -$14.2B stack), on the stacked side at half the size. My -56.00 booking covered it by $17.71B, so guiding low worked. But we named the risk and didn't book it, and we discounted a rival's stated sequencing. The lesson, adopted: a named risk with a negative midpoint gets its midpoint booked in the round we find it, and a rival's stated sequencing is not data. SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no new CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. An Open Fan with no airframer path would need a reason why Safran would agree, and there is none: a 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base. Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot. Any CFM price, terms or capacity is joint [CX-0184], including any answer to the airframer's backstop rate request. GEnx is GE alone. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove these parts: - Lobby only beside a live Open Fan (no lobbying evidence in my record). - Embraer held (my record is silent on it). - No reaction to the Joint Venture (profile.md §5, §7). - Supply and raw materials: Ali's supply record is my own description of his job, so I checked it against doctrine (OE first, spares never crowding out OE). BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. But admission buys a seat, and both airframes are flying. There is no seat until an airframer wants one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. My ramp optimism [CX-0590, CX-0592] is checked by publishing no rate, and no capacity commitment on the backstop request without field data and Safran. WHAT CHANGES MY MIND: - A durability or safety flag. That means fleet action and a reserve in the round it is found; it lowers the booking, not the orders. - A widebody move on the record. I re-price it in 2050. - A firm airframer launch that wants RISE [CX-0469]. None is possible in the NB window. Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444]. No veto stands. Ghai's binding vetoes and Ali's advice all fall on orders I don't make, so there are no overrides.

Weighing the CFO. Weighed in full. His record is High confidence on money, and his profit calls land [CX-0910]. He reproduced every grid row and the -$7.09B Joint Venture move exactly. I adopted his corrections: - the penalty starts in 2045; - strain is not added because the $2B is already in hold, not because it is 'one project'; - Dominate falls to 21.0%/23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 35.2%/37.8% with Lobby, on renormalised shares. I also adopted his Joint Venture lesson: book the midpoint of a named negative risk in the round we find it, and treat a rival's stated sequencing as no data. I took his booking advice: -39.60, not lower and not -38.29. His tests pass: - pays for itself (hold is best); - volumes first (nothing launched); - capex ($0 new against $2.55B a year of room, with no rating effect); - premium ($0, $0 of $4.0B, RISE allowance unused). His terms flag on the airframer's backstop rate request became a private other move: joint with Safran, on standard terms, no price attached, no rate published. His binding vetoes (Open Fan, Open Fan + Lobby, Lobby alone, price talk without Safran) all fall on orders and words I don't use. The statement says only that capacity commitments are made with Safran; there is no price or terms talk. He concurs with hold.

Weighing the operating head. Weighed as a thin record. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, so he is Medium confidence on durability, test standard and RISE physics. On supply his record is only my description of his job [CX-0633], so I weighed that part against doctrine. On dates I deferred fully: - The Ducted's launch + 6 = 2036 and Embraer's 2037 were met, neither early. - GEnx: 2033, counted from 2042. - An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, and one launched in 2050 in 2060. I accepted his correction of my frame: 18 and 15 years, not eight and five. It appears in no statement or move. He is candid that the brief carries shares, not cycles. He raises no flag and does not certify that none exists. I took his wording advice: - the statement claims no durable fleet; - time on wing is reported in cycles on field data against the CFM56 yardstick, hot and harsh service first; - no RISE date and no progress claimed past his evidence; - the Ducted is never called the next generation. My statement promise of 'durable engines in service' from the frame was dropped for that reason. On supply he has no evidence after 2024 and follows doctrine. I carried his raw-materials flag and the backstop capacity call into private other moves, with OE first and the call joint with Safran. He concurs with hold.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), at weight 1.0. It is the brief's only column and the backlog on the record [CX-0248]. fps is on CFM (code 3, in service 2040) and NGSA on CFM, P&W and RR (code 7, in service 2037). The Joint Venture engine has been in service since 2036. Codes are locked, and the Delay Tactics window on fps closed at its 2040 entry.

Best grid plan in that scenario. Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%) in S1, the only column. The alternatives against hold are Open Fan + Lobby -21.89 and Open Fan -30.56. My submitted plan is this plan.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. Premium this round: $0.00. Game to date: $0.00 of the $4.0B cap. The submitted plan is the best grid plan in the only column, so no doctrine or objective premium arises. RISE allowance, stated apart: $0 of $15B, unused. It cannot be used this round. Every Open Fan route waits on an airframe already in service, so it fails the airframer-path test. Objective premium declined for 'Introduce the Open Fan', against the best non-RISE plan (hold): - $21.89B for the cheapest route (Open Fan + Lobby), which is $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap; - $30.56B for the Open Fan alone. Neither buys anything toward the objective, since the engine is ready in 2055, after the 2050 test. Both would also break 'Dominate', so this is a net objective loss, not a premium.

  • R3-1 Safety and quality in service: Ali to report in-service durability and safety of the Ducted, Embraer and LEAP on test and field evidence, with cross-functional gate calls alongside Safran's engineers; any flag before next orders with its fleet action. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in his evidence. - He looks first at the Ducted in hot and harsh service, where LEAP first fell short. - I made this a public other move: time on wing reported in cycles on field data, against the CFM56 yardstick. Gate calls are made cross-functionally with Safran's engineers [CX-0012, CX-0633]. - Any flag reaches you before the 2050 orders with its fleet action. Ghai confirms the penalty starts in 2045. Dominate, met today, would fall to 21.0%/23.5% (2045/2050) with the Open Fan alone and 35.2%/37.8% with Lobby, on his renormalised reading (inference). That confirms your reading. There is no reaction or price cut on Joint Venture news.

Taken up. - S1 is weighted at 1.0 and I book -39.60, $1.31B below S1. The named risks enter no grid row and no column; the $1.31B sits only in the booking as a guide-low cushion, sized by the largest named risk, which fits your 'or below'. - Ghai's reconciliation: -$7.09B exactly. Our -56.00 booking covered it by $17.71B. - Lesson adopted: a named risk with a negative midpoint gets its midpoint booked in the round we find it. - The risks are named in predictions: WB (-$0.76-0.8B for a Trent 1000 upgrade, -$1.08-1.3B for UltraFan WB, exclusive), Ducted durability and raw materials. Taken up. - The statement names no rival and blames no one. - It gives only the in-service years on the record (2036, 2037, 2033) and no Open Fan or RISE date. My frame's 'eight and five years' slip, corrected by Ali to 18 and 15, appears nowhere. - It has no price or terms talk; capacity commitments are said to be made with Safran. - It says the Ducted 'isn't our next-generation engine' and that RISE's entry 'is really not for us to say'. - It publishes no rate and claims no durable fleet without field data.

Objective. PD-briefing objective: dominate narrowbody engines and introduce the Open Fan. It never changes the payoff. (1) Dominate NB engines (CFM at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is MET on the brief. The shares are 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year, now locked), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050. An Open Fan launch would break it. On Ghai's renormalised reading (inference) the shares would be 21.0% (2045) and 23.5% (2050) with the Open Fan alone, and 35.2% and 37.8% with Lobby. (2) Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050) is UNREACHABLE in this game on any order. - A 2045 launch is ready no earlier than 2055 (launch + 10). - A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056. - The last launch that could have been ready by 2050 was in 2035, and it would have waited on both airframes. RISE is not given up. It continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214]. It goes into a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].

Predictions. COLUMN WEIGHTS: S1 1.0, the only column. Hold is -38.29 there. I book -39.60. What I expect on the record: nothing moves on the narrowbody. The codes are locked, both airframes and the Joint Venture engine are in service, and our NB share follows the brief: 54.3% in 2045, rising to 56.8% from 2049. WB stays at 44.8% unless someone moves. RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMN (named; in no grid row; only the largest sets the $1.31B guide-low cushion in my booking): (a) Widebody, against GEnx's 44.8%. The two cases are exclusive. - An RR Trent 1000 upgrade (+5 pp WB from 2048): about -$0.76B (Ghai) or -$0.8B (Board). - An UltraFan WB re-engine (+10 pp once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service): -$1.08B from a 2045 launch, -$1.22B from 2050 (Ghai), or about -$1.3B (Board). The signals: Boeing will look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, and it now is; RR does no widebody spend without a Re-engine; Airbus's focus is the A350. I can't put a probability on it, because looking is not moving. (b) A 787 or A350 re-engine shifting WB airframe share. Unpriced, and it could cut either way for GEnx. (c) Ducted and Embraer in-service durability, hot and harsh service first. On LEAP, time-on-wing shortfalls became reserves in the quarter they were found. This lowers the booking, not the orders. (d) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths. Unquantified. (e) The airframer's backstop rate call on the same supplier base. Any answer is joint with Safran, and OE comes first. (f) Supplier-dependent volumes, and macro (recession, tariffs) that the board's fixed narrowbody market leaves out. Upside is not booked. If the 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, I raise toward -38.29, and not before.

Expected ΔPV. −39.60 $B (board after the round: −38.29 $B)

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • 1. The fleet comes first now that the engine is in service. The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (the folded GTF2) has been ready since 2036. It has been fitted on NGSA since NGSA entered service in 2037 (code 7, fitted CFM + PW + RR). Restore credibility is met, and it stays met only while that engine earns its place on time on wing, life-limited-part life and spares. The GTF fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, shops and engineers. Product safety and quality are a matter the Board reserves to itself, through Governance and Public Policy [P-1360, P-1214, PG-0050, P-1028, PX-0080].
  • 2. No Board item is possible this round. The brief (section 3) offers only hold for both GTF2 Solo and Joint Venture with RR. - The Joint Venture formed in 2035, so a withdraw is gone: it is allowed only before formation. - The engine is ready, so a cancel is gone too. - launch if selected is not on the list, and every live airframe is already in service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040). The Miss-a-cycle rule therefore asks for nothing. The orders will be hold/hold and will not reach Board review, so this guidance is the Board's only formal input for 2045 [PG-0047, P-1285, P-1875].
  • 3. The annual programme NPV review, written plainly. If nobody moves again, ΔPV is -2.93 (yield 97.34%): engine value -0.93 plus R&D -2.00, which the board books undiscounted. Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV >= 0) is not met, and no order on the grid can meet it. - The gap comes from the airframe split, not from P&W's engine. P&W's NB share peaked at 24.8% in 2039 and was 23.2% in 2044. It falls to 21.6% from 2049 as Boeing's CFM-only fps (in service since 2040) wins share back from Airbus, whose NGSA carries P&W. - Engine value falls below the status quo from 2043 (8.1 against 8.3), and the gap reaches 8.7 against 9.7 by 2050. - Looking back, the $2B bought a place on NGSA worth about $24.8B: -2.93 against -27.76, the round-1 hold row with NGSA off P&W. That figure is an inference from the round-1 grid. The Board does not ask management to chase the gap with spend, discounts or terms [P-1191, PG-0024, P-1165, P-0731].
  • 4. The capital order, now that no programme spend is left. GTF2's last ~$0.33B went out in 2035, and the brief shows no R&D or write-off after 2035, so no fresh $2B Joint Venture share was charged. The order of cash uses: - the dividend first; - then debt back to pre-ASR levels; - then buybacks as the fill-in. At ΔPV 0 on the 10% grid, a buyback is the benchmark any future spend must beat. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch was never used and now has nothing to fund [P-0566, P-0686, PX-0353, P-0669, P-1357, P-0499].
  • 5. Disclosure that reports what is done, not what is hoped. Two lines of the 2035 statement are now out of date: 'GTF2 is in development, not yet proven' and 'our share ... has held at 24% since 2026'. The engine is in service, and the public record shows 23.2% in 2044. Report both plainly. Claim no durability the fleet record does not show, and say nothing on airframers' rates or shares. The derivative suits over GTF oversight make the accuracy of this text a Board matter [PG-0039, PG-0050, P-1367].

Expects to see. No Board item can be submitted, so the package will not come to review. The Board expects to read the following in the round-3 ExCo notes and sealed orders, and will check them at the 2050 guidance. (a) Orders and scoring. - Orders hold/hold, the brief's only legal row: -2.93 in S1, the only column. - predictions S1 1.00; expected ΔPV -2.93; premium 0; overrides empty. (b) From Calio. - An objective_note: credibility met (the Joint Venture engine on NGSA since 2037); Capitalise not met at -2.93 (engine value -0.93, R&D -2.00); PV given up for either objective $0. - The public statement text. - board_response answers to every round-2 review recommendation, with the moot ones marked closed. (c) From Mitchill. - The annual NPV review of the GTF2/Joint Venture programme: - the two components; - the year-by-year profile: small gains in 2038-40 (7.6 against 7.5, 7.9 against 7.6, 7.9 against 7.8), then losses from 2043; - the look-back against the round-1 grid. - Confirmation that the board charges no fresh $2B share or write-off after 2035. - Cash against the ~$6B self-funded envelope, with $0 of new R&D. - The dividend covered; debt measured against pre-ASR levels; and when buybacks return as the standard fill-in. - His four grounds marked not engaged. - The standing 2045 withdraw review closed as moot, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035. (d) From Eddy. - The four-point Joint Venture report the Board asked for in round 2: - P&W's gear and core remain one P&W module with design authority; - there is no technology licence; - GTF2's certification baseline was left untouched; - the engine was ready in 2036 (the bulletin confirms 2036, carried over from the folded GTF2). - A fleet report on the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and on the GTF fleet, built from measured data (time on wing, LLP life, shop visits, AOG), or a plain statement that the brief holds none. - His parts result, with the fleet and A320neo deliveries first. - Both of his veto checks. (e) Any red-line flag, and how it was struck or rebutted. If a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so next round.

Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: hold. This is not a Board item; it is the only value the brief offers, and the Board endorses it. Grid: -2.93 (S1). GTF2 has been folded into the Joint Venture, has been ready since 2036 and is on NGSA, so there is nothing left to launch or cancel.
  • Joint Venture with RR: hold. This is not a Board item; the commitment the Board approved in 2035 stands. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine has been ready since 2036. The Board endorses hold: the published terms, not an order, now protect the gear and core.
  • Other moves, which the Board recommends on rather than votes on: - the GTF durability kit at shop visits on standard terms; - the fleet-first order of call on pacing parts; - the readiness report each round, now a fleet report; - an accurate public status statement with no dated recovery claims.

Would veto.

  • None this round. The Board never vetoes a hold, and hold is the only value the brief offers for either field. Any value outside the brief's section-3 list is not a legal order and is read as hold.
  • Standing for 2050, the last round, if that brief offers any engine order: - An unconditional GTF2 Solo: launch fails Committed airframe if no live airframe outside service selects P&W. No franchise-defence case is left, because NGSA and fps are both in service. It also fails Return hurdle: a 2050 launch would be ready in 2056, the last year the board counts the NB market, so it would book $2B for almost no share. Acceptable alternatives: hold, or launch if selected where it is legal. - A launch if selected passes only where a live airframe not yet in service could select P&W and GTF2 would be ready by its EIS.
  • Any order in either round that does one of the following: - books share, a selection or partner money that is not on the public record; - carries a premium that is undeclared, above $0.5B or off the objective; - strains the dividend; - hands P&W's gear or core to the Joint Venture or to Rolls-Royce.

Recommendations.

  • Close out the Joint Venture report the Board asked for in its round-2 review, now that the Joint Venture has formed. Eddy should confirm, in a private note to the Board: - the gear and core remain one P&W module with design authority; - there is no technology licence; - GTF2's certification baseline was left untouched; - the engine was ready in 2036. In future, any merged Joint Venture or UltraFan content should reach the engine only as a derivative, fully tested before its own entry into service. It should never touch the gear and core, and never come through a licence. Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model.
  • Turn the GTF2 readiness report into a fleet report each round. Base it on measured data for the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and for the GTF fleet: time on wing, life-limited-part life, shop visits and AOG. Where the brief holds no data, say so rather than give a figure. Any durability or safety-critical-part finding should reach Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the next round's orders, with the plan, and should be disclosed early. The 2023 lesson was to put testing ahead of service and to let the Safety Board act.

Question. Control what you can control [PX-0020]. The engine is done and the money is spent. The Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce (the folded GTF2) has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. Its budget was GTF2's $2B, booked in 2035, and nothing has been charged since. The bad news first. We are at -2.93 $B against the status quo, and Capitalise on the GTF is not met. Our NB engine share peaked at 24.8% in 2039 and was 23.2% in 2044. On the board it falls to 21.6% from 2049, and the brief offers no order that changes that. The brief offers one row: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR hold. So the 2045 questions are not about capital. They are about the fleet and the record: 1. Fleet. Is the new engine earning its place on time on wing, life-limited-part (LLP) life and spares? Do the GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, shops and engineers? What does the brief actually let us report? 2. Joint Venture. Did the published terms hold: gear and core one P&W module, no licence, GTF2's certification baseline untouched? And how does merged content reach the engine from here? 3. Record. We put the programme NPV review on the record, correct the 2035 statement (it said 'in development' and '24% since 2026'), and close the round-2 items that are now moot. 4. Last round. We set the 2050 rule now, so that no engine spend goes out without a live airframer. Safety and durability first [PX-0035], then Neil's gate, then the Board. No Board item can arise this round.

Private: the fleet report to the Board each round, on measured data or a plain 'none in the brief'. Findings go to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the next orders. 3. Private: the order of call. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo deliveries come first [PX-0099]. 4. Private: the Joint Venture close-out (Shane's four points), plus the rule that merged content comes only as a tested derivative, off the gear and core, with no licence. 5. Private: Neil's annual programme NPV review, with both look-backs labelled as inference. 6. Private: the 2050 rule. No engine order without a live airframe not yet in service selecting P&W, ready by its entry into service. BOARD I will answer each round-2 recommendation and each round-3 recommendation in board_response. These are closed as moot: - the Joint Venture ready-date question (the bulletin shows 2036); - the 2045 withdraw test (formed 2035); - the same-round sequencing question; - the S2 exposure (code 7, in service). PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement), for Shane and Neil to check 'Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with deliveries when we promised them. What is done: the engine we developed with Rolls-Royce in our Joint Venture has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence. Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We are not starting a new engine programme today. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.' WHAT COULD CHANGE THIS - Hold/hold cannot change. - The statement and other moves change if any of these comes in: - Shane reports a fleet or safety-critical-part finding; it then leads the statement, with the plan; - Neil finds a line that books upside; - the Board flags a figure.

R&D is -2.00: one undiscounted line, booked once, nothing charged since 2035. Cash went out at about $0.33B a year, 2030-35. Engine value is -0.93: gains in 2038-40 worth +0.15, losses from 2043 worth -1.12, about -0.97 on rounded figures. That reconciles to the brief. My first read of the 2043 turn was timing. It isn't. It's more pervasive. Our share has tracked Airbus's NB share exactly, 0.32 points per point, every year since 2037, and the board holds 21.6% from 2049 to 2056. No order of ours reaches that, and we will not chase it with price. Both look-backs are inference. The 2035 commit added +5.51 for no new cash, on the round-2 grid. The +24.8 for not being off NGSA holds as arithmetic, but it's the top of the range: round 2 showed a Joint Venture without GTF2 reaching the same engine value. Keep both private. I was wrong on Rolls-Royce. I gave its commitment 10%. The statement books nothing unproven. We hold no fleet data, so we claim none. 2050: a launch would be ready in 2056, the last counted year, worth about $0.26B against $2B. It fails my gate.

Rationale. THE DECISION: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR hold. premium 0. predictions S1 1.00. expected ΔPV -2.93. overrides empty. No Board item. 1. START FROM EDDY'S PROPOSAL. STRIKE WHAT FAILS A BINDING VETO. - Mitchill invoked one binding veto, on ground 3 (aggressive terms): any share-recovery or pricing campaign to close the Capitalise gap. Ground 2 passes: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem. - No colleague flagged a company red-line breach. 3. The cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035, and no live airframe can still select us. - A rival's discount never moves the answer. 5. PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE. - premium 0. I accept that rather than invent one. - I note his candour: his round-2 weights were low on Rolls-Royce.

Weighing the operating head. Weighed as binding on the technical grounds and as the best engineering read available. His seat's record is one event, June 2023, Low; the rest is seat doctrine, and I say so. - I adopted his proposal (hold/hold), his four-point Joint Venture close-out and his derivative rule. - I adopted his order of call. His bias is fleet lift first [PX-0123]; mine is to balance Airbus and the fleet jointly [PX-0099]. So steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily with Airbus as a tie-break, not a starvation rule. - His plain fleet report, 'none in the brief, no figure', is preferred to an invented one. - He was candid that full LLP life at NGSA's 2037 entry into service is not confirmed. - His point (c), the certification baseline, rests on the 2035 freeze and the ready date, not on a file. I label it inference. - Neither of his grounds is engaged. His standing conditions on durability claims, derivatives and capacity carry into 2050. - I took his wording fix to the statement. I keep the promise to disclose early that he flagged, because fast disclosure is my record [PX-0030][PX-0034].

CONFIRMED as an inference from the 2035 configuration freeze and from the ready year, 2036 = GTF2 launch + 6, neither reset to 2041 nor compressed. The brief holds no certification file. (d) Ready in 2036. CONFIRMED by the bulletin. The bulletin's 'in service since 2036' is the ready year; the engine has flown since NGSA's 2037 entry into service. DERIVATIVE RULE. Rolls-Royce's technology, or any merged Joint Venture or UltraFan content, reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine: - with its own full test programme, severe-environment testing included, and all LLPs at full life at its own entry into service; - as a new build standard or a certified kit at shop visits; - never through a licence, and never into the gear and core. The integrated-team rule [P-1240] holds only while team boundaries follow module boundaries: the gear and core stay one P&W team with design authority, Rolls-Royce's content sits in modules it owns behind controlled interfaces, and one engine-level authority runs certification. A derivative that crosses the gear-and-core boundary is opposed under red line P-1233 and flagged to the Board. Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. Rolls-Royce's technology is protected on the same terms as ours, and we keep the partner whole [PX-0038]. No derivative spend goes out without a live airframer need.
  • Annual programme NPV review of GTF2 and the Joint Venture (Mitchill) (private): ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is one undiscounted line, booked once in 2035 as the folded GTF2 share. Nothing has been charged since: no fresh $2B and no write-off. Cash went out at about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. Discounted, that phasing would be about -1.09, and we book none of the difference. Engine value against the status quo, nominal $B: - level 2026-37; - +0.1 in 2038, +0.3 in 2039, +0.1 in 2040; - level 2041-42; - then losses from 2043: -0.2, -0.3, -0.4, -0.6, -0.7, -0.8, then -1.0 a year in 2049-53 and -1.1 a year in 2054-56. In PV terms the gains are +0.15 and the losses -1.12, a net -0.97 against the brief's -0.93 (rounding). That fits the board's 2056 NB cut. Why the share drifts: P&W's NB share tracks Airbus's NB share at 0.317 pp per point (Mitchill's fit, exact to 0.1 pp for 2037-44). No P&W order reaches that. LOOK-BACKS (inference, private): - About +24.8 against being left off NGSA (-2.93 against -27.76). This is the top of the range, not a point estimate: round 2 showed that a Joint Venture without GTF2 could reach the same engine value, but only on events that were not on the record in 2030. - +5.51 for the 2035 commit, read off the round-2 grid, for $0 of new R&D. - Mitchill's own record: he weighted S4 at 0.10 and was low on Rolls-Royce.
  • Capital order report (private): New R&D in 2045 is $0, which is 0% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope [PX-0268]. The last GTF2 tranche, about $0.33B in 2035, was 5.5% of it. The dividend is covered and comes first [PX-0081]. Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The board carries no debt path, so Mitchill gives no date rather than invent one; he will report it at 2050 if that brief carries it. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch was never used and has nothing to fund. At the 10% grid rate a buyback scores ΔPV 0, and it is the benchmark any future spend must beat.
  • Standing 2050 rule (private): No engine order unless a live airframe not yet in service selects P&W, on the public record, and the engine can be ready by its entry into service [P-0746][PX-0109]. A 2050 unconditional launch would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts. At best it is worth about +$0.26B PV against $2.00B, an edge of at most -1.74 in every column, with no cancel round. Mitchill's ground 2 and the Board's Committed-airframe and Return-hurdle tests would both veto it. launch if selected only where it is legal and a live airframe outside service could select us. Eddy's default 2050 proposal is hold.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety comes first, and the engine is now in service. The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA since 2036, on the schedule it inherited from GTF2 (bulletin). What matters most to us now is the fleet: time on wing, full-life parts, and support through partner shops. Any safety or durability flag must reach us before the next round's orders. No date for a new engine goes public this round [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0287].
  • Protect what is working. Both parts of the objective are met on hold. RR's narrowbody share is 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050. Its widebody share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns (+20.55 in S1, +20.80 in S2). Keeping either part needs no premium and no new programme. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [R-1561, R-1582, R-1005, R-1574].
  • One big programme at a time, and the strain is still in the grid. In 2035 we expected the Trent 1000 upgrade to come back in 2045 without strain, once UltraFan NB was out of development. The grid says otherwise. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain stacks on any widebody item (dashboard_game.md section 2). Against hold, the upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.02 (S1 / S2). Each loses more than its own bill and breaks the premium caps. Both stay at hold [RG-0019, RG-0033, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214].
  • The balance sheet and returns. Narrowbody R&D is behind us: our $4B Joint Venture share and the $1.71B write-off are already booked. Cash follows the capital frame: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat and Trent durability stays funded. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. This test does not apply unless McCabe invokes a balance-sheet veto [RX-0242, R-0900, R-0909, RG-0059, RG-0041, RX-0214].

Expects to see. The package should contain the following. (1) Grid rows. The row of the submitted orders and the row with each Board item at hold, column by column (S1 / S2). On all-hold that is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +20.55 / +20.80. For a widebody item, its row against that row: 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' (+14.07 / +14.34) or 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' (+11.55 / +12.78). (2) The CEO's expected scenario and predictions, with weights on S1 and S2 under the ExCo rule. Our illustrative case is S1 0.85, S2 0.15. Boeing said in 2035 it would look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, which is a signal for one Re-engine. Airbus's statement that the A350 family remains its focus is nothing on the other, and S2 needs both. All-hold is then +20.59 expected. (3) McCabe. Her co-signature on any launch, her weights, the worst column for each item and capex a year. On all-hold, we want her to confirm three things: no narrowbody R&D remains; the plan fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the distribution plan after 2028; and leverage stays at or below about 1.5x. We also ask for an off-grid figure: our exposure under the Joint Venture's shared-risk terms to an in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine. It books nothing. (4) Watson. His report should cover what the 2036 EIS-readiness review found on gearbox durability, and RR fitted at NGSA's entry (24.1% of narrowbody engines in 2037). It should also cover the Joint Venture engine's in-service time on wing and full-life parts, and support through our partner shops without relying on P&W's shops. For any widebody item, he should give the ready year (UltraFan WB 2051; the upgrade counts from 2048), the years of strain and the support plan. (5) Both veto checks, with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in rationale and overrides empty. (6) premium item by item. We expect $0 on all-hold. (7) A public statement with no date for any new engine, no Joint Venture date and nothing on any airframer's dates. (8) board_response to each round-2 recommendation. The 2045 withdrawal review should be closed formally: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, so it is moot. If a figure is missing, we will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • All four fields at hold. For UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W, hold is the only legal value, and the Joint Venture stands as formed. UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade also stay at hold. None of these is a Board item, and we never veto a hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 (S1) and +20.80 (S2), or +20.59 on our illustrative case (S1 0.85, S2 0.15). Both parts of the objective are met (narrowbody 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050; widebody at least 55.2%). Premium is $0B.
  • Qualitative other moves raise no Board item and we would support them: Trent fleet durability (time on wing, about £1bn over four years); UltraFan technology funded as technology, using public R&D money where it is available; in-service support for the Joint Venture engine; and pricing discipline. They change no payoff on the grid.

Would veto.

  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -6.48 (S1) and -6.46 (S2), so -6.48 under any weights. It fails the reasonable worst case: both columns are below minus its $2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks on the bill while the Joint Venture runs. It fails declared premium: the $6.48B shortfall is above the $3B cap for the round. Without strain it would still be about -1.48 (inference: +0.52 of engine value against $2B of R&D), so it does not pay even then. The company's one-programme rule is not engaged as written, since no UltraFan is in development, but the strain is the cost of running a second programme beside the Joint Venture. Acceptable alternative: hold [RG-0033, RG-0068, R-1574, RX-0214, R-1127].
  • UltraFan WB: launch. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -9.00 (S1) and -8.02 (S2), or -8.85 on our case. It fails the airframe test: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. S2 is a grid column, not the record, and Boeing's 2035 remark on the 787's next step is a signal, not a launch. It fails declared premium: the shortfall is far above both the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap and the $3B cap. It fails the reasonable worst case: S1 at -9.00 is below minus its $4B bill. Even in S2 it would be ready in 2051 against Re-engines in service in 2050, and would earn about +0.98 against $9B of R&D and strain. Acceptable alternative: hold [R-1574, R-1005, RG-0033, RG-0021, R-0929].
  • Any Board item that lacks McCabe's co-signature (as defined in our profile), or that comes in a package where a binding ExCo veto went unrespected, a red-line flag is left unresolved or overrides is not empty. Acceptable alternative: hold [RX-0213, R-1579, RG-0044].

Recommendations.

  • Hold all four fields and say why in rationale: this round we protect what is working. The Joint Venture engine is in service, both parts of the objective are met on hold, and 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns. The CEO has our total support for this frame.
  • Close the 2035 widebody plan. We recommended then that the Trent 1000 upgrade come back in 2045, once UltraFan NB was out of development, against a Re-engine or as a declared premium inside $3B. That rested on the strain lifting, and the grid shows it does not: the Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain stays on any widebody item for the rest of the game. For 2050, bring a widebody item only if a Re-engine is on the record and the grid puts the item within its own bill and the caps. Note that UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061.
  • Product safety in service. Watson should report four things. First, what the 2036 EIS-readiness review found on gearbox durability. Second, the Joint Venture engine's time on wing and full-life parts since 2036. Under P&W's published terms, P&W held design authority through certification, so we want our own view of maturity. Third, support through our partner shops on the Singapore model: P&W has said the GTF fleet has first call on its shops. Fourth, any safety or durability flag, which must reach us before the next round's orders. 'We have a moral obligation to do these things properly.'
  • Precaution on shared risk. McCabe should size, off the grid, RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine under its shared-risk terms. P&W's published terms cite partners carrying 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge. She should confirm that it fits without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and without touching the dividend. It books nothing and is not a veto ground.
  • Capital. No new programme spend this round. Distributions should come from sustainable free cash flow, after the cash needs of the business, in the order of the capital frame: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then extra distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) continues, and UltraFan technology continues as technology, using public R&D money where available.
  • Widebody watch. The franchise test does not trigger. Our share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, and no rival-engined Re-engine is on the record. The GEnx upgrade has taken 2.8 pp since 2042. In 2050, watch for a 787 next step from Boeing and any A350 Re-engine. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we hold today.
  • The public statement, pricing and housekeeping. The statement should cover the Joint Venture engine in service, with durability and support first. It should give no date for any new engine and say nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, and it should keep 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'. 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.' Make no price concessions. Formally close the 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review: the Joint Venture formed in 2035.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, the 2045 question, in cash and quality of earnings. The Joint Venture engine is in service and is now a business. On hold the board gives us +20.55 (S1) and +20.80 (S2), and both legs of the objective are met. The question is whether anything on this grid adds cash. It does not. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain sits on top of either widebody item. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 against hold, and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.02. Each loses more than its own bill in both columns, under any weights. So this round is about harvesting and protecting what we have: the fleet, the Joint Venture engine's durability and support, and the Trent franchise. We fund durability, not new engines. We are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582]. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].

Situation. Public record, 2045. - NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037, code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). Fitted: CFM + PW + RR. - fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on the 10-year path, in service since 2040, code 3 (CFM). - Joint Venture with P&W: formed 2035, when both of us committed. Our UltraFan NB Solo and P&W's GTF2 folded in. The engine took GTF2's schedule and has been in service since 2036. - P&W's published terms: shared risk, investment and revenue on the partner model under which partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge. P&W's gear and core stay its own module, and it keeps design authority through certification. There is no technology licence. The GTF fleet has first call on P&W's shops. - Rivals: CFM ducted engine in service since 2036, CFM-Embraer since 2037, RISE kept as technology. The GEnx upgrade has been in service since 2033 and has counted since 2042, taking 2.8 pp of widebody from us (58.0% to 55.2%). - Widebody: no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. Boeing says it will look at the 787's next step once fps is in service. That is a signal for a 787 Re-engine, not a launch, and Boeing has named no engine. Airbus says the A350 family, including the A350F, remains its focus: nothing toward a Re-engine. - Observed 2044: narrowbody engines CFM 53.7 / P&W 23.2 / RR 23.2; widebody engines CFM/GE 44.8 / RR 55.2. Our position on hold: ΔPV +20.55 $B, yield 118.68%. - Components: engine value +26.26; R&D -4.00 (our Joint Venture share); write-offs -1.71 (UltraFan NB spend beyond our share). All of it was booked in 2035. No narrowbody R&D remains on the board (Helen to confirm). - RR narrowbody engines: 965 in 2037, a peak of 990 in 2039, 914 in 2045, 863 a year from 2049. Our share drifts down from 24.8% to 21.6% as fps gains on CFM only. That is airframe mix, not a lever we hold. - Widebody engines: 188 a year from 2042. - The board counts narrowbody to 2056 and widebody to 2061. Objective: both legs met on hold. - Narrowbody entry: 22.9% in 2045, 21.6% in 2050. - Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. The worst year is 55.2%, 5.2 pp of headroom. - The S2 hold row is +0.25 above S1, which I read as no loss of widebody share in S2 (inference; Rob to confirm against the 50% line). Grid, each item against 'UltraFan NB: hold' (S1 / S2): - T1000 upgrade: -6.48 / -6.46. That is the $2B bill plus the $5B strain against about +0.52 / +0.54 of engine value. - UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.02. That is the $4B bill plus the $5B strain against 0 / +0.98 of engine value. It would be ready in 2051, after S2's Re-engines enter service in 2050. - Best plan in both columns: 'UltraFan NB: hold'. Housekeeping: the 2045 withdrawal review set in 2035 is moot, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035; I close it formally. The 2035 widebody plan (bring the upgrade back once UltraFan NB was out of development) assumed the strain would lift. The grid shows it does not, so I close that plan too. Board guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 2.5): it would approve all four fields at hold, with premium $0B. It would veto Trent 1000 upgrade: launch, UltraFan WB: launch, and any item lacking McCabe's co-signature or sitting in a package with an unrespected veto, an unresolved red-line flag or non-empty overrides.

Options to test.

  • Weights (mine; Helen to confirm or replace): S1 0.90, S2 0.10. Under our rule, S2 needs both Re-engines. Boeing's '787 next step once fps is in service' is a signal (0.2). Airbus's 'A350 family remains our focus' is nothing (0.1). A column that needs both legs can be no likelier than its weaker leg, so S2 gets 0.10. The Board's case is 0.85 / 0.15. The choice is weight-proof: both widebody items are negative in both columns. Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold.
  • A. All four at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold' (my lean). - +20.55 / +20.80. EV +20.58 on my weights, +20.59 on the Board's case. - Best row in both columns. Worst column +20.55. Premium $0B. - Both legs of the objective met. Never a Board item. - Four-part gate: nothing new to gate. It keeps a business that passed the gate and is now earning.
  • B. 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade'. - Row +14.07 / +14.34; EV +14.10 (Board case +14.11). - Item -6.48 / -6.46; EV -6.48 under any weights; worst column -6.48. - That is below minus its own $2B bill in both columns, and the $6.48B shortfall is above the $3B cap. It cannot be carried as a declared premium. - Fails the gate on business model: even without strain it is about -1.48. - My 'regain share, why not?' instinct [RX-0101, RX-0117] does not survive the numbers. Board veto. Priced only.
  • C. 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB'. - Row +11.55 / +12.78; EV +11.67 (Board case +11.73). - Item -9.00 / -8.02; EV -8.90 (Board case -8.85); worst column -9.00, below minus its $4B bill. - Fails airframers first: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has not named UltraFan on a 787 Re-engine. - Even in S2 it is ready in 2051, after the Re-engines' 2050 entry, and earns about +0.98 against $9B of bill and strain. - Far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap and the $3B cap. Fails the gate on airframe, market and business model. Board veto. Priced only.
  • D. Upgrade and UltraFan WB together: not a legal plan, because the two are exclusive. Not tested.

Red lines.

  • Safety first [RX-0053]. The Joint Venture engine and the Trent fleet come before any new spend. No compressed maturity. Any safety or durability flag on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent fleet reaches the Board before the next round's orders [RG-0027, RX-0296].
  • No date for any new engine in public this round. No Joint Venture date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices [R-0970, R-1476].
  • UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W stay at hold, the only legal values. The Joint Venture stands as formed. Nothing is cancelled, because no programme is in development.
  • One big programme at a time. On this board the Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project, so any widebody item carries $5B of strain. The upgrade and UltraFan WB are exclusive [R-0929, R-1127].
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column: upgrade -$2B, UltraFan WB -$4B. Today they are -6.48 and -9.00. Board veto on both [RG-0033].
  • No UltraFan WB without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan. Neither is on the record. Any UltraFan WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574, R-1005].
  • Doctrine premium at most $3B per round against the best expected grid plan, declared item by item. A widebody shortfall can be kept only as a declared premium inside that cap.
  • McCabe's joint sign-off on any launch against mid-to-high-teens hurdles [RX-0213, R-1579]. Her balance-sheet vetoes: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Watson's Civil veto binds: compressed maturity, an early disclosed date, or no support before EIS. overrides stays empty, and we revise once within any veto.
  • Capital frame: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D broadly flat [RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].
  • No price concessions: win-win terms, value remunerated, every contract through the Investment Committee [RX-0097, R-1582].

Initial lean. Proposal: all four at hold. UltraFan NB Solo: hold, Joint Venture with P&W: hold (the Joint Venture stands as formed), UltraFan WB: hold, Trent 1000 upgrade: hold. No Board item. Premium $0B. EV +20.58 on my weights (+20.59 on the Board's case); S1 outcome +20.55. So, frankly, there is nothing to buy this round. The Joint Venture engine is flying and earning. Both legs of the objective are met. Every new item on the grid destroys value: - the upgrade: -6.48; - UltraFan WB: -9.00 in S1, -8.02 even in S2. I said in 2023 we would regain share on the 787 [RX-0101, RX-0117]. Not at any price. We are not after market share. 'Actually, I've seen this movie before': two programmes in parallel, and the strain eats the return. What we do instead is control what we control: - the Joint Venture fleet's time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops; - Trent fleet durability, about £1bn over four years [RX-0123]; - UltraFan technology kept as technology, with public R&D money where available [RX-0094]. Cash follows the frame: balance sheet, dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. I formally close two plans. The 2045 withdrawal review is moot: the Joint Venture formed in 2035. The 2035 widebody plan assumed the strain would lift, and it does not. For 2050, a widebody item comes only with a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within its own bill and the caps. Other moves. Public: - the Joint Venture engine in service, with durability and support first; - Trent fleet durability continues; - UltraFan technology continues as technology. Private: - the in-service support plan through partner shops, not P&W's; - any safety or durability flag to the Board before the next round's orders; - pricing discipline; - both reviews closed; - the 2050 widebody watch; - Helen's off-grid shared-risk sizing, booking nothing. What would change my lean: - a widebody item that Helen and Rob show within its own bill and the $3B cap (the $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB) against a Re-engine on the record. None exists on this grid. - a durability or safety flag from Rob. That changes the support plan and the statement, not the orders. Draft public statement: 'So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our job now is the fleet. Safety is at the top, then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.' Subject to Helen's numbers and Rob's fleet report.

Helen McCabe (CFO) tests

Plan on it for 2050. Off the grid, our own Trent 1000 experience is the reasonable worst case: £2.4bn over seven years. That's our best view at the minute.
