It did not: on this board the formed Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project. That assumption was wrong, and I say so. - What the miss costs: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, a premium we could have chosen to declare inside $3B. With strain it is off the table. - What the Joint Venture brought: 24.1% of NGSA engines from entry, both legs of the objective met, and the $2.29B of Solo spend not needed in 2036-37. 8. Off-grid, as the Board asked. - Watson: the gearbox that flies is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip, RR was fitted at NGSA's entry (965 engines, 24.1%), and there is no durability or safety flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no number, and neither do I. - His oversight note becomes a private move: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data, and gear-and-core repair data or a module pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops. - McCabe sizes our share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge at about £1.2-2.9bn, with a peak year of £0.3-0.7bn. Twice that still fits without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and with the dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first. It books nothing. 9. Where my record is thin. Joint Venture terms and P&W are Low confidence for me (erginbilgic.md §6). On the gear and core, support and shop capacity I defer to Watson. On the shared-risk sizing I take McCabe's test as the evidence. The in-service oversight and the worst-case sizing are company doctrine and Board asks (profile.md §4; RG-0027, RG-0033), not my own words. 'Actually, I've seen this movie before': two programmes in parallel, and the strain eats the return. We control what we control: the fleet, durability and cash.

Weighing the CFO. Taken in full; she decided the numbers. I adopt her weights (S1 0.90 / S2 0.10, the generous case for the widebody items) and her item values: upgrade -6.48 / -6.46, UltraFan WB -9.00 / -8.02, -8.90 expected. I adopt her worst columns and her premium of $0B. Her withheld co-signatures on the upgrade and UltraFan WB are binding and respected. She invokes no balance-sheet veto: no funding, net cash, leverage at or below about 1.5x. She confirms no narrowbody R&D remains and the fit with a flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan. Her capex figures go on the record: about £0.49bn a year for either item, £1.47bn or £2.94bn in total, with £3.68bn of strain on top. Her off-grid shared-risk sizing (£1.2-2.9bn, peak £0.3-0.7bn, twice that still funded from free cash flow) becomes a private cash-plan move that books nothing. Her 2050 view goes to the 2050 watch: strain planned as permanent, and an upgrade launched in 2050 worth only about +0.28 of engine value against $7B. No disagreement with my proposal.

Weighing the operating head. Taken in full on readiness, support and the franchise. He confirms: the Joint Venture engine ready in 2036 on GTF2's clock with nothing compressed; RR fitted at NGSA's entry (24.1%, 965 engines); no safety or durability flag on the record; widebody at 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with S2 at or above S1 and so above the 50% line. He confirms the board carries the Joint Venture as a running narrowbody project, so $5B of strain falls on either widebody item; he withdraws his own 2035 upgrade plan. His oversight note on the P&W gear and core becomes two private moves: technical review rights, and repair data or a module-exchange pool. His support plan is carried privately without reliance on P&W's shops, and his in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders. He checked the public statement for early dates; it carries none, and I added only 'UltraFan technology continues as technology', with no date. He invokes no Civil veto. His capacity view and the unreconciled shop-visit figures (1,100-1,200 against 1,400-1,500) are advice, recorded. His ranking for 2050, the upgrade first among widebody items and only within its bill or against a threatening Re-engine, goes into the 2050 watch.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1: rivals hold (weight 0.90). No 787 or A350 Re-engine this round. Boeing has only signalled a look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, and Airbus keeps the A350 family as its focus. S2 (both Re-engines) is weighted 0.10, capped by its weaker leg.

Best grid plan in that scenario. 'UltraFan NB: hold' (all four fields at hold): +20.55 in S1, and also the best row in S2 at +20.80. EV +20.58 on 0.90 / 0.10 (+20.59 on the Board's 0.85 / 0.15). It beats 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' (+14.07 / +14.34) by 6.48 / 6.46, and 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' (+11.55 / +12.78) by 9.00 / 8.02.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. None. The submitted orders are the best grid row in both columns, so no doctrine-favoured order is kept against PV. Item by item: UltraFan NB Solo hold, $0; Joint Venture with P&W hold, $0; UltraFan WB hold, $0; Trent 1000 upgrade hold, $0. For the record, choosing the upgrade would have cost $6.48B under any weights, and UltraFan WB $8.90B ($8.85B on the Board's case). Both are above the $3B cap, and UltraFan WB is also above its $1B sub-cap, so neither could be carried as a declared premium.

Answers to the Board.

  • R3-1: Hold all four fields and say why in rationale: protect what is working. Taken up in full. All four fields are at hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 / +20.80, +20.58 on our weights and +20.59 on yours. Both legs of the objective are met. Premium $0B. No Board item. The why is in rationale items 2-5.
  • R3-2: Close the 2035 widebody plan; for 2050 bring a widebody item only with a Re-engine on the record and within its own bill and the caps. Taken up. The plan is closed formally in a private move, and I admit plainly that it rested on the strain lifting, which it does not. The cost: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, inside the $3B cap; with strain it is -6.48. For 2050 the rule is a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within the item's own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB), with the upgrade first per Watson. Noted: UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. McCabe makes an upgrade launched in 2050 about +0.28 of engine value against $7B of bill and strain.
  • R3-3: Product safety in service: Watson to report the 2036 review on gearbox durability, time on wing and full-life parts, partner-shop support, and any flag. Taken up. Watson reports that the gearbox in service is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip or reset, and RR was fitted at NGSA's entry at 24.1% (965 engines), holding equal shares with P&W through 2044. There is no safety or durability flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no figure. Two private moves answer the maturity point: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data under the shared-risk terms, and gear-and-core repair data or a module-exchange pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. His in-service report, and any flag, reach you before the 2050 orders.
  • R3-4: Precaution on shared risk: McCabe to size, off the grid, RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine. Taken up. McCabe bases it on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn over seven years), taken at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model and scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. She rebases it on any durability flag or on fleet data worse than plan.
  • R3-5: Capital: no new programme spend; distributions from sustainable free cash flow in the capital-frame order; R&D broadly flat; Trent durability and UltraFan technology continue. Taken up. No new programme spend on the board. The capital frame is held as a private move: balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. McCabe confirms it fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) and UltraFan as technology (public R&D money where available) continue as public, qualitative moves.
  • R3-6: Widebody watch: the franchise test does not trigger; watch for a 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine in 2050; time on wing is the lever today. Taken up. 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with S2 at or above S1 (Watson). The test does not trigger. The 2050 watch is a private move: a Boeing 787 next step, any A350 Re-engine, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom. Watson puts the GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp at about $0.53B of PV, already in the hold row. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we fund today; it is worth $0 on this grid but keeps the fleet earning.
  • R3-7: Public statement, pricing and housekeeping: Joint Venture engine in service with durability and support first; no new-engine date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframers' or P&W's plans; 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'; no price concessions; close the 2045 withdrawal review. Taken up. The statement leads with safety, time on wing, full-life parts and partner-shop support. It carries no date of any kind and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, and it keeps 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' and 'We do not want to underestimate the risks'. Watson checked it for early dates. Pricing discipline is a private move: no concessions, and every contract through the Investment Committee. The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed formally as moot: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation.
  • R2-1 (closing): zero margin at NGSA; the 2036 review to clear gearbox durability on test evidence; in 2045 report what it found and whether RR was fitted at entry. Closed. After the fold the engine flew on GTF2's clock, ready in 2036 with one year of margin to NGSA's 2037 entry, better than the zero margin UltraFan alone carried. The review's subject became that engine, whose gear P&W designs. The record shows entry on schedule, RR fitted at entry (24.1%) and no flag. No 2036 date was ever put on an RR engine in public. The 2035 line 'ready in 2037' is superseded by the fold and is not repeated.
  • R2-2 (closing): the 2045 withdrawal review: a sealed withdrawal unless the grid supports the commitment, in the same round as any widebody item; settle the fold question. Closed as moot. P&W committed in 2035, so the Joint Venture formed that round and withdraw is not on the 2045 menu. The fold question is moot too. The strain concern did materialise, through the formed Joint Venture as a running project rather than through a later formation. That is why both widebody items stay at hold.
  • R2-3 (closing): keep the private Joint Venture conditions: RR funds only its $4B share, a folded programme keeps its own test clock, no P&W gear or core change, support not counting on P&W's shops. Kept. RR's R&D on the board is its $4.00B share. The $1.71B write-off is our own UltraFan spend before formation, not a P&W cost. No combined design was offered: the engine took GTF2's own clock with P&W's gear and core. Our support does not count on P&W's shops. The one gap, the gear-and-core module, is now addressed through repair data or a module pool under the shared-risk terms.
  • R2-4 (closing): support and capacity: confirm the 2035 contracts placed, and the spares pool and field service standing in 2036; capacity is advice. Confirmed by Watson. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts were placed in 2035, and the spares pool and field service stood up in 2036, before NGSA's entry. They are now scaled to 914 narrowbody engines in 2045 and 863 a year from 2049, against 188 widebody. Capacity is recorded as advice.
  • R2-5 (closing): cash: report the remaining Solo spend; if not spent, that saving is no reason to bring widebody spend beside the commitment. Confirmed. The Joint Venture took GTF2's schedule, so the remaining $2.29B (about £1.68bn) of Solo spend was never needed. It is not redeployed into widebody: both widebody items stay at hold, and gross R&D stays broadly flat.
  • R2-6 (closing): widebody franchise for 2045: bring the Trent 1000 upgrade first, against a Re-engine on the record or as a declared premium inside $3B; UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap. Brought and priced, then held. The upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 against hold because the $5B strain stays beside the formed Joint Venture. That is beyond its own $2B bill and the $3B cap, so it cannot be a declared premium, and McCabe withholds her signature. UltraFan WB has no Re-engine on the record and runs -9.00 / -8.02, far beyond the $1B sub-cap. Both are at hold. The watch carries to 2050.
  • R2-7 (closing): pricing discipline; in later statements give no Joint Venture ready date and nothing beside any airframer's dates. Kept. No concessions. This statement carries no Joint Venture date, no new-engine date and nothing on any airframer's dates.

Objective. Both legs are met on hold, with no premium and no new programme. Narrowbody entry: RR narrowbody share 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050, through the Joint Venture engine on NGSA. Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in S1, with 5.2 pp of headroom. S2 is at or above S1 on Watson's reading, since the hold row is +0.25 higher. Neither widebody item is needed to hold 50%. A further CFM widebody gain the size of the GEnx upgrade would leave about 52.4%, still above the line (Watson, inference). The narrowbody drift from 24.8% to 21.6% is airframe mix (fps gains on CFM), not a lever we hold.

Predictions. Weights: S1 0.90, S2 0.10. - No 787 Re-engine this round (0.80). Boeing has only said it will look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, and has named no engine. - No A350 Re-engine (0.90). Airbus says the A350 family, including the A350F, remains its focus. - Both Re-engines together (S2): 0.10 at most. - CFM/GE holds. The ducted engine and Embraer stay in service, RISE stays as technology, and the GEnx upgrade keeps its 2.8 pp of widebody. - P&W stays in the Joint Venture on its published terms. The GTF fleet keeps first call on its shops. - The Joint Venture engine stays in service with no durability or safety flag on the record. Watson's in-service report reaches the Board before the 2050 orders. - RR on hold: narrowbody share 21.6% from 2049; widebody 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. Both legs of the objective are met. - The $5B strain stays on any widebody item in 2050, to be confirmed from that grid. Expected ΔPV of the chosen orders: +20.58 $B on my weights (+20.59 on the Board's case). S1 outcome +20.55; S2 outcome +20.80.

Expected ΔPV. +20.58 $B (board after the round: +20.55 $B)

Other moves.

  • Joint Venture engine in service: safety, durability and support first (public): The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our priorities for it, in order: safety, then time on wing and full-life parts, then support through our partner shops. No date for any next build standard and no Joint Venture date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices [RX-0053, RX-0296, R-1476, R-0970].
  • Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded (public): About £1bn over four years, kept apart from UltraFan money and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. This is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0123, RX-0246, RX-0214].
  • UltraFan technology continues as technology (public): UltraFan technology keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, using public R&D money where available. No product launch, no ready date and no entry date. Qualitative only [RX-0094, RG-0065].
  • Joint Venture in-service support plan (Watson) (private): This carries over the 2035 support build: partner-shop agreements on our Singapore model, castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts, and the spares pool and field service stood up before NGSA's entry. Now scaled to the fleet: 914 RR-share narrowbody engines in 2045, 863 a year from 2049, about 8,600 delivered by end-2045 and about 13,000 by 2050. Field service sits near NGSA operators. The gap is the gear and core. To close it, we seek P&W's repair data, or a gear-and-core module-exchange pool, under the shared-risk terms, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops (the GTF fleet keeps first call on them). Capacity is advice, not a ground [RX-0283, RX-0286, RX-0287].
  • Technical review rights and in-service reporting to the Board (private): We carry shared risk on a gear and core that P&W designs and certifies, with no technology licence. So we ask, under the shared-risk terms, for RR access to P&W's test, certification and fleet data. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. Our engineers give their own view of maturity, from test and fleet evidence, not slides. Watson's in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders, and any safety or durability flag goes to the Board at once [RG-0027, RX-0296, RX-0284].
  • Off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine (McCabe) (private): The reasonable worst case, on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn of cash over seven years) at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model, scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that, about £5.7bn, peaking near £1.4bn, it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. It is rebased on any durability flag, or on time-on-wing or shop-visit data worse than plan [RG-0033, RX-0242, RX-0260].
  • Capital frame held: no new programme spend (private): Nothing new is funded on the board this round. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the 30-40% dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0042, RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].
  • Pricing discipline (private): No price concessions on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent fleet. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee. Joint Venture terms stay shared risk and investment, with no RR funding of P&W's costs [RX-0097, RX-0081, R-1582].
  • Housekeeping: two 2035 plans formally closed (private): (1) The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed as moot. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation. Watson's question on folding an already-ready UltraFan is moot for the same reason. (2) The 2035 widebody plan is closed: it would have brought back the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2045 without strain. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project on this board, so the $5B strain stays on any widebody item. That plan rested on an assumption that proved wrong, and we say so plainly [RX-0077, R-1573].
  • 2050 widebody watch (private): In 2050 we watch for a Boeing 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine on the record, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom above 50%. A widebody item comes to the ExCo only with a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within its own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB). The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, per Watson. UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. We plan on the strain staying, and confirm it from the 2050 grid [R-1574, R-0361, RG-0068].

Round 4 · decision year 2050

2050: everyone holds again, and the final state is the 2035 state

Every company held, and no value has changed since 2035. A Re-engine ordered in 2050 would enter service only in 2055. Airbus's A350 Re-engine was worth +$0.57B if Boeing held and −$0.42B if not; Boeing's 787 Re-engine +$0.04B or −$1.00B.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It came in on the date we gave you. The line is at 940 airplanes a year, and we got there one step at a time: on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line had shown it was stable at the rate it was on. If we take another step, it works the same way. We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 47%. That's up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and it's still short of half. I won't dress it up. We earn every point one delivery at a time, and that includes supporting the airplanes our customers already fly. We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step again. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready, and today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched. Paying down debt is still far and away our priority. We fund the business from our operations, with no new equity, and I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers. Some things don't change. We certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us, and we keep working with CFM, our engine partner, on time on wing and support for the fleet. A while back I said we were turning this big ship, but it hadn't turned yet. We've come a long way since then. There's still work to do, and we'll keep doing it the same way: do less, do it better, and let our own readiness set the pace. The financials will follow our production performance.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Our first task now is the fleet in service. We put fleet safety and operational integrity above all, and with our engine partners we follow how these engines perform in service, on field data. We continue production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected. On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We continue to study the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock, and we will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before. We also continue to prepare the technologies for the generations of aircraft that will follow. We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes, and we keep recruiting the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft. We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility. On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we started this, and it's how we'll finish it. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: there's a CFM engine on both new single-aisle airplanes. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 was ready in 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We still don't have a birthright on the next order. We earn it by delivering: LEAP and the ducted engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines. What we don't know yet is how the newest of these engines hold up over the long haul, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. We're not raising a flag today. That isn't a claim that the job is done. The field data decides that, not us. So we measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we share it with our airframers and regulators through one team, with Safran's engineers alongside. When a customer's safety review looks hard at our engines, we welcome it. Where we find something, we fix it, with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery. The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, 50-50, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that. We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. We size our own supply base to our own needs, and we keep the shop and inspection capacity our fleet relies on. Anything on CFM capacity or terms, we work through together with Safran, and with our customers in private. You won't see us pointing fingers. You'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyDo Nothing

Public statement: “Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them. What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected. Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, measured on the fleet, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, sold on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready not before six years from launch, and it will enter service only once durability is proven. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.”

Rolls-RoyceDo Nothing

Public statement: “So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and the fleet is our job. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. If we find an issue, we will say so early, with the plan. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.”

How each company decided: Board guidance, ExCo, Board review (private during the game)

Boeing: the decision chain (Kelly Ortberg, Jay Malave, Stephanie Pope; Boeing Board)
StepWhat happened
Board guidanceBoeing Board: risk appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged in our tests for this final round. On Malave's conservative case, debt is not back to $45B until 2053, so we do not yet ease toward 4 (inference). The tests stand: a launch must clear +$1B in the expected column, and no Board item may fall …
FrameKelly Ortberg: initial lean: Orders I lean to: Do Nothing. - fps: hold - fps engine code: null - 737 rate: hold - 787 Re-engine: hold Row: +0.66 / +0.57. Every order is a hold, so no item goes to the Board. I'll still answer every one of its recommendations in board_response, including those …
Test (CFO)Jay Malave recommends: Do Nothing. Options failing a test: Full cost of a slip: one year of certification slip on plan B, for scale (ask 3); Re-engine against the Board's business-case bar (advice to the Board). Vetoes: B: fps hold + 787 Re-engine (row 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine', +0.71 / -0.43) (not binding)
Test (operating head)Stephanie Pope recommends: Do Nothing. Options failing a test: On-time, predictable delivery: 787 Re-engine with EIS 2055, row B (record [BX-1331] by inference; doctrine slip prior); Technology readiness for a 2055 EIS (doctrine; CEO ask 6; advice, not a veto ground, not priced on the board). Vetoes: 737 rate: increase (any combination) (not binding); fps: hold + 787 Re-engine: launch (row B) (not binding)
DecideKelly Ortberg: Do Nothing
Veto check (CFO)Jay Malave concurs
Veto check (operating head)Stephanie Pope concurs
Board reviewBoeing Board: not called; every order is the default (a hold is never a Board item)

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality first, in service and on the line. The fps has flown since 2040 and holds 940 deliveries a year from 2049. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, and the bulletin carries no CFM durability flag. The Aerospace Safety Committee wants the year's results directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer: fps in-service safety and reliability, the CFM ducted engine's durability on field data (hot and harsh service first), supplier and quality KPIs, and the 737 and 787 results. Any production step stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA [BG-0043, BG-0025, BG-0014, BX-1271, B-2236, BG-0069].
  • The rating comes first. Malave's conservative case put debt at $60.9B at end-2049 (47% of EV), back to $45B in 2053, with 2047 as upside. Operating profit runs at 16.9 a year from 2049, 10.2 above the status quo. Debt is the first call on that uplift. There is no new equity. Shareholder returns come last and are a matter reserved to this board, to be taken up only once the rating is solid [BG-0029, BG-0062, BG-0034, B-2259, B-2327, BX-1305, BX-0556, BG-0044].
  • One well-founded launch, not a bet. The only Board item on offer is 787 Re-engine: launch. Its item value is +0.05 / -1.00 (S1 / S2). It clears the $1B business-case bar in neither column and sits exactly at our -$1B downside limit in S2, which the bulletin does not rule out. We expect 787 Re-engine: hold. fps and 737 rate are offered only at hold [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581, BG-0066, BX-1239, BX-0548].
  • The long cycle and candour at the close of the game. Report narrowbody share plainly: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045, and 47% from 2049 through 2060, a 47/53 long-run split. Both objectives stay recorded as not met. No order on offer moves that path, so the objective premium is 0. Tie no order to Airbus's timing, attribute nothing to anyone, log every premium, and answer every recommendation now, because 2050 is the last decision year [BG-0006, BG-0005, BG-0003, B-2313, BG-0022, BG-0026].

Expects to see. 1. Ortberg's frame and his expected_scenario (S1, rivals hold; or S2, Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine), argued from the bulletin. Airbus keeps the A350 family as its widebody focus and will decide 'when the technology and the case are mature'. Rolls-Royce spends nothing new on a widebody engine without a Re-engine. Neither rules S2 out, so both columns count as plausible. 2. The submitted row from the round-4 grid. If 787 Re-engine: launch is submitted, show the same row with 787 Re-engine at hold, column by column: - Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.57. - fps: hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.71 / -0.43. - Item value: +0.05 / -1.00. It breaks even at a 4.8% chance of S2. State whether the grid ties out to Malave's round-3 estimate of about +0.04 for a 2050 launch in S1. 3. Malave's buffer test with numbers. We expect 'not applicable', since there is no column labelled 'Risk case' and the fps has no slip leg. On the S2 proxy floor of -1.43, Do Nothing passes by 2.00 and the Re-engine row by 1.00. 'Fundable when the 777X turns' does not apply, since no fps launch is offered. 4. Malave's close-out funding report to the Finance Committee: - actual end-2049 debt against his conservative case ($60.9B) and upper bound ($16.4B); - whether the 2047 upside was met; - the investment-grade year, restated, including the effect of any Re-engine ($5B, about $1.0B a year over 2050-54, 5.9% of 16.9 a year of operating profit); - confirmation of no new equity, and no dividend or buyback proposal before the rating is solid. 5. Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results and her veto check. The KPI veto is not in play, since 737 rate is hold-only and no live problem is reported. We still want: - her results on the fps line at 940; - CFM allocation and the CFM ducted engine's durability in service; - the 737 and 787 results; - strain for any Re-engine: 0 years of overlap, with the fps counted 2033-40 and a 2050 Re-engine counted 2050-55; - her technology readiness view for a 2055 EIS (UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056; the upgraded GEnx has been on the 787 since 2033). This is advice, not a veto ground. 6. The CEO's rulings for any Re-engine: - H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. - H4: 0 years of overlap. - H5: once launched, never cancelled. This is the last round, so S2's -1.00 would be locked in. - H1, H2 and H6 do not apply. 7. premium with its reason: - If S1 is expected and the Re-engine is held: 0.05 forgone, a tie inside ε. The cumulative total becomes 0.81 against the $2B cap. - If S2 is expected: 0, with the cumulative total staying at 0.76. - Objective premium: 0. - Hard-rule costs logged apart: H3 2.20 (round 1), H4 0.65 (round 2), none in rounds 3 and 4. 8. A board_response answering each recommendation below. This is the final round, so nothing can be carried forward. 9. A public statement that gives no Re-engine date, no rating year and no attribution, and ties no order to Airbus.

Would approve.

  • Do Nothing: fps: hold, 737 rate: hold and 787 Re-engine: hold. The fps stays in service at 940 a year. The row is +0.66 / +0.57 (S1 / S2). On the S2 proxy it sits 2.00 above the -1.43 floor, and its worst column is higher than the Re-engine row's by 1.00 (+0.57 against -0.43). Holds are not Board items and are never vetoed. If every order is a hold, the GM does not call us to review. This is the last round, so we ask that board_response close out our recommendations in this package.
  • fps engine code: none. The fps has flown CFM since its 2040 EIS, and the brief offers only None. This is not a Board item and never a veto ground.

Would veto.

  • 787 Re-engine: launch (with fps: hold). The row is +0.71 / -0.43 against Do Nothing's +0.66 / +0.57, an item value of +0.05 / -1.00. Ground, the business case: a launch needs an item value above $1B in the expected column. It falls short by 0.95 in S1 and by 2.00 in S2, so it fails whichever column the CEO expects. Downside: -1.00 in S2 sits exactly at our -$1B limit, with no margin. It is not below the limit on the printed grid, so we do not count it as a ground. It passes the other tests: - Rating first: not applicable, since there is no risk-case column. On the S2 proxy it is -0.43 against -1.43, passing by 1.00. - One development at a time: 0 years of overlap. - H3: no A350 Re-engine is on the record. - Safety: the brief reports no live problem. Funding is not our ground. The $5B is about 5.9% of operating profit over 2050-54. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Board item that carries a binding ExCo veto still standing after revision, a red-line flag the CEO neither struck nor rebutted in the rationale, or a premium above $2B or unlogged. We would veto the item whose reversion to the default cures it, here 787 Re-engine: launch, and name hold as the alternative.
  • fps and 737 rate are offered only at hold this round (the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order), so no other value is valid and there is nothing to veto. We never veto a hold.

Recommendations.

  • Hold the 787 Re-engine. Its item value is +0.05 / -1.00. It clears $1B in neither column, and in S2 it sits at our -$1B limit. Launched in the last decision year, H5 would lock that in with no exit. In S1, +0.05 is inside ε, and the tie goes to doing less, better and to the plan whose worst column is higher, by 1.00. Holding is the better call whenever the chance of S2 is above 4.8%. Malave's round-3 estimate of about +0.04 tied out to the grid's +0.05. Record the forgone Re-engine as a loss accepted, not a wait. On the 787's future: - Grow it from Charleston. - Keep the readiness work going without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. - Publish no Re-engine date. - If Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine, H3's second half bars a 787 Re-engine from then on.
  • Bring the Finance Committee a close-out report from Malave. It should cover: - actual end-2049 debt against his conservative case ($60.9B, 47% of EV) and his upper bound ($16.4B), and whether the 2047 upside was met; - the investment-grade year, restated once, on operating profit of 16.9 a year from 2049 (10.2 above the status quo); - the debt path to $45B, with no new equity. Debt stays the first call on cash, and the rating year stays internal. Shareholder returns stay last. Do not put a dividend reinstatement or buyback in other_moves. Either is a matter reserved to this board, and comes to us as a Finance Committee proposal only once debt is back at $45B and the rating is solid.
  • The Aerospace Safety Committee asks to hear directly, each year, from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. Their report should cover: - fps in-service safety and reliability at 940 a year; - the CFM ducted engine's durability on field data, with hot and harsh service first, as CFM has committed in public; - supplier and quality KPIs; - the 737 and 787 results. On the line and the supply base: - A CFM durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step until the fleet action is in place. - Any step above 940 stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next. - Certify before building at rate on any derivative, with no production-certification concurrency. - Keep the CFM line, long-lead structures, titanium forgings and rare-earth parts contracted and funded for the rate in front of us, and track CFM allocation by airframer. - Attribute nothing to anyone.
  • Disclosure and the long cycle, at the close. Report the narrowbody path honestly: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045, and 47% from 2049 through 2060, the 47/53 long-run split. Both objectives stay recorded as not met. No order on offer can change that, so no objective premium applies. Tie no order to Airbus in either direction: do not launch to pre-empt an A350 Re-engine, and do not hold because of one. The hold rests on ε and on debt first. We judge this plan on the long cycle, and we will continue to use shareholders' feedback in our decisions.
  • Premium log and board_response. The premium: - If S1 is expected and the Re-engine is held, log 0.05 as a doctrine premium within ε. The cumulative total becomes 0.46 + 0 + 0.30 + 0.05 = 0.81 against the $2B cap. - If S2 is expected, log 0, and the cumulative total stays at 0.76. Keep hard-rule costs in their own log: H3 2.20 (round 1), H4 0.65 (round 2), none in rounds 3 and 4. This is the last decision year, so answer every recommendation here in board_response, including those carried from rounds 2 and 3. Nothing can be raised again later.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. 2050 is the last decision year on this board. The fps has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave, and it holds 940 deliveries a year from 2049. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Only one order is live: 787 Re-engine. A 787 Re-engine launched now would enter service in 2055. Does it earn a place? Or do we hold, keep doing less and doing it better, and accept that the Re-engine is forgone on this board? Two things sit under that question, and I owe the Board both at the close: the KPI record on the fps at 940, and a straight funding report on debt and the rating. My four questions to this ExCo: (1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live problem. I want Pope's seat to put that on the record for the fps at 940, the 737 and the 787 [BX-1271, BX-1259]. (2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready for a second development? A Re-engine is a second development, even with the fps out of development [BX-1296, BX-1305]. (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? No column is labelled 'Risk case' this year. The fps is in service, so it has no slip leg. I still want Malave to read S2 first, as the Board does, and to cost a slip of the Re-engine for scale [BX-1319]. (4) Is each plan doing less, better? Every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.57. - Components: narrowbody operating profit +20.30, programme investment -14.91, debt penalty -4.73. - The penalty is already netted and never subtracted again. Kelly Ortberg decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision: Do Nothing. - Orders: fps hold, fps engine code null, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. - Row: +0.66 / +0.57 (S1 / S2). - Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board. 1. The team rule, applied. - Malave's buffer test: not applicable. The brief labels no column 'Risk case', and the fps has been in service since 2040, so it has no slip leg. He confirms he holds no veto, and no plan is out on this ground. - The Board's S2 proxy (floor 0.57 - 2.00 = -1.43): A passes by 2.00 and B by 1.00. - KPI doctrine (Pope's seat): not in play. 737 rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. She checked her veto and did not invoke it. - Neither colleague flagged a red line. I override nothing. The rest is my call. 2. The grid (round4.md §3): - A, Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.57. - B, fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.71 / -0.43. - B's item is +0.05 / -1.00. Holding is the better call whenever the chance of S2 is above 4.8% (0.05 / 1.05). - Malave's independent rebuild gives +0.042 / -1.001 (operating gain +0.758, bill -0.276, penalty -0.439). That ties to the grid and to his round-3 estimate of about +0.04. Pope's rebuild of the operating gain ties as well. 3. My tests. - KPI stability: pass. No live problem in the brief, and no dip in the numbers: 860 to 940 over 2045-49, exactly on the path. Delivery counts are not KPIs, so the record comes from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer [BX-1271, BX-1259]. - Three work streams: not converged [BX-1296]. - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2055, share doesn't move and our 787 margin falls from 20% to 15.77%, about $0.76B a year. - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been the 787's engine since 2033. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056, after a 2055 EIS. RISE has no product date. My technology risk appetite is Low [BX-1298]. This isn't priced on the board and it isn't why I hold, but it means that work stream isn't there. - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 5.9% of operating profit, with no new equity. Funding isn't the issue; the return is. - Debt before the next airplane: B fails. A second development has to beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does it in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326]. - B adds +$3.10B of undiscounted penalty on top of $105.32B of debt (I accept Malave's wording fix). That's about 0.44 PV, already inside the grid and never subtracted again. For scale, the fps 10-year's own undiscounted penalty is $19.1B. - B would keep the conservative investment-grade year at 2053, but it cuts the room from $4.5B to $0.5B and gives up the 2052 upside. - FAA process: pass. No certification trouble is reported [BX-1309]. - Certification slip: there's no risk-case column, so this is for scale only. - Malave: one year of slip costs about 0.09 priced, which takes B's S1 item to about -0.05 before concessions and rework. - Pope: one year defers about 0.07 of gain, more than the whole item. - So all of B's S1 value rests on a nominal 2055 date with no headroom. I don't plan that way [BX-1318, BX-1319, BX-1275]. - Doing less, better: +0.05 in S1 is inside ε, so the plan with less to execute wins [BX-1239]. A is also the higher-confidence plan: its worst column is higher by 1.00 [BX-0548]. In S2, A leads outright by 1.00. - Airbus doesn't set the date. I'm not holding because of Airbus, and I wouldn't launch to pre-empt it either [B-2313]. On the grid, entering service in the same year costs us 1.00, so B is no hedge. The hold rests on ε, debt first and readiness. - Premium cap: 0.05 this round, 0.81 cumulative, against $2B. 4. Hard rules and red lines. - H1: does not apply. The fps is in service; I lifted H1 in Round 1, with evidence. - H2: cannot bind. - H3, first half: lapsed after Round 1. - H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. If Airbus launches one this round, we stand aside (company doctrine [B-0917, B-0858], not my record). - H4: 0 years of overlap (fps 2033-40, a Re-engine 2050-55). It would pass, so it isn't binding. - H5: the fps can't be cancelled. A launched Re-engine is never cancelled, so in this last round S2's -1.00 would have been locked in. - H6: not in play. H7: no trigger. - H8: 0.81 of $2B, logged. - My own lines: none is tested by a hold. Certify before rate, no fixed-price development, no blame on the FAA, and no attribution all stand. 5. Board risks. The Board would veto 787 Re-engine: launch on its business case: 0.95 short of $1B in S1 and 2.00 short in S2, with S2 sitting exactly at its -$1B limit. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned." [BX-1300] We're further along now, and the same discipline holds.

Weighing the CFO. I weighed it heavily, as my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. It's still a thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and beyond the buffer test his views are advice. What I took: - His buffer test is not applicable, since there is no risk-case column. The grid governs, and nothing is netted twice. - The cash path: one $5B bill at EIS 2055, about $1.0B a year of real spend, fundable from operations with no new equity. - His debt table: both plans reach $45B during 2053. B cuts the room to $0.53B and gives up 2052. - The slip cost for scale: one year is about 0.09 priced, which takes B's S1 item below zero. - The premium log: 0.05, cumulative 0.81. I agree. We don't claim what the data doesn't show. Caveats: the pro-rata penalty allocation, the half-the-uplift-to-debt case and the 2053 year are his inferences, not grid outputs. Weighing the operating head. I weighed it as advice from a doctrine seat. Pope's evidence on the airplane business is Very low; her own record covers delivery, cash and IP, applied by inference. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer give that record. - The line ran 860 to 940 on the path. At a flat 940 the in-service tail binds, not a step: about 8,500 fps, rising to about 14,100 by 2055. - The supply binding order: the CFM line, structures, titanium forgings, rare earths. Certify-before-rate confirmed. - IP: a Solo airframe with an engine partner is the right split. - Charleston grows the 787 with or without a Re-engine. I note her reading that the board carries no new-build 737 deliveries; the 737 fleet and spares are off the board. Her note on another airframer resizing its supply agreements is an ordinary market move, and I attribute nothing to it.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), provisional. My confidence on Airbus is Low. For S1: - Airbus repeats that the A350 family, including the A350F, remains its focus, and that it will decide 'when the technology and the case are mature, and not before'. - It held its widebody in 2030, 2035 and 2045. - Rolls-Royce's line, no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, is a condition on its own spending, not an Airbus commitment. - A move is real only when it is launched. S2 stays plausible: - NGSA has been in service since 2037, which frees Airbus engineering. - Doctrine expects an A350 Re-engine attempt. The orders are the same in either column. Hold ties within ε in S1 and wins by 1.00 in S2.

Best grid plan in that scenario. In S1 the top row is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, at +0.71. That's 0.05 above Do Nothing's +0.66, well inside ε ($1B). I order Do Nothing (fps: hold + 787: hold, +0.66 / +0.57): - The tie goes to doing less, better [BX-1239] and to the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548], whose worst column is higher by 1.00. - Debt first and the Board's business case also rule out the Re-engine row. It clears ε in neither column. In S2, Do Nothing is the top row outright (+0.57 against -0.43).. B's +0.71 against A's +0.66 is inside ε, so doing less, better and the higher-confidence plan decide the tie. - In S2 the premium would be 0, since holding gains 1.00 there. Holding is the better call whenever the chance of S2 is above 4.8%. - Objective premium: 0. No order on offer moves the narrowbody path. Final log: - Round 1: 0.46 (the 10-year ramp over the 7-year). - Round 2: 0. - Round 3: 0.30. - Round 4: 0.05. - Cumulative: 0.81, within the $2B cap (H8). Nothing carries forward. It entered service on its 2040 date, and no reset was needed. - Re-engine window and holds (R1 1, R2 2, R3 1): met. - Held in 2035 under H4, logged as a 0.65 hard-rule cost. - Held in 2045 and 2050 on ε and debt first. - The 2050 test you set was applied, and the Re-engine failed it. - Yearly funding reports (R1 2, R2 3, R3 2): closed by Malave's close-out report. - Safety reporting, certify-before-rate, suppliers funded (R1 3, R2 4, R3 3): in place, and they continue. - The 10-year ramp row (R1 5): 0.46 logged. Objective. The briefing objective is to hold the 50/50 narrowbody split and defend incumbency. It's the company's mission, not on my own ranked list, and it never changes the payoff. The path, reported plainly: - 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39, while NGSA flew alone. - 38% in 2040, the worst year, at fps EIS. - Up a point a year to 43% in 2045. - 47% from 2049 through 2060: a long-run split of 47/53. Both objectives are recorded as not met: - 50/50: below 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050. - Incumbency (40% or more in 2030-50): the worst year was 38%. No order on offer this round moves that path; the 787 Re-engine is widebody only. So the objective premium is 0.

Predictions. Airbus (Low confidence): - Most likely holds the A350 again (S1). - An A350 Re-engine (S2) is plausible. If it launches, H3's second half means we stand aside, and our hold avoids the -1.00. - NGSA stays in service on code 7. Engine makers: - Rolls-Royce launches no UltraFan WB without a Re-engine. - CFM holds RISE as technology, with no product date, and raises no durability flag on the Ducted. - The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine stays on NGSA. Boeing: - The Board isn't called to review, since all four orders are holds. - The fps holds 940 a year, with narrowbody share at 47% through 2060. Widebody stays at 100 a year (58.8%). - No live problem is expected. The CFM line and the in-service tail are the watch items. - Debt falls on Malave's conservative path, solidly investment grade during 2053, with 2052 as upside. Final ΔPV: +0.66 in S1, +0.57 in S2.

Expected ΔPV. +0.66 $B (board after the round: +0.66 $B)

Other moves.

  • fps line holds at 940 a year; any step above it is KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA (public): The fps went from 860 deliveries in 2045 to 940 in 2049, on the briefed path, one KPI-gated step at a time. The board holds the line flat at 940 (47% of 2,000) through 2060, so demand calls for no step above it. Any step that commercial demand does call for stays KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next. If a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem goes live, the line holds at its current rate until the KPIs show stability again [BX-1271, BX-1259, BX-1322]. Unpriced.
  • Chief Engineer and Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee each year (public): The report covers: - fps in-service safety and reliability at 940 a year; - the CFM ducted engine's durability on field data, hot and harsh service first; - supplier and quality KPIs; - the 737 and 787 results. The board carries deliveries only, so their results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record. A CFM durability or allocation flag holds any step above 940 until the fleet action is in place: root cause, inspection, parts fix, shop visits and spares. The commitment is public; the reports are internal [BG-0043, BX-1298, B-2304].
  • Certify before building at rate on any derivative; no fixed-price development (public): No production-certification concurrency on any derivative, including any future 787 step [BX-1263, B-2228]. Development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Neither is priced on the board.
  • Supply base funded and hot for 940 plus spares, not contracted above it (private): Pope's binding order at a flat rate: 1. the CFM engine line (sole source, OE engines and Ducted spares); 2. long-lead airframe structures; 3. titanium forgings; 4. rare-earth parts. All four stay funded and hot for 940 plus spares for the in-service fleet. We don't contract above that, which would tie up working capital. Staff are embedded at any supplier that falls behind [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. We name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing to anyone.
  • CFM allocation tracked by airframer (private): In 2049 we took 1,880 of CFM's 2,272 narrowbody engines, 82.7%, up from 78.2% in 2044. That leaves 392 OE engines for NGSA and the A320neo. The exposure is concentration: one sole-source line carries all of our narrowbody deliveries. We track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and keep delivery commitments contracted for the rate in front of us [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923].
  • In-service support for the fps fleet (private): About 8,500 fps were delivered in 2040-49 (about 17,000 engines), rising to about 14,100 by 2055 as shop visits come due. Spares and support go on time to that fleet, and every transaction should build customers' trust [BX-1273]. Unpriced; off the board.
  • Close-out funding report to the Finance Committee; debt first, no new equity (private): Malave's close-out report is the record: - Operating profit came in on the path: 74.4 over 2040-44 and 81.5 over 2045-49, then 16.9 a year (10.2 above the status quo). - Actual end-2049 debt is not observable on the board, so he reports the planning figure: conservative case $60.9B (47% of EV), upper bound $16.4B. Peak was $105.32B at EIS 2040 (81% of EV). - The 2047 upside is not shown, and we don't claim it. - Investment-grade year, restated once: 2053, with $4.5B of room and 2052 held as upside ($0.57B short). With no Re-engine launched, that stands. - No new equity. Debt stays the first call on cash. No shareholder-return proposal comes from management; that is a matter reserved to the Board, once the rating is solid [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Publicly we say debt first and give no rating year [BX-1268].
  • 787 grows from Charleston; no Re-engine launch (public): The 787 holds 100 a year on the board (58.8%). Charleston has headroom above that [BX-1317, B-2336]. We give no Re-engine date. Internally, readiness work on the 787's next step continues without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. Pope finds no matured widebody engine for a 2055 EIS [BX-1296]. On this board the Re-engine is forgone: a loss accepted, not a wait.
  • Independent estimate check and early-warning rule continue (private): Malave stays the independent check on every programme estimate [BX-1316]. Any reset is planned once and reported early, with the mitigation attached [BX-1318, BX-1306].
  • Customer slots quoted only against the KPI-gated line (private): fps delivery slots are offered only against what the gated line at 940 supports, never against an earlier internal number [BX-1273, B-2315].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety first, now on a fleet in service. NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM ducted and P&W-RR Joint Venture engines, and both engine families are now in hot and harsh service. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce all say they make no durability claim until field data shows it. The Board's twice-yearly safety review should take three reports together: Wagner's NGSA line, the A320neo transition, and the in-service durability record of both NGSA engine families. Nothing added this round may draw on the people, shops or supplier slots that carry them [AG-0038, AX-0081, AX-0015, A-0303, A-0331, AG-0067, AG-0068].
  • Liquidity and the A+/A1 rating, with room. No programme cash is running. An A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 would spend $1.0B a year over 2050-54. That is about 19% of the $5.2B line and leaves $4.2B of headroom, with no overlap with NGSA and no two-front strain. Operating profit on the brief is $15.9B a year from 2049, against $8.8B in the status quo. Cash is not the constraint this round [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104, A-0343].
  • The widebody decided on proof, in the last decision year. The A350 Re-engine is the only possible Board item, and its case is thinner than in 2045. It is worth +0.57 in S1 (rivals hold) and -0.41 in S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine), and it breaks even at a 58% chance of S2. In 2045 it was +0.89 / -0.50. No later round exists in which to gate, re-test or cancel it. On the record, no widebody engine would be ready for a 2055 entry into service. The Board does not press for the launch and will not stand in its way if every test passes [A-0302, AX-0019, A-0364, AX-0007, AG-0029, AG-0033].
  • Governance of any Board item. The A350 Re-engine is a launch above EUR 800m, so it needs a Qualified Majority. No override can carry it. At +0.57 in S1 it falls $0.43B short of the $1B the Board's override review requires over hold. It also trails hold by $0.41B in S2, the worst plausible column. The game's one override has been unused in rounds 1 to 3 and should stay unused [AG-0049, AG-0011, AX-0008, AX-0027, AG-0026].
  • Integrity, returns and the long view at the close of the game. Delay Tactics are closed: the menu offers only none, and none has been ordered in this game. No unpriced move may do by other means what the Board refused. Returns stay within the 30-50% payout and the AGM buyback authority, sized after programme cash. There is to be no equity raise, and state money is upside only. The Board supplies the long view that pay does not: preparation of the generation after NGSA stays funded as research and technology [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0034, AG-0039, AG-0006].

Expects to see. (1) The grid rows. On the Board's reading of round4.md: - NGSA hold + A350 hold: +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2; - NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine: +23.94 in S1 and +22.92 in S2; - item value of the A350 Re-engine: +0.57 in S1 and -0.41 in S2. It breaks even at a 58% chance of S2, and is worth about +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%; - holding gives up only $0.04B in S2, the cost of a lone 787 Re-engine entering service in 2055. (2) The CEO's expected column, with a probability reasoned from the bulletin. - Against S2, Boeing said in 2045: - "We're not launching a new program today"; - the market, the technology and Boeing are not yet ready ("Today all three aren't there"); - it gives no date; - debt reduction is "far and away our priority". - Boeing's other move also records no matured widebody engine for a 2050 entry into service. That rules out a 2050 EIS, not a 2050 launch. - For S2: Charleston has headroom, and readiness work on the 787's next step continues. The bulletin has not ruled S2 out, so it is the worst plausible column. (3) Toepfer's paper: - cash if launched: $1.0B a year over 2050-54 and entry into service in 2055, with no overlap, no strain, one launch and $4.2B of headroom; - cash if held: no programme cash; - his added-move gate (at least $1B in the expected column and not negative in the 787 Re-engine column). The Board reads +0.57 / -0.41 as failing it; - a check of his 2045 option-to-wait estimate (about +0.6) against the grid's +0.57; - the net-cash proxy, base case beside stress case, with the payout and the buyback room under the AGM authority; - the A+/A1 headroom proxy. (4) Wagner's memo: - safety and quality on NGSA, the A320neo and the A350; - the NGSA line at 1,060 deliveries from 2049 and the A320neo transition; - the in-service durability record of the CFM ducted and Joint Venture engines on NGSA (time on wing, shop visits, any flag); - the Joint Venture watch item: two of three makers ride on one engine, with CFM as backstop; - the outcome of the supply-agreement resizing; - his gates on the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages, from line data, or a statement that the record is silent; - the engineering ring-fence; - the widebody engine path for a 2055 entry into service. Rolls-Royce spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine, and an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056. Wagner should say whether this fails production readiness again. (5) Overrides. None is expected. Any override must be reported with its margin over hold in both columns. (6) Confirmation of the remaining fields: ngsa hold, NGSA engine code none, Delay Tactics none. (7) A closing record of the staged widebody case, gate by gate, including rule 3. No 787 Re-engine is on the record, and a same-year Boeing launch is the S2 column, not a launch after Boeing. (8) A public statement that: - leads with the five pillars; - gives windows, not dates; - ties no widebody step to Boeing; - never mentions Delay Tactics. Where a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so. A missing piece alone is not a veto ground.

Would approve.

  • NGSA: hold. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so this is not a Board item, and there is no cancel on the menu. NGSA engine code none: the fitted CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce engines stand.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold. This is the default and is never vetoed. The row is +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2, the better row in the worst plausible column, and it gives up only $0.04B in S2.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch (entry into service 2055), but only if every one of these conditions holds: - the CEO's expected column is S1, where the item adds +0.57, and his S2 probability is below the 58% break-even; - its worst plausible column, S2, is at -0.41, inside the Board's $2B loss line; - spend is $1.0B a year over 2050-54 against the $5.2B line, with no overlap, no strain and one launch in the round; - rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record; - Toepfer and Wagner pass it on their own tests, with no override, and Wagner names an engine ready by 2055 or passes production readiness; - it carries a Qualified Majority as a launch above EUR 800m.
  • Delay Tactics: none. This is the only value on the menu. The question has been closed since fps entered service in 2040.

Would veto.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch where the CEO's expected column is S2, or where his probability for S2 is 58% or more. Ground: downside. The item does not gain in his expected scenario: it is -0.41 against hold in S2. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch carried by an override of a CFO or Wagner soft veto, for example Toepfer's added-move gate or Wagner's production-readiness test. Ground: governance, because the override fails the Board's review. +0.57 is under $1B over hold in S1, and on a Qualified Majority item it trails hold by $0.41B in S2, the worst plausible column. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch that carries a binding ExCo veto the CEO neither respected nor overrode as the rule allows, or a red-line flag he neither struck nor rebutted. Ground: governance. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch that Wagner fails on safety, quality, the NGSA or A320neo ramp shield, or a supply crunch. This includes an engine-durability flag on the NGSA fleet that the launch would draw on. Ground: safety and ramp. The Board accepts no override of these tests. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Delay Tactics value other than none, or any NGSA cancel, should either appear. Neither is on the brief's menu. Integrity and abnormal risk, and reactive cancellation, would be the grounds. Acceptable alternatives: none and hold.

Recommendations.

  • Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and on an explicit read of Boeing. Put a probability on S2 and reason it from the bulletin. Boeing gave no Re-engine date and said the market, the technology and Boeing were not yet ready, but its readiness work continues and Charleston has headroom. - The item breaks even at 58%: it is worth about +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%. - Even at 0% it is only +0.57, under the $1B test, which is smaller than in 2045, as Toepfer's discount predicted. - If his gate or Wagner's readiness test fails it, the right answer is hold. The Board will not read that as a lost opportunity, and it would not accept an override to carry it.
  • Treat this as the last decision year. No later round exists to gate, re-test or cancel a launch, so an A350 Re-engine ordered now is an unconditional commitment through its 2055 entry into service. The proof must therefore come first. If it is launched: - the Audit Committee (chair Gemkow) runs an annual cash gate at $1.0B a year over 2050-54; - the write-off schedule is $5B x years elapsed / 5; - cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. A 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 enters service in 2055 at the earliest, so no Boeing move can meet that condition, and the case must stand on its own.
  • Engine path. Rolls-Royce is the A350 incumbent, but it spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine and keeps UltraFan as technology, with no product launch. An UltraFan WB launched alongside a 2050 airframe would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. Boeing's own record finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 entry into service. Wagner should name the engine, its readiness and the fallback. The engine path is not a veto ground on its own, unless he fails the launch on production readiness and that failure is overridden.
  • Safety, durability and the NGSA line. The twice-yearly safety review should take three reports as one package: - Wagner's NGSA line report; - the A320neo transition report; - the in-service durability record of the CFM ducted and P&W-RR Joint Venture engines on NGSA (time on wing, life-limited parts, shop visits). The Joint Venture watch item stays on the agenda: two of the three makers ride on one engine, and CFM is the backstop within resized needs. A flag from any engine maker comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. It is answered through supply and fleet action, never by an NGSA re-timing. Widebody engineering draws on neither NGSA in-service support nor the A320neo transition.
  • Returns and rating. The CFO should show: - the payout within the 30-50% policy; - buyback room under the 18-month AGM authority, sized after the year's programme cash, with the A350 Re-engine first if it is launched; - the base case beside the stress case; - the A+/A1 headroom proxy. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State support stays upside only and is never assumed in the case.
  • Integrity and the briefing objective. The 60/40 edge is not met: narrowbody share is 53% in 2050, on the long-run split, and no order on this menu moves it. The Board will not trade value or integrity for it. The ECSC should report the outcome of its review: - each supply agreement resized to Airbus's own needs (1,060 a year from 2049), never held at the 2039 peak, with any agreement over EUR 300m brought to the Board; - hiring that never targets rival teams; - pricing within ordinary competition. Delay Tactics stay none, and no unpriced move may recreate them.
  • The long view beyond the board's horizon. Pay measures nothing beyond about four years, so the Board supplies the long view. Research and technology for the generation after NGSA, and studies on the A350 family's future, stay funded inside the Board-approved R&D budget as staged studies, each below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate. An NGSA derivative or an A220 variant comes to the Board as its own item if it crosses EUR 300m, and a launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority. None is presented as a launch in public. The Board's annual off-site should review the staged portfolio.
  • Public statement. - Lead with the five pillars and with NGSA's fleet safety and durability. - Give windows, not dates. - If the A350 Re-engine is launched, give no window the engine cannot meet, and make no reference to Boeing. - If it is held, say the A350 family, including the A350F, remains the focus, decided on Airbus's own technology and industrial clock, and commit to nothing either way. - Never mention Delay Tactics. The Board vets the final text.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. It is 2050, the last decision year of the game. Do we keep the A350 at Do Nothing, the company default? That row is +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2, with no Board item. Or do we launch the A350 Re-engine for entry into service in 2055? That row is +23.94 / +22.92, so the item alone is worth +0.57 in S1 and -0.41 in S2. No later round exists in which to gate, re-test or cancel it, so a launch now is an unconditional commitment. To launch, it must pass all of these: - the five pillars, now including the in-service durability of NGSA's engines; - the company's $1B launch test; - Toepfer's added-move gate; - Wagner's gates: an engine ready by entry into service, the A350F and Spirit A350 packages, and the ring-fence; - a Qualified Majority of the Board.

Situation. Round 4, decision year 2050. In round 3 (2045) the GM recorded no public events, and the brief reports no inject. Public record (bulletin) - Boeing. - fps has been in service since 2040 on CFM. It is at 43% of narrowbody deliveries, and its ramp is gated on KPIs agreed with the FAA (860 deliveries in 2045, 940 in 2049). - No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase is on the record. The 787 holds 100 a year, and Charleston has headroom. - In 2045 Boeing said: "We're not launching a new program today"; the market, the technology and Boeing are not ready ("Today all three aren't there"); "I'm not going to give you a date"; and "Paying down debt is far and away our priority". - Readiness work on the 787's next step continues internally, on engine durability data and customer requirements. Boeing's other move finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 entry into service. That rules out a 2050 entry, not a 2050 launch. S2 is not ruled out, so it stays the worst plausible column. - Airbus. NGSA has been in service since 2037, three years ahead of fps. It flies CFM, P&W and RR (fitted set CFM + PW + RR). - Engines. Every NGSA engine is in service: CFM ducted since 2036, and the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine since 2036, with GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded in. The question has moved from delivery to durability in service. - CFM makes no durability claim until field data shows it. Hot and harsh service goes first on the ducted engine; that is Ali's inference from the LEAP history, and CFM labels it "not a flag". CFM says any flag reaches the Board before the 2050 orders with its fleet action. None is on the record. - P&W will report the fleet record (time on wing, life-limited-part life, shop visits) and gives no dated recovery. Its GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on its parts, shops and engineers. - Rolls-Royce: "there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine". UltraFan continues as technology only. Trent durability work of about £1bn runs over four years. - No widebody engine for a 2055 A350 Re-engine is on the record. An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056. - Observed shares. - Narrowbody: 63% at the 2039 peak, 57% in 2045, 53% in 2049. - Widebody: flat at 41.2% (70 a year). - Narrowbody engines in 2049: CFM 56.8%, P&W 21.6%, RR 21.6%. - Problems. The brief reports no safety, quality, durability or supply problem. Our position (brief section 1) - If nobody moves, ΔPV is +23.37: narrowbody profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 (booked at the 2037 entry into service) and debt penalty -0.53. - Operating profit is $15.9B a year from 2049, against $8.8B in the status quo, on 1,060 narrowbody deliveries at the long-run 47/53 split. - No programme cash is running. The line stays at $5.2B, one year's FCF [AX-0104]. An A350 Re-engine would spend $1.0B a year over 2050-54: about 19% of the line, leaving $4.2B of headroom. It has no overlap with NGSA and no two-front strain. That is below the 2045 figure (+0.89 / -0.50), as Toepfer's five-year discount predicted (about +0.61). - Holding gives up only $0.04B in S2, the cost of a lone 787 Re-engine entering service in 2055. Objective (scored by the GM, never part of the payoff) - Protect the A320 family: met (60% in every year before NGSA entered service). - Defend the 60/40 edge: not met (62% in 2040, 57% in 2045, 53% in 2050). - No order on this menu moves narrowbody share, and I trade no PV for the objective. Wagner's NGSA line report, the A320neo transition report and the in-service durability record of both NGSA engine families go to the safety review as one package. - Cash is not the constraint. - The widebody is decided on proof, in the last decision year. Options to test.

  • A. The company default, and my lean: NGSA hold, engine code none, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. - Grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2. - No Board item. - Its worst column (+23.33) is better than plan B's (+22.92). - It wins every tie-break: no added entry into service, no strain, no capex start, fewer Board items. - It gives up $0.57B in S1 and about $0.28B in expectation at my 30% for S2. That is within the $1B doctrine default.

Initial lean. My lean is plan A, the company default: - NGSA: hold; - NGSA engine code: none; - A350 Re-engine: hold; - Delay Tactics: none. That gives +23.37 in S1, my expected column at about 70%, and +23.33 in S2 at about 30%. Expected PV is about $23.36B, and there is no Board item. Why, in the order I am paid to protect - Five pillars. The task in 2050 is a fleet in service. Two new engine families are going into hot and harsh service, and every maker withholds a durability claim until field data shows it. Hold adds nothing that could draw on the people, shops or supplier slots behind that work [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015]. - The ramp. NGSA production continues in a disciplined and controlled way at 1,060 a year, alongside the A320neo transition, with supply agreements sized to our own needs [AX-0010, AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. - The Airbus of the 2030s. That aircraft is delivered. The widebody derivative is where my instinct pulls, as with the A330neo, re-engined late and cheaply [A-0090, A-0091]. On this grid it does not clear our own tests: - At +0.57 it falls short of the $1B launch test even if Boeing never moves. My decision therefore rests on our tests, not on our read of Boeing, which keeps us on our own clock. - It is negative in S2. - No widebody engine is on the record for 2055. An UltraFan WB launched alongside us would be a year late. - This is the last decision year, so a launch could never be gated or re-tested. - The Board. It approves hold as readily as a launch, and no override could carry the launch [AX-0026, AG-0049]. Robustness. Hold's worst column (+23.33) beats the launch's (+22.92). The expected cost of holding, about $0.28B at my 30% for S2, is inside the $1B doctrine default. It is not a premium, and no PV is traded for the 60/40 objective. My read of Boeing (it is not decisive). I put S2 at about 30%, within a range of 20-40%. That is lower than my 40% in 2045. - Against S2: Boeing said "We're not launching a new program today" and "Today all three aren't there", and gave no date. It puts debt reduction "far and away" first. Its fps ramp is still climbing step by step. No widebody engine maker has committed new money: Rolls-Royce spends none without a Re-engine. - For S2: Charleston has headroom, readiness work on the 787's next step continues, and this is the last round. S2 stays the worst plausible column. What would change my lean. Toepfer and Wagner would both have to pass the launch on their own tests, with no override. Wagner would have to name an engine ready by 2055. And the item would have to clear $1B over hold in my expected column without going negative in S2. This grid cannot show that: +0.57 is its ceiling. Any durability, safety, quality or supply flag would only strengthen hold. Public line - The five pillars first, then NGSA fleet safety and durability. - NGSA production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family. - The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We decide on our own technology and industrial clock and commit to nothing either way. - A more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes. - Our financial framework, in Toepfer's register. - Zero-for-zero trade. - Windows, not dates. Nothing on Boeing, and nothing on Delay Tactics.
