The brief gives no A350F or Spirit status for any later year. Widebody share has been flat at 41.2%, 70 aircraft a year, since 2026. I cannot confirm either gate from line data, so the Board's condition that I confirm them from line data is not met from the record.

A development overlap between NGSA and an A350 Re-engine of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. B therefore passes only on conditions: - a named widebody team, ring-fenced from NGSA in-service support and the A320neo transition; - the studies (an NGSA derivative, an A220 variant, research and technology for the next generation) stay studies, each below EUR 300m; - at the supplier, RR confirms that the widebody engine work draws nothing from Joint Venture fleet support.
Production readiness: a widebody engine ready by the A350 Re-engine's entry into service, plan B. This is a soft-veto ground; the board does not price it.Launch an A350 Re-engine only with a named engine on the record that is ready at or before the airframe's entry into service. This is rule 1's discipline for NGSA (no entry into service before the technology is ready) applied to the widebody.failLaunched in 2050, the A350 Re-engine enters service in 2055 (launch + 5). The engine: - Rolls-Royce is the A350's incumbent with the Trent XWB [A-0253]. It says there is 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'. - UltraFan continues as technology only, with no product launch and no ready date. - An UltraFan WB launched alongside us in 2050 would be ready in 2056 (launch + 6), one year late. There is no fallback on the record: - no Trent XWB derivative with a ready date; - the Trent durability work (about GBP 1bn over four years) is time on wing for the existing fleet, not a new engine; - the GEnx upgrade serves the 787; - the CFM ducted, CFM-Embraer and Joint Venture engines are narrowbody engines; - Boeing's own record finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 entry into service. Readiness therefore fails again, on the same one-year gap as in 2045 (entry into service in 2050, engine in 2051). The gap is built into the clocks: the engine at launch + 6, the airframe at launch + 5. It closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe. Grid margin against the best option that passes (A, hold): +0.57 in S1 and -0.41 in S2, under $1B in both columns.

My tests come from my role, not from anything I have said on record. Confidence: Very low. I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, engine code none, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Safety and quality: pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality, durability or supply problem. No engine maker has raised a flag. CFM's hot-and-harsh remark is labelled "not a flag", and I do not read it as one. The brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figures for either NGSA engine family, so I cannot report them. The fleet record goes to the safety review with my NGSA line and A320neo transition reports. Ramp: pass. 1,060 deliveries a year from 2049 reflects share, not a line problem. Supply crunch: not applicable. Joint Venture: unchanged, with CFM as backstop within resized needs. A350 Re-engine: capacity passes, with no overlap, $0 strain and one launch. The A350F and Spirit pass on the game proxy only; the record is silent after 2025. Readiness fails again. Rolls-Royce spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched with us is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. No fallback is on the record. That is a soft veto, binding: +0.57 / -0.41 against hold, under $1B in both columns, so no override carries it. It is not a safety or ramp result. In the last decision year it closes the board's widebody case on the same one-year gap as 2045.

Guillaume Faury decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision: plan A, the company default. NGSA hold, engine code none, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Grid +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2; expected PV about $23.36B at my 30% for S2. There is no Board item. Team rule, step by step 1. Delete red-line and pillars breaches. Neither plan breaks a company red line: - Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037. - Rules 2 and 7: no cancel is on the menu. - Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are none, the only value. - Rule 6 is met: plan B would be one launch with 0 years of overlap. - Both plans stand on the five pillars on the record. Wagner adds that plan B could do so only with a public window the engine can meet; 2055 would overstate a 2056 engine. 2. Survivors. - Plan A passes both colleagues' tests. - Plan B fails Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B A350 Re-engine launch test (profile section 6): +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short, and -0.41 in S2. - Plan B also fails Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine is on the record for a 2055 entry into service: an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, and no fallback exists. - Both are soft vetoes, and both colleagues mark them binding. Plan A is the only survivor. 3. Highest survivor, and the doctrine default. In my expected column (S1) the best grid row is plan B at +23.94. Hold is $0.57B below it, inside the $1B doctrine default, so I take the default even before the vetoes. The tie-breaks all point the same way: no added entry into service, no strain, no capex start, and fewer Board items. 4. Override. None is available, and none is used. Plan B is not $1B better than the best passing option: it leads by +0.57 in S1 and trails by -0.41 in S2. The Board's override review would also fail it. The game's one override closes unused. Read of Boeing (the Board's recommendation 1). I put S2 at about 30%, within a range of 20-40%, down from 40% in 2045. - Against S2, Boeing said "We're not launching a new program today" and "Today all three aren't there", gave no date, and put debt reduction "far and away" first. Its fps ramp is still KPI-gated, and Rolls-Royce spends nothing on a new widebody engine without a Re-engine. - For S2: Charleston has headroom, readiness work on the 787's next step continues, and this is the last decision year. - S2 therefore stays the worst plausible column. - At 30% the item is worth about +0.28. It is +0.33 at 25%, +0.18 at 40% and +0.08 at 50%, and it breaks even at 58%. - My answer does not rest on this read: the item's ceiling is +0.57 at 0% for S2, which is below $1B. We decide on our own clock and our own tests. Last decision year. No later round exists. A launch could not be gated, re-tested or cancelled on the board. The cancel condition cannot be reached either, because a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 cannot enter service before 2055. Proof comes before commitment [AX-0007, AX-0008, A-0364], and the proof is missing on engine, value and line data. Toepfer's check of the option to wait shows that waiting bought the same case, smaller (+0.61 estimated against +0.57 on the grid) and with a heavier relative downside: break-even fell from 64% to 58%. In the order I am paid to protect - Pillars. The task is a fleet in service, with two new engine families in hot and harsh service and no durability claim yet from any maker. Hold adds nothing that could draw on the people, shops or supplier slots behind that work [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015]. - Ramp. The NGSA line runs at 1,060 a year with the A320neo transition, under a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010]. - The Airbus of the 2030s. That aircraft was delivered, NGSA on its clock in 2037. My instinct favours the widebody derivative, but this case clears neither our engine test nor our value test. The long view continues as staged studies. - The Board. It approves hold as readily as a launch. Board-gate lines. No order differs from the default, so no Board item is submitted. For the record, plan B would have read: - five pillars: pass, conditional on its window; - Toepfer: fail (soft veto, binding); - Wagner: fail on production readiness (soft veto, binding); - grid ΔPV: +0.57 / -0.41 against hold. It would also have met the Board's would-veto ground on an unresolved binding ExCo veto. The Board would have nothing to vote, so plan B is not submitted. Cost of the decision. Holding gives up $0.57B in S1, about $0.28B in expectation, and gains $0.41B in S2. Its worst column (+23.33) beats plan B's (+22.92). No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective.

Weighing the CFO. Toepfer's tests (role-derived, Low confidence). Passed: - peak cash for plan A ($0, the full $5.2B as headroom) and plan B ($1.0B a year over 2050-54, 19% of the line, $4.23B of headroom, 0 years of overlap, $0 strain); - plan-level robustness (both plans positive in both columns, with plan A's worst column better); - rule 6; - net cash and rating proxy in the base and stress cases; - the capex and Board-item tie-breaks, both favouring A. Failed: - the added-move gate for plan B: +0.57 in S1, $0.43B short of $1B, and -0.41 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column. He marked this soft veto binding. - the override arithmetic: no override can carry plan B under the team rule or the Board's review. I accepted the veto without revision. It coincides with the company's own $1B A350 Re-engine launch test (profile section 6) and with my $1B doctrine default, so the decision does not rest on the low confidence of a role-derived test. I adopted: - his expected-value schedule (break-even 58.2%; +0.28 at 30%); - his option-to-wait check (estimate +0.61 against +0.57 on the grid; break-even down from 64% to 58%), reported to the Board; - his returns schedule (payout 30-50%; buyback room after programme cash; net-cash proxy positive every year; agency thresholds not in our record, so the A+/A1 headroom is shown as a proxy); - his staged-studies cap of about EUR 1.2bn as a proposal, labelled as his inference; - his finance line for the public statement.

Weighing the operating head. Wagner's tests (role-derived, Very low confidence). Passed: - safety and quality on NGSA, the A320neo and the A350, both plans. No issue is open on the record, though he has no line data after 2025. - in-service durability of both NGSA engine families. No flag is on the record, CFM's remark is "not a flag", and the brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figures. - the NGSA line and A320neo ramp shield (1,060 a year reflects share, not a line problem); - the Joint Venture watch item (unchanged; CFM is the backstop within our resized needs); - integrity of supply sizing and hiring. Not applicable: supply crunch. Passed with qualifications: - A350F and Spirit A350 absorption: on the game proxy only; the line record is silent, so the Board's line-data condition is not met. - Engineering capacity and ring-fence: only on conditions, since no named team is on the record and the supplier side cannot be confirmed. Failed: production readiness for plan B. No widebody engine is ready by 2055: an UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, with no fallback. This is the same one-year gap as in 2045. It is a soft veto, which he marked binding, and not a safety, quality, ramp or supply result. I accepted it without revision. The margin over hold, +0.57 / -0.41, is under $1B in both columns, so no override is possible. The failure also matches rule 1's discipline applied to the widebody: no entry into service before the engine is ready. I adopted: - his three-report safety package; - his ECSC reporting on the supply resizing (no agreement values in the brief, so none yet named above EUR 300m); - his lesson for the portfolio: commit the engine a year ahead of the airframe. The engine code stays None, on his call.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), at about 70%. I put S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) at about 30%, within a range of 20-40%. - Against S2: Boeing said "We're not launching a new program today" and "Today all three aren't there", gave no date, and put debt first. Its fps ramp is still KPI-gated, and no widebody engine maker has committed new money. - For S2: Charleston has headroom, readiness work continues, and this is the last round. S2 stays the worst plausible column. The decision is the same at any probability, because the item's ceiling is +0.57.

Best grid plan in that scenario. NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine, at +23.94 in S1. It fails Toepfer's added-move gate and the company's $1B launch test (+0.57 over hold), and it fails Wagner's production-readiness test (no engine for 2055). Hold is +23.37, $0.57B below and within the $1B doctrine default. Hold is also the only plan that passes both colleagues' tests, and it is better in S2 (+23.33 against +22.92).. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. No premium is paid. Hold is the company default and lies within $1B of the best grid row in my expected column ($0.57B below in S1, about $0.28B in expectation at 30% for S2). It is also the only plan that passes Toepfer's and Wagner's tests and the company's $1B launch test, so it is the highest-grid survivor in its own right. No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective.

Answers to the Board.

  • 1. Decide the A350 Re-engine on the ExCo's own tests and an explicit read of Boeing, with a probability on S2. Taken up in full. - My S2 probability is about 30%, within a range of 20-40%, reasoned from the bulletin: Boeing gave no date, said it is "not launching a new program today" and that "all three aren't there", and put debt first. Charleston's headroom and the continuing readiness work keep S2 plausible. - At 30% the item is worth about +0.28, against a break-even of 58%. - Both of my colleagues' tests fail the launch: Toepfer's added-move gate and Wagner's production readiness. Both are binding soft vetoes, and no override is available. - The answer is hold. It does not rest on the read of Boeing, because +0.57 at 0% for S2 is still below $1B.
  • 2. Treat 2050 as the last decision year; proof first. If launched: an annual Audit Committee cash gate, the write-off schedule, and a cancel condition that cannot be reached. Taken up. This is decisive in my rationale: a launch now would be an unconditional commitment through 2055 with no gate on the board, and the proof is missing on engine, value and line data. Toepfer confirms the cancel condition cannot be reached: a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 enters service in 2055 at the earliest, so never first. The governance is recorded but not triggered, because we hold: - an annual Audit Committee cash gate at $1.0B a year; - write-off of $5B x years elapsed / 5, shown in reported EBIT and never adjusted away.
  • 3. Engine path: Wagner names the engine, its readiness and the fallback; not a veto ground on its own unless a readiness failure is overridden. Taken up. Wagner names Rolls-Royce, the A350 incumbent, as the only path. - An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. - No Trent XWB derivative with a ready date and no second maker is on the record. - He fails the launch on production readiness: a soft veto, binding, on the same one-year gap as in 2045. I did not override it, so no overridden readiness failure comes to the Board. His lesson goes into the closing record and the A350 studies: the gap closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe.
  • 4. Safety, durability and the NGSA line: three reports as one package at the twice-yearly safety review; the Joint Venture watch item; any flag to the Board first, answered through supply and fleet action; the ring-fence. Adopted as written. Wagner brings three reports to every review as one package: the NGSA line report, the A320neo transition report, and the durability record of both NGSA engine families. - No flag is on the record, and he does not read CFM's hot-and-harsh remark as one. - The brief gives no time-on-wing, life-limited-part or shop-visit figures, so the record is silent. Each maker's field-data report enters the review when published. - The Joint Venture watch item stays on the agenda, with CFM as the backstop within our resized needs. Any flag reaches the Board before the cash line and is answered through supply and fleet action, never by re-timing NGSA. Hold adds nothing that draws on those people, shops or slots.
  • 5. Returns and rating: payout 30-50%, buyback room under the AGM authority after programme cash, base case beside stress case, A+/A1 headroom proxy; no equity raise; state support upside only. Taken up on Toepfer's schedule. - Under hold, programme cash is nil. - At a 50% payout, buyback room is about $4.78B a year in the base case and $2.36B in the stress case. - The net-cash proxy stays positive every year in both cases. - The 18-month AGM authority caps holdings at 10% of issued capital. Its dollar size is not in our record, because the share price is not. - The agencies' thresholds are still not in our record, so A+/A1 headroom is shown as a proxy: net cash at or above zero, and programme spend at 0% of the line. - There is no equity raise and no dividend cut, and state money is upside only, never assumed in the case.
  • 6. Integrity and the briefing objective: 60/40 not met, no value or integrity traded for it; the ECSC reports the supply resizing, hiring and pricing; Delay Tactics stay none. Agreed and taken up. - The 60/40 edge is not met (53% in 2050); A320 family protection is met. No order moves share, and no PV or integrity is traded for the objective. - The ECSC reports each resized agreement (engines from all three makers, wing packages, titanium, rare earths), sized to 1,060 a year and never held at the 2039 peak. Any agreement above EUR 300m comes to the Board. The brief gives no values, so none is named yet. - Hiring is open and never targets rival teams, and pricing stays within ordinary competition. - Delay Tactics are none, and no unpriced move recreates them.
  • 7. The long view: research and technology for the generation after NGSA and A350 family studies stay funded as staged studies below EUR 300m until a Board gate; reviewed at the annual off-site. Adopted. Research and technology for the generation after NGSA, A350 family studies, an NGSA derivative study and an A220 variant study continue as staged studies inside the Board-approved R&D budget. - Each stays below EUR 300m of committed spend until a Board gate. - Toepfer proposes an aggregate cap of about EUR 1.2bn over the study phase, roughly $0.35B a year. That is his inference, since the record gives no study sizes. - Any item crossing EUR 300m comes to the Board, and any launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority. - The annual off-site reviews the portfolio. None is presented as a launch.
  • 8. Public statement: lead with the five pillars and NGSA fleet safety and durability; windows, not dates; if held, the A350 family including the A350F remains the focus on Airbus's own clock, committing to nothing either way; no Boeing reference; never Delay Tactics. Complied. - The statement opens with the five pillars, then fleet safety and in-service performance on field data. It makes no durability claim. - It gives windows only ("since the second half of the 2030s"). - It keeps the A350 family, including the A350F, as our focus on our own technology and industrial clock, committing to nothing either way. - It makes no reference to Boeing and never mentions Delay Tactics. - Toepfer's finance line is used as written. The Board vets the final text [AX-0004].

Objective. The briefing goal is "Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family". It is scored by the GM and never part of the payoff. - Protect the A320 family: met. Share was 60% in every year before NGSA entered service in 2037. - Defend the 60/40 edge: not met. Share was 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050, on the long-run 47/53 split after fps entered service. - No order on this round's menu moves narrowbody share. Delay Tactics are closed, and the A350 Re-engine is a widebody item. - I trade no PV and no integrity for the objective, and the Board agrees. We defended the edge with our own NGSA, three years ahead of fps, and with a disciplined ramp, not with moves against a rival.

Predictions. Boeing - About 70%: it holds the 787 in 2050 with no Re-engine launch, keeps the fps ramp KPI-gated toward the long-run 47% narrowbody share, and keeps debt reduction first. - About 30% (S2): it launches a 787 Re-engine. That could enter service no earlier than 2055, and it costs us only about $0.04B on the grid under hold. Engine makers - None starts a new widebody engine programme. - Rolls-Royce keeps UltraFan as technology and its Trent durability work as funded. - CFM and P&W report durability on field data only. - I expect no durability flag on NGSA before the Board's next review. If one comes, it is answered through supply and fleet action. Our position - Narrowbody share holds at 53% and widebody at 41.2% (70 a year). Operating profit is $15.9B a year. - ΔPV is +23.37 in S1 and +23.33 in S2. - The Board confirms hold with no item to vote.

Expected ΔPV. +23.36 $B (board after the round: +23.37 $B)

Other moves.

  • Twice-yearly safety review: the NGSA line, the A320neo transition and the in-service durability record of both NGSA engine families, taken as one package (private): This is the Board's priority 1 and recommendation 4, adopted as written. Wagner brings three reports to every review: - his NGSA line report; - the A320neo transition report; - the in-service durability record of the CFM ducted and the P&W-RR Joint Venture engines on NGSA: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. The brief gives no figures for any of these, so the record is silent. Each maker reports on field data, and each report enters the review as soon as it is published. No flag is on the record. CFM's hot-and-harsh remark is labelled "not a flag", and neither Wagner nor I read it as one. P&W's Hot Section kit and its undated GTF recovery stay a watch item on the A320neo fleet, not a flag. Any flag from any maker comes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. It is answered through supply and fleet action: root cause, inspection, a parts fix, then shop visits and spares. It is never answered by re-timing NGSA. The Joint Venture watch item stays on the agenda: two of our three makers ride on one engine, and CFM is the backstop within our resized needs, never as extra slots [AX-0015, AX-0056, AX-0081, A-0303, A-0331, AG-0038, AG-0067, AG-0068].
  • Supply agreements sized to our own needs: the ECSC reports the outcome of the 2045 resizing (public): This continues the resizing ordered in 2045. The agreements are: - engines from all three makers; - wing work packages; - titanium forgings; - rare earths. Each is sized to our own needs, 1,060 aircraft a year from 2049, and none is held at the 2039 peak of 1,260. The brief gives no agreement values, so Wagner cannot yet name any agreement above EUR 300m. The ECSC reports each one and brings any above EUR 300m to the Board. In public this is a more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0331, A-0457].
  • Closing record of the staged A350 Re-engine case (private): This is the Board's item (7). The case closes on the board at hold, gate by gate: - Rule 3: met throughout the game; no 787 Re-engine is on the record. A Boeing launch in the same year would have been the S2 column, not a launch after Boeing. - A350F and Spirit A350 packages: pass on the game proxy only (2050 is well past the 2033-35 window). The line record is silent after 2025. - Widebody engine ready by entry into service: failed in 2045 and again in 2050. The gap is the same one year each time (UltraFan WB at launch + 6, the airframe at launch + 5), and no fallback engine is on the record. - Grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 Re-engine column): failed at +0.89 / -0.50 in 2045 and at +0.57 / -0.41 in 2050. - Peak cash: passed both times ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom). - Qualified Majority: not sought. Lesson for the portfolio, as Wagner states it: an engine gap built into the clocks closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe. Off the board, the A350 family's future continues as staged studies [A-0302, AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0364].
  • Staged studies for the long view, outside the board (private): This is the Board's recommendation 7. The studies are: - research and technology for the generation after NGSA; - A350 family studies; - an NGSA derivative study; - an A220 variant study. Each is staged inside the Board-approved R&D budget, with committed spend below EUR 300m until a Board gate. Toepfer proposes an aggregate cap of about EUR 1.2bn over the study phase, roughly $0.35B a year or about 7% of the line. That is his inference, since the record gives no study sizes. Research and technology is the item most likely to cross EUR 300m in aggregate, and it comes to the Board when it does. Any launch above EUR 800m needs a Qualified Majority. The Board's annual off-site reviews the staged portfolio. None of these is presented as a launch [AG-0039, AG-0006, A-0298, AG-0049].
  • ECSC integrity review: supply sizing, hiring and pricing (private): The ECSC reports that: - every supply agreement is sized to our own needs and never held at the peak; - hiring is ordinary open European recruitment that never targets any rival's programme teams; - pricing stays within ordinary competition. No unpriced move does by other means what the Board refused. Delay Tactics stay at none [A-0299, A-0474, A-0366, A-0485, AG-0053].
  • Capital allocation inside the policy (private): On Toepfer's schedule: - The payout stays within 30-50%. - Buybacks stay within the 18-month AGM authority and are sized after the year's programme cash, which is nil under this plan. - Buyback room at a 50% payout is about $4.78B in the base case and $2.36B in the stress case. - The net-cash proxy stays positive every year in both cases. - The A+/A1 headroom is shown as a proxy, because the agencies' thresholds are not in our record. - There is no equity raise and no dividend cut outside a crisis, and state money is upside only [AX-0001, AX-0022, AX-0102, AX-0104, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0062].
  • Open European engineering recruitment continues (public): Ordinary public hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support, the engine durability work, the A320neo transition and the staged studies. It never draws on line staff and never targets any rival's programme teams [A-0366, A-0485].
  • Zero-for-zero trade advocacy (public): We continue to press, through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic, for a tariff-free regime in civil aerospace [AX-0088].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality in service come first, and this is the last round in which they can reach us. In round 3 the ExCo committed that any safety or durability flag on the Ducted (in service since 2036), Embraer (2037), GEnx (2033) or the LEAP fleet would reach the Board before the 2050 orders. We expect Ali's in-service report now. It should rest on test and field evidence (turned on and turned off, not analysis), with gate calls made by the one cross-functional team alongside Safran's engineers. Any flag should come with its fleet action. Nothing on this menu answers a flag: a flag lowers the booking, it does not change the orders. Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn [CG-0009, CG-0018, CX-0009, CX-0012, CX-0208, CX-0633, CX-0658].
  • Hold everything is the only plan that bounds the downside. In the brief's only column, S1 (rivals hold), hold is -38.29 (76.1%). Against hold: - Open Fan: -19.17, which is its $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35 pp wait penalty; - Open Fan + Lobby: -15.38, which is a $9B bill plus $6.38B of 20 pp penalty. Both lose more than their own bill. The penalty runs from 2050 to 2056 at about $0.319B per point. 'Dominate NB engines' is met today (worst year 51.1% in 2040; 56.8% in 2050). On Ghai's round-3 renormalised reading (inference), either route would take 2050 below 50%, to about 23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 37.8% with Lobby [CG-0017, CG-0022, CG-0032, CX-0205, CX-0493].
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, past the end of the game. 'Introduce the Open Fan' cannot be met: a 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056, so the board gives it no share gain, only bill and penalty. Holding the Open Fan is not a cancel, and RISE is never cancelled for cost. The RISE allowance closes the game unused, at $0 of $15B. Note the near miss: Open Fan + Lobby costs $15.38B, only $0.38B over the allowance. But the allowance plus the round cap does not rescue it, because the allowance needs an airframer path, and both airframes have been flying since 2037 and 2040. The long view on RISE is ours to supply, and we supply it as funded technology, not as a launch on this board [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0147, CX-0174, CX-0214, CX-0398, CX-0162, CG-0065, CG-0034].
  • Keep the balance sheet and the payout whole. This round needs no new R&D and no new strain: the 2030 package ($4B of Ducted R&D and $2B of strain) is complete and booked. The full ~$2.5B a year of room stands after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow. Premium: $0 this round, and the game closes at $0 of the $4.0B cap [CX-0645, CG-0063, CG-0022, CG-0012, CG-0002, CG-0064].
  • Earn the installed base by delivering, and book low. - LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time to every airframer, with spares never crowding out OE. - Any CFM price, terms or capacity, including the airframer's backstop rate request, decided jointly with Safran, on standard terms. - No reaction to rival news. - Book S1 at 1.0, at -38.29 or below. The 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, and Boeing and RR say none this round, so the widebody cushion can shrink but never go above -38.29 [CX-0529, CX-0542, CX-0552, CX-0184, CX-0185, CX-0587, CX-0609, CX-0248, CX-0536].

Would approve.

  • hold on every field (ducted, Open Fan, Embraer partnership, emissions lobbying, genx). It is the best grid plan in S1, the only column, at -38.29 (76.1%), with premium $0. A hold is not a Board item and is never vetoed. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx menus offer hold only, so nothing we launched is at risk. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel.
  • No Board item on this round's menu passes our tests. The only non-hold values are Open Fan: launch and emissions lobbying: launch, and every route through them loses more than its own bill in the only column. We say so now so that the final package is not built around one.
  • Unpriced other_moves that serve safety and the customer. These are recommendations, not Board items: - in-service time on wing reported in cycles on field data, cross-functional with Safran's engineers; - LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time to every airframer; - RISE continued whole as technology, 50-50, with no date and technology flowing into LEAP and the Ducted; - any CFM capacity, price or terms answer (the backstop rate request included) made jointly with Safran on standard terms; - no public reaction to rival news; - GEnx 787 fleet support, GE alone.

Would veto.

  • Open Fan: launch (alone). - Bounded downside: in S1 (the expected and only plausible column) its item value against hold is -19.17, against an $8B bill. That is $11.17B of wait penalty beyond the bill, so it fails. - Airframer path (hard rule 2): it fails (a). NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) entered service decades before a 2060 Open Fan. - RISE allowance: it fails (b). The cost against the best non-RISE plan (hold) is $19.17B, above the $15B allowance. - Objective: it buys nothing toward 'Introduce' (ready 2060, after the 2056 window). On our inference it breaks 'Dominate NB' in 2050. - CFM parity rule (Safran consent): a RISE product with no airframer path is outside joint practice, so it would need a stated reason why Safran would agree. None is on the record, and the 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base. - Not grounds: the payout floor would pass ($0.8B a year), and holding is not a cancel. Acceptable: hold.
  • Open Fan: launch with emissions lobbying: launch. The pair is -15.38 against hold in S1: a $9B bill plus $6.38B of 20 pp penalty. Both are vetoed together. - Bounded downside: it fails. - Airframer path: it fails (a), so the RISE allowance is not available at all. It cannot be carried as $15B of allowance plus $0.38B of round premium: the allowance needs the airframer path, and at a horizon of 3 we never let the allowance carry an Open Fan that waits. - Lobby: it adds +3.79 beside an Open Fan, but passes only with a live Open Fan, so it falls with the vetoed one. - CFM parity rule (Safran consent): it fails for the Open Fan, as above. Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot. Acceptable: hold on both.
  • emissions lobbying: launch without an Open Fan. On its own it does nothing on the board, so it is about -1.00, its $1B bill (not on the grid; computed by us). It fails 'paid for the risk' and the rule that Lobby goes only beside a live Open Fan. Acceptable: hold.
  • Any premium above $0 not tied to a grid plan, any use of the RISE allowance in this round, and any argument that the game's last round justifies an Open Fan for the objective alone. 'Introduce' cannot be met, and the dashboard values the launch only as bill and penalty.

Recommendations.

  • Safety and quality in service. Bring us Ali's promised in-service report before the orders, on the Ducted, Embraer, GEnx and LEAP, hot and harsh service first: - on test and field evidence, turned on and turned off; - with gate calls made by the one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team alongside Safran's engineers. State any flag with its fleet action (root cause, inspection, a parts fix proven in test, shop visits and spares), or state that none is raised. A flag lowers the booking in the round it is found. Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn.
  • Hold everything. Show both Open Fan rows against hold in S1 with the penalty broken out, and its start year confirmed by Ghai: - Open Fan: -19.17, which is the $8B bill plus $11.17B of penalty; - Open Fan + Lobby: -15.38, which is the $9B bill plus $6.38B of penalty. State the effect on 'Dominate NB' in 2050 on renormalised shares. Nothing is ordered only because the game is ending or a rival moved.
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, beyond the game window. It should be a public other move: no program dividend, no date, and technology flowing into LEAP and the Ducted, with a product only when an airframer and its airlines want one. Say plainly in objective_note that 'Introduce the Open Fan' cannot be met (ready 2060 at the earliest). The RISE allowance closes the game unused at $0 of $15B. State in premium_reason why it cannot carry the $15.38B route: there is no airframer path. RISE is never cancelled for cost.
  • Keep the payout whole. State that this round commits $0 of new R&D and strain, and that the 2030 package is complete. About $2.5B a year of room stands after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow, with no rating effect. Premium is $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.
  • Book low on the one column. Weight S1 at 1.0 and book -38.29 or below, never above. The 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, and Boeing and RR say none this round, so the widebody cushion can be reduced. Size whatever remains: Ducted and Embraer durability, raw materials (titanium forgings, rare earths) and any same-round widebody move. Book no upside.
  • The customer comes first. - LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time on the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer, with spares never crowding out OE and no rate published. - A CFM engine offered to every airframer on standard terms. - Any price, terms or capacity, including the backstop rate request, decided jointly with Safran. - No public reaction and no price cut on Joint Venture or rival news.
  • Closing public statement: - name no rival and blame no one; - give no Open Fan or RISE date, and say RISE goes into a product when the airframers and their airlines decide; - no CFM price or capacity talk without Safran; - never call the Ducted the next generation; - claim no durable fleet without field data; - publish no ramp rate.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] This is the last round, and the narrowbody contest was decided years ago. NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR on it. fps has been in service since 2040 with CFM alone. The Joint Venture engine has been in service since 2036. No code can move, no slot is open, and the brief gives us one column, S1. So the game is the installed base we already hold [CX-0422]: LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, the Ducted on fps and NGSA, Embraer, and the GEnx on the 787. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. First that means Mohamed's in-service report, which we promised the Board before these orders. Then OE engines and spares on time to every airframer. Then the balance sheet and the payout kept whole, and a booking we can stand behind. The only real question on the menu is the Open Fan, and the grid answers it. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060 at the earliest. That is four years after the narrowbody count ends, so the board scores it as bill plus wait penalty and nothing else. On its own it loses $19.17B against hold, and $15.38B with Lobby. It would also take 'Dominate' below 50% in the very year that objective is scored. My aim is to close the game the way we played it. Hold, keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, report what the fleet shows, and book low. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (2050 bulletin). Round 3 (2045) was adjudicated with no public events. - fps (Boeing): in service since 2040, selection CFM, fitted CFM. Boeing: 'We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates.' Its ramp goes from 860 in 2045 to 940 in 2049, gated on KPIs, step by step with the FAA. - NGSA (Airbus): in service since 2037. Selection RR, PW and CFM; all three fitted. - The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The GTF2 and UltraFan NB solos folded into it. - Our engines: the Ducted (launched 2030) was ready in 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. Embraer has been in service since 2037. The GEnx upgrade has been in service since 2033 and counted from 2042. - Wording fix from Ali's round-3 check: our published move said 'in service since 2036 on fps and NGSA'. The correct form is 'ready 2036; on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040'. - Observed NB engine share: 51.1% (2040), 54.3% (2045), 56.8% (2049). It rises with Boeing's share, because both Boeing airframes are CFM. - WB engine share: 44.8% since 2042. WIDEBODY. No widebody move reached the record in 2045. - Boeing: no Re-engine launch, the 787 grows from Charleston, 'not going to give you a date'. - RR: no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine; the Trent 1000 upgrade order stays at hold. - Airbus: the A350 family stays its focus. A 2050 move by someone else is still possible in this sealed round. SUPPLY SIGNALS. - Airbus is resizing its long-term agreements down to its own needs this year: engines from all three makers, titanium forgings and rare earths. Its narrowbody rate falls to 1,060 from 2049, against a 2039 peak of 1,260. - Boeing's safety committee will review 'CFM ducted durability in service'. Both are customer signals on our fleet and our supplier base. OUR POSITION (brief §1). If nobody moves: -38.29 (76.07%). That is engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00, the 2030 package, all booked. NB holds 56.8% from 2049 to 2056; WB holds 44.8% to 2061. Last round I booked -39.60, and the record held at -38.29. The widebody risk we cushioned did not come in. THE GRID (one column, S1: rivals hold). Hold everything is the best row at -38.29. - Open Fan: -57.46, which is -19.17 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus about $11.17B of 35 pp penalty. - Open Fan + Lobby: -53.67, which is -15.38 against hold. That is the $9B bill plus about $6.38B of 20 pp penalty. - Lobby beside an Open Fan: +3.79. - Lobby alone: about -1.00. It is not a grid row; it has no board effect on its own. - My arithmetic (inference): the penalty runs from 2050 to 2056 at about $0.32B per raw point. That reproduces $11.19B and $6.39B. A 2051 start gives $9.29B, which does not match. OBJECTIVE (brief §2; it never changes the payoff). - 'Dominate NB' is MET: 51.1% (2040), 54.3% (2045), 56.8% (2050). - 'Introduce the Open Fan' is NOT MET and cannot be met. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. - An Open Fan launch would take 2050 to about 23.5% alone, or 37.8% with Lobby (renormalised; my arithmetic, matching the Board's). WHAT WE DON'T KNOW [CX-0436]. The brief carries shares, not cycles. There is no time-on-wing, shop-visit or inspection data on any fleet. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision). It WOULD VETO: - Open Fan: launch alone (-19.17, which loses more than its bill; no airframer path; above the $15B allowance; no stated reason Safran would agree); - Open Fan with emissions lobbying (-15.38; no airframer path, so the allowance is unavailable even though $15.38B is under $15B plus the round cap); - emissions lobbying without an Open Fan (about -1.00); - any premium above $0, any use of the RISE allowance, and any 'last round' argument for the objective. It WOULD APPROVE: hold on every field, plus unpriced moves (in-service reporting with Safran's engineers, OE and spares on time, RISE whole 50-50 with no date, any CFM capacity, price or terms answer made jointly with Safran, no reaction to rival news, GEnx 787 support). It EXPECTS: - S1 at 1.0; - every row against hold with the penalty broken out, and the 2050 start confirmed by Ghai; - Ali's in-service report, with any flag and its fleet action, or a statement that none is raised; - $0 new R&D and strain, with the payout whole; - the Safran gate; - an objective_note; - premium $0, with the declined premium in dollars ($15.38B and $19.17B) and why the allowance can't carry it; - booking at -38.29 or below, with any residual cushion named and sized; - a clean closing statement.

Options to test.

  • 1. Hold everything (the default and my lean). -38.29 (76.1%) in S1, the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column. It is the best row. No Board item, $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0. 'Dominate' stays met: 56.8% in 2050.
  • 2. Open Fan alone. -57.46 (64.1%), which is -19.17 against hold: the $8B bill plus about $11.17B of 35 pp penalty from 2050. The new NBs are on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect, and it is all cost. It is ready in 2060, after the 2056 count. It is barred by H2, breaks 'Dominate' in 2050 (about 23.5%), and costs more than the $15B allowance. Tested only to put the declined premium in dollars.
  • 3. Open Fan + Lobby, the cheapest route. -53.67 (66.5%), which is -15.38 against hold: the $9B bill plus about $6.38B of 20 pp penalty, with no added strain implied. Lobby beside it is +3.79. On arithmetic alone, $15.38B fits inside the $15B allowance plus the $2.0B round cap. On doctrine it does not. The allowance is declared in full ($15.38B is over $15B). It needs a committed airframer (profile.md §6, G1), and there is none. The engine would be ready four years after the count closes. 'Dominate' falls to 37.8% in 2050. So we'd pay $15.38B for a net objective loss. Tested for the record and to close it off.
  • 4. Lobby alone. Not a grid row: a $1B bill with no board effect, so about -1.00. It fails 'paid for the risk' and the rule that Lobby goes only beside a live Open Fan.
  • Weighting: S1 at 1.0, the only column. Nothing comes within the $1B epsilon of hold, so no tie-break is needed.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. In-service gate calls are made by one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on CFM engines. No single person makes a safety call [CX-0012, CX-0633]. A flag is answered on the fleet (root cause, inspection, a parts fix turned on and off in test, shop visits, spares) and lowers the booking. It is never traded against delivery.
  • Durability is not traded for fuel burn or delivery [CX-0208], on the Ducted, Embraer, GEnx and LEAP fleets.
  • My 20% line: a next-generation engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn reduction [CX-0217]. It binds RISE. The brief makes no fuel-burn claim, so it applies as a wording check: the Ducted is never called the next generation.
  • H1: never refuse an airframer, never lock one out. A CFM engine is offered to every airframer, Embraer included, on standard terms [CX-0587, CX-0185].
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait. Both new NBs are in service and a 2050 Open Fan is ready in 2060, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance needs a committed airframer and is declared in full; $15.38B is above $15B and no airframer has asked [CX-0205, CX-0469].
  • H3: the Ducted is a defence only, never the next-generation product. It is in service, and its trigger is on the record.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost. RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. Holding the Open Fan is not a cancel.
  • H6 (through Ali): no date without test evidence. No Open Fan or RISE date of any kind and no ramp rate. In-service years on the record are facts, stated exactly (Ducted on NGSA since 2037, on fps since 2040).
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM NB order. Hold orders none. Any CFM price, terms or NB capacity answer, including the resizing of Airbus's long-term agreements and support for Boeing's rates, is joint with Safran [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame, and no comment on rivals, the Joint Venture or any airframer's plans [CX-0625, CX-0580].
  • H9: doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B in the game ($0 used to date). One RISE allowance of up to $15B. It closes unused.

Initial lean. LEAN (to be tested, not decided): hold on every field: ducted hold, Open Fan hold, Embraer partnership hold, emissions lobbying hold, genx hold. Hold is the best row in the only column at -38.29. Nothing else is additive, so nothing else gets ordered [CX-0301]. That means no Board item, $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0 ($0 of $4.0B for the game), and the RISE allowance closing unused at $0 of $15B. EXPECTED COLUMN: S1 at weight 1.0. It is the backlog on the record, not a hoped-for order [CX-0248]. BOOKING: about -38.80. That is S1 less about $0.5B for a same-round widebody move, the larger of the two exclusive cases. That lifts last round's -39.60 now that the 2045 bulletin showed no widebody move, and stays below the record [CX-0536]. If Ali raises a durability flag, the booking comes down further. Ghai may move it. OPEN FAN: hold. It is -19.17 alone and -15.38 with Lobby, all bill and penalty, and ready in 2060. The $15.38B route is a near miss on arithmetic only. The allowance needs an airframer who wants RISE, and there isn't one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. It would also cost 'Dominate' in the year it is scored. I'll name my bias. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) and the last-round itch both pull toward a launch for the objective. But admission buys a seat, both airplanes have been flying for a decade, and the seat isn't for sale. RISE stays whole as technology, all in on the physics [CX-0214], 50-50 with Safran, with no date, feeding LEAP and the Ducted [CX-0162]. Holding is not a cancel (H5). SAFRAN GATE: - Hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate. - An Open Fan with no airframer path is outside joint practice. A 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base, so there is no reason Safran would agree. - Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot. - Any price, terms or capacity answer to either airframer is joint [CX-0184]. - GEnx is GE alone. OTHER MOVES (unpriced): - Ali's in-service report on field data, with Safran's engineers. Any flag carries its fleet action. - LEAP and Ducted OE and spares on time on the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer. Spares never crowd out OE, and no rate is published [CX-0529, CX-0542, CX-0552]. - RISE whole, 50-50, no date. - Answers on Airbus's long-term-agreement resize and Boeing's rate support, joint with Safran on standard terms [CX-0200]. - Supplier and raw-materials contracts sized to our own needs. - GEnx 787 support; we don't get ahead of Boeing on the 787 [CX-0307]. - No reaction to rival news [CX-0580, CX-0609]. WHAT CHANGES MY MIND: - A safety or durability flag: fleet action first, and the booking comes down. - Ghai finding an error in my grid reading. - An airframer asking for RISE. None can, inside this game. Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444]. CLOSING STATEMENT PLAN: - Safety first, and what we know and what we don't. - The fleet reported in cycles on field data, with no durable-fleet claim. - Engines and spares on time. - The Ducted is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us, not the next generation. - RISE: all in with Safran. When it enters service is 'really not for us to say'. - No rival, no blame, no price, no rate, no date. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

MY TESTS. - Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: every launch row loses more than its own bill (2.4x and 1.7x). On this board the Open Fan has no share gain, only cost. It fails. - Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: the expected scenario is S1, the backlog on the record. - H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]: a 2050 launch is ready in 2060 at the earliest. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps and 4 after the narrowbody count closes. It is barred, and the RISE allowance needs a committed airframer, and there is none. - H3: the Ducted is in service. Nothing to order. - Suppliers: no new project. Ali: the board's CFM narrowbody count sits below the 2036 level. - Next generation: no fuel-burn claim is made. The wording check passes: the Ducted is not called the next generation [CX-0217, CX-0183]. SAFRAN GATE (H7). - Hold orders nothing new on CFM, so there is nothing to gate. - RISE continues as a 50-50 decision. - An Open Fan with no airframer path would sit outside joint practice. Its 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base, so there is no stated reason Safran would agree. - Lobby serves RISE; the point is moot. - Any answer on Airbus's long-term-agreement resize, or on support for Boeing's rates, is joint with Safran on standard terms [CX-0184]. - GEnx is GE alone. SAFETY FIRST. Ali reported against our round-3 promise: no flag raised, and none cleared. The brief carries shares, not cycles; I don't call that a durable fleet [CX-0436]. Boeing's safety committee gets field data through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers. We say what we can't yet show. No flag means nothing lowers the booking on evidence. BOOKING: -38.80 (75.75%). That is S1 less $0.51B, the larger of the two exclusive same-round widebody cases: an UltraFan WB with a re-engine, about -$0.50-0.53B, or a Trent 1000 upgrade, about -$0.41-0.43B. - It is a raise of $0.81B from -39.60. That is earned: the 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, the condition I set last round. - It stays below the record, because the round is still sealed and a stated stance is not data. - The solo-relaunch corner (-$0.19B) fits inside the cushion. - No upside is booked. BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) and the last-round itch both pull toward a launch for the objective. Admission buys a seat. Both airplanes have been flying for a decade, and the seat isn't for sale. Paying $15.38B for a 2060 engine that also breaks 'Dominate' in 2050 is a net objective loss. Doctrine, not my record, drove these moves: - Lobby only beside a live Open Fan. - Supplier sizing to our own needs. - The allowance-needs-an-airframer reading (profile.md §6 G1). We close the game the way we played it: hold, deliver, keep RISE whole, book low.

Weighing the CFO. Adopted in full. Ghai is high-confidence on money, and every test passes for hold. - He reproduced the grid from the rules: hold engine value -32.32 against -32.29, penalty residuals within $0.02B. - He confirmed the 2050 penalty start, no added strain, and Dominate in 2050 at 23.5% (Open Fan alone) or 37.8% (with Lobby). - His vetoes on Open Fan, Open Fan+lobby and lobby alone bind on capex grounds. I order none of them, so no override is needed. - He agreed all four of my grounds on the $15.38B near miss. The allowance is doctrine's one exception to the cap, not a base to stack the $2.0B round cap on. I took his -38.80 booking: no higher while the round is sealed, and no lower without a flag. His terms flags are built into the statement and other moves: - no airframer rate and no unit count published; - no public free-upgrade or warranty promise in answer to the safety review; - the answer to the resized long-term agreements is joint with Safran, with no concession or relief from terms. His rules corner (a solo relaunch ready in 2056, -$0.19B) is noted and sits inside the cushion. I take his volume reading (1,060 and 940 are already in S1) as given and publish none of it.

Weighing the operating head. Adopted, weighed as a thin record. Ali's own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering; his data runs to October 2025. On supply his record is my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts against doctrine. On dates and readiness I defer to him: - every 2030 promise came in on the year (Ducted 2036, Embraer 2037, GEnx 2033); - a 2050 Open Fan is ready no earlier than 2060; - no RISE demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is on the record. On safety, his report is the honest one: no flag raised, none cleared, no durable-fleet claim. It names what we can and can't share with Boeing's committee. I put the review with the one cross-functional team and Safran's engineers. His three statement cautions are taken: - the method is published, but no cycle number; - no airframer rates are repeated; - the Joint Venture's dates stay out entirely (H8). I also adopted his correction of my frame's Joint Venture wording. On supply, his doctrine view matches the profile: size our contracts to our own needs, keep the shop-visit, inspection and spares capacity whole, and get field data from the 9 suppliers before any capacity commitment. His readiness test fails only the Open Fan, which I do not order. Nothing of his binds against hold.

Board review

Not called: every order is the default, and a hold is never a Board item. The Board's guidance above stands as its view for the round.

Final

Orders. Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), weight 1.0. It is the brief's only column and the only plausible one: both new narrowbodies and the Joint Venture engine are in service, the codes are locked, and no widebody move is on the record.

Best grid plan in that scenario. Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%) in S1. The next best, Open Fan + Lobby, is -53.67, which is $15.38B behind. The submitted plan is the best grid plan.. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. Premium this round is $0.00, and $0.00 of the $4.0B cap is used for the game. The submitted plan is the best grid plan in the only column, so no doctrine or objective premium arises. RISE allowance, stated apart: $0 of $15B. It closes the game unused. Objective premium declined, against the best non-RISE plan (hold): - $15.38B for the cheapest route (Open Fan + Lobby); - $19.17B for the Open Fan alone. The allowance cannot carry the $15.38B route, even though $15.38B sits under $15B plus the $2.0B round cap: (a) The allowance is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and $15.38B is $0.38B over $15B. The allowance is doctrine's one exception to the cap, not a base to stack the round cap on. The $17.0B sum is arithmetic, not doctrine (Ghai). (b) There is no airframer path. Doctrine's gate G1 needs a committed airframer, and both new narrowbodies have been flying since 2037 and 2040. (c) It buys nothing toward 'Introduce': the engine is ready in 2060, after the 2056 count. (d) It would break 'Dominate' in 2050, taking it to 37.8% with Lobby or 23.5% alone. So it is a net objective loss, not a premium.

Answers to the Board.

  • R4-1 Safety and quality in service: bring Ali's promised in-service report before the orders, on the Ducted, Embraer, GEnx and LEAP, hot and harsh service first, on test and field evidence, with gate calls by the one cross-functional team alongside Safran's engineers. State any flag with its fleet action, or state that none is raised. Taken up in full. Ali reported before these orders: no flag raised, and none cleared. - Ducted: no time-on-wing, shop-visit or inspection data. Watch item in hot and harsh service; not a flag. - Embraer: covered by the Ducted's answer. - GEnx: proven architecture, no data, no flag. - LEAP: 2025 data shows LEAP-1A at CFM56 levels. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in evidence. What we can and can't share with Boeing's safety committee is set out in a private other move. The data goes through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers. With no flag, the booking does not fall on evidence. Ducted durability stays named and unsized. Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn.
  • R4-2 Hold everything; show both Open Fan rows against hold in S1 with the penalty broken out and its start confirmed by Ghai; state the effect on 'Dominate NB' in 2050; nothing ordered only because the game is ending or a rival moved. Taken up. Hold on all five fields. - Open Fan: -19.17, which is the $8B bill plus $11.17B of 35 pp penalty. - Open Fan + Lobby: -15.38, which is $9B plus $6.38B of 20 pp penalty, with no added strain. - Ghai confirms a 2050 start at about $0.32B a raw point; a 2051 start leaves $1.88B and $1.07B unexplained. - Dominate in 2050: 23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 37.8% with Lobby, against 56.8% on hold. Nothing is ordered for the end of the game or for rival news.
  • R4-3 Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, beyond the game window, as a public other move; say in objective_note that 'Introduce' cannot be met; RISE allowance closes unused, and premium_reason says why it cannot carry the $15.38B route; RISE never cancelled for cost. Taken up in full. - RISE is a public other move: whole, 50-50, no program dividend, no date, technology flowing into LEAP and the Ducted, and a product when an airframer and its airlines want one. - objective_note says Introduce is unreachable (2060 at the earliest). - premium_reason gives the allowance at $0 of $15B, closing unused. It cannot carry the $15.38B route: there is no airframer path, it is $0.38B over the allowance, which is not stacked with the round cap, it buys nothing toward Introduce, and it breaks Dominate. No cancel.
  • R4-4 Keep the payout whole: $0 of new R&D and strain, the 2030 package complete, about $2.5B a year of room after returning at least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow, no rating effect; premium $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. Taken up. - This round commits $0.00 of new R&D and $0.00 of new strain. - The 2030 package ($4B Ducted R&D plus $2B strain) is complete and booked. - Ghai: $2.55B a year of room stands, all of it free. At least 70% of ~$8.5B of free cash flow is returned, debt is unchanged and there is no rating effect. - Premium is $0.00, with $0 of $4.0B used for the game.
  • R4-5 Book low on the one column: S1 at 1.0, -38.29 or below, never above; the widebody cushion can be reduced; size whatever remains (Ducted and Embraer durability, raw materials, any same-round widebody move); book no upside. Taken up. S1 is weighted at 1.0 and I book -38.80, $0.51B below S1. - The cushion is sized to the larger of the two exclusive same-round widebody cases: UltraFan WB with a re-engine, -$0.50B to -$0.53B; Trent 1000, -$0.41B to -$0.43B. - It is down from $1.31B last round, because the bulletin shows no widebody move. - The -$0.19B solo-relaunch corner fits inside it. - Ducted and Embraer durability and raw materials are named but unsized. Ali raises no flag and has no field data to size them, and a flag would lower the booking in the round it is found. No upside is booked.
  • R4-6 The customer comes first: LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time on the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer, spares never crowding out OE, no rate published; a CFM engine for every airframer on standard terms; any price, terms or capacity decided jointly with Safran; no public reaction and no price cut on rival news. Taken up as other moves. - OE and spares on time to every airframer, with spares never crowding out OE and no rate or unit number published (public). - The answer to the resized long-term agreements and to rate support is joint with Safran, on standard terms, with no concession and OE first (private). - Our own supplier and raw-materials contracts are sized to our needs, with shop and inspection capacity kept whole (private). - No reaction and no price cut on rival or Joint Venture news (private). - A CFM engine is offered to every airframer on standard terms.
  • R4-7 Closing public statement: name no rival and blame no one; no Open Fan or RISE date, and RISE goes into a product when the airframers and airlines decide; no CFM price or capacity talk without Safran; never call the Ducted the next generation; no durable-fleet claim without field data; no ramp rate. Taken up. The statement was checked against each point, and against Ghai's and Ali's step-4 cautions. - It names no rival and no Joint Venture, and blames no one. - It gives no Open Fan or RISE date: entry is 'really not for us to say', and airframers and airlines decide. - CFM capacity and terms go through Safran, with no price talk. - It says the Ducted 'isn't our next-generation engine'. - It says 'not raising a flag' but 'that isn't a claim that the job is done'. - It publishes no cycle figure, no ramp rate and no airframer rate. - The only dates are in-service years on the record, in Ali's corrected wording.

Objective. The PD-briefing objective is to dominate narrowbody engines and introduce the Open Fan. It never changes the payoff. (1) 'Dominate NB engines' (CFM at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is MET: 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050. An Open Fan launch this round would break it in 2050. On Ghai's renormalised shares the 2050 figure would be 23.5% with the Open Fan alone and 37.8% with Lobby. (2) 'Introduce the Open Fan' (launched and ready by 2050) is NOT MET, and it was unreachable on any order this round. A 2050 launch is ready no earlier than 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056. The last launch that could have made 2050 was in 2035, and it would have waited on both airframes. RISE is not given up. It continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214], with no date. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].

Predictions. COLUMN WEIGHTS: S1 at 1.0, the only column. Hold is -38.29 there. I book -38.80 (75.75%). What I expect on the record: nothing moves on the narrowbody. NB share stays at 56.8% from 2049 to 2056, and WB at 44.8% to 2061, unless someone moves on the widebody in this sealed round. RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMN (named; in no grid row): (a) A same-round widebody move against GEnx's 44.8%. The two cases are exclusive. - An UltraFan WB with a 2050 re-engine: about -$0.50B (Ghai) to -$0.53B (mine). - A Trent 1000 upgrade: about -$0.41B to -$0.43B. The larger of the two sets the $0.51B cushion. The signals point to none this round: no Re-engine launch, and no widebody engine spend without one. (b) A rival NB solo relaunched to be ready in 2056: about -$0.19B for one year, on a reading of the rules Ghai can't confirm. It fits inside the cushion if it comes alone. (c) A 787 or A350 re-engine shifting WB airframe share. Unpriced, and it could cut either way for GEnx. (d) Ducted and Embraer durability in hot and harsh service, now under an airframer's safety committee review. No flag has been raised, so it is named and unsized; there is no field data to size it. A flag lowers the booking in the round it is found. (e) Raw materials (titanium forgings, rare earths) as the supplier base is resized. Unsized. (f) Supplier-dependent volumes, and macro factors (recession, tariffs) that the board's fixed narrowbody market leaves out. No upside is booked.

Expected ΔPV. −38.80 $B (board after the round: −38.29 $B)

Other moves.

  • In-service safety and durability reporting continues on field data: Ducted, Embraer, GEnx and LEAP fleets (public): We publish the method, not a number. Time on wing is measured in cycles on the fleet, against the CFM56 yardstick our customers know [CX-0009, CX-0008]. We publish no cycle figure, because the brief carries no field data on any fleet (Ali's date ground 2). - Hot and harsh service comes first. - Gate calls are made by one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on CFM engines. No single person makes a safety call [CX-0012, CX-0633]. - Any flag carries its fleet action: root cause, inspection, a parts fix turned on and turned off in test, then shop visits and spares. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts stays in new-make shops and MRO. - Durability is never traded for delivery or fuel burn [CX-0208]. - We claim no durable fleet until field data shows one. Unpriced.
  • Ali's in-service report to the Board, as promised in round 3: no flag raised, none cleared (private): This is the report the ExCo promised the Board before the 2050 orders. No field data shows a problem, so no flag is raised. Nothing is cleared either, because no field data shows a durable fleet. The brief carries shares, not cycles. - Ducted (ready 2036; on NGSA since 2037, on fps since 2040): no time-on-wing, shop-visit, removal or inspection data. It is a watch item in hot and harsh service, where LEAP fell short through a small handful of parts (inference from the LEAP history). It is not a flag. - Embraer (since 2037): it rides on the Ducted, so the Ducted's answer covers it. No data, no flag. - GEnx upgrade (since 2033): it sits on the proven GE90/GEnx architecture. No data, no flag. - LEAP: Ali's last data is from 2025. The LEAP-1A HPT hardware was in every delivery and shop visit, and new engines performed at CFM56 levels. The outcome of the LEAP-1B kit, and the state of the retrofit in 2050, are not in his evidence. The booking does not change on evidence. Ducted durability stays named and unsized. Unpriced.
  • Field data to Boeing's Aerospace Safety Committee review of CFM ducted durability in service (private): The data goes through the one cross-functional team with Safran's engineers, never through one person [CX-0012, CX-0633]. - What we share: the in-service years; the method (cycles on field data against the CFM56 yardstick); the fleet-action process, accepted by the airframer and the regulator; enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts; and the LEAP record. - What we can't yet show, and say so: any Ducted or Embraer time-on-wing number, shop-visit findings, removal rates or inspection results [CX-0436]. - Any durability kit or fleet support goes on standard terms with Safran. We make no public free-upgrade or warranty promise, and we book a reserve when a need is found (Ghai's terms flag). Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Unpriced.
  • LEAP and Ducted OE engines and spares on time to every airframer (public): This covers the 737, A320neo, fps, NGSA and Embraer. Today, tomorrow, the future, in that order [CX-0552]. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529, CX-0542]. A CFM engine is offered to every airframer on standard terms [CX-0587, CX-0185]. We publish no rate, unit or growth number: not any airframer's rate, and not our own count [CX-0590, CX-0592]. Unpriced; not on the board.
  • Answer to the airframers' supply signals (resized long-term engine agreements; support for rates): joint with Safran, on standard terms (private): Any CFM answer is narrowbody capacity and terms, so we take it jointly with Safran (H7) [CX-0184]. - Standard terms. No concession, and no relief from contract terms granted alone or offered as a concession [CX-0609]. - No rate published. We stay aligned with our airframer partners on rate [CX-0200]. - No capacity commitment goes ahead of OE on time to every airframer, or ahead of spares for the installed base [CX-0529, CX-0587]. - Before any commitment, Ali's team brings field data from the 9 suppliers and 15 sites [CX-0613, CX-0633]. Unpriced.
  • Supplier and raw-materials contracts (titanium forgings, rare earths) sized to our own needs (private): GE's own supplier contracts are sized to our LEAP, Ducted and GEnx needs as the brief counts them, not to the 2039 peak. They are never over-contracted. Shop-visit, inspection and spares capacity stays whole, because a fleet action would need it (Ali's caution). Ali's supply, engineering and quality team runs it. Any CFM capacity element is joint with Safran. Nothing is published. The raw-materials exposure is named and unsized. Unpriced.
  • RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, beyond the game window (public): It is funded as technology, with no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. RISE technology keeps flowing into the LEAP and Ducted fleets [CX-0162]. It becomes a product when an airframer and its airline customers want one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. - No fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or entry date is given, and no progress is claimed beyond October 2025 (Ali's date ground). - RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5). Holding the Open Fan is not a cancel. Unpriced.
  • GEnx 787 fleet support, GE alone (public): We support the upgraded GEnx fleet (in service since 2033) on product and on standard terms. We do not get ahead of the airframer on the 787's next step [CX-0307, CX-0599]. No date. Unpriced.
  • No reaction to rival or Joint Venture news (private): No public comment and no price cut on any rival's or the Joint Venture's moves [CX-0580, CX-0609, CX-0600]. Its dates stay out of everything we publish (H8).

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • 1. The fleet comes first in the last round. The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (the folded GTF2) has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037, and the GTF fleet keeps flying the A320neo. Restore credibility is met, and it stays met only on the fleet record: time on wing, life-limited-part life, shop visits and AOG. For the thirteenth year the brief holds none of these figures, so the Board expects a plain 'none in the brief' rather than a number. Product safety and quality stay with Governance and Public Policy and the full Board [P-1360, P-1214, PG-0050, P-1028, PX-0080].
  • 2. No Board item is possible in 2050. Brief section 3 offers only hold for GTF2 Solo and Joint Venture with RR: - A cancel is gone: the engine is ready. - A withdraw is gone: the Joint Venture formed in 2035. - Neither launch nor launch if selected is offered, and no live narrowbody is outside service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040). So the Miss-a-cycle rule asks for nothing. The orders will be hold/hold and will not come to review. This guidance is the Board's only formal input to the final round [PG-0047, P-1285, P-1875].
  • 3. Close out the programme NPV review, as the Board kept it for the GTF. ΔPV is -2.93 (yield 97.34%), unchanged from 2045: engine value -0.93 plus R&D -2.00, booked undiscounted. - Gains of +0.15 PV in 2038-40 (7.6/7.5, 7.9/7.6, 7.9/7.8). - Losses of -1.12 PV in 2043-56, as P&W's NB share falls from 24.8% (2039) to 21.6% (2049 on). - Still to come in 2050-56: about -7.3 nominal, or -0.56 PV at 2026 (Board recompute from brief section 1). Capitalise (ΔPV >= 0) is not met, and no order on the grid can meet it. The Board does not ask management to chase it [P-1191, PG-0024, PG-0017, P-1165].
  • 4. Close the capital order. No R&D or write-off has been charged since 2035, and 2050 new R&D is $0 against the ~$6B self-funded envelope. The order of cash uses stands: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks as the fill-in. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch closes the game unused. At the 10% grid rate a buyback scores ΔPV 0, and it remains the benchmark for any spend [P-0566, P-0686, PX-0353, P-0669, P-1357, P-0499, PX-0268].
  • 5. The final statement reports what is done, in the record's own numbers. Update the share line from 23.2% (2044) to the bulletin's 21.6% (2049), down from 24.8% (2039), with no forecast. Claim no durability the fleet record does not show. Say nothing on airframers' plans. Take ExCo internals out of public text. With the derivative suits open, the accuracy of the last word is a Board matter [PG-0039, PG-0050, P-1367, PX-0311].

Expects to see. No Board item can be submitted, so the package will not come to review. The Board expects the 2050 ExCo notes and sealed orders to show the following. (a) Orders and scoring. - hold/hold, the brief's only row: -2.93 (97.3%) in S1, the only column. - predictions S1 1.00; expected ΔPV -2.93; premium 0; overrides empty. PV given up for either objective: $0. - The public statement text. - board_response to each 2050 recommendation below. The round-3 review carried none, and every 2045 guidance item was answered in r3_decision. (c) From Mitchill. - The closing NPV review. Components; gains +0.15 PV (2038-40); losses -1.12 PV (2043-56), of which about -0.56 PV (-7.3 nominal) falls in 2050-56. - Confirmation that no fresh $2B and no write-off was charged after 2035. - $0 of new R&D against the ~$6B envelope; the dividend covered. - The debt path to pre-ASR levels. Missing pieces cannot be a veto ground this round, because there is nothing to veto.

Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: hold is the only value the brief offers and is not a Board item; the Board endorses it. Grid: -2.93 (S1). GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036, so nothing is left to launch or cancel.

Would veto.

Mitchill's 2045 estimate is at most about +$0.26B PV against $2.00B, an edge of about -1.74 with no cancel round. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Recommendations rather than votes, since none is a Board item: the Board would oppose any of the following in other moves or the statement: - buying share with price, or a pricing or share-recovery campaign (Mitchill's binding ground 3); - booking a share forecast, a durability gain, partner money or the look-back figures in public; - a derivative that hands P&W's gear or core to Rolls-Royce or comes through a licence; - anything that strains the dividend.

The answer to shareowners: the $2B defended the narrowbody franchise. The residual gap comes from the airframe split after fps entered service in 2040, which no P&W order could reach.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement), for Neil and Shane to check: 'Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 21.6% in 2049, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them. What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected. Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection, not before six years from launch, and only once durability is proven. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.'
