CFM now reports field-data time on wing in public, hot-and-harsh first, on an engine that flies beside ours on NGSA. Our standard from here: report on field data, or don't report. FINDINGS: the 2050 brief and bulletin hold no durability or safety-critical-part finding. 'No finding in the brief' means no data. It does not mean a clean fleet. STANDING RULE PAST 2050: any finding goes first, with its plan, to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board [P-1360][P-1214][PG-0050]. It is contained first, disclosed early, and leads the public statement. No dated recovery is given.
  • Order of call on pacing parts, shops and engineers, and the 2050 parts result (private): Eddy's order, kept past 2050: 1. Safety-critical parts and any airworthiness action, on any fleet [PX-0035]. 2. Fleet lift: GTF MRO and Joint Venture engine support. 3. A320neo engine deliveries. 4. Joint Venture new builds for NGSA. 5. Derivatives. None is live. Steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily and set jointly with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0099][PX-0123][PX-0131]. This is a tie-break, not a starvation rule: NGSA new builds remain a commitment to Airbus. Parts result: ground 2 passes, with no fleet, quality or supply problem in the brief. - P&W NB OE builds are 863 a year from 2049, down 127 from the 2039 peak and 51 from 2045. - Airbus's public resizing of its supply agreements is already inside the brief's 863. It is no further cut and no surge. - The risk sits in the sub-tier. Suppliers sized for the peak may cut powder-metal or castings capacity just as the fleet ages into heavier shop visits. - So we do not cut pacing-part capacity on the OE count. Freed OE slots go to spares and shops. Any supplier change or requalification runs under records discipline and contain-first [P-1040][PX-0125]. - We give no count of freed capacity, because the brief holds none. - Nothing on Airbus's numbers goes in public [PX-0062].
  • Closing programme NPV review to the Board (Mitchill's review, adopted) (private): This is the last of the annual programme NPV reviews the Board kept for the GTF. ΔPV is -2.93 $B (yield 97.34%) = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is undiscounted and booked once, in 2035. Cash went out at about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. - No fresh $2B and no write-off after 2035. - $0 of new R&D from 2036 to 2050. Engine value against the status quo, PV at 2026: - gains of +0.145 in 2038-40 (7.6/7.5, 7.9/7.6, 7.9/7.8); - losses of -1.115 in 2043-56: -0.553 in 2043-49, and -0.563 in 2050-56 (-7.3 nominal) still to come; - net -0.97 on the brief's rounded nominal rows, against -0.93. The 0.04 is rounding. Mitchill's calculation, my frame script and my decide check (work/r4_decide_check.py) all agree. Look-backs, labelled as INFERENCE and kept private: - +5.51 for the 2035 commit at $0 of new R&D (-2.93 against the round-2 hold row of -8.44 in S4); - about +24.8 against being left off NGSA (-2.93 against the round-1 hold row of -27.76). This is the top of the range, not a point estimate. Answer to shareowners: the $2B defended the narrowbody franchise. The residual gap comes from the airframe split after fps entered service in 2040, which no P&W order could reach. That attribution stays private and is never said in public about an airframer. Objectives: Restore credibility met; Capitalise not met at -2.93; PV given up for either: $0.
  • Capital-order close, and the after-game technology rule (private): Capital order: - $0 of new R&D in 2050, against the ~$6B self-funded envelope [PX-0268]. - The dividend is covered and declared by the Board each quarter [PX-0081]. - Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next [P-0686]. The brief carries no debt path, so the date is 'no date'; we invent none. - Buybacks are the fill-in [P-0669]. - The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch closes the game unused. - At the 10% grid rate a buyback scores ΔPV 0. It stays the benchmark any spend must beat. After-game rule: technology work beyond the board's horizon stays inside the self-funded envelope as technology, not as a programme. It comes to Finance as a programme only with an airframer's selection on the record, and then passes the payback test [P-0746][PX-0109].
  • Joint Venture and derivative discipline, standing after the game (private): This is company doctrine and Eddy's engineering. My own record on a Joint Venture is Low. - P&W's gear and core stay one P&W module with P&W design authority, with no technology licence [P-1233][P-1240]. - Rolls-Royce, merged or UltraFan content reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine. It needs its own full test programme, with severe-environment testing and all LLPs at full life at its own entry into service, completed before that entry into service [PX-0128][P-1214]. It never touches the gear and core. - Integrated teams follow module boundaries [P-1240]. - Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. - Both partners stay on the same engine [P-1875], and each partner's technology is protected on the same terms [PX-0038]. - No derivative without an airframer need, and derivatives sit last in the order of call. - Any proposal that needs our gear or core, merges the gear systems or comes by licence is flagged to the Board as a red-line matter.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety comes first, and our fleet is now large. The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA since 2037. On the brief's year table that is about 12,100 RR-share narrowbody engines delivered from 2037 to 2049, and about 13,000 by the end of 2050. Watson's in-service report was promised to us before the 2050 orders, and we expect it in this package: time on wing, full-life parts and shop visits on fleet data, plus any safety or durability flag with its fleet action. No date for any new engine goes public [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0287].
  • Protect what is working. This is the last decision year, so there is no later round in which to cancel, revise or recover. Both parts of the objective are met on hold. Narrowbody share is 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050. Widebody share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns, at +20.55 (S1) and +20.90 (S2), or about +20.59 on our illustrative weights. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [R-1561, R-1582, R-1005, R-1574].
  • One big programme at a time, and the strain stays in the grid. The Joint Venture still counts as a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain stacks on any widebody item, and the 2050 grid confirms it. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.73 / -6.63 against hold: about +0.27 / +0.37 of engine value against a $2B bill plus $5B of strain. UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.33: 0 / +0.67 of engine value against $4B plus $5B. Neither item can change the 2050 widebody measurement. The upgrade counts from 2053 at the earliest, and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056. Both stay at hold [RG-0019, RG-0033, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214].
  • The balance sheet and returns. No narrowbody R&D remains: our $4.00B Joint Venture share and the $1.71B write-off were booked in 2035. Cash follows the capital frame: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat and Trent durability stays funded. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. The balance-sheet test does not apply unless McCabe invokes a veto [RX-0242, R-0900, R-0909, RG-0059, RG-0041, RX-0214].

Expects to see. The package should contain the following. (1) Grid rows: the row of the submitted orders and the row with each Board item at hold, column by column (S1 / S2). All-hold is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +20.55 / +20.90. For any widebody item, show its row against that one: 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' at +13.82 / +14.27 (item -6.73 / -6.63), or 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' at +11.55 / +12.57 (item -9.00 / -8.33). (2) The CEO's expected scenario, his predictions, and S1 / S2 weights under the ExCo rule. Our illustrative case is S1 0.90 / S2 0.10. S2 needs both Re-engines, so it can be no likelier than its weaker leg. Boeing gave no date and said 'Today all three aren't there', with readiness work continuing internally: at most a signal. Airbus 'keeps studying the options' on its own clock: at most a signal. On our case, all-hold is about +20.59 expected (20.585), the upgrade item -6.72 and the UltraFan WB item -8.93. On 0.85 / 0.15 these are +20.60, -6.72 and -8.90. No sign changes under any weights. (3) From McCabe: her co-signature or withheld signature on any launch, her weights, the worst column for each item, and capex a year. Our figures are about £0.49bn a year for either item (the upgrade over three years, UltraFan WB over six), with about £3.68bn of strain on top. On all-hold we want three confirmations: no narrowbody R&D remains; the plan fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the distribution plan; leverage stays at or below about 1.5x. We also want her off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine rebased on Watson's in-service report. It books nothing. (4) From Watson: the in-service report promised before the 2050 orders, on test and fleet evidence, not slides. It should cover time on wing, full-life parts and shop visits; any safety or durability flag with its fleet action; whether RR has secured technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data; the gear-and-core repair data or module-exchange pool; and support through partner shops without relying on P&W's shops. For any widebody item he should give the ready or counting year against each live Re-engine's EIS: the upgrade counts from 2053 at the earliest; UltraFan WB is ready in 2056, against 2055 for S2's Re-engines. He should also give the years of strain and the support plan. (5) Both veto checks, with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in rationale and overrides empty. (6) premium item by item. We expect $0 on all-hold. (7) A public statement with no date for any new engine, no date for a Joint Venture build standard, and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. (8) A board_response to each recommendation below. If a figure is missing, we will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • All four fields at hold. For UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W, hold is the only legal value, and the Joint Venture stands as formed. UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade also stay at hold. None of these is a Board item, and we never veto a hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 (S1) and +20.90 (S2), or about +20.59 on S1 0.90 / S2 0.10 (+20.60 on 0.85 / 0.15). Both parts of the objective are met: narrowbody 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050, widebody at least 55.2%. Premium is $0B.
  • Qualitative other moves raise no Board item, and we would support them. They are: in-service safety, durability and partner-shop support for the Joint Venture engine; RR technical review rights and a gear-and-core module pool under the shared-risk terms; Trent fleet durability (about £1bn over four years); UltraFan technology funded as technology, using public R&D money where available, with no product launch or dates; the capital frame held; and pricing discipline. None changes a payoff on the grid.

Would veto.

  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -6.73 (S1) and -6.63 (S2), or -6.72 on our case, and it is negative under any weights. It fails the reasonable worst case, since both columns are below minus its $2B bill: the $5B strain stacks on the bill beside the Joint Venture. It also fails the declared-premium test, because a $6.72B shortfall is above the $3B cap for the round. Without strain it would still be about -1.73 / -1.63 (inference: about +0.27 / +0.37 of engine value counting from 2053, against $2B), so it does not pay even then. It cannot change the 2050 widebody measurement either. The company's one-programme rule is not engaged as written, since no UltraFan is in development; the strain is the priced cost of running a second programme. We expect McCabe to withhold her signature. Acceptable alternative: hold [RG-0033, RG-0068, R-1574, RX-0214, R-1127].
  • UltraFan WB: launch. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -9.00 (S1) and -8.33 (S2), or -8.93 on our case. It fails the airframe test, because no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. Boeing gave no date and found no matured widebody engine for a 2050 EIS, and Airbus is only studying options. S2 is a grid column, not the record. It fails the declared-premium test, since the shortfall is far above both the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap and the $3B cap. It fails the reasonable worst case too: S1 at -9.00 is below minus its $4B bill. Even in S2 it would be ready in 2056, a year after Re-engines entering in 2055, and would earn about +0.67 against $9B of bill and strain. Acceptable alternative: hold [R-1574, R-1005, RX-0058, RG-0033, RG-0021, R-0929].
  • Any Board item that lacks McCabe's co-signature (as our profile defines it), or that sits in a package where a binding ExCo veto went unrespected, a red-line flag is left unresolved or overrides is not empty. Acceptable alternative: hold [RX-0213, R-1579, RG-0044].

Recommendations.

  • R4-1. Hold all four fields and say why in rationale. In the last decision year we protect what is working: the Joint Venture engine is in service, both parts of the objective are met on hold, and 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns (+20.55 / +20.90). Nothing taken now can be cancelled or revised in a later round, so no commitment whose downside cannot be recovered should be made. The CEO has our total support for this frame.
  • R4-2. Close the widebody watch. The franchise test does not trigger: our share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, and no rival-engined Re-engine is on the record. Neither widebody item can affect the 2050 measurement: the upgrade counts from 2053 at the earliest, and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056. With the $5B strain permanent beside the Joint Venture, the upgrade buys about +0.27 / +0.37 of engine value for $7B, and UltraFan WB 0 / +0.67 for $9B. Keep 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we hold, worth $0 on this grid but what keeps the franchise earning.
  • R4-3. Product safety in service. Watson's in-service report on the Joint Venture engine is due to us with these orders. It should cover time on wing, full-life parts and shop visits on fleet data, not analysis; the status of RR's technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data; the gear-and-core repair data or module-exchange pool; and partner-shop support without relying on P&W's shops. Any safety or durability flag should come to us with its fleet action and be said early in public, with the plan and no dated recovery. 'We have a moral obligation to do these things properly.'
  • R4-4. Precaution on shared risk. McCabe should rebase her off-grid sizing of RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine on Watson's report. Last round it was about £1.2-2.9bn, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn, and twice that still fitted. She should confirm again: no equity, leverage at or below about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground.
  • R4-5. Capital. No new programme spend this round. Distributions should come from sustainable free cash flow, after the cash needs of the business, in the order of the capital frame: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then extra distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) continues. UltraFan technology continues as technology, using public R&D money and a partner where available, with no product launch, ready date or entry date.
  • R4-6. The public statement and pricing. Lead with the Joint Venture fleet: safety, then time on wing and full-life parts, then support through partner shops. Give no date of any kind: no new engine, no Joint Venture build standard, no widebody. Say nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. Make no market-share promise: the narrowbody drift from 24.8% to 21.6% is airframe mix, with fps on CFM, not a lever we hold. Keep 'We do not want to underestimate the risks'. Make no price concessions.
  • R4-7. Close the record. This is the last decision year, so put a short closing account in rationale. Say what the airframe-first choice of 2030 and the partner-once-P&W-committed choice of 2035 delivered: RR fitted on NGSA from 2037 at 24.1%, both parts of the objective met, and $4.00B of R&D plus the $1.71B write-off against +26.26 of engine value, for ΔPV +20.55 on hold. Say plainly what the 2035 widebody plan missed, the strain. Answer each recommendation above in board_response.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, the 2050 question, and the last one, in cash and quality of earnings. The Joint Venture engine has been earning on NGSA since 2037. Both parts of the objective are met on hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is +20.55 (S1) and +20.90 (S2), the best row in both columns. Does anything on this grid add cash? Frankly, no. The Joint Venture still counts as a running narrowbody project, so $5B of strain sits on any widebody item. - Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.73 / -6.63 against hold. - UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.33. Each loses more than its own bill in both columns, under any weights. Neither can move the 2050 widebody measurement: the upgrade counts from 2053 and UltraFan WB is ready in 2056. This is the last decision year. Nothing ordered now can be cancelled or revised later, so we take on no commitment whose downside we cannot recover. This round we harvest and protect: fleet safety first, then time on wing, full-life parts, partner-shop support and the Trent franchise. Cash stays in the capital frame. We are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582]. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058]. I also close the record: what 2030 and 2035 delivered, and what the 2035 widebody plan missed.

Situation. Public record, 2050 (round 3 adjudicated; no public events). - NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037, code 7. Fitted: CFM + PW + RR. - fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on the 10-year path, in service since 2040, code 3 (CFM). Its ramp is KPI-gated, 860 deliveries in 2045 and 940 in 2049. No narrowbody airframe is still live, so no selection is open. - Joint Venture with P&W: formed 2035. Our UltraFan NB Solo and P&W's GTF2 folded in. The engine was ready in 2036 on GTF2's clock and has been in service on NGSA since 2037. - P&W's stance: it keeps its published terms (shared risk, investment and revenue). The gear and core stay P&W's own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on P&W's parts, shops and engineers. It reports on the fleet record, says flags early and gives no dated recovery. No flag is on the record. - Rivals: the CFM ducted engine (since 2036) and CFM-Embraer (since 2037) are in service. RISE is held as technology. The GEnx upgrade has counted since 2042 (2.8 pp of widebody). CFM now reports durability on field data. - Airbus is resizing its long-term engine and supply agreements with all three makers down to its own needs. That is advice for Rob's supplier plan. It is not ours to repeat in public. - Widebody: no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. Boeing: 'Today all three aren't there', no date, readiness work continuing internally, and no matured widebody engine found for a 2050 EIS. Airbus 'keeps studying the options' on its own clock. Boeing's line is close to nothing and Airbus's is at most a signal. - Observed 2049 engine shares. Narrowbody: CFM 56.8 / P&W 21.6 / RR 21.6. Widebody: CFM/GE 44.8 / RR 55.2. Our position on hold: ΔPV +20.55 $B, yield 118.68%. - Components: engine value +26.26; R&D -4.00 (our Joint Venture share); write-offs -1.71 (UltraFan NB spend beyond our share). All were booked in 2035. No narrowbody R&D remains. - RR narrowbody engines: 965 in 2037, a peak of 990 in 2039, 914 in 2045, then 863 a year from 2049. - Fleet on the brief's year table: about 12,100 RR-share narrowbody engines delivered in 2037-2049, about 13,000 by the end of 2050. - Widebody: 188 engines a year from 2042. - The board counts narrowbody to 2056 and widebody to 2061. Objective: met on hold, and locked. - Narrowbody entry: 22.9% in 2045, 21.6% in 2050. - Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040, then 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with 5.2 pp of headroom. - No order this round can change a measured year. The upgrade counts from 2053, UltraFan WB is ready in 2056, and S2's Re-engines enter in 2055. - The narrowbody drift from 24.8% to 21.6% is airframe mix, with fps on CFM. It is not a lever we hold. Grid, each item against 'UltraFan NB: hold' (S1 / S2): - T1000 upgrade: -6.73 / -6.63. That is about +0.27 / +0.37 of engine value against the $2B bill and $5B of strain. - UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.33. That is 0 / +0.67 of engine value against $4B and $5B. - Best plan in both columns: 'UltraFan NB: hold'. Board guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 2.5): it would approve all four fields at hold, premium $0B. It would veto Trent 1000 upgrade: launch, UltraFan WB: launch, and any item that lacks McCabe's co-signature or sits in a package with an unrespected veto, an unresolved red-line flag or non-empty overrides. It expects Watson's in-service report on the Joint Venture engine in this package.

Options to test.

  • Weights (mine; Helen to confirm or replace): S1 0.90 / S2 0.10. - S2 needs both Re-engines, so it can be no likelier than its weaker leg. - Boeing's 'Today all three aren't there', with no date and no matured engine for a 2050 EIS, is close to nothing (0.1). - Airbus 'keeps studying the options' on its own clock: at most a signal (0.2). - So S2 gets 0.10 at most. That is also the Board's illustrative case and the generous one for the widebody items. - Sensitivity: 0.85 / 0.15 and 0.95 / 0.05. The choice is weight-proof, because both widebody items are negative in both columns. - Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold.
  • A. All four at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold' (my lean). - +20.55 / +20.90. EV 20.585, about +20.59 on 0.90 / 0.10; +20.60 on 0.85 / 0.15; +20.57 on 0.95 / 0.05. - Best row in both columns. Worst column +20.55. Premium $0B. - Both parts of the objective met. No Board item. - Four-part gate: nothing new to gate. It keeps a business that passed the gate in 2030 and 2035 and is now earning.
  • B. 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade'. - Row +13.82 / +14.27; EV +13.87 (+13.89 on the Board's alternative). - Item -6.73 / -6.63; EV -6.72 under any weights; worst column -6.73. - Below minus its own $2B bill in both columns. The $6.72B shortfall is above the $3B cap, so it cannot be a declared premium. - Fails the gate on business model: about -1.73 even without strain. - It counts from 2053, so it cannot touch the 2050 measurement. It cannot be cancelled later. - My 787 'Why not?' [RX-0101, RX-0117] does not survive the numbers. Board veto. Priced only.
  • C. 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB'. - Row +11.55 / +12.57; EV +11.65 (+11.70 on the Board's alternative). - Item -9.00 / -8.33; EV -8.93 (-8.90 on 0.85 / 0.15); worst column -9.00, below minus its $4B bill. - Fails airframers first: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has not named UltraFan. - Even in S2 it is ready in 2056, after the 2055 Re-engine entries, and earns +0.67 against $9B of bill and strain. - Far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap and the $3B cap. Fails the gate on airframe, market and business model. Board veto. Priced only.
  • D. Upgrade and UltraFan WB together: not a legal plan, because the two are exclusive. Not tested.

Red lines.

  • Safety first [RX-0053]. The Joint Venture fleet and the Trent fleet come before any new spend. Any safety or durability flag comes to the Board in this package, with its fleet action: root cause, inspection, parts fix, then shop visits and spares. It is said early in public, with the plan and no dated recovery [RG-0027, RX-0296].
  • No date of any kind in public: no new engine, no Joint Venture build standard, no widebody date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. That includes Airbus's supply resizing and Boeing's fps ramp [R-0970, R-1476].
  • UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W stay at hold, the only legal values. The Joint Venture stands as formed. Nothing is cancelled, because no programme is in development.
  • Last decision year: no commitment whose downside cannot be recovered. A launch now runs to the board's end, with no round left to cancel it [RG-0033, RG-0021].
  • One big programme at a time. The Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project, so any widebody item carries $5B of strain. The upgrade and UltraFan WB are exclusive. The 'no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development' line is not engaged as written, because no UltraFan is in development. The strain is the priced cost, not deducted again [R-0929, R-1127].
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column (Board doctrine): upgrade no worse than -$2B, UltraFan WB no worse than -$4B. Today they are -6.73 and -9.00. Board veto on both [RG-0033].
  • No UltraFan WB without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan. Neither exists. Any UltraFan WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574, R-1005, RX-0058].
  • Doctrine premium of at most $3B a round against the best expected grid plan, declared item by item. A widebody shortfall stays only as a declared premium inside that cap. None qualifies this round.
  • McCabe's joint sign-off on any launch against mid-to-high-teens hurdles [RX-0213, R-1579]. Her balance-sheet vetoes: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Watson's Civil veto binds: compressed maturity, an early disclosed date, or no support. overrides stays empty. We revise once within any veto, and no Board item goes up without her co-signature.
  • Capital frame: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D broadly flat [RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].
  • No price concessions and no market-share promise. Terms are win-win, and every contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0097, R-1582].

Initial lean. Proposal: all four fields at hold. - UltraFan NB Solo: hold and Joint Venture with P&W: hold. These are the only legal values, and the Joint Venture stands as formed. - UltraFan WB: hold and Trent 1000 upgrade: hold. No Board item. Premium $0B. EV about +20.59 on 0.90 / 0.10 (20.585); S1 outcome +20.55, S2 +20.90. So, frankly, there is nothing to buy in the last round. The Joint Venture engine is flying and earning. Both parts of the objective are met and cannot be changed by anything we order now. Every new item on the grid destroys value: - the upgrade: -6.73, and it counts only from 2053; - UltraFan WB: -9.00 in S1 and -8.33 even in S2, ready a year after the Re-engines it would serve. I said we would regain share on the 787 [RX-0101, RX-0117]. Not at any price, and never with a downside we cannot recover. 'I worry about tomorrow's financials' [RX-0125]. 'Actually, I've seen this movie before': two programmes in parallel, and the strain eats the return. What we do instead is control what we control. Public: - the Joint Venture engine in service: safety, then time on wing and full-life parts, then support through our partner shops; - Trent fleet durability continues, about £1bn over four years [RX-0123]; - UltraFan technology continues as technology, with public R&D money where available and no dates [RX-0094, RG-0065]. Private: - Rob's in-service report to the Board, with RR technical review rights and a gear-and-core module pool; - the partner-shop support plan; - Helen's off-grid shared-risk sizing, rebased on Rob's report and booking nothing; - the capital frame held; - pricing discipline; - 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' kept as policy, with the widebody watch closed. Closing account (for the rationale, subject to the memos): - 2030: airframers first. launch if selected spent nothing until NGSA chose us [RX-0058]. - 2035: partner first once P&W had committed. That halved the bill, and the engine flew on GTF2's clock. RR was fitted on NGSA from 2037 at 24.1%. - Result: $4.00B of R&D plus the $1.71B write-off against +26.26 of engine value, for +20.55. Both parts of the objective met. - What we missed, said plainly: the 2035 widebody plan assumed the strain would lift once UltraFan NB left development. It did not. On this board the formed Joint Venture is a running project, and that closed the upgrade for good. - 'A milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062]. What would change my lean: - a widebody item within its own bill and the caps against a Re-engine on the record. None exists. - a safety or durability flag from Rob. That changes the statement, the support plan and Helen's sizing, not the orders. Draft public statement: 'So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and the fleet is our job. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. If we find an issue, we will say so early, with the plan. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.' Subject to Helen's numbers and Rob's fleet report.

Review rights and a module pool stay unsecured this round (inference). - No safety or durability flag on the Joint Venture engine reaches the record in 2050. - CFM keeps reporting durability on field data. The GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp is already in the hold row. - Outcome: ΔPV +20.55 (S1) / +20.90 (S2). Both parts of the objective are met.

Gearbox contracts sized to UltraFan technology work. Keep concentrating work on high-performing suppliers. Not for the public statement [RX-0286, RX-0279].

The airframers' regret is in the widebody Re-engines and, for Airbus, the Delay Tactics it did not order. Rolls-Royce's is its fold-in write-off. CFM/GE's and P&W's orders were the best reply in every round. The played outcome is on none of the snapshot's equilibrium lists.
  • Your snapshot's four Pure Nash all pair fps on the 10-year ramp with NGSA plus one Delay Tactics move, with one airframer re-engining.
  • The game's cell, with no Delay Tactics and no Re-engine, is neither Pure nor Near-Nash: not at the snapshot's dates (Airbus +$25.05B, Boeing −$0.06B), and not at the game's own fps date of 2040 (+$23.37B, +$0.66B).
  • Moving fps from 2041 to 2040 cuts the Near-Nash from 12 to 8, and every remaining one has Delay Tactics. One Delay Tactics move is worth $1.45B to Airbus at 2041, inside the dashboard's Near-Nash band of 1% of value ($1.5B), and $1.57B at 2040, outside it.
The stage game is Chicken on the widebody through 2050.
  • In every round the two pure equilibria have one airframer re-engine and the other hold. Both survive to 2050 on this dashboard; on the earlier version only Airbus re-engining was left by 2050.
  • 2045: Boeing gains $0.29B by re-engining if Airbus holds, and loses $1.26B if Airbus re-engines too. Airbus gains $0.89B, or loses $0.50B.
  • 2050: Boeing gains $0.04B or loses $1.00B; Airbus gains $0.57B or loses $0.42B.
  • Both holding was within $1B of each side's best reply in 2045 and 2050, the only Near-Nash cell in those rounds. In 2030 and 2035 it was not: Airbus's best reply was worth $3.30B and $3.19B more.
Regret: Airbus gave up most, $3.30B in 2030, in a Delay Tactics move and the A350 Re-engine.
  • Boeing: $2.20B in 2030, falling to $0.04B in 2050, all from the 787 Re-engine. It was kept out by the one-development-at-a-time rule and the Board's downside test in 2030, by the 2-year overlap limit in 2035, and in 2045 and 2050 by the Board's $1B business case (and its downside test in 2045) and Ortberg's tie-break toward doing less.
  • With Boeing's other orders as played, the 7-year ramp was worth $0.46B more, its logged premium. Regret counts the best full set of orders, a 787 Re-engine with the 10-year ramp (+$2.86B against +$2.39B with the 7-year), so the ramp does not appear in it.
  • Airbus: $3.30B in 2030 and $3.19B in 2035, from one Delay Tactics move and the A350 Re-engine together; either alone was worth about $1.5B to $1.7B. Then $0.89B and $0.57B for the A350 Re-engine.
  • Rolls-Royce: $1.71B in 2030, exactly its fold-in write-off. Holding UltraFan NB in 2030 and joining in 2035 would have brought the same Joint Venture without it. Had no Joint Venture formed, holding would have left it at −$0.56B, so the conditional launch was right when made.
  • P&W's GTF2 had spent $1.67B by 2035, under its $2B Joint Venture share, so P&W wrote off nothing. Rolls-Royce had spent $5.71B against a $4B share.
Calibration: the airframers were exact on the case that came true; the engine makers missed by up to $19.21B in 2030.
  • Airbus expected +$23.37B in 2030 and got +$23.37B. Boeing expected −$1.96B, in the case where Airbus also re-engined the A350, which the Airbus Board had ruled out in private guidance Boeing could not see. Its figure for the case that came true, +$0.66B, was exact.
  • The airframers' own logged premiums and the value their fixed rules cost match the game master's regret to within $0.01B in every round.
  • The engine makers missed badly in 2030. CFM/GE expected −$50.41B and got −$31.20B; P&W +$3.15B against −$8.44B; Rolls-Royce +$3.37B against +$18.26B. The actual selection (fps on CFM alone, NGSA on all three) was not a case in P&W's or Rolls-Royce's grid.
  • In 2035 each put "rivals hold" first and under-weighted the other's Joint Venture commitment: P&W expected −$10.14B and got −$2.93B, Rolls-Royce +$15.99B against +$20.55B. From 2045 every company was within $1.31B, and all but CFM/GE within $0.05B.
Only Boeing logged premiums: $0.81B in all, within its $2B cap.
  • Boeing declared $0.46B in 2030 for the 10-year ramp, then $0.30B and $0.05B in 2045 and 2050 for holding the 787 Re-engine. The last two were holds its Board said it would have vetoed anyway. By the Board's own rule, which measures premiums against the best plan that passes its tests, they need not have been logged.
  • Boeing logged separately what its fixed rules cost: $2.20B in 2030 and $0.65B in 2035.
  • Every other company declared no premium in any round. Airbus logged its gaps as the cost of its red lines and binding tests (2030-35), and as within the $1B by which its rules let the default trail the best plan (2045-50). CFM/GE declined to pay $37.34B in 2035 for the Open Fan objective.
  • No company cancelled a programme.
All 20 company-rounds kept to their own information.
  • An audit of every tool call found all 20 company-rounds clean: no company reached another's material, the dashboard or the game master's files.
  • Each company's chain ran as its own workflow, in parallel, in every round, and nothing passed between companies.

Against the earlier game

The orders differ in only four places, all in 2030 and 2035; in 2045 and 2050 every company held in both games. The earlier game had one strategist agent per company, deciding as its leadership team, on the earlier version of the dashboard. This game had four agents per company on the new version. Both changed at once, so the comparison alone cannot say what the ExCo-and-Board structure did. The decision records show why each order differs. The table below values each game's final state on both versions of the dashboard.

Reading across a row on one board isolates the decisions; reading the same game on both boards isolates the board change. A state carries over as it stands: the same programmes, dates, engine selections and covert moves, revalued.

Four orders differ.
  • 2030, Boeing: the 10-year ramp here, the 7-year before; and no 737 rate increase here, an increase before.
  • 2035, Airbus: no Delay Tactics here, a covert bottleneck before.
  • 2035, Rolls-Royce: a Joint Venture commitment here, a hold before. P&W committed in both games.
  • Everything else matches: NGSA on all three makers, fps on CFM alone, CFM/GE's three 2030 moves, and P&W's and Rolls-Royce's conditional launches.
In value, the dashboard change repriced one decision: Boeing's ramp.
  • The earlier version gave the 7-year ramp a 5-point first-mover bonus. On it the 7-year led in every case, by $5.20B where Airbus launched NGSA alone. The earlier strategist: the 10-year "costs $5.2B against NGSA, beyond the $2B cap".
  • The new version drops the bonus: the first new narrowbody in service gains 1 point a year while alone, and keeps it. In Boeing's expected case the two ramps were $0.46B apart, inside the $1B margin its rules treat as a tie, and the CEO's stated preferences took the 10-year.
  • The 2030 stage game agrees: its pure equilibria have the 7-year ramp on the earlier version and the 10-year on the new one.
  • A replay of all 16 combinations of the four differences on both versions (data/replay16.json) finds the rate hold, the absent Delay Tactics move and the Joint Venture worth the same on either, within $0.01B. Each order's effect quoted below is averaged over every combination of the other three; the ramp and the Delay Tactics move interact, by about ±$0.25B.
  • All of the dashboard change's effect on the value of the four differences sits in the ramp. It also cut Airbus's cash headroom (see Delay Tactics).
The 737 rate increase: a test declared in advance, and kept.
  • The grid was the same on both versions: beside an fps launch the increase cost $0.74B in every case.
  • The earlier strategist took it anyway, as a $0.74B premium under its team rule to raise the rate in the first round.
  • Here the Boeing Board listed it among the orders it would veto ("Its item value is −0.74 in every column"), and Ortberg's profile allows the increase only if it adds value. The CEO held; his CFO and operating head advised the same.
  • Effect of holding the rate, on either version: +$0.74B for Boeing and +$1.86B for Airbus. Boeing stays at 40% in 2032-36 instead of 45%, and Airbus meets its A320 objective (60% against 55%).
Delay Tactics: integrity read two ways, a stricter condition and a cash line.
  • One move was worth less here (+$1.65B against +$2.16B). The replay puts that on Boeing's 10-year ramp, not the dashboard: against a 7-year fps the move is worth $2.15B to $2.16B on either version.
  • The earlier strategist read the bottleneck as Airbus's "first claim on scarce capacity", the only form inside its integrity pillar. It read the team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) as met, and passed its $5.2B cash guardrail at $4.8B of peak spend.
  • Here the Airbus Board, its CFO and its operating head barred the bottleneck on integrity. Faury kept the team's stricter condition, which on its own keeps poaching off, and the Board's cash line also ruled poaching out. NGSA's bill is larger on the new version ($35.52B against $30.07B), which left only $0.13B of headroom.
  • Effect of no Delay Tactics move: Boeing +$1.69B, Airbus −$1.90B, CFM/GE +$1.61B, P&W and Rolls-Royce −$0.66B each.
The Joint Venture: a red-line clause taken from the Board's test.
  • In both games a Rolls-Royce commitment in 2035 was worth +$2.29B, but only if P&W committed in the same round, which it did in both.
  • The earlier strategist's rule was to commit only after P&W's commitment was public, so with sealed orders it held. By 2045 joining was worth nothing.
  • Here the CEO's red line also allowed a commitment once a live airframe's engine selection included P&W, the Board's partner test, and NGSA met it. For Rolls-Royce, the governance allowed the commitment; no test required it. For P&W, the RTX Board recommended it.
  • Worth the same on both versions: Rolls-Royce +$2.29B, P&W +$5.51B, CFM/GE −$7.09B.
Company by company. Each change splits into the dashboard change (the earlier game's state on both versions) and the order change (both states on the new version).
  • Boeing −$1.18B: dashboard change −$3.42B, order change +$2.23B.
  • Airbus +$7.76B: dashboard change +$1.98B, order change +$5.79B, mostly Boeing's ramp (+$5.83B) and rate hold (+$1.86B), less Airbus's own forgone Delay Tactics move (−$1.90B).
  • CFM/GE −$13.11B, with the same orders in both games: dashboard change −$3.45B, others' orders −$9.66B, mostly the Joint Venture (−$7.09B).
  • P&W +$7.71B, also with the same orders: dashboard change +$1.24B, others' orders +$6.47B, mostly the Joint Venture (+$5.51B).
  • Rolls-Royce +$4.87B: dashboard change +$1.62B, order change +$3.25B, of which its own commitment +$2.29B.
  • Objectives: five of ten met in each game, but different ones. Boeing kept incumbency before and lost it here, a cost the CEO and Board recorded when choosing the 10-year ramp; Airbus lost A320 protection before and kept it here.
What the comparison cannot say.
  • The table values fixed end states. It replays no game, so it says nothing about what the companies would have chosen on the other version of the dashboard.
  • An order change swaps every company's orders at once. CFM/GE's and P&W's own orders were the same in both games.
  • Where the records show a governance mechanism (the rate increase, Delay Tactics, the Joint Venture), it is a test declared in advance and complied with, never a veto exercised. The ramp changed with the dashboard, and the ExCo chose it against its Board's advice.

Method

How the game was run

  • Dashboard. Your combined_dash.py, run headless (never in Streamlit) at the Game_v3.txt snapshot. Solved by the game master (GM), it reproduces the snapshot: airframers 4 Pure Nash and 12 Near-Nash, engines 1 Pure Nash and 11 Near-Nash, with every rounded yield matching. Changes from the earlier version of the dashboard:
    • The second new narrowbody no longer climbs to 50/50. The first in service gains 1 point a year while alone and keeps that edge: the long-run split is 50/50 shifted 1 point per year of lead, with the leader capped at 80%.
    • No 7-year fps share bonus. The two-front strain is overlap-aware and built in. Re-engines default to 2042.
    • Bills: fps $65.00B (7-year) and $60.32B (10-year), NGSA $35.52B. Narrowbody obsolescence 30%.
  • Players. 20 AI agents. In each company, the CEO, CFO and operating head of the default 2026 executive committee, each profiled from that person's own public words (transcripts and filings), and the Board, profiled from transcripts, filings and web search, with a culture score (risk aversion, time horizon). Where an executive's record was thin, the seat's tests were derived from the role or company doctrine and labelled low confidence (Pope, Toepfer, Wagner).
    • Boeing: Kelly Ortberg, Jay Malave, Stephanie Pope and the Boeing Board.
    • Airbus: Guillaume Faury, Thomas Toepfer, Lars Wagner and the Airbus Board.
    • CFM/GE: Larry Culp, Rahul Ghai, Mohamed Ali and the GE Aerospace Board, with Safran's consent on CFM programmes.
    • P&W: Chris Calio, Neil Mitchill, Shane Eddy and the RTX Board.
    • Rolls-Royce: Tufan Erginbilgic, Helen McCabe, Rob Watson and the Rolls-Royce Board.
    • They are AI agents, not the people.
  • Each round, in each company.
    • The Board gives guidance. The CEO frames the choice. The CFO and the operating head test it, independently.
    • The CEO decides. The CFO and operating head run a veto check, and the CEO revises once if a binding veto or a red-line flag stands.
    • Each Board item (any order other than hold) goes to Board review: approve, or veto with acceptable alternatives. The CEO revises once within a Board veto. The Board confirms, and a still-vetoed item reverts to the default. A missing Board review fails closed.
    • Each company's decision rule and veto grounds come from its team profile.
    • Each company's chain ran as its own workflow, in parallel, in every round; nothing passed between companies. Within a company the GM passed only that company's own memos between seats.
  • Information. As in the earlier game: the public bulletin plus a private brief per company, with its own position, projection and objective status, and its own payoff grid against a few public scenarios. Only the GM saw the dashboard.
  • Isolation. The hardened path hook from the earlier game, extended to the new dashboard file and snapshot. It denies other companies' files and briefs, the dashboard file, the snapshot, GM code, earlier reports and runs, and the GM's scratch files and transcripts. From 2035 each company had its own scratch folder.
    • An audit of every tool call found all 20 company-rounds clean.
    • In 2030 the agents tried 13 times to write drafts to the session scratchpad their environment advertises. The hook denied every attempt, and nothing was written.
    • Other denials were the hook's conservative rules (command substitution, wildcards) applied to the companies' own files.
  • Out-of-date figures. The agents' standing instructions load when the session starts, before the Boeing and Airbus files were updated for the new dashboard. So the running agents still quoted the earlier dashboard's fps and NGSA bills, and figures derived from them (NGSA's yearly spend, Boeing's debt penalties), in eleven lines.
    • Everything they read during play (brief, public rules, game guide) used the new dashboard.
    • In 2030 both airframers' agents noticed. Airbus used the current $35.52B NGSA bill; its CFO noted the difference moves headroom, not any result. Malave flagged Boeing's old debt-penalty figures as stale, so the current ones were used.
    • From 2035 each company's prompts stated its own current figures. The engine makers' files had no changed figures.
  • Rounds. Four sealed, simultaneous rounds: 2030, 2035, 2045, 2050. Each round's value is the GM valuation of the state after that round, assuming nobody moves again. The final round's value is the game outcome.

Rules the GM added to the static dashboard (as in the earlier game)

  • Time. A programme enters service, or an engine is ready, after its development time from the decision year.
    • Airframes: fps 7 or 10 years, fps via Embraer 10, NGSA 7, Re-engines 5.
    • Engines: ducted 6, GTF2 6, UltraFan NB 7, UltraFan WB 6, Trent and GEnx upgrades 3, the Embraer partnership 7, the Joint Venture 6 or an inherited schedule. Open Fan takes 10 years and is never ready before 2045.
  • Cancellations. Airframes write off the bill × years elapsed ÷ development years, with the dashboard's debt penalty. Engines write off R&D × years elapsed ÷ development years, undiscounted like the dashboard's R&D.
  • Delay Tactics are covert: the order and its cause are never published. None was ordered in this game.
  • Engines. The dashboard's engine game is applied year by year, splitting each airframer's narrowbody share equally among the engines fitted to it.
    • Each narrowbody engine move counts from the later of its ready year and the first new narrowbody's entry into service (2037 here).
    • One change from the earlier game: widebody engine upgrades now count from the year the dashboard starts its widebody changes (the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042), as the dashboard does. On the earlier version that year was always 2035, so the earlier game is unchanged.
  • Joint Venture. It forms when both makers commit, without an airframer selecting the Joint Venture engine. It folds in solo programmes, writing off spend beyond the maker's share, and inherits the most advanced folded schedule.
  • Tests. The model tests, on both versions of the dashboard: dashboard reproduction, 648 engine move combinations and the snapshot equilibria. The replay tests: both games replay exactly, and no played year changes. The isolation tests: 292 cases.

What the numbers are

  • ΔPV and yield. ΔPV is the change in present value at 2026 against the status quo (nobody launches anything), at each company's dashboard WACC: Boeing 10.5%, Airbus 8%, CFM/GE 8.5%, P&W and Rolls-Royce 10%. Yield = 100 + 100 × ΔPV ÷ enterprise value.
  • Dashboard conventions. Airframe programme spend is charged in full at entry into service. Engine R&D is undiscounted. Engine value is the lifetime value per engine delivered: price × 1.6, rising 2.2% a year.
  • Regret. The final ΔPV a company would have had with its best alternative orders in that round, holding every other order in the game as played (later rounds re-run), minus its actual final ΔPV.
  • Your dashboard alone. The table below sets each final value next to your dashboard alone. The airframers match exactly. For the engine makers the dashboard fixes a 50/50 airframer split and locks P&W to GTF2 Solo for the engine selections in this game; the GM's Joint Venture and year-by-year split account for the difference.
